```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

Dixon, Gary E.; Crookston, Nicholas L. 2016. Model Structure of the Forest Vegetation Simulator. Internal Rep. Fort Collins, CO: U. S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Forest Management Service Center. 128p. (Revised: June 29, 2016)

This document describes basic model structure for the Forest Vegetation Simulator (FVS) computer software. This guide explains model flow, logic considerations, subcomponents, and subroutines for the base model including the regeneration establishment and event monitor extensions. It also discusses how to accomplish common programming tasks associated with code maintenance or enhancement. This document is meant to serve as an initial reference for people involved with design or modification of the FVS model computer code.

Keywords: Forest Vegetation Simulator, forest management, simulation models, resource management.

## About the Authors {-}

Gary E. Dixon (retired) is a biometrician and served as the Forest Vegetation Simulator Group leader at the Forest Service’s Washington Office Forest Management Service Center in Fort Collins, Colorado. Dr. Dixon received his B.S. (1973), M.S. (1974), and Ph.D. (1977) in forest biometrics at Colorado State University. He has worked on the development of tree growth models throughout most of his career. He joined the Forest Management Staff in 1982 and has worked with the model now known as the Forest Vegetation Simulator since that time. He retired from the Forest Service in 2008 but still actively participates in FVS development.

Nicholas L. Crookston (retired) was an operations research analyst and worked at the Forest Service’s Rocky Mountain Research Station, Forestry Sciences Laboratory in Moscow, Idaho. He has participated in the development of FVS from about 1977 to the present time. Dr. Crookston received his B.S. (1973) in botany at Weber State University, M.S. (1977) and Honorary Doctorate of Natural Resources (2015) from the University of Idaho. He retired from the Forest Service in 2015 but still actively participates in FVS development.

We would like to thank all those people that contributed to the development, testing, and support of the FVS software system. We would also like to thank the many FVS users who have provided feedback and suggested model improvements over the years.

## About this Guide {-}

This document is meant to serve as a technical guide to the FVS model and document program flow and programming considerations of the model. As such it is intended for people involved with FVS model development and code modification. This document a technical supplement to the two FVS user’s guides referenced in the following section.

## How to use this Guide {-}

Anyone reading this document should also have “Essential FVS: A user’s guide to the Forest Vegetation Simulator” and the “Keyword Reference Guide for the Forest Vegetation Simulator” at hand. These can be downloaded from the Forest Management Service Center’s web site. Any references in this document to the “EFVS Guide” or “Keyword Guide” are referencing these documents. When a keyword record name is mentioned in this document, it should be looked up in the keyword guide for a detailed discussion of the parameter fields and other explanatory notes.

Developers should also obtain the FVS overview document for the variant pertaining to their geographic area from the same web site. With these three documents, plus this one, model developers should have a good start towards understanding the FVS model structure.

Users wanting to interface with FVS using the Suppose graphical user interface should obtain that software along with the “exercise guide” pertaining to their geographic area. These products are also available from the FMSC web site. A new online tool for running FVS, called FVSOnline, is now available.  FVSOnline is intended to replace Suppose and takes advantage of some newer programming constructs documented in this document. FVSOnline can also be run on a local machine.

# Introduction

The Forest Vegetation Simulator (FVS) is a model used for predicting forest stand dynamics that is used extensively in the United States. User’s guides exist for those people interested in running their data through FVS (Dixon 2002, Van Dyck and Smith-Mateja 2000) and model relationships specific to geographic variants are presented in the various variant overview guides (e.g. Keyser and Dixon 2008). However, formal technical documentation of the programming flow and logic has not been previously available in a consolidated place. This document provides this type of documentation for the FVS base model including the regeneration establishment and event monitor extensions. Some mention will be made of other FVS extensions, such as the database extension, where appropriate.

[General Flow Overview](#sec-general-flow-overview) discusses general FVS structure and programming considerations. [Projection Initialization Phase](#sec-projection-initialization-phase), [Projection Cycling Phase](#sec-projection-cycling-phase), and [Projection Summarization Phase](#sec-projection-summarization-phase) are arranged in the order that FVS processes a stand. [Option Processing Logic](#sec-option-processing-logic), [Event monitor logic](#sec-event-monitor-logic), [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api), and [Regeneration establishment in FVS variants](#sec-regeneration-establishment-in-fvs-variants) are devoted entirely to describing the program flow and logic in a particular section of the FVS code, or a particular FVS feature. [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants) describes structural differences in the two ORGANON-FVS variants. [Database Input and Output Extension](#sec-database-input-and-output-extension) describes the database extension, including SQLite input and output.

# General Flow Overview {#sec-general-flow-overview}

The general processing sequence for FVS is shown in figure 2-1 and discussed in section 3.4 of the EFVS guide. Each of the major task groupings shown in this processing sequence will be further broken down in following sections.

FVS can process a single stand in one model run or many stands in one model run. When running FVS there are two processing modes, serial or parallel. A serial run occurs when each stand is processed to completion before the next stand starts. A parallel run occurs when all the stands are processed up to a common stopping year, typically before the end of the projection, and then the program is stopped. Other processes can then be run that can include the creation of information FVS can use when a simulation is resumed. Once the simulation resumes, all the stands are processed up to the next common stopping point or the end of the projection.

Prior to about 2012, running stands in the parallel mode required the use of a separate version of FVS that included the Parallel Processing Extension (PPE, Crookston and Stage, 1991).  However, given the complexity of that program and its lack of use, The PPE was removed and FVS was modified to include the ability to stop and restart itself. This will be discussed in further detail in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api).

Most of this document is devoted to explaining the processing sequence for a single stand serial model run. A multiple stand serial model run follows the same processing sequence as a single stand serial model run, repeated for each stand. A parallel model run follows virtually the same flow as its serial counterpart for each stand in the projection initialization, projection cycling, and projection summarization phases. Details on how this is accomplished are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api).

The general processing flow for a single stand serial model run can be broken down into three phases. The projection initialization phase gets the stand ready to run; the projection cycling phase projects the stand through time; and the projection summarization phase produces the output reports.

## Input and Output Arrays {-}

The following tables summarize the major FVS subroutines and the arrays they use:

### Subroutine Summary Tables {-}

#### Main Control Flow Functions {-}

```{r main-control-table, echo=FALSE}
main_control <- data.frame(
  Function = c("FVS", "INITRE", "TREGRO"),
  Purpose = c(
    "Main simulation driver that orchestrates the entire projection cycle",
    "Initializes prognosis run, processes keywords and options",
    "Main tree growth routine called each cycle"
  ),
  Input_Arrays = c(
    "PRGPRM.F77, ARRAYS.F77, PLOT.F77, CONTRL.F77, OUTCOM.F77, PDEN.F77, ECON.F77, WORKCM.F77",
    "All major common blocks, keyword file data, stand parameters",
    "PRGPRM.F77, CONTRL.F77, Cycle number (ICYC)"
  ),
  Output = c(
    "IRTNCD (error/status code)",
    "Initialized stand variables, control flags",
    "Calls GRINCR and GRADD to compute increments"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(main_control,
      col.names = c("Function Name", "Purpose", "Input Arrays", "Output"),
      caption = "Main Control Flow Functions",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

#### Growth and Mortality Processing Functions {-}

```{r growth-mort-table, echo=FALSE}
growth_mort <- data.frame(
  Function = c("GRINCR", "GRADD", "UPDATE", "MORTS"),
  Purpose = c(
    "Computes growth and mortality for each tree record",
    "Updates tree descriptions and adds increments",
    "Adds growth increment, deducts mortality, computes volumes",
    "Calculates tree mortality rates (variant-specific)"
  ),
  Input_Arrays = c(
    "PLOT.F77, ARRAYS.F77, CONTRL.F77, PDEN.F77; DBH(), HT(), ISP(), DG(), HTG()",
    "ARRAYS.F77, COEFFS.F77, CONTRL.F77; DG(), HTG(), DBH(), HT(), PROB()",
    "ARRAYS.F77, COEFFS.F77, CONTRL.F77; HT(), HTG(), DBH(), DG(), WK2(), IMC()",
    "Variant-specific common blocks; Stand density (BA, SDI, CCF), tree attributes"
  ),
  Output = c(
    "DG() - inside bark diameter increment on the YR basis; HTG() - height growth; WK2() - mortality (TPA)",
    "Updated DBH(), HT(), scaled DG() to cycle length",
    "Updated HT(), DBH(), PROB(); WK6() - mortality volume; OMORT() - mortality summary",
    "WK2() - mortality (trees/acre)"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(growth_mort,
      col.names = c("Function Name", "Purpose", "Input Arrays", "Output"),
      caption = "Growth and Mortality Processing Functions",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

#### Stand Density and Statistics Functions {-}

```{r density-stats-table, echo=FALSE}
density_stats <- data.frame(
  Function = c("DENSE", "NOTRE", "SETUP", "STATS"),
  Purpose = c(
    "Calculates stand density statistics",
    "Calculates trees per acre from sampling design",
    "Sets up index pointers for species-ordered sort",
    "Computes statistical description of input data"
  ),
  Input_Arrays = c(
    "PLOT.F77, ARRAYS.F77; DBH(), HT(), PROB(), ISP(), ICR(), DG()",
    "PRGPRM.F77, ARRAYS.F77; PROB(), DBH(), BAF, FPA, BRK, PI",
    "PRGPRM.F77, ARRAYS.F77; IREF(), KOUNT(), IBEGIN(), IND2(), IREC1",
    "ARRAYS.F77, CONTRL.F77; DBH(), PROB(), CFV(), BFV(), ISP(), PI, ALPHA"
  ),
  Output = c(
    "BA, TPROB, RELDEN (CCF), RMSQD (QMD), AVH, PCT(), RELDSP(), DR016, RELDM1, OLDBA, PCCF(), PTPA(), PTPAA(), BAAA(), PRDA(), PTBAA(), PTBALT()",
    "PROB() - trees/acre based on plot design",
    "IND1() - species-ordered indices; ISCT(,1-2) - first/last by species; ITRN",
    "Stand statistics (mean, std dev, CV, confidence intervals); Species summaries"

kable(density_stats,
      col.names = c("Function Name", "Purpose", "Input Arrays", "Output"),

                full_width = FALSE) %>%
```


## Overall Model Design and Control

This section describes some underlying concepts behind FVS structure and discusses the routines involved in overall program control.

### Programming Language, Comments, and Debugging

FVS code has evolved through time as computer systems and languages have changed. FVS was developed in FORTRAN IV, upgraded in places to FORTRAN V, ultimately converted to FORTRAN 77, and currently contains FORTRAN 90, 95, and 2003 constructs. The code is continually upgraded and older code constructs eliminated as time permits. FVS is fully compatible with a FORTRAN compiler that supports the 2003 standard. The code was originally designed to run on a mainframe computer system and was changed to also run on personal computer (PC) systems around 1985. Mainframe usage has dwindled and many applications of FVS are now run on a PC. However, there are many uses of FVS and some of them are accomplished on large servers where hundreds of thousands of runs are done. The FVS code is supported on a range of computer systems, including Windows, Linux-based systems, and Unix-based systems like MAC OSX. Building FVS from source code can be done using various approaches. These are documented in wiki pages at url:https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki.

FVS code contains many comment statements to describe the function of each subroutine, document the date it was last changed, and explain what is going on within code segments. These comments are extensive enough to serve fairly well as a programmer’s guide and are likely the reason a document like this one has not seemed critical to develop.

FVS code also has an internal debugging feature in the form of WRITE statements that output various program calculations and model controls. Outputs from these WRITE statements are included in the FVS main output file. This internal debug feature is turned on using the DEBUG keyword record. It can be activated for individual subroutines or globally throughout the model, and for individual cycles or all cycles. This feature produces a lot of output when turned on globally for all cycles. However, this feature is powerful enough that some programmers use it exclusively to find program bugs rather than implementing an off-the-shelf debugging product.

Subroutine INITRE processes model keyword records, including the DEBUG keyword record. INITRE calls subroutines DBPRSE or DBALL to schedule debug requests to the activity table. Subroutine DBCHK is used throughout program to check the activity table and see if the internal debug feature is active in an individual subroutine at the time the subroutine is called. A local logical variable, usually named DEBUG, is set to a value of “.TRUE.” when the internal DEBUG feature is on for that subroutine in that cycle or “.FALSE.” when it is not.

In some instances, the logical variable DEBUG is passed through a subroutine call list to a secondary subroutine. This occurs when the secondary subroutine is an integral part of the subroutine that called it, or when the secondary subroutine is called from multiple places for different purposes and you may want the debug output for only one of those places. An example of the first case is subroutine VARMRT that is variant-specific and only called from subroutine MORTS in the processing logic. However, if you are debugging mortality calculations, then it only makes sense that turning on debug for  subroutine MORTS also turns on debug in subroutine VARMRT so all mortality calculations are displayed. An example of the second case is subroutine FINDAG that estimates tree age from tree height and a site index curve for the individual species.  Subroutine FINDAG is called from various other subroutines. You may want debug output from FINDAG during model calibration in the projection initialization phase, but not during height growth estimation in the projection cycling phase.

Another important reason why the DEBUG variable is sometimes passed from one subroutine to another is that the subroutine DBCHK takes a lot of computer time. It is very inefficient to call it, for example, from within loops that are running over the entire tree list that might result in several thousand calls per growth cycle. It is much more efficient to call DBCHK at a higher level in the processing sequence and pass the value of DEBUG to subroutines that are called within a tree loop.

The NODEBUG keyword record can be used to turn the internal debug feature off. It is seldom, if ever, used in a single stand serial run. However, it may be useful in a multiple stand serial run. The DEBUG feature can be turned on globally for all stands, and then NODEBUG can be inserted for specific stands to omit those stands from producing debug output. Subroutine DBINIT is called for processing NODEBUG keyword record requests.

### Passing Data throughout the program

FVS makes heavy use of labeled COMMON blocks to make data available throughout the program. The COMMON block name gives an indication of the types of variables the COMMON block contains. For example, the PLOT labeled COMMON block contains plot level variables such as slope, aspect, elevation, and basal area per acre, while the ARRAYS labeled COMMON block contains individual tree arrays such as diameter at breast height, total tree height, and trees per acre that the tree record represents. Labeled COMMON blocks are the same across all geographic variants. An effort is made to provide variable definitions via comment statements within each labeled COMMON block for all variables contained in the labeled COMMON.

Many computer scientists discourage the use of COMMON blocks. However, FVS uses them for more than simple historical purposes and wholesale removal of them in favor of some other construct would break some model features. A key feature involves the ability to stop the program and restart it from the point where it left off (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)). COMMON blocks are like global structures in C; judicious use is often the only viable alternative to getting the job done.

Some variants utilize variables that are unique to the variant. The VARCOM labeled COMMON block was created to pass variant-specific variables. However, other even more variant-specific labeled COMMON blocks have been created over the years: CICOM is used in the CI variant; EMCOM is used in the EM variant; GGCOM is used in variants that use the GENGYM model logic; TWIGCOM is used in variants that use the Twigs model logic; and ORGANON is used in the two variants that use the ORGANON model logic (see [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants)). These variant-specific COMMON blocks tend to be very small.

Global array dimensions and other controlling scalars are set in parameter statements in the PRGPRM, ESPARM, and other similar code segments. These code segments are variant-specific and set dimensions such as the total number of tree records allowed in the simulation, the number of species contained in the variant, and the FVS sequence numbers for which species will automatically regenerate (sprout) following harvesting.

FVS also makes extensive use of subroutine argument lists to pass arrays and scalars from one code segment to another. These are generally used where program control is only transferred from the calling subroutine to the called subroutine for a short calculation or task.

In recent years, an effort has been made to explicitly type all variables. However, some code segments, especially in the insect and disease extensions may still contain some implicitly typed arrays and scalars. Implicit typing is an old FORTRAN construct whereby variables with names that start with the letters I, J, K, L, M, or N (or in lowercase) are considered integers and other variables are 32-bit reals. Any time one of these subroutines is worked on, the change to explicit typing should be added and an IMPLICIT NONE directive added to the subroutine.

Two other techniques are used to cut down on storage space requirements and passing of coefficients. Limited use is still made of EQUIVALENCE statements although these are outdated and should be replaced with pointers or some other more modern FORTRAN code constructs.  In general, the EQUIVALENCE statements can be safely removed, but not in every case. They should be removed where possible.

There are several “work arrays” which reside in the WORKCM labeled COMMON block and are used to pass data from one part of the model to another, and then reused for the same purpose but with different data in a different part of the model. Some of these arrays are dimensioned by the maximum number of species the variant accommodates and some by the maximum number of tree records allowed. Usage of these arrays must be carefully documented in the COMMON block in which they reside to avoid corruption of the data they contain.

A unique 2-character alpha code identifies which variant is being run. For example the alpha code “IE” is used to identify the Inland Empire geographic variant. This alpha code is stored in the variable VARACD that is carried in the CONTRL.F77 labelled COMMON block.

### General Model Architecture

Three types of input data are needed by FVS: 1) data containing information communicating FVS parameter settings and what the user wants FVS to do, 2) data communicating stand-level information, and 3) data containing information about the individual tree inventory. The second and third type of information can be read directly out of a database, or contained in two external files called the keyword record file and tree data file. These two external files will be referred to throughout this document but keep in mind the data could easily come from a database instead. However, even when a database is used, the keyword record file is required and controls the basic input, even if it is brief. There is one exception. The stop and restart capability of FVS is discussed in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). When a restart file is used to start FVS from where it left off, a keyword record file is not used.

Users set projection parameters and communicate management activities to FVS through the use of keyword records. Keyword records containing parameter and stand-level information are handled differently than those indicating management activities. How FVS processes keyword records will be discussed in [Processing keyword record requests](#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests).

Management activities can be scheduled by year, projection cycle, or by defining a condition using an IF-THEN-ENDIF keyword record sequence. Conceptually there is an activity schedule table inside FVS where each row corresponds to a particular management activity and the columns correspond to the parameters associated with that management activity including the year it is scheduled. As keyword records get processed in the projection initialization phase, activities will be posted to the activity schedule table. During the projection cycling phase stand conditions will be monitored and any management activities scheduled by condition will be posted to the activity schedule table if the condition is satisfied. Each projection cycle the activity schedule table is consulted to see if any management activities need to be done. Some activities may not get done for various reasons. Activities get tagged as “DONE”, “NOT DONE”, or “CANCELLED” depending upon their disposition (see [Keyword records that need to be scheduled](#sec-keyword-records-that-need-to-be-scheduled) for more information on this topic).

How FVS processes tree input data will be discussed in [Reading stand and tree record input data](#sec-reading-stand-and-tree-record-input-data). Data for individual tree records is kept in various arrays in the ARRAYS labeled COMMON block. These arrays get updated as the projection progresses through time and summarized across all tree records to calculate stand level statistics. For example, one key variable, PROB(i), where “i” is the tree record index, is the number of trees per acre that the tree record represents. This variable is used extensively throughout the model.

### Code Organization and Linking Considerations {#sec-code-organization-and-linking-considerations}

There are about 25 different geographic variants of FVS either used or under development in the United States. An efficient source code system avoiding duplication cuts down on maintenance requirements and speeds up change implementation. For example, if an equation is changed in a subroutine that is used in all variants, it is more efficient to change it in one place and have that change implemented in all 25 variants rather than having to change it in all 25 variants. This is the motivation behind the FVS code storage structure shown in Appendix A.

Individual code segments are linked together to form an FVS executable program. In FVS nomenclature there is the base model and there are extensions to the base model. For each base model extension there is a code segment in the base model source directory containing all the external references needed by the base model for that extension. These are identifiable by the letters “EX” at the beginning of the subroutine name. For example, for the fire and fuels extension (FFE, Rebain 2010), there is a subroutine named EXFIRE in the base model source directory containing all the external references needed by the base model to run the FFE. To link an executable without any extensions, all these “EX” subroutines must be included in the link instructions. To include an extension, simply remove the corresponding EX subroutine in the link instructions and insert the code segment names making up the extension. Subroutine EXTREE, that is used to assign example trees to the output arrays, is currently the only “EX” named base model subroutine that is not a container of external references for a model extension.

With the code structure of FVS it is a simple matter to change some of the model limits specified in the PRGPRM code segments. For example, the default number of tree records allowed in FVS is limited to 3000. To change this, first change it in PRGPRM and then re-compile the source code and re-link the program executable. While this limit can be increased or decreased, it should not be reduced below about 1000 to maintain statistical properties of the model and because some of the work arrays dimensioned by this variable are used for other purposes. This fact may indeed be unfortunate and should be changed, but it is a current reality. Also, it should be kept as a multiple of 3 (e.g. 999 or 1002) to be consistent with the model’s record tripling process.

### Accessing Tree Records {#sec-accessing-tree-records}

FVS has a tree list that holds up to 3000 tree records (the default limit). The number of tree records in a simulation during any cycle can vary depending on the number of tree data records input, record tripling, harvesting, mortality, and regeneration. Knowing how to efficiently access the tree information is important for programming efficiency.

Tree record data is initially stored in tree data arrays in the order that the data was input. This order can change through one of the other FVS processes listed above. The main point being that the tree data is not stored in any kind of sorted order. The number of tree records in a simulation, at any point of the simulation, is carried in the variable ITRN stored in the CONTRL labeled COMMON block. An internal FVS sequence number is assigned to each tree record. These internal sequence numbers range from 1 to ITRN and indicate the storage index, or pointer, in the tree data arrays containing the information for that tree record. For example, if the internal sequence number is 5, the tree diameter represented by that tree record is in location DBH(5), the total tree height is in HT(5) and the trees per acre is in PROB(5).

In the computer code it is more efficient to loop over all tree records for some operations and over all tree records of a given species for other operations. For example, to compute quadratic mean diameter you just need to loop over all tree records in the stand, in any order, and get the sum of squared diameters and trees per acre. There aren’t any species-specific coefficients to access in that calculation. However, if you are in a growth projection loop it is more efficient to access species coefficients once and then loop through all the tree records of that species predicting growth than it would be to access species coefficients for each and every tree record as it is encountered.

Looping over all tree records is a simple matter. The looping just needs to take place from indices 1 to ITRN. The actual code might look something like the 10 lines shown below for computing quadratic mean diameter (QMD). Note that code is included to handle the case where there are no tree records (ITRN = 0), or where the number of trees per acre is too small to compute a reasonable QMD. For this example, the test for computing a reasonable QMD compares SUMTPA to 0.001; perhaps a different threshold should be used. However, comparing SUMTPA to exactly zero should be avoided.

```fortran
QMD = 0.
IF (ITRN .GT. 0) THEN
SUMD2 = 0.
SUMTPA=0.
DO I=1,ITRN
SUMD2 = SUMD2 + DBH(I)*DBH(I)*PROB(I)
SUMTPA= SUMTPA + PROB(I)
ENDDO
IF (SUMTPA .GT. 0.001) QMD = SUMD2 / SUMTPA
ENDIF
```

There are three arrays in the ARRAYS labeled COMMON block that facilitate looping over all tree records, in individual species groups, or by size. These arrays also facilitate many FVS internal calculations that are dependent on tree size, such as a trees percentile ranking by some attribute.

The IND(i) array contains integer pointers, or indices, to locations in the tree data arrays containing information for a particular tree record. The IND(i) array is in sorted order by descending diameter. For example, if IND(1) = 20 then the tree record with information stored in the tree data arrays in location 20 is for the largest diameter tree in the stand.

The IND1(k) array is used to access tree data in species order. IND1(k) contains sectors such that each sector contains indices to the internal FVS sequence numbers for all records of a given species. A companion array, ISCT(i,j), is used to access the IND1(k) array. There are two elements in the ISCT(i,j) array for each species. ISCT(i,1) points to the first record in the sector of IND1(k) that is associated with species i; ISCT(i,2) points to the last record in the sector of IND1(k) that is associated with species i. If there are no records for species i, then ISCT(i,1) and ISCT(i,2) will contain zeroes. The actual code to access tree data in species order might look something like this (also notice an example of the internal debug feature near the end of this code segment):

```fortran
C----------
C  BEGIN SPECIES LOOP
C----------
DO 20 ISPC=1,MAXSP
I1=ISCT(ISPC,1)
IF(I1.EQ.0) GO TO 20
I2=ISCT(ISPC,2)
CONSPP= DGCON(ISPC) + COR(ISPC) + 0.01*DGCCF(ISPC)*RELDEN
DGLDS= DGLD(ISPC)
DGBALS = DGBAL(ISPC)
DGCRS= DGCR(ISPC)
DGCRS2=DGCRSQ(ISPC)
DGDSQS=DGDSQ(ISPC)
DGDBLS=DGDBAL(ISPC)
C----------
C  BEGIN TREE LOOP WITHIN SPECIES LOOP
C----------
DO 10 I3=I1,I2
I=IND1(I3)
D=DIAM(I)
IF (D.LE.0.0) GOTO 10
ALD=ALOG(D)
CR=ICR(I)*0.01
BAL=(1.0 - (PCT(I)/100.)) * BA100
DDS=CONSPP + DGLDS*ALD + DGBALS*BAL + CR* (DGCRS +
&  CR*DGCRS2) +DGDSQS*D*D + DGDBLS*BAL/(ALOG(D+1.0))
IF(DDS.LT.-9.21) DDS=-9.21
WK2(I)=DDS
C----------
C  PRINT DEBUG INFORMATION, IF DESIRED
C----------
IF(DEBUG)THEN
WRITE(JOSTND,9001) I,ISPC,D,BAL,CR,RELDEN,BA,DDS
9001FORMAT(' IN DGF, I=',I4,',  ISPC=',I3,',  DBH=',F7.2,
&',  BAL=',F7.2,',  CR=',F7.4/
&5X,'CCF=',F9.3,',  BA=',F9.3,',   LN(DDS)=',F7.4)
ENDIF
C----------
C  END OF TREE LOOP
C----------
10  CONTINUE
C----------
C  END OF SPECIES LOOP
C----------
20  CONTINUE
```

## The Main FVS Routine

The main routine for the FVS model is appropriately called PROGRAM MAIN (source file base/main.f90). MAIN first checks whether the first command line argument is --version or --build-info. If it is, MAIN writes the version string (--version) or the build information (--build-info), taken from the FVSVERSION module in base/version.f90 (version, organization, remote, branch, commit hash, and commit date, set by the makefile when the program is built), and stops before any simulation is initialized; no keyword file is needed. Otherwise MAIN calls subroutine fvsSetCmdLine (the source code for this subroutine is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) to retrieve any options that may, optionally, have been specified in the command that starts FVS (those may include the name of the keyword record file, the name of the restart file, or parameters that control stopping points (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)).  PROGRAM MAIN is very short and most programmers can ignore it. It calls one major subroutine, named FVS, which orchestrates all other subroutines, and it is the only program unit that executes a STOP statement. When the projection ends, MAIN calls fvsGetICCode, which returns the highest condition code set by subroutines ERRGRO and RCDSET during the run, and uses it as the exit status of the program: 0 when no condition code was set, and 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 for condition codes 1 to 5. In short, subroutine FVS contains what was once the MAIN program. This top-level organization was introduced in about 2010 to support the use of FVS as a shared library that is called by other upper-level programs (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)).

As part of its projection initialization phase, subroutine FVS calls subroutines to perform the following tasks:

check (again) for command line options,

check for return codes that may have been set at various stages,

check for restart codes causing the program to restart from a previously created stop point file if specified on the command line (a restart from stop point 7 resumes at the model calibration step; any other restart code resumes in the projection cycling phase; see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)),

open the key input and output files that will be required for the projection,

initialize parameters to their default condition,

process all keyword record requests, including reading stand and tree data from a database (the DATABASE – END sequence with STANDSQL and TREESQL) or from a tree data file,

set up the main projection cycling array (cycle lengths and any additional cycle boundaries requested with the CYCLEAT keyword record),

process and list the activity schedule, including the option lists of insect, disease, and economic extensions,

establish the initial species sort,

expand the tree data to a trees per acre basis based on the specified sample design,

initialize any data needed by extensions such as the root disease and insect models,

process stop point 7 (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)),

calibrate internal equations to match the incoming tree data,

flag best trees for regeneration establishment model use,

compute initial tree record level variables such as volumes and crown width,

compute initial stand level variables such as basal area per acre,

compute the initial percentile distributions of various tree attributes,

assign example trees to the sample tree output arrays, compute cover statistics if the cover extension is being used,

compute a statistical description of the input data,

write any initial stand data that needs to be saved for output, visualization, or use with other programs (for example the database inventory reference table, the output headings, the cycle 0 stand statistics, the tree list, and the stand visualization),

initialize the root disease and blister rust extensions, and

mark the end of the projection initialization phase and initialize the event monitor variables that are computed at inventory time.

As part of the projection cycling phase, subroutine FVS calls various subroutines to estimate tree growth and mortality, process management requests, establish regeneration, and write any stand data that needs to be saved for output, visualization, or use with other programs.

As part of the projection summarization phase, subroutine FVS calls various subroutines to produce the final output reports.

Subroutine FVS then returns to its caller, PROGRAM MAIN (or the calling program when FVS is a shared library), which calls FVS again for the next stand and the sequence is repeated. The run ends when the next call finds no more stands.

A logical variable, LSTART, has a value of “.TRUE.” during the projection initialization phase and “.FALSE.” when that phase is completed. This variable is used extensively during model calibration, discussed in [Model calibration and other setup tasks](#sec-model-calibration-and-other-setup-tasks), to control program logic flow.

The differences in program flow for a parallel run will be discussed in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api).

# Projection Initialization Phase {#sec-projection-initialization-phase}

The FVS model must go through various steps and checks in preparation for a single stand growth projection. Model parameters and variables must be initialized to their default starting values. User model controls must be input and stored. Tree data (if any) must be input, any missing data values filled in, and the data expanded to a per-acre basis. Self-calibration of model equations to the input data needs to take place. Once this phase is completed FVS is calibrated to local stand conditions, knows what projection to make in terms of projection length, management actions, model output, and other user instructions, and has the tree data to make it. Upon completion of the projection initialization phase, tree data may not yet exist if this is a bare ground projection.

## Opening the necessary input and output files

FVS needs to open various input and output files that are required in a projection and establish database connections if stand or tree data is coming from a database. When the keyword record file name is not specified as a command line option, FVS will prompt users for 6 file names. These names can be provided via keyboard input or the names can be supplied in a response file. The FVSOnline interface, provided by the fvsOL R package (code is at https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator-Interface and more information is at https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/FVSOnline), runs FVS through the rFVS package and supplies the keyword record file name directly, so FVS does not prompt for file names.

Most FVS runs take stand and tree data from, and write results to, SQLite databases. In these runs the keyword record file is still required. Inside a DATABASE – END keyword record sequence it names the input database with the DSNIN keyword record (the default is FVS_Data.db) and the output database with the DSNOUT keyword record (the default is FVSOut.db), and it contains the STANDSQL and TREESQL keyword records that retrieve the stand and tree records. No tree data file is needed in this case; the tree data file described below applies only to flat file input.

The first file opened is the file containing FVS keyword records, referred to as the “keyword record file” (or simply “keyword file”). A keyword record file is required to make an FVS projection. A detailed description of the keyword record file can be found in section 4.1 of the EFVS guide. How FVS reads this file will be discussed in [Processing keyword record requests](#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests) and [Processing event monitor instructions](#sec-processing-event-monitor-instructions) of this document.

If needed, the second file opened is a file containing individual tree data records, referred to as the “tree data file”. A detailed description of the tree data file is provided in section 4.2 of the EFVS guide.  A tree data file is not required when making a bare ground simulation or when all of the tree data will be read from a database table. In these instances, the file name “NUL” (or /dev/null on Unix-like platforms) should be specified for the tree data file name if FVS prompts for it. In a bare ground simulation the NOTREES keyword record must also be included as one of the keyword records in the keyword record file.

The next four prompts are for output file names. The third prompt is for the main FVS output file; the fourth for the tree list output file (requested with the TREELIST keyword record); the fifth is for the summary output file (requested with the ECHOSUM keyword record); and the sixth is for an auxiliary file used for input to post-processing programs like CHEAPOII. Default file names exist for these files if the user enters “NUL” or a blank when FVS prompts for these file names. Detailed descriptions of these output files are provided in section 4.3 of the EFVS guide. In multi-stand runs, output from all stands included in the keyword record file will be written to these files. When you enter the name of the keyword record file on the command line, FVS does not prompt for these file names. It automatically creates the files if and when they are needed by replacing the suffix of the keyword record file name (generally, “.key”) with other suffices, as follows: “.out” for the output, “.trl” for tree list, “.chp” for the CHEAPOII file, and “.tre” for the input tree list (see table 3-2).

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine fvsSetCmdLine (source code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) which then calls subroutine GENRPT to initialize the multiple report file. The multiple report file is a scratch file that FVS uses to temporarily store information that will eventually end up in the main output file. Information for several output reports is written to this file as the output is computed along with a report number identifying which output report the information will eventually go to. At the end of a simulation of each stand, all the reports will be written to the FVS output files in proper projection sequence. If there are over 200 different reports saved in the file, then the file is converted to a permanent file and saved for post-projection processing.

Subroutine fvsSetCmdLine (source code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) then calls subroutine FILOPN to open the keyword record file and the output file.  The tree data file and other FVS output files are opened when, and if, they are needed. Subroutine FILOPN sets up the file specification parameters and issues OPEN commands or calls subroutine MYOPEN to open files. FILOPN prompts for file names when the name of the keyword record file is not specified on the command line. When the keyword record file is specified on the command line, the names of other needed files are automatically formed using the keyword record file prefix as the common prefix, and suffices as listed in table 3-2.

Programmers need to be aware that subroutine MYOPEN once contained operating-system dependent code that needed to be modified for different operating environments. However, since about 2005, FVS is being coded using modern FORTRAN standards, so the need for this operating-system dependent code has evaporated and MYOPEN should therefore be phased out. In some of the more recent code its use has been avoided.

Sometime in the early 2000s, a new file handling subroutine was added called “openIfClosed” (the source code for this subroutine is part of the source code of subroutine FILOPN). An example using this code is in subroutine PRTRLS, the subroutine that writes the tree list output table. Subroutine openIfClosed is called prior to writing to the designed unit number. It checks to see if the file is opened, and opens it if it is not. It always opens a file with POSITION=’append’, so if a fresh file is desired, the old one needs to be discarded prior to the run starting. The assigned file name is the prefix name of the keyword record file and the suffix that is passed to subroutine openIfClosed (in the case of the tree list, the suffix is “.trl” as shown in table 3-2). This strategy was introduced so FVS does not create many unused empty files that need to be deleted later. It also simplified the coding of the stop/restart capability ([Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)) because the upper-level programming code need not open files until, and unless, they are actually needed for output.

A unit number is associated with each file. Those used by the FVS base model are specified in subroutine BLKDAT; those used in the regeneration establishment extension can be found in subroutine ESBLKD; those associated with other extensions can be found in various other places. Table 3-1 shows unit numbers and associated variable names that are used for some purpose in FVS. Programmers should avoid using these unit numbers for any other purpose in FVS when adding new features to the model. Furthermore, there is a capability in modern FORTRAN that provides a file unit number for use. An example of its use is in the Climate-FVS extension’s CLIN subroutine where the OPEN statement uses the NEWUNIT feature of the FORTRAN OPEN statement. This construct should replace the fixed unit assignments for many files listed in table 3-1. Unit 30 associated with variable KOLIST is a good example of where the OPEN(NEWUNIT =…) construct could easily replace the unit assignment, and should be changed.
