If some, or all, of the stand initialization parameters or individual tree data is being read directly from a database, database connections are not established at this point. Database connections will be established during the processing of keyword records, see [Processing keyword record requests](#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests) and [Reading stand and tree record input data](#sec-reading-stand-and-tree-record-input-data), when the DATABASE - END keyword record sequence is encountered in the keyword record file.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Various other subroutines serve minor, but either necessary or nice, roles in this process.

Subroutine REVISE is used to retrieve the date (YYYYMMDD) of the last git commit at the time the program was built, which is stored in the FVSVERSION module (source file base/version.f90); the value is “unknown” if the build could not read it from git. REVISE formerly returned a revision date stored for each variant. This date is used, along with the 2-character unique alpha variant code, to label FVS output files.

Subroutine UNBLNK is used to remove blanks from a character string, leaving the nonblank contents of the string left justified in the string and the rest of the string blank. It also returns the length of the nonblank portion of the string.

Subroutine RCDSET is used to set the FVS error severity value (10, 20, or 30) and is called from several places in the program. It has two arguments, the second indicates if the error warrants ending the run. This case, when the call is from subroutine FILOPN, will cause FVS to end processing when the keyword record file is not present and there is no restart file (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)). FVS requires a keyword record file to set the projection parameters, specifications, and management activities. If a keyword record file is not present and there is no restart file, the run will stop.

KEYFN, an entry point in subroutine KEYRDR, is used to save the keyword record file name from subroutine FILOPN for writing to the output file. This feature documents the name of the keyword record file that was used to create the run, in the output file. It is also used when automatic filenames are generated in the case where the keyword record file is input on the command line. Lastly, this name is added to the CASES table of the database output and is used to relate all the output tables in the database that were created from a single FVS run. A case is a single run of a single stand as defined in the database extension documentation (Crookston and others 2003).

## Initializing parameters to their starting values

FVS needs to initialize all model parameters to their starting values. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine INITRE to accomplish this task. In multi-stand runs each stand is processed by a separate call to subroutine FVS, so this is the point reached at the beginning of each stand in the run.

The goal upon completion of this task is that every model control parameter needed for the FVS projection of the individual stand will have a value. The value may be the model’s default value or a value set by the user, but all parameters will have a value. This is accomplished in three steps: 1) default values are assigned to all model control parameters; 2) keyword records are processed and user specified values replace some of the default values; and 3) default values for parameters that were not set by the user, but are dependent on other parameter values set by the user, are assigned.

### Subroutines involved and their function

For step 1, subroutine INITRE calls subroutine GRINIT to set the default conditions for the beginning of the simulation for a stand. Subroutine GRINIT contains variant-specific initializations for many model variables, including those variables that are either species-specific, used for output summarization, or stand-specific such as slope, aspect, and elevation.

Step 2, processing of the keyword records, is done by subroutine INITRE along with the help of many other subroutines. This will be explained in greater detail in the next section.

For step 3, subroutine INITRE calls subroutine SITSET that is another variant-specific subroutine. The role of subroutine SITSET is to make sure those model control parameters that may be dependent on other parameter settings, all have a value. Examples are species-specific site index values or stand density index values where the user may have set values for a few, but not all, species recognized by the variant.

### Auxiliary subroutines

The purpose of this document is to describe the program flow during model execution. However, from a programmer’s perspective it is worth mentioning there are other FVS subroutines involved in model initialization. Some are base model subroutines where values are loaded at compile time rather than run time.

Subroutine BLKDAT is a variant-specific BLOCK DATA subroutine that contains base model parameter settings such as the species codes the variant recognizes. These are all set with DATA statements and loaded at compile time. Other variant-specific and base model subroutines contain DATA statements that load default equation coefficients and model parameters at compile time.

Subroutine ESBLKD is another BLOCK DATA subroutine that contains regeneration establishment extension settings that are loaded at compile time. These settings are not variant-specific.

Subroutine DBSINIT, called from subroutine INITRE, initializes the database extension for each stand. It turns off every database output table (the summary, compute, tree list, cut list, FIA-VBC, and other tables each have a control variable that is set when the corresponding keyword record is processed in a DATABASE – END sequence) and clears the case identifier. It does not open any database connection; connections are opened when the DSNIN or DSNOUT keyword records are processed.

Various other extensions have their own initialization subroutines. Some have DATA statements that load at compile time, while others like subroutine FMINIT for the fire and fuels extension load at run time. Some of these, like subroutine FMINIT, are extension specific and some are variant-specific, like subroutine MISINTCR for the mistletoe extension in the Central Rockies variant. Initialization subroutines for the various base model extensions include: ESINIT, MPBINT, DFBINT, TMINIT, BWEINT, CVINIT, RDINIT, MISIN0, MISINT, BRINIT, ISSTAG, FMINIT, SVINIT, ECINIT, DBSINIT, and CLINIT. Subroutine INITRE also calls subroutines OPINIT, to initialize the activity schedule, and RANSED, to set the random number seed, at this point.

And finally, the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP), contain a section of code in subroutine GRINIT to initialize variables needed to run the ORGANON subroutines. These variables also load at run time. Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants).

## Processing keyword record requests {#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests}

Users communicate run control information to FVS through the use of keyword records. Consequently, use of the keyword record system is described throughout the EFVS guide and is the basis of FVS training sessions and tutorials. Keyword record processing is echoed to the main FVS output file unless a user turns this feature off with the NOECHO keyword record.

### Subroutines involved and their function {#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests-subroutines-involved-and-their-function}

Subroutine INITRE orchestrates the processing of all keyword records. If the PARMS format, discussed in section 6.1 of the EFVS guide, is not being used, subroutine INITRE also checks the keyword record parameter fields for valid values and assigns default parameter values if some of the parameter values are missing. If values for required parameter fields are missing, or if supplied values are incorrect, then the keyword record is rejected. In this case, subroutine KEYDMP is called to echo the keyword record to the FVS main output file and subroutine ERRGRO is called to write an error message to the FVS main output file giving the user some idea of what problem was encountered. Processing then continues with the next keyword record. If the PARMS format is being used, parameter field checking is not done.

Keyword records convey different types of information to FVS and are dealt with in different ways. Keyword records may be used to set constants, schedule management activities, or serve as flags to indicate program control needs to be temporarily transferred to a different part of FVS, such as one of the FVS extensions, for processing to continue.

#### Keyword records that can be dealt with once {#sec-keyword-records-that-can-be-dealt-with-once}

Some keyword records can be dealt with once and then FVS is done with them for the simulation of a particular stand. Keyword records that simply convey parameter settings FVS should use instead of the model default values are of this type. Examples of these are the BAMAX keyword record that sets the biological basal area maximum for the stand and the DEFECT keyword record that sets species-specific defect corrections for volume estimates. Keyword records that allow users to enter equation coefficients are also of this type. An example is the CWEQN keyword record that allows users to enter their own species-specific crown width equation coefficients.

In both of these cases subroutine INITRE directly stores the new parameter values in the appropriate variable or array, echoes the information to the output file unless keyword record echoing is turned off, and FVS is done with processing that particular keyword record request.

#### Keyword records that transfer control to another part of FVS for processing

A special case of keyword records that can be dealt with once in FVS by subroutine INITRE are those that transfer control to another keyword record processing subroutine within the FVS structure. Examples are the COMPUTE keyword record that transfers control to the event monitor subroutine EVUSRV, and the FMIN keyword record that transfers control to the fire and fuels extension keyword record processing subroutine FMIN.

Control remains in the location outside of subroutine INITRE until an END keyword record is encountered at which time control returns to subroutine INITRE. Any keyword records encountered between these special signal keyword records are processed by the designated components of FVS. Some of these between keyword records will be handled directly by the receiving subroutine as discussed above, and some will be scheduled as discussed below. In either case, keyword records are handled in the same way as discussed for subroutine INITRE base model keyword record processing, with one exception. Processing of event monitor instructions is quite different and will be discussed in [Processing event monitor instructions](#sec-processing-event-monitor-instructions). Subroutines that process extension specific keyword records include: BGCIN, BMPPIN, BRIN, BWEIN, CVIN, CLIN, DBSIN, DFBIN, DFTMIN, ESIN, FMIN, MISIN, MPBIN, ORIN, and RDIN.

#### Keyword records that need to be scheduled {#sec-keyword-records-that-need-to-be-scheduled}

Many FVS model instructions can be issued by year (often called “date”) or projection cycle. Examples are management activities such as thinning requests and model multipliers that alter predicted model outputs. Instructions of this type must be handled by the option processing subroutines within FVS that posts the instructions to the activity schedule table and then retrieves them at the appropriate time by the appropriate portion of the FVS code for implementation. Most keyword records of this type support the PARMS format discussed in section 6.1 of the EFVS guide. For some, like the TREELIST keyword record, the PARMS format would not make sense and is not supported; there aren’t any parameter fields on the TREELIST keyword record that are dynamic. How FVS processes the PARMS format is discussed in [Compiling the PARMS notation](#sec-compiling-the-parms-notation).

##### Scheduling the Option {#sec-scheduling-the-option}

Subroutine INITRE calls subroutine KEYRDR to read a keyword record. That subroutine (which is also used by the extensions) checks the parameter fields if the PARMS format is not being used. If the checks are satisfied, subroutine OPNEW is called to post the activity to the activity schedule table. If the PARMS format is in use, parameter fields are not checked and subroutine OPNEWC is called to post the activity to the activity schedule table. In either case, a unique option code (also called an activity number) is associated with each activity. Information posted to the activity schedule includes the unique option code, the year the activity is being scheduled, and the parameters associated with the activity. Option codes associated with FVS keyword records are shown in subroutine OPLIST (see [Option Processing Logic](#sec-option-processing-logic)).

##### Retrieving and Processing the Option

It is the responsibility of individual subroutines pertaining to the activity to check the activity schedule, retrieve any activities posted there for the current cycle, and process the information contained in the associated parameters. For example, it is the responsibility of subroutine CUTS to retrieve any thinning-related activities from the activity schedule each projection cycle. The processing subroutine, in this example CUTS, contains a list of unique option codes it is responsible for processing. This list is typically stored in a local array called MYACTS(i). Subroutine OPFIND is called to see if any activities on the activity schedule for the current cycle match those in the list. If there are, then OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called for each of the scheduled activities to retrieve the parameters associated with the activity. These activities are returned in the order they are scheduled (the year), or, when activities are scheduled in the same year, then in the order they were specified. The processing subroutine then stores the associated parameters in the appropriate variables for processing. OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to post the activity and its disposition to the activity summary. Possible dispositions include “DONE”, “NOT DONE”, or “DELETED OR CANCELLED”.

“DONE” means the activity was processed successfully.

“NOT DONE” usually means there was an error at some point in processing the keyword record. With improvements in keyword record parameter checking and defaulting, it is extremely rare to encounter this disposition for this reason. Other reasons an activity would get marked “NOT DONE” are that the activity was posted to occur in a year that is not within the time scope of the simulation; or it was dynamically posted for a year that has already past in simulation time. In those cases, the activity is simply never explicitly considered. Lastly, a “NOT DONE” can be seen when a programmer has failed to include a call to OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, where one should exist.

“DELETED OR CANCELLED” means the activity was considered but parameter settings could not be satisfied. For example, if a diameter limit thinning in the DBH range 0.0” – 5.0” was specified for cycle 3, and there were no trees in the stand with diameters less than 5.0” in cycle 3, then this diameter limit thinning request would be “DELETED OR CANCELLED”.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutines used in reading event monitor instructions will be discussed in [Processing event monitor instructions](#sec-processing-event-monitor-instructions).

Subroutine DUNN is a variant-specific subroutine that translates Dunning site codes to regular site index values. Dunning site codes are valid for FVS variants used in Forest Service Region 5 and may be entered using the SITECODE keyword record.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine FFIN is used to process parameters on the FERTILIZ keyword record and schedule the fertilization activity.

Subroutine FNDKEY is used to find a keyword record name in the keyword record name table. FVS base model keyword record names are in an array called TABLE(i) which is loaded in the BLOCK DATA code segment KEYWDS, and carried in the KEYCOM labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine FORKOD is used to translate the forest code entered on the STDINFO keyword record into a subscript that is stored in variable IFOR and used to index forest specific growth constants or coefficients in various parts of FVS. If the forest code is missing, or invalid, a default value is assigned. The actual forest code corresponding to the forest index is stored in variable KODFOR. Both IFOR and KODFOR are stored in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine GETSED is called to generate a seed value for the FVS random number generator. The seed value is passed to RANSED, an entry point in subroutine RANN, to reseed the random number generator.

Subroutine HABTYP is used to translate the habitat type entered on the STDINFO keyword record into a subscript that is stored in variable ITYPE and used to index habitat specific growth constants or coefficients in various parts of FVS. If the habitat type is missing, or invalid, a default value is assigned. The actual habitat type corresponding to the habitat type index is stored in variable KODTYP.  Both ITYPE and KODTYP are stored in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine KEYDMP writes a keyword record to the main output file when the parameter values contain errors severe enough that the keyword record is being rejected.

Subroutine KEYOPN opens an external file for input or output as requested with the OPEN keyword record.

Subroutine KEYRDR is used to read the FVS base model keyword records. Keyword records are read in both character and real formats. Keyword records are decoded and scanned for the PARMS format. If a STOP keyword record is encountered, subroutine KEYRDR calls GRSTOP, an entry point in subroutine ERRGRO, to close database connections, close any open file units, set an appropriate return code, and return back to subroutine FVS.

Subroutine KSSTAG is called to process parameters associated with structural call calculations entered with the STRCLASS keyword record.

Subroutine LBAGLR is used to read the activity group label for the current activity group entered with the AGPLABEL keyword record.

Subroutine LBDSET writes the default stand label set to the FVS main output table and assigns the stand label set to all activity groups for which no activity group label set has been specified.

Subroutine LBSPLR is used to read the stand policy label set entered with the SPLABEL keyword record.

Subroutine SDEFLN is called to process parameters associated with the BFFDLN and MCFDLN keyword records that are used to set species-specific defect coefficients for volume calculations.

Subroutine SDEFET is called to schedule activities associated with the MCDEFECT and BFDEFECT keyword records. These keyword records are used to enter species-specific defect correction factors used in volume calculations.

Subroutine SPDECD decodes the species code for keyword records that contain species-specific parameters. The species code entered on the keyword record may be the FVS species sequence number, the FVS alpha species code, the species group name, or a value of zero indicating the parameters apply to all species.

Subroutine SVKEY is called to process parameters associated with the Stand Visualization System and entered with the SVS keyword record.

Subroutine TRNASP translates the aspect in degrees entered on the STDINFO keyword record to a value in radians by multiplying the degree aspect by the constant 0.0174533. The translated value of stand aspect is stored in variable ASPECT in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine TRNSLO translates the slope percent entered on the STDINFO keyword record to a ratio value by dividing the slope percent by 100. The translated value of stand slope is stored in variable SLOPE in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

## Processing event monitor instructions {#sec-processing-event-monitor-instructions}

The event monitor within FVS can be used to conditionally schedule activities, create user-defined output variables, and make the value of keyword record parameter fields the result of a mathematical expression rather than constant values. Certain limits exist that govern the number of events, the amount of memory available to hold expressions, and so on. A PARAMETER statement at the beginning of the OPCOM labeled COMMON block sets these limits. To increase these limits, programmers should modify the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, recompile all the FVS code segments that use the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, and re-link the program executable. Some of these limits can be increased; other limits cannot, without a major rewriting of event monitor computer code. Programmers should pay attention to comment statements giving variable definitions in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block to see which of these limits can be adjusted.

### Processing an IF-THEN-ENDIF expression

Stand management activities can be scheduled by year or cycle. They can also be scheduled contingent upon several factors, which can be called an event. An event is designated in FVS by an IF keyword record followed by a logical expression of some sort that defines the event. Following the logical expression, a THEN keyword record signals the end of the logical expression and the beginning of the activities that will be scheduled only when the event is true. The activities can include one or more FVS keyword records (including those found in extensions) that can be scheduled by year or cycle number. An ENDIF keyword record is entered to signal the end of an event monitor sequence.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

When subroutine INITRE encounters an IF keyword record, it immediately calls subroutine EVIF to begin processing the event monitor sequence. The variable LOPEVN is a logical variable having a value of “.TRUE.” if keyword records being currently entered by the user are part of an event monitor sequence. Subroutine EVIF first checks to see if LOPEVN is “.TRUE.” indicating that another event monitor sequence is already open. If it is, subroutine EVIF calls EVEND, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT, to close the event monitor sequence that is already open so a new sequence may be started.

Subroutine EVIF next checks to make sure adding this new event monitor sequence will not exceed the maximum number allowed in FVS. If the maximum has already been reached, subroutine ERRGRO is called to write an error message to the output file. If room exists in the activity storage arrays, subroutine EVIF calls subroutine EVCOMP to process the logical expression.

[Event monitor logic](#sec-event-monitor-logic) describes how FVS compiles the expressions; [Projection Cycling Phase](#sec-projection-cycling-phase) discusses the processing sequence FVS uses for evaluating logical expressions during a projection cycle.

When subroutine INITRE encounters a THEN keyword record, it calls EVTHEN, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT. EVTHEN links the internal event number, assigned when the logical expression was compiled, with the specified management activities and stores them for future scheduling. These get stored in array IEVACT(i,j) contained in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block.

When subroutine INITRE encounters an ENDIF keyword record, it calls EVEND, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT. EVEND signals an end to processing the event monitor sequence and increments the internal event number.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ALGSPP is used to check for valid species codes or species group names.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine EVKEY is used by subroutine ALGKEY to check for user-defined variables in an expression.

Subroutine EVMKV is used to create a new variable.

Subroutine KEYDMP writes a keyword record to the main output file when the parameter values contain errors severe enough that the keyword record is being rejected.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to convert lower case characters to upper case characters.

### Defining new variables

Allowing users to define their own variables is one powerful feature of the event monitor. Values of these variables will be displayed in the Activity Summary portion of the main output file and can be used in logical expressions or specifications of keyword record parameter settings in a PARMS format. New variables are defined using the COMPUTE keyword record followed by a number of supplemental records defining the new variables. The sequence is closed with an END keyword record.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

When subroutine INITRE encounters a COMPUTE keyword record it calls subroutine EVUSRV to compile and store the expressions defining the variables contained on the supplemental records. Subroutine EVUSRV calls subroutine ALGEXP to read an expression from a supplemental record and utilizes subroutines ALGKEY and EVMKV in a similar fashion as done in processing an IF-THEN-ENDIF sequence. Subroutine EVUSRV then calls subroutine ALGCMP to compile the expression. And since the computation of user-defined variables can be scheduled by year or cycle, subroutine EVUSRV calls subroutine OPNEW to place the action into the activity schedule with an activity code, or option code, 33.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages and sets return status codes.

### Compiling the PARMS notation {#sec-compiling-the-parms-notation}

With most keyword records that can be scheduled by year or cycle, users have the option of using the PARMS format to specify parameter values. The PARMS format allows users to specify expressions that will be used to calculate parameter values at the time the logical expression becomes true and the management activity is being done. This is a very powerful feature of the event monitor.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

As stated above, when subroutine INITRE encounters a keyword record using the PARMS option it calls subroutine OPNEWC to process it. Subroutine INITRE does not check any of the parameter fields for valid values when the PARMS statement is used (it can’t because their values are not known until the option is retrieved from the activity schedule with OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND).  Subroutine OPNEWC calls subroutine ALGCMP to compile expressions making up the parameter specifications, as described in the IF-THEN-ENDIF specification above. If valid parameters specifications are found, OPNEWC stores the activity in the activity schedule and marks it as “NOT ACCOMPLISHED”.  Parameter specifications will be evaluated at the time the management activity specified by the keyword record is triggered by year, cycle, or condition.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to convert lower case characters to upper case characters.

## Reading stand and tree record input data {#sec-reading-stand-and-tree-record-input-data}

There are two ways to get stand and tree record input data into FVS: from SQLite database tables, which is how most FVS runs are set up, or from ASCII flat files. In both cases a keyword record file is required. For database input, the keyword record file contains a DATABASE – END keyword record sequence. Within this sequence the DSNIN keyword record names the input database (the default is FVS_Data.db), and the STANDSQL and TREESQL keyword records, each followed by an SQL SELECT statement and a closing EndSQL line, retrieve the stand and tree records. By convention the stand level data are in a table named FVS_StandInit (or FVS_PlotInit when plots are projected as stands) and the tree data are in a table named FVS_TreeInit, both identified by the stand identifier, so a typical query is `SELECT * FROM FVS_StandInit WHERE Stand_ID = '%StandID%'`. Text wrapped in percent signs is replaced with a value for the current stand before the query is run (%StandID%, %MgmtID%, %Stand_CN%, %Variant%, and %FVSCase%). Each stand is projected by its own call to subroutine FVS, so the queries return the records for the current stand only. As a shortcut, the STANDIN keyword record lists the columns to retrieve, and FVS builds a query on table FVS_StandInit using the current stand identifier and the inventory year. The SQLIN keyword record executes other SQL statements against the input database.

Stand level information can also be entered on FVS keyword records such as STDINFO and DESIGN. These are processed as detailed above in [Keyword records that can be dealt with once](#sec-keyword-records-that-can-be-dealt-with-once). Values are applied in the order the keyword records are processed, so the placement of the DATABASE – END sequence in the keyword record file is critical. If the DATABASE – END sequence is after keyword records, like STDINFO, that specify stand parameters, parameter values from the database will replace those that were entered by the previous keyword records. The opposite is also true: if the keyword records follow the database sequence, parameter values from the keyword records will replace values that came from the database.

Tree record data, if there is any, may be read from a database or from a flat file, or both. It would be unusual for some of the tree data to be in a database and some of it in a flat file, but it can happen. When flat files are used, several tree data files may be read, in effect, concatenating the individual files. Two keyword records signal FVS to input tree record data from a flat file. These are the TREEDATA and PROCESS keyword records; TREEDATA directly signals FVS to input tree record data from a flat file; PROCESS indirectly signals FVS to input tree record data if none has been read and a NOTREES keyword record was not present in the keyword record file.

If there are there are not enough projectable tree records for a simulation, then one of two things will happen. If the variant includes the full regeneration establishment extension, subroutine INITRE calls ESEZCR, an entry point in subroutine ESINIT, to set flags that will trigger the regeneration establishment model to predict some advanced regeneration to start the simulation. If the variant includes the partial regeneration establishment extension model, entry ESEZCR in subroutine ESINIT is still called and the flags get set but the partial regeneration establishment model does not predict natural regeneration. In this case, the projection will run with no tree records (but they could be added using the PLANT or NATURAL keyword records).

### Subroutines involved and their function {#sec-reading-stand-and-tree-record-input-data-subroutines-involved-and-their-function}

When subroutine INITRE encounters a DATABASE keyword record, signaling that the next set of keyword records pertains to the database extension, it calls subroutine DBSIN. Subroutine DBSIN reads and processes the database extension keyword records until an END keyword record is found, and then returns control to INITRE. The DSNIN keyword record causes subroutine DBSOPEN to open the input database immediately. For a STANDSQL keyword record, subroutine DBSPRSSQL replaces the percent sign delimited tokens in the SQL statement and subroutine DBSSTANDIN runs the query and stores the returned columns in the corresponding FVS stand level variables (the same variables that are set by keyword records such as STDINFO and DESIGN). For a TREESQL keyword record, subroutine DBSPRSSQL replaces the tokens, DBSIN prepares the query on the input database (opening the database first if necessary), and calls subroutine INTREE, which obtains each tree record from subroutine DBSTREESIN. If an SQL statement fails or a token cannot be replaced, a message is written to the main output file and the error severity is set so that FVS stops processing the stand.

Subroutine INTREE processes tree input data and this may occur at different places in the keyword record processing sequence.

When subroutine INITRE encounters a TREEDATA keyword record, tree data input occurs at that point in the FVS keyword record processing sequence. INITRE immediately calls subroutine INTREE to read the tree record input data.

However, a TREEDATA keyword record is not required in a keyword record set. When subroutine INITRE encounters the PROCESS keyword record it checks to see if the tree record data has been read. If it hasn’t, then subroutine INITRE calls subroutine INTREE to read the tree record input data at this point in the FVS processing sequence. A PROCESS keyword record is required in a keyword record set.

Subroutine INTREE calls subroutine DAMCDS that calls subroutine BASDAM to process damage and severity ratings pertaining to the base model. Subroutine DAMCDS stores insect and disease damage and severity ratings for later processing by subroutine DAMPRO.

Subroutine DAMPRO is called from subroutine INITRE to process damage codes for insect and disease extensions.

Subroutine TRESOR is called from subroutine INITRE to match tree identification numbers with tree index numbers for FVS extensions

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if a user has called for triggering extra write statements to the output file which will be useful in program debugging.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine ESPLT1 is called to store point specific information for the regeneration establishment extension.

Subroutine LNKCHN is called for each tree record to establish it in the sorting sequence.

RDATV and RDTRES are used to see if the western root disease model extension is active and tree list initialization is being used. These two routines will exist as subroutines if the western root disease model extension is part of the variant, or as entry points in subroutine EXRD if the western root disease model extension is not part of the variant.

Subroutine SPCTRN is used to translate unidentified species codes to the closest valid species code in the variant.

Subroutine SPDECD is used to check field 5 of the TREEDATA keyword record for valid species codes when field 5 is used for data screening.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to change lower case species codes to upper case.

## Model calibration and other setup tasks {#sec-model-calibration-and-other-setup-tasks}

At this point in the FVS processing sequence the user’s simulation control information and tree data information have been input into FVS. However, subroutine FVS still has many tasks to complete as part of the projection initialization phase. It must initialize any simulation control variables not yet initialized or set by keyword record input, expand the tree data input to a per-acre basis, fill in any missing data values, and calibrate certain model relationships to match the input data.

### Initialization tasks {#sec-initialization-tasks}

Subroutine FVS sets up the IY(i) array which specifies cycle boundaries for the entire projection. The number of cycles is limited to the array dimension, a cycle length that was not specified defaults to 10 years, and an additional cycle boundary is inserted for each year requested with the CYCLEAT keyword record that falls inside the projection. The first and last years of the projection are not changed. Subroutine FVS then processes and writes option lists for any insect, disease, and economic extensions that are part of the variant and the simulation.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutines OPEXPN, OPCYCL, and OPLIST to process and list the activity schedule. Subroutine OPEXPN expands the activity list so activities specified for all cycles are duplicated once for each cycle. Subroutine OPLIST writes the activity schedule to the main output file.

Subroutine FVS next calls subroutine SETUP to set up the index pointers for species sorting (see discussion of array IND1(k) in [Accessing Tree Records](#sec-accessing-tree-records)), and subroutine NOTRE to expand the inventory data to a per-acre basis. This is followed by calls to insect and disease code segments, Code segments will exist as subroutines in the appropriate extension if the extension is part of the variant, or as entry points in the appropriate EX__ subroutine if the extension is not part of the variant. If the model is being run with insect and disease extensions, these calls initialize parameters and compute variables needed by those extensions. The calls made here include RDMN1 (first call, root disease), MPSDLP (mountain pine beetle: dead lodgepole pine per acre) and DFBINV (Douglas-fir beetle: dead trees per acre).

The variable ICYC carries the FVS cycle number and is used in various locations throughout the model. ICYC is set to 0 at the start of a stand, before subroutine INITRE is called. “Cycle 0” is another way of saying “at inventory time”. The variable ICYC is used as an index to the IY(i) array throughout the model, and in a few places (e.g. subroutines DGDRIV and MORTS) to control program logic. For the next tasks, ICYC is set to 1, and it is set back to 0 after subroutine ESFLTR is called (see [Final projection initialization tasks](#sec-final-projection-initialization-tasks)). Certain activities scheduled for cycle 1 (e.g. TREELIST for cycle 1 with field 4 not set to 1) also occur at inventory time.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine OPCSET to set the option pointers for the initialization phase to the cycle 1 options (ICYC = 1). Subroutine OPCSET sets up the IOPCYC(i) array containing the activities scheduled for that cycle sorted by ascending activity number.

Subroutine FVS then processes stop point 7 by calling subroutine fvsStopPoint. If a stop at this point has been requested, FVS returns to its caller here, before model calibration. A restart from stop point 7 resumes at the next step (SDICLS and CRATET) without repeating the steps described above (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)).

SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the maximum Stand Density Index for a stand. This will be needed in variants using a Weibull-based crown change model to correctly fill in missing crown ratio values.

### Model calibration and data dubbing

Next is a major task that distinguishes FVS from many other growth models. The primary growth functions for the large and small tree sub-models, and the height-diameter relationships are calibrated to the input data. Calibration of the model to match the input data improves projection results in most cases. However, users may not want this to happen under some conditions and can turn this FVS feature off using the NOCALIB keyword record.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine CRATET, a variant-dependent subroutine, to perform calibration related tasks. Subroutine CRATET also directs writing of the Calibration Statistics section of the main output file and directs the filling in (or “dubbing”) of any data values missing in the input data (e.g. total tree height or crown ratio).

Subroutine CRATET has an extra task in the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). That is to direct: 1) calibration of the ORGANON growth model equations; and 2) dubbing data values missing in the input data using ORGANON equations for valid ORGANON trees. This step is done by calling the ORGANON subroutine PREPARE and does not occur in any of the other FVS variants. Processing then continues as described below. Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants).

#### Calculate site and stand level variables

Some variants use the stands’ mean annual increment as a growth predictor variable; some variants use the species representing the most basal area, also called the “site species” as a growth predictor variable. Subroutine CRATET calls subroutine MBACAL to identify the site species based on plurality of basal area, and subroutine MAICAL to compute mean annual increment. In a bare ground simulation, the call to MBACAL is skipped.

Most growth equations in FVS contain terms for site level variables that have constant values for a stand projection unless climate change modeling is taking place. Examples of these variables include habitat type, site index, slope, aspect, and elevation. In the absence of climate change, these terms only need to be aggregated once with the results stored in vectors that are subscripted by species; these aggregations get used when processing each tree record. Subroutine CRATET calls subroutine RCON to direct the calculation of these terms. In climate change modeling, if any site level variables change, subroutine RCON gets called again from subroutine GRINCR and these aggregations get recomputed. Subroutine GRINCR will be discussed in [Projection Cycling Phase](#sec-projection-cycling-phase).

Subroutine RCON calls special entry points that are contained in growth modeling subroutines to load site dependent terms. These are: entry DGCONS in subroutine DGF; entry HTCONS in subroutine HTGF; entry REGCON in subroutine REGENT; entry MORCON in subroutine MORTS; and entry CRCONS in subroutine CROWN. All of these subroutines are variant-specific.

Subroutine CRATET then calls subroutine DENSE to compute stand metrics needed during model calibration. FVS is a forward projecting model. Tree input data includes a tree’s current diameter and height, past diameter growth and height growth over some measurement period, and tree mortality. The basic idea in calibrating the growth models is to backdate the stand to its condition 10-years in the past, project the stand forward 10-years using the imbedded growth and mortality functions, compare the projected current stand to the observed current stand, and scale the growth functions so the projected current stand matches the observed current stand.

Subroutine DENSE is called from various places in FVS. A logical variable, LBKDEN, is set to “.TRUE.” by subroutine CRATET when the input diameter growth data are previous increments or previous diameters (IDG less than 2), indicating DENSE needs to backdate the stand for model calibration. Backdating is not possible when there are no growth sample trees. Subroutine DENSE backdates the stand if it needs to, and calculates various other values and adjusts them for non-stockable points in the inventory. These other values include average height of the stand, crown competition factor by species, and point basal area in larger trees, for all tree records.

#### Dead tree records

Subroutine CRATET next deals with the non-projectable tree records (aka mortality). When tree level data is read, subroutine INTREE stores parameters associated with dead tree records in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Trees coded as recent mortality (within the last 5 years) get stored with a tree value class (IMC) of 7; trees that have been dead for a longer period of time (tree history codes 8 and 9) get stored with a tree value class of 9.

Subroutine CRATET identifies the non-projectable tree records. The numbers of records coded as recent mortality, by species, get written to the FVS main output file. Subroutine CRATET then realigns the pointers to the species-ordered sort, eliminating the dead tree indices. (See the discussion of the IND1(i) and ISCT(i,j) arrays in [Accessing Tree Records](#sec-accessing-tree-records).)

It is important to note that FVS is not done with the dead tree information yet, and this information is still stored in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Missing information about dead trees still needs to be filled in, dead tree information needs to be passed to the fire and fuels extension, and dead trees in the inventory data get printed in the tree list output file. Dead tree information will get purged from FVS later in the processing sequence by subroutine FVS (see [Final projection initialization tasks](#sec-final-projection-initialization-tasks)).

#### Calibrate height-diameter equation and dub missing heights

Subroutine CRATET works through the live tree records one species at a time. For each species it calibrates the height-diameter equation when the conditions below are met, and then estimates (dubs) the total heights that are missing. Height-diameter equations vary by variant, and the variant overview documents give the coefficients. The variables named in this section are defined in the next table.

```{r htdbh-variables, echo=FALSE}
htdbh_variables <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variable, ~Definition,
  "HT", "Total tree height, in feet",
  "DBH", "Tree diameter at breast height, in inches",
  "B1", "Intercept of equation {3.6.2.3.1}",
  "B2", "Slope of equation {3.6.2.3.1}",
  "HT1", "Default value of B1 for a species, set by the variant",
  "HT2", "Default value of B2 for a species, set by the variant",
  "AA", "Intercept calibrated to the trees of a species, equation {3.6.2.3.2}",
  "K1", "Number of trees in the calibration sample of a species",
  "LHTDRG", "Logical variable by species; true when calibration is turned on",
  "IABFLG", "Integer flag by species; 1 when the default intercept is used and 0 when the calibrated intercept AA is used; 1 at the start of a run",
  "NORMHT", "Height of the tree without the broken or dead top, in hundredths of a foot; negative on input for a record with a broken or dead top",
  "ITRUNC", "Broken height, the height of the tree with a broken or dead top, in hundredths of a foot",
  "HTDBH", "Subroutine that calculates the height of a tree from its diameter",
  "HTONT", "Subroutine in the ON variant that calculates the height of a tree with the Ontario equations",
  "IWYKCA", "Integer flag by species in subroutine HTDBH of CS, LS, NE and ON; 0 for the Wykoff equation and 1 for the Curtis-Arney equation",
  "IFOR", "Forest code of the stand",
  "P2", "Coefficient of equation {3.6.2.3.4}",
  "P3", "Coefficient of equation {3.6.2.3.4}",
  "P4", "Coefficient of equation {3.6.2.3.4}",
  "Z", "Join diameter by species in subroutine HTDBH of CA and WS, in inches",
  "DB", "Diameter by species in subroutine HTDBH of SN, CS, LS, NE and ON at which the interpolated height is 4.51 feet, in inches",
  "HTT11", "Coefficient A of the Chapman-Richards equation in AK, by species",
  "HTT12", "Coefficient B of the Chapman-Richards equation in AK, by species",
  "HTT13", "Coefficient C of the Chapman-Richards equation in AK, by species",
  "BB", "Slope of the regression of height on the square root of diameter in KT",
  "SMDBH", "Diameter by species in KT that separates the small-tree line from the height equation, in inches",
  "SMA", "Slope by species of the small-tree line in KT, HT = SMA x DBH + 4.5",
  "LMHTDUB", "Logical variable by species in BC; true when the metric form of the equation is used"
)

kable(htdbh_variables,
      col.names = c("Variable", "Definition"),
      caption = "Variables used in the height-diameter calibration and the dubbing of heights",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Default equation.** In most variants the default equation is the logistic height-diameter equation of Wykoff et al. (1982), shown in equation {3.6.2.3.1}, with species-specific coefficients B1 = HT1 and B2 = HT2. The variants in which another form is used for the calibration or the dubbing are listed under "Variant differences" below.

$$
HT = 4.5 + \exp\left(B_1 + \frac{B_2}{DBH + 1.0}\right)
\tag{3.6.2.3.1}
$$

Where:

- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- B1: Intercept (the default value is HT1; the calibrated value is AA)
- B2: Slope (the default value is HT2)


**Trees used for the calibration.** A live tree record is used for a species only when all of the following are true: the total height is greater than 4.5 feet, the tree does not have a broken or dead top (NORMHT is not negative), and the diameter is at least the minimum diameter for the variant and species. The minimum diameter is 3.0 inches in the variants and species not listed in the next table.

```{r htdbh-min-dbh, echo=FALSE}
htdbh_min_dbh <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Species, ~Minimum_DBH,
  "AK", "All", "5.0",
  "HI", "All", "5.0",
  "OP", "All", "5.0",
  "WC", "All", "5.0",
  "PN", "All", "5.0",
  "BM", "PY, YC, CW and OH", "5.0",
  "EC", "WH, PY, WB, NF, LL, YC, WJ, BM, VN, RA, PB, GC, DG, AS, CW, WO, PL, WI and OH", "5.0",
  "SO", "NF, WH, PY, WA, RA, BM, CW, CH, WI, GC, MC, MB and OH", "5.0",
  "WS", "LP, WB, PM, KP, FP, CP, LM, GP, WE, WJ, UJ and CJ", "5.0",
  "CI", "MC", "5.0",
  "TT", "BI and MC", "5.0",
  "UT", "MC and BI", "5.0"
)

kable(htdbh_min_dbh,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Species", "Minimum DBH (inches)"),
      caption = "Minimum diameter of the trees used to calibrate the height-diameter equation, where it is not 3.0 inches",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The species are identified by the two character FVS species codes of the variant. PN is compiled with the WC version of CRATET. The remaining variants use 3.0 inches for all species.

**Calibration.** The calibration is done separately for each species. It replaces the intercept of equation {3.6.2.3.1}, B1, with an intercept, AA, that is fitted to the measured heights of the species in the inventory. The slope, B2, is not changed, and the default coefficients, HT1 and HT2, are not changed. The steps are:

1. The calibration sample is selected, as described above: the live trees of the species with a measured total height greater than 4.5 feet, without a broken or dead top, and with a diameter at or above the minimum diameter.
2. The trees in the sample are counted. K1 is the number of trees in the sample. The calibration is done only when K1 is 3 or more, and when calibration has not been turned off for the species (LHTDRG is true).
3. The intercept AA is calculated with equation {3.6.2.3.2}. It is the intercept that makes the mean residual of the sample trees equal to zero on the scale of ln(HT - 4.5), with the slope B2 kept.
4. The intercept AA is tested. When AA is negative, the calibration is discarded and the default intercept, HT1, is kept.
5. When AA is zero or positive, IABFLG for the species is set to 0. IABFLG is 1 for all species at the start of a run. There is no upper limit on AA.

$$
AA = \frac{1}{K_1}\sum_{i=1}^{K_1}\left[\ln\left(HT_i - 4.5\right) - \frac{B_2}{DBH_i + 1.0}\right]
\tag{3.6.2.3.2}
$$

Where:

- AA: Calibrated intercept
- K1: Number of trees in the calibration sample of the species
- $HT_i$: Total height of tree $i$ (feet)
- $DBH_i$: Diameter at breast height of tree $i$ (inches)
- B2: Slope of equation {3.6.2.3.1}

When the species is calibrated (IABFLG is 0), the calibrated equation is equation {3.6.2.3.1} with AA in place of B1, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.3}. When the species is not calibrated (IABFLG is 1), equation {3.6.2.3.1} is used with the default intercept, B1 equal to HT1.

$$
HT = 4.5 + \exp\left(AA + \frac{B_2}{DBH + 1.0}\right)
\tag{3.6.2.3.3}
$$

Where:

- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- AA: Calibrated intercept from equation {3.6.2.3.2}
- B2: Slope of equation {3.6.2.3.1} (the default value is HT2)

The calibrated equation is used by CRATET to dub the missing heights of the species, as described below. The calibration is also used after CRATET, as described next.

**Use of the calibration after CRATET.** Subroutine REGENT, which grows the small trees, uses the calibrated intercept when it calculates the diameter of a small tree from its height. REGENT does this for the trees that are smaller than the breakpoint diameter of the variant and species (3.0 inches in SN and EC, for example; the breakpoint is set by variant and species in the other variants). It inverts equation {3.6.2.3.1}, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.5}, and applies the inverted equation twice: to the height at the start of the cycle, and to the height at the end of the cycle. The diameter increment of the tree is the difference between the two diameters, adjusted by the bark ratio and the user-supplied diameter increment multiplier. When REGENT is called from the regeneration establishment extension, the inverted diameter is assigned as the diameter of the new tree.

$$
DBH = \frac{B_2}{\ln\left(HT - 4.5\right) - B_1} - 1.0
\tag{3.6.2.3.5}
$$

Where:

- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- HT: Total tree height (feet), at the start or at the end of the cycle
- B1: Intercept, equal to HT1 when IABFLG is 1, and equal to AA otherwise
- B2: Slope (the value is HT2)

REGENT contains this calculation in AK, BM, CA, CI, CR, CS, EC, EM, HI, IE, LS, NC, NE, OC, ON, OP, SN, SO, TT, UT, WC, WS and PN (PN is compiled with the WC version of REGENT). In CI, CR, EM, IE, TT, UT and WS, the calculation is used only for some of the species, and the other species use other equations. In SO, the slope, B2, and the intercept, B1, are HTT2 and HTT1 of the species and the crown ratio class JCR for species 1 to 8, 10, 12, 13 and 32 when IABFLG is 1, and AA is used when IABFLG is not 1. The other variants use the following rules:

- KT does not refer to AA or to IABFLG in REGENT.
- BC does not use the calibrated intercept. Its REGENT sets its own intercept and slope from the arrays HHT1 and HHT2.
- When the variant has subroutine HTDBH and calibration is off for the species, or the species was not calibrated (LHTDRG is false, or IABFLG is 1), REGENT calls subroutine HTDBH, which calculates the diameter from the height, in place of equation {3.6.2.3.5}. AK uses the inverted Chapman-Richards equation in place of equation {3.6.2.3.5} under the same condition.
- In BM (species PY, YC, CW and OH), EC (species BM, VN, RA, PB, GC, DG, AS, CW, WO, PL, WI and OH), TT and UT, a diameter increment of 0.1 x HTG x XRDGRO is used for some species when calibration was done (LHTDRG is true and IABFLG is 0), where HTG is the height increment and XRDGRO is the user-supplied diameter increment multiplier.
- In BM, EC, TT and UT, for some species, the diameter assigned to a new tree is adjusted when calibration was done, so that the regression passes through the bud width at a height of 4.5 feet.

**Default setting of the calibration.** The calibration is turned on by default (LHTDRG is true) in the variants and species listed as on in the next table, and is turned off by default in the other variants. The NOHTDREG keyword changes the setting. Its first field is a species code, a species group, or 0 for all species. If its second field is greater than 0 the calibration is turned on; if the second field is blank or 0 the calibration is turned off.

```{r htdbh-calib-default, echo=FALSE}
htdbh_calib_default <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Default, ~Exceptions,
  "AK", "Off", "None",
  "BC", "On", "None",
  "BM", "Off", "Species WJ, WB, LM and AS are on",
  "CA", "Off", "None",
  "CI", "On", "Species MC is off",
  "CR", "On", "None",
  "CS", "Off", "None",
  "EC", "Off", "None",
  "EM", "On", "None",
  "HI", "Off", "None",
  "IE", "On", "None",
  "KT", "On", "None",
  "LS", "Off", "None",
  "NC", "Off", "None",
  "NE", "Off", "None",
  "OC", "Off", "None",
  "ON", "Off", "None",
  "OP", "Off", "None",
  "PN", "Off", "None",
  "SN", "Off", "None",
  "SO", "Off", "None",
  "TT", "On", "Species BI and MC are off",
  "UT", "On", "Species MC and BI are off",
  "WC", "Off", "None",
  "WS", "On", "Species LP, WB, PM, KP, FP, CP, LM, GP, WE, WJ, UJ, CJ and MC are off"
)

kable(htdbh_calib_default,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Calibration by Default", "Exceptions"),
      caption = "Default setting of the height-diameter calibration (LHTDRG)",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Dubbing the missing heights.** CRATET then estimates the height of every live and dead tree record that has no height. A record that has a diameter of 0.1 inch or less is given a height of 1.01 feet. For the other records the height is calculated from equation {3.6.2.3.1}, with B1 equal to AA when the species was calibrated, and equal to HT1 otherwise. A height below 4.5 feet is set to 4.5 feet. In the variants that have subroutine HTDBH (see the next table), the height from that subroutine replaces this height when calibration is off for the species (LHTDRG is false), or when the species was not calibrated (IABFLG is 1). Subroutine HTDBH calculates the height from the diameter alone. Dead trees are dubbed in the same way. For a species with no live tree records, B1 is equal to HT1, and subroutine HTDBH replaces the height where the same condition holds.

**Broken and dead tops.** For a record with a broken or dead top (NORMHT, the height of the tree without the damage, is negative), CRATET dubs the height the tree would have without the damage, and stores it in NORMHT, in hundredths of a foot. When the record has a measured height and the broken height, ITRUNC, is zero, ITRUNC is set to 80 percent of the measured height. When the height is missing and ITRUNC is zero, ITRUNC is set to 80 percent of the dubbed height, and the tree height is set to the dubbed height. When ITRUNC is given, a tree height that is smaller than ITRUNC is raised to ITRUNC.

```{r htdbh-forms, echo=FALSE}
htdbh_forms <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Equation_In_HTDBH,
  "BM", "Curtis-Arney",
  "EC", "Curtis-Arney",
  "HI", "Curtis-Arney, with two special cases (see below)",
  "NC", "Curtis-Arney",
  "PN", "Curtis-Arney, with two special cases (see below)",
  "OP", "Curtis-Arney (uses the HTDBH subroutine of PN)",
  "SO", "Curtis-Arney",
  "WC", "Curtis-Arney",
  "SN", "Curtis-Arney, with a height of 4.51 feet at a diameter DB",
  "CA", "Curtis-Arney, with a join diameter Z",
  "OC", "Curtis-Arney, with a join diameter Z (uses the HTDBH subroutine of CA)",
  "WS", "Curtis-Arney, with a join diameter Z",
  "CS", "Wykoff or Curtis-Arney by species (IWYKCA)",
  "LS", "Wykoff or Curtis-Arney by species (IWYKCA)",
  "NE", "Wykoff or Curtis-Arney by species (IWYKCA)",
  "ON", "Wykoff or Curtis-Arney by species (IWYKCA)"
)

kable(htdbh_forms,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Equation in HTDBH"),
      caption = "Equation forms in subroutine HTDBH",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The Curtis-Arney form is shown in equation {3.6.2.3.4}, where P2, P3 and P4 are coefficients by species (and by forest in some variants).

$$
HT = 4.5 + P_2 \exp\left(-P_3 \, DBH^{P_4}\right)
\tag{3.6.2.3.4}
$$

Where:

- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- P2: Coefficient by species (and by forest in some variants)
- P3: Coefficient by species (and by forest in some variants)
- P4: Coefficient by species (and by forest in some variants)


Below the join diameter, the height is interpolated linearly between two points. The upper point is the height from equation {3.6.2.3.4} at the join diameter. The join diameter is 3.0 inches, except in CA and WS, where it is Z, a diameter by species. The lower point is a height of 4.51 feet at a diameter of 0.3 inch, except in SN, CS, LS, NE and ON, where the diameter is DB, a value by species.

Subroutine HTDBH in the HI and PN variants has two special cases. For the forest codes, IFOR, 2, 4 and 6 and the species DF, the join diameter is 5.0 inches instead of 3.0 inches (the code comment refers to Douglas-fir on the Siuslaw). For a diameter of 100 inches or more, the species SS and the forest code 1 or 3, the height is 0.25 x DBH + 248 (the code comment refers to Sitka spruce on the Olympic National Forest).

**Variant differences.** The following variants differ from the description above.

- AK does not call subroutine HTDBH. When calibration is off, or the species was not calibrated, the Chapman-Richards equation $HT = 4.5 + A(1 - e^{B \cdot DBH})^{C}$ is used, with the coefficients A, B and C coming from the arrays HTT11, HTT12 and HTT13. The dubbed height is then multiplied by 0.45 for the species AD, WI and OH, and by 0.65 for the species SU.

  Where:

  - $HT$: Total tree height (feet)
  - $DBH$: Diameter at breast height (inches)
  - $A$: Coefficient HTT11 of the species
  - $B$: Coefficient HTT12 of the species
  - $C$: Coefficient HTT13 of the species
  - $e$: Base of the natural logarithm

- KT regresses the heights on the square root of the diameter, $HT = AA + BB\sqrt{DBH}$, using the calibration trees, and uses the default coefficients when the slope, BB, is negative. Trees smaller than the diameter SMDBH are given the height SMA x DBH + 4.5 when the default coefficients are used, and the regression is joined to this line at the diameter where the two equations meet.

  Where:

  - $HT$: Total tree height (feet)
  - $DBH$: Diameter at breast height (inches)
  - $AA$: Intercept of the regression (feet)
  - $BB$: Slope of the regression (feet per square root of inch)

- BC calibrates and dubs in metric units (height and diameter converted to meters and centimeters, with a breast height of 1.3 meters) for the species for which LMHTDUB, a logical variable, is true.
- ON calculates the calibrated intercept as above, but the dubbed height comes from subroutine HTONT, and subroutine HTDBH replaces it when calibration is off or the species was not calibrated. Dead trees are dubbed with HTONT only.
- CR, when the model type is 3 (Black Hills) and the species was not calibrated, uses a logistic equation based on the site index to dub the height.
- CI (species MC), TT (species BI and MC) and UT (species MC and BI) use the Curtis-Arney equation of this section directly, with coefficients written in CRATET, when calibration is off or the species was not calibrated. When the species was calibrated, the height is 0.0994 + 4.9767 x DBH below 5.0 inches and equation {3.6.2.3.1} at 5.0 inches or more.
- BM, EC, HI, OP, PN, SO, WC and WS use small-tree equations for trees below 5.0 inches in diameter for some species. These equations are in CRATET and are applied before the HTDBH replacement.
- WS replaces the dubbed height with a Region 5 equation based on site index for some species when the species was not calibrated.

The details of each of these variants are given in the variant overview documents. The unverified items found while reading the code are listed in OpenQuestions.md.

#### Add dead trees to the snag list

Subroutine CRATET calls FMSSEE to add the dead trees to the FFE snag list. FMSSEE will exist as a subroutine if the fire and fuels extension is part of the variant, or an entry point in subroutine EXFIRE if the fire and fuels extension in not part of the variant.

#### Dub missing crown ratios

After the heights have been dubbed, subroutine CRATET dubs the crown ratios that are missing in the input data, for the live and the dead tree records. The variables named in this section are defined in the next table.

```{r crown-variables, echo=FALSE}

kable(crown_variables,
      col.names = c("Variable", "Definition"),

                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
```

**ORGANON height calibration (OC and OP).** In the two ORGANON-FVS variants, subroutine CRATET calls ORGANON subroutine PREPARE once for the stand, before the FVS height calibration described above. The call is skipped when the data were already prepared (LORGPREP is true), when there are no tree records, when ORGANON is not used for the stand (LORGANON is false), and when none of the records is a major ORGANON species (`oc/cratet.f:146,206-219`, `op/cratet.f:139,195-208`). PREPARE edits the tree records, dubs missing heights and crown ratios, and calibrates the ORGANON height-diameter equation (subroutine HDCALIB), the crown equation (subroutine CRCALIB) and, when radial growth data are present, the diameter growth equation (subroutine DGCALIB) (`organon/prepare.f:119-141`). The height-diameter calibration multiplier of species group g is stored in ACALIB(1, g).

A record is a valid ORGANON tree when its diameter is 0.1 inch or more, its height is missing or above 4.5 feet, and its species is one of the valid species of the variant (IORG = 1). The next table lists the ORGANON model type, the number of ORGANON species groups (NSPN), the number of major species groups (IB), the valid species and the species that allow PREPARE to run. The names of the species groups are in the LABEL arrays of `oc/cratet.f` and `op/cratet.f`.

```{r organon-valid-species, echo=FALSE}
organon_valid_species <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Model_Type, ~Species_Groups_NSPN, ~Major_Groups_IB, ~Valid_Species, ~Species_That_Allow_PREPARE,
  "OC", "1 (SWO), the only valid type", "18", "5", "IC, RC, GF, DF, WH, SP, PP, PY, CY, WO, BO, BM, RA, MA, GC, DG, TO, WI", "IC, GF, DF, SP, PP",
  "OP", "2 (NWO), or 3 (SMC); 2 when not set", "11", "3", "GF, DF, RC, WH, BM, RA, MA, WO, PY, DG, WI", "GF, DF"
)

kable(organon_valid_species,
      col.names = c("Variant", "ORGANON model type", "Species groups (NSPN)", "Major groups (IB)", "Valid FVS species", "Species that allow PREPARE to run"),
      caption = "ORGANON model type, species groups and valid species of OC and OP (sources: oc/cratet.f:166-205, op/cratet.f:155-194, organon/prepare.f:243-252, vorganon/orin.f)",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "4em") %>%
  column_spec(5, width = "16em")
```

For each species group, HDCALIB predicts the height of every tree with a measured height with the ORGANON height-diameter equation of the model type, PTRHT, which is calculated as described after this paragraph (species group equations A_HD_SWO, HD_NWO and HD_SMC, or the stand equations HD40_SWO, HD40_NWO and HD40_SMC for the species that makes up 80 percent or more of an even-aged stand) (`organon/start2.f:96-185`). The multiplier of the group is the ratio estimator of equation {3.6.2.3.6}. It is calculated only when the group has at least 2 trees with a measured height; otherwise it is 1.0 (`start2.f:162-167`).

$$
\begin{aligned} \beta &= \frac{\sum_i Y_i X_i / DBH_i}{\sum_i X_i^{2} / DBH_i} \\ Y_i &= HT_i - 4.5, \qquad X_i = PTRHT_i - 4.5 \end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.6}
$$

Where:

- β: Height calibration multiplier of the species group, ACALIB(1, g)
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of tree i (inches)
- HT_i: Measured total height of tree i (feet)
- PTRHT_i: Total height of tree i predicted by the ORGANON height-diameter equation (feet)

Subroutine CALTST then tests whether β differs from 1.0, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.7}. When t is less than the critical value, β is set to 1.0. The critical value is taken from the array TVAL of CALTST, with N - 1 degrees of freedom: 63.657 for 1 degree of freedom, 2.750 for 30, interpolated between 30 and 40, 40 and 60, 60 and 120, and 120 and 1000 degrees of freedom, and 2.576 above 1000. Otherwise, and when the variance is not positive, β is limited to 0.5 to 2.0 (`organon/start2.f:1037-1085`).

$$
\begin{aligned} t &= \frac{\left|\beta - 1\right|}{\sqrt{MSE \Big/ \sum_i X_i^{2} / DBH_i}} \\ MSE &= \frac{\sum_i Y_i^{2} / DBH_i - 2\beta \sum_i Y_i X_i / DBH_i + \beta^{2} \sum_i X_i^{2} / DBH_i}{N - 1} \\ Y_i &= HT_i - 4.5, \qquad X_i = PTRHT_i - 4.5 \end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.7}
$$

Where:

- t: Test statistic of the multiplier
- β: Height calibration multiplier of the species group from equation {3.6.2.3.6}
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of tree i (inches)
- HT_i: Measured total height of tree i (feet)
- PTRHT_i: Total height of tree i predicted by the ORGANON height-diameter equation (feet)
- N: Number of trees of the species group with a measured height (trees)

When records have a missing height, PREPARE dubs it with the calibrated equation, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.8}, with a minimum of 4.6 feet (`organon/start2.f:225-226`). CRATET then loads the DBH, height and crown ratio of the valid ORGANON trees back into the FVS arrays, and counts the heights that ORGANON dubbed by species (KNTOHT) (`oc/cratet.f:350-360`). The FVS calibration described above then runs on all the records, including the heights that ORGANON dubbed; the source comment says that this brings the FVS and ORGANON equations closer together (`oc/cratet.f:210-213`).

$$
HT_i = \max\left[4.6, \; 4.5 + \beta \left(PTRHT_i - 4.5\right)\right]
\tag{3.6.2.3.8}
$$

Where:

- HT_i: Dubbed total height of tree i (feet)
- β: Height calibration multiplier of the species group from equation {3.6.2.3.6}
- PTRHT_i: Total height of tree i predicted by the ORGANON height-diameter equation (feet)

The multiplier that ORGANON uses in each cycle is attenuated toward the midpoint between 1.0 and β, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.9}, when the height calibration flag INDS(1) is 1; otherwise it is 1.0 (`organon/execute2.f:232-240`). CYCLG is ICYC - 1 (`oc/dgdriv.f:180`, `op/dgdriv.f:175`), so the multiplier of the first cycle is β. ORGANON uses it to calibrate the predicted heights in the height growth of the minor species groups (the groups above IB), where the 5-year height is the height of the tree multiplied by the ratio of the calibrated height-diameter predictions at the diameter DBH and at DBH minus the diameter growth of the tree (`organon/htgrowth.f:225-236`), and in the diameter growth calibration (`organon/diamcal.f:256-257`).

$$
CALIB_1 = \frac{1 + \beta}{2} + 0.5^{\,0.5 \, CYCLG} \, \frac{\beta - 1}{2}
\tag{3.6.2.3.9}
$$

Where:

- CALIB_1: Height calibration multiplier that ORGANON uses in the cycle
- β: Height calibration multiplier of the species group, ACALIB(1, g)
- CYCLG: Number of cycles grown in ORGANON, which is the FVS cycle number minus 1

The height calibration is controlled in three ways. The default of INDS(1) is 1 (calibration on) in `oc/grinit.f:356` and `op/grinit.f:354`, and field 4 of the ORGINFO keyword (0 or 1; an invalid value is set to 1) sets it (`vorganon/orin.f:186-196`). Calibration values read from lines 2 to 4 of the ORGANON .INP file replace the calculated value of a species group when they are not 1.0 (`vorganon/org_intree.f:141-148`), and a calibration value computed by PREPARE is loaded into ACALIB only where the value of ACALIB is still 1.0 (`oc/cratet.f:394-400`). ORGANON stops with an error when any calibration value is below 0.5 or above 2.0 (`organon/execute2.f:591-596`).

**ORGANON predicted height (PTRHT).** ORGANON assigns each tree to a species group from the FIA species code that ORGSPC returns for the FVS species (`oc/orgspc.f:55-65`, `op/orgspc.f:47-55`). Subroutine SPGROUP_EDIT (called by PREPARE, `organon/prepare.f:309`) and subroutine SPGROUP_RUN (`organon/execute2.f:917-961`) compare the code with the list of the model type, which are SCODE1 (model type 1, 19 codes in which 15 and 17 are both group 2) and SCODE2 (model types 2 and 3, 11 codes). The next table lists the FIA code and the species group of the valid species of each variant.
