ORGANON predicts the height of a tree with one of two equation forms, and the form depends on the use and on the stand. The species group form, equation {3.6.2.3.10}, has three coefficients per species group g, held in the array HDPAR(g, 1..3) of the subroutine of the model type. The stand form, equation {3.6.2.3.11}, is used only in HDCALIB and PRDHT, and only for a tree of a species group that makes up 80 percent or more of the basal area of an even-aged stand (conditions in the table below).

- **HDCALIB and PRDHT (calibration and dubbing of heights):** the stand form when its conditions are met, and otherwise the species group form from A_HD_SWO for model type 1 (`organon/start2.f:259-276`), HD_NWO for model type 2 (`organon/htgrowth.f:818-829`) or HD_SMC for model type 3 (`organon/htgrowth.f:858-869`) (`organon/start2.f:84-150,189-220`).
- **Diameter growth calibration (DGCALIB):** the species group form only, from A_HD_SWO, HD_NWO or HD_SMC for model types 1, 2 and 3 (`organon/diamcal.f:244-251`).
- **Height growth of the minor species groups (the groups above IB):** the species group form only, from HD_SWO for model type 1 (`organon/htgrowth.f:773-790`) and from HD_NWO or HD_SMC for model types 2 and 3 (`organon/htgrowth.f:223-230`). HD_SWO is a second array of the same form for model type 1.

The source comments say that A_HD_SWO has parameters for all (undamaged and damaged) trees and that HD_SWO has parameters for undamaged trees, except RC, WO and RA (`start2.f:236-237`, `htgrowth.f:752`). Subroutine INGRO_FILL (`organon/execute2.f:1153`) also uses HD_SWO, but no source file calls it.

$$
PTRHT = 4.5 + \exp\left(B_0 + B_1 \, DBH^{B_2}\right)
\tag{3.6.2.3.10}
$$

Where:

- PTRHT: Total height of the tree predicted by the species group equation (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height of the tree (inches)
- B_0, B_1, B_2: Coefficients of the species group of the tree, HDPAR(g, 1), HDPAR(g, 2) and HDPAR(g, 3) of the subroutine named above

The stand form, equation {3.6.2.3.11}, uses the top height HT40 and the diameter D40 of the stand. Its coefficients are in the array HD40PAR(e, 1..3), where e is 1, 2 or 3 for Douglas-fir, true fir and ponderosa pine in HD40_SWO (`start2.f:931-934`) and 1 or 2 for Douglas-fir and western hemlock in HD40_NWO and HD40_SMC (`start2.f:955-958`, `start2.f:980-983`).

$$
PTRHT = 4.5 + \left(HT40 - 4.5\right) \frac{\exp\left(B_0 \, DBH^{\,B_1 + B_2 \left(HT40 - 4.5\right)}\right)}{\exp\left(B_0 \, D40^{\,B_1 + B_2 \left(HT40 - 4.5\right)}\right)}
\tag{3.6.2.3.11}
$$

Where:

- PTRHT: Total height of the tree predicted by the stand equation (feet)
- HT40: Top height of the stand (feet), equations {3.6.2.3.14} to {3.6.2.3.16}
- D40: Diameter of the 40 largest trees per acre (inches), equation {3.6.2.3.12}
- DBH: Diameter at breast height of the tree (inches)
- B_0, B_1, B_2: Coefficients HD40PAR(e, 1), HD40PAR(e, 2) and HD40PAR(e, 3) of equation e of the subroutine of the model type

HDCALIB and PRDHT use the stand form for a tree only when the stand is even-aged (the flag INDS(4) is 1) and the species of the tree makes up 80 percent or more of the basal area, with the proportions of equation {3.6.2.3.13}. Otherwise they use the species group form (`organon/start2.f:84-150,189-220`). The default of INDS(4) is 1 in `oc/grinit.f:359` and `op/grinit.f:357`; field 2 of the ORGINFO keyword sets it (`vorganon/orin.f:163-170`), and SITSET sets it to 0 when the stand age (IAGE) is 0 (`oc/sitset.f:317-321`, `op/sitset.f:315-319`). The conditions are in the next table.

```{r organon-ptrht-selection, echo=FALSE}
organon_ptrht_selection <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Model_Type, ~Stand_Equation, ~Condition, ~Top_Height, ~Otherwise,
  "1 (SWO, OC)", "HD40_SWO(1)", "Group 1 and PDF >= 0.80", "HS_H40 with the Douglas-fir coefficients, SI_1", "A_HD_SWO",
  "1 (SWO, OC)", "HD40_SWO(2)", "Group 2 and PTF >= 0.80", "HS_H40 with the Douglas-fir coefficients, SI_1", "A_HD_SWO",
  "1 (SWO, OC)", "HD40_SWO(3)", "Group 3 and PPP >= 0.80", "HS_H40 with the ponderosa pine coefficients, SI_2", "A_HD_SWO",
  "2 (NWO, OP)", "HD40_NWO(1)", "Group 1 and PDF >= 0.80", "B_H40, SI_1", "HD_NWO",
  "2 (NWO, OP)", "HD40_NWO(2)", "Group 3 and PWH >= 0.80", "F_H40, SI_2", "HD_NWO",
  "3 (SMC, OP)", "HD40_SMC(1)", "Group 1 and PDF >= 0.80", "B_H40, SI_1", "HD_SMC",
  "3 (SMC, OP)", "HD40_SMC(2)", "Group 3 and PWH >= 0.80", "F_H40, SI_2", "HD_SMC"
)

kable(organon_ptrht_selection,
      col.names = c("ORGANON model type", "Stand equation", "Condition", "Top height HT40 from", "Otherwise"),
      caption = "Selection of the PTRHT equation in HDCALIB and PRDHT (source: organon/start2.f:84-150,189-220)",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "6em")
```

The diameter D40 is the mean diameter of the 40 largest trees per acre of the major species groups (the groups up to IB), as calculated by subroutine DFORTY (`start2.f:833-877`). The records with a diameter above zero are accumulated in diameter classes of 0.1 inch, from the largest class down, until the trees per acre exceed 40. The class that crosses 40 is prorated so that the total is exactly 40 trees per acre. D40 is 0 when no record is eligible. The trees per acre of a record are TDATAR(i, 4) divided by the number of points NPTS.

$$
D40 = \frac{\sum_i DBH_i \, TPA_i}{\sum_i TPA_i}
\tag{3.6.2.3.12}
$$

Where:

- D40: Mean diameter of the 40 largest trees per acre (inches)
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of record i (inches)
- TPA_i: Trees per acre represented by record i (trees per acre), with the last class prorated so that the sum of TPA_i is 40

The proportions PDF, PTF, PPP, PWH and PRA are calculated by subroutine SPMIX (`start2.f:879-918`). Their species are the Douglas-fir (FIA code 202), the true firs (15 and 17), ponderosa pine (122), western hemlock (263) and red alder (351). The basal area of all the records is the denominator.

$$
P_s = \frac{\sum_{i \in s} DBH_i^{2} \, TPA_i}{\sum_i DBH_i^{2} \, TPA_i}
\tag{3.6.2.3.13}
$$

Where:

- P_s: Proportion of the basal area of species s, which is PDF, PTF, PPP, PWH or PRA
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of record i (inches)
- TPA_i: Trees per acre represented by record i (trees per acre)

The top height HT40 is the height of the site index curve at the breast-height age. The age is BHAGE, which CRATET sets to STAGE - 6, where STAGE is the stand age IAGE plus the years from the first cycle to the current cycle, IY(ICYC) - IY(1) (`oc/cratet.f:257-264`, `op/cratet.f:246-253`). The site indices are SI_1, the Douglas-fir site index, and SI_2, the ponderosa pine site index in OC and the western hemlock site index in OP (`oc/sitset.f:324-325`, `op/sitset.f:322-323`; in the equations below the site index of the species is the SI of the equation). When EDIT finds that one of them is missing, it sets it from the other (`organon/prepare.f:356-368`): for model type 1, SI_1 = 1.062934 SI_2 and SI_2 = 0.940792 SI_1; for model types 2 and 3, SI_1 = 0.480 + 1.110 SI_2 and SI_2 = -0.432 + 0.899 SI_1 (Nigh 1995, as stated in the source comment).

Model type 1 uses subroutine HS_H40, the dominant height curves of Hann and Scrivani (1987) for Douglas-fir (ISP = 1) and ponderosa pine (ISP = 2) (`start2.f:606-636`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
HT40 &= 4.5 + \left(SI - 4.5\right) \frac{X(AGE)}{X(50)} \\
X(t) &= 1 - \exp\left(-\exp\left(a + b \ln\left(SI - 4.5\right) + c \ln t\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.14}
$$

Where:

- HT40: Top height of the stand (feet)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- AGE: Breast-height age of the stand, BHAGE (years)
- a, b, c: Coefficients of the species, which are -6.21693, 0.281176 and 1.14354 for Douglas-fir and -6.54707, 0.288169 and 1.21297 for ponderosa pine (`start2.f:622-630`)

Model types 2 and 3 use subroutine B_H40 for Douglas-fir, the equation of Bruce (1981) (`start2.f:638-657`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
HT40 &= SI \exp\left(A_1 \left[\left(AGE + 13.25 - \frac{SI}{20}\right)^{A_2} - \left(63.25 - \frac{SI}{20}\right)^{A_2}\right]\right) \\
A_2 &= -0.447762 - 0.894427 \frac{SI}{100} + 0.793548 \left(\frac{SI}{100}\right)^{2} - 0.17166 \left(\frac{SI}{100}\right)^{3} \\
A_1 &= \frac{\ln\left(4.5 / SI\right)}{\left(13.25 - SI/20\right)^{A_2} - \left(63.25 - SI/20\right)^{A_2}}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.15}
$$

Where:

- HT40: Top height of the stand (feet)
- SI: Site index of Douglas-fir, SI_1 (feet)
- AGE: Breast-height age of the stand, BHAGE (years)

Model types 2 and 3 use subroutine F_H40 for western hemlock, the unpublished metric curves of J. Flewelling, as stated in the source comment (`start2.f:659-680`). The site index is converted to meters (0.3048) and the top height back to feet (3.2808). The age is not converted. The height-age equation is in SITECV_F_EDIT (`start2.f:723-763`), its parameters are in SITEF_C_EDIT (`start2.f:765-796`) and the productivity index ψ is approximated from the site index in SITEF_SI_EDIT (`start2.f:798-831`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
HT40 &= 3.2808 \, HTOP \\
HTOP &= \begin{cases} h_1 + \psi x + \dfrac{\left(1 - w\right) \psi x_k}{c + 1} \left[\left(\dfrac{x_k - x}{x_k}\right)^{c+1} - 1\right] & x < x_k \\[2ex] y_k + \alpha \left(1 - e^{-\beta \left(x - x_k\right)}\right) & x \ge x_k \end{cases} \\
x &= AGE - 1 \\
x_k &= 128.326 \, e^{-2.54871 \, \psi} \\
w &= 0.2 + \frac{0.8}{1 + e^{5.33208 - 9.00622 \, \psi}} \\
c &= 1 + 1.2 \, \psi \\
\alpha &= 52.7948 \, \psi, \qquad \beta = \frac{\psi}{\alpha} \\
h_1 &= \mathrm{INT}\left(1.3 + \frac{w \psi}{2}\right) \\
y_k &= h_1 + \psi x_k \left(1 - \frac{1 - w}{c + 1}\right) \\
\psi &= 0.75 + z \left(b_{1j} + z \left(b_{2j} + z \left(b_{3j} + z \left(b_{4j} + z \left(b_{5j} + z \, b_{6j}\right)\right)\right)\right)\right) \\
z &= \frac{0.3048 \, SI - 32.25953}{10}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.16}
$$

Where:

- HT40: Top height of the stand (feet)
- SI: Site index of western hemlock, SI_2 (feet)
- AGE: Breast-height age of the stand, BHAGE (years)
- b_kj: Coefficient k of the array b(6, 2) of SITEF_SI_EDIT (`start2.f:814-817`), with j = 1 when 0.3048 SI is 32.25953 or less and j = 2 otherwise

**ORGANON crown ratio dubbing and calibration (OC and OP).** CRATET sends every live record to PREPARE with its crown ratio as a fraction, ICR/100, so a missing crown ratio is 0 (`oc/cratet.f:235`, `op/cratet.f:224`). EDIT sets MISSCR when any crown ratio is 0 or less, and treats a crown ratio above 1.0 as an error (`organon/prepare.f:262-267`). PREPARE then calls HDCALIB, PRDHT (only when a height is missing), CRCALIB (always) and PRDCR (only when MISSCR is set), in that order (`organon/prepare.f:119-132`), so the crown ratios are dubbed from heights that are already dubbed.

CRCALIB and PRDCR predict the height to the crown base, HCB, of a tree, and the predicted crown ratio is PCR = 1 - HCB/HT (`organon/start2.f:353-373`, `start2.f:426-446`). They use subroutine A_HCB_SWO for model type 1 (`organon/start2.f:454`), and HCB_NWO and HCB_SMC for model types 2 and 3 (`organon/crngrow.f:244`, `organon/crngrow.f:311`). The three subroutines have the same form, equation {3.6.2.3.21}, and differ in the coefficient array HCBPAR(g, 1..7): A_HCB_SWO (`start2.f:482-523`), HCB_NWO (`crngrow.f:264-291`) and HCB_SMC (`crngrow.f:331-358`). Model type 1 also has HCB_SWO (`crngrow.f:155`, array at `crngrow.f:183`), a second array of the same form that ORGANON uses in the crown recession of the cycles (`crngrow.f:67`, `crngrow.f:92`). The species groups g are those of the table above.

The inputs of equation {3.6.2.3.21} are the maximum crown width MCW of the trees, equation {3.6.2.3.17}, from subroutines MCW_SWO, MCW_NWO and MCW_SMC (`crngrow.f:440`, `514`, `573`, arrays `471-496`, `538-555`, `597-614`), and the stand summaries of subroutines SSUM and OLDGROWTH, which CRCALIB calls with the heights that were already dubbed (`start2.f:343-345`). The crown competition factor of the larger trees, CCFL, is equation {3.6.2.3.18}. It is read for the diameter of a tree by subroutine GET_CCFL_EDIT (`start2.f:1021-1035`): the diameter classes are 0.1 inch up to 50 inches; a tree above 50 inches uses a table by inch with the class INT(DBH - 49), and a tree above 100 inches has a CCFL of 0 (`organon/diamcal.f:486-560`). The stand basal area SBA is equation {3.6.2.3.19} and the old-growth indicator OG is equation {3.6.2.3.20} (`organon/diamcal.f:563-611`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
MCW &= \begin{cases} \dfrac{HT}{4.5} \, B_0 & HT < 4.501 \\[1ex] B_0 + B_1 D' + B_2 D'^{2} & HT \ge 4.501 \end{cases} \\
D' &= \min\left(DBH, \, PKDBH\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.17}
$$

Where:

- MCW: Maximum crown width of the tree (feet)
- HT: Total height of the tree (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height of the tree (inches)
- B_0, B_1, B_2: Coefficients MCWPAR(g, 1), MCWPAR(g, 2) and MCWPAR(g, 3) of the species group of the tree
- PKDBH: Diameter above which the crown width no longer increases (inches), MCWPAR(g, 4)

$$
\begin{aligned}
CCFL_j &= \sum_{i:\,k_i > k_j} 0.001803 \, MCW_i^{2} \, TPA_i \\
k_i &= \mathrm{INT}\left(10 \, DBH_i + 0.5\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.18}
$$

Where:

- CCFL_j: Crown competition factor of the trees that are in a larger diameter class than tree j
- MCW_i: Maximum crown width of record i from equation {3.6.2.3.17} (feet)
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of record i (inches)
- TPA_i: Trees per acre represented by record i, TDATAR(i, 4) divided by NPTS (trees per acre)

$$
SBA = 0.005454154 \sum_i DBH_i^{2} \, TPA_i
\tag{3.6.2.3.19}
$$

Where:

- SBA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of record i (inches)
- TPA_i: Trees per acre represented by record i (trees per acre)

The indicator OG uses the 5 largest trees per acre of the major species groups (the groups up to IB). The records are accumulated in diameter classes of 1 inch, class INT(DBH) + 1 with a maximum of 100, from the largest class down, and the class that crosses 5 trees per acre is prorated so that the total is 5 trees per acre. OG is 0 when there is no such tree.

$$
\begin{aligned}
OG &= \frac{DBH5 \times HT5}{10000} \\
DBH5 &= \frac{\sum_i DBH_i \, TPA_i}{\sum_i TPA_i}, \qquad HT5 = \frac{\sum_i HT_i \, TPA_i}{\sum_i TPA_i}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.20}
$$

Where:

- OG: Old-growth indicator
- DBH5: Mean diameter of the 5 largest trees per acre (inches)
- HT5: Mean height of the 5 largest trees per acre (feet)
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of record i (inches)
- HT_i: Total height of record i (feet)
- TPA_i: Trees per acre represented by record i, with the last class prorated so that the sum of TPA_i is 5 (trees per acre)

The coefficients are HCBPAR(g, 1..7). The species group 3 (ponderosa pine in OC, western hemlock in OP) uses the site index SI_2, and every other group uses SI_1. Both site indices are reduced by 4.5 feet before the call (`start2.f:351-352`, `start2.f:426-427`).

$$
HCB = \frac{HT}{1 + \exp\left(B_0 + B_1 HT + B_2 CCFL + B_3 \ln SBA + B_4 \dfrac{DBH}{HT} + B_5 SI + B_6 OG^{2}\right)}
\tag{3.6.2.3.21}
$$

Where:

- HCB: Height to the crown base of the tree (feet)
- HT: Total height of the tree (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height of the tree (inches)
- CCFL: Crown competition factor of the larger trees from equation {3.6.2.3.18}
- SBA: Stand basal area from equation {3.6.2.3.19} (square feet per acre)
- SI: Site index minus 4.5 feet, SI_1 or SI_2 as stated above (feet)
- OG: Old-growth indicator from equation {3.6.2.3.20}
- B_0 to B_6: Coefficients HCBPAR(g, 1) to HCBPAR(g, 7) of the species group of the tree

CRCALIB uses the trees with a measured crown ratio. For each group it calculates the ratio estimator of equation {3.6.2.3.22}, only when the group has at least 2 such trees and at least 1 record; otherwise the multiplier is 1.0 (`start2.f:337-387`). It then applies subroutine CALTST, as for the height calibration, with sums that are not weighted by the diameter; equation {3.6.2.3.7} applies with the DBH_i weights taken as 1. The multiplier is stored in ACALIB(2, g).

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta &= \frac{\sum_i Y_i X_i}{\sum_i X_i^{2}} \\
X_i &= PCR_i = 1 - \frac{HCB_i}{HT_i}, \qquad Y_i = CR_i
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.22}
$$

Where:

- β: Crown ratio calibration multiplier of the species group, ACALIB(2, g)
- HCB_i: Height to the crown base of tree i from equation {3.6.2.3.21} (feet)
- HT_i: Total height of tree i (feet)
- CR_i: Measured crown ratio of tree i (fraction)

PRDCR dubs each record with a crown ratio of 0 or less and a diameter above 0. The predicted crown ratio is multiplied by the calibration multiplier and limited to 0.05 to 1.0, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.23} (`start2.f:447-449`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
CR &= \min\left[1.0, \, \max\left(0.05, \, \beta \, PCR\right)\right] \\
PCR &= 1 - \frac{HCB}{HT}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.3.23}
$$

Where:

- CR: Dubbed crown ratio of the tree (fraction)
- β: Crown ratio calibration multiplier of the species group from equation {3.6.2.3.22}
- HCB: Height to the crown base of the tree from equation {3.6.2.3.21} (feet)
- HT: Total height of the tree (feet)

CRATET then loads the crown ratio of the valid ORGANON trees back as ICR = NINT(100 CR) (`oc/cratet.f:359`, `op/cratet.f:348`). This value is not limited to 95 and has no minimum of 10. The records that are not valid ORGANON trees keep their missing crown ratio, and CROWN dubs them with the Weibull model, as described under "Crown ratio models" (CROWN returns without a change for a tree that has a crown ratio when it is first called; `oc/crown.f:228`).

The multiplier that ORGANON uses in each cycle is attenuated, as shown in equation {3.6.2.3.24}, when the crown calibration flag INDS(2) is 1; otherwise it is 1.0 (`organon/execute2.f:94-96`, `execute2.f:241-246`). The default of INDS(2) is 1 (`oc/grinit.f:357`, `op/grinit.f:355`), and field 5 of the ORGINFO keyword sets it (`vorganon/orin.f:206-209`).

$$
CALIB_2 = \frac{1 + \beta}{2} + 0.5^{\,0.5 \, CYCLG} \, \frac{\beta - 1}{2}
\tag{3.6.2.3.24}
$$

Where:

- CALIB_2: Crown calibration multiplier that ORGANON uses in the cycle
- β: Crown ratio calibration multiplier of the species group, ACALIB(2, g)
- CYCLG: Number of cycles grown in ORGANON, which is the FVS cycle number minus 1

The attenuated multiplier CALIB(2, g) is used only in the crown recession of model type 2: CROWGRO multiplies the predicted crown ratio by CALIB(2, g) for model type 2, and does not use it for model types 1, 3 and 4 (`organon/crngrow.f:69-81`, `crngrow.f:95-110`). In OC (model type 1) and in OP with model type 3 the crown calibration therefore affects only the dubbed crown ratios.

**Missing crown ratios.** Subroutine INTREE converts the crown ratio of each input record. A value from 1 to 9 is a crown class code and is converted to a percent, ICR = 10 x code - 5 (the classes become 5, 15, and so on to 85). A value from 10 to 99 is kept as a percent, and a value above 99 is set to 99. A value of 0 or a negative value is not changed, and the crown ratio is considered missing. Dead tree records are converted in the same way before they are moved to the bottom of the tree arrays.

CRATET sets a logical variable, MISSCR, to true when any live or dead tree record has a crown ratio that is 0 or negative, and calls subroutine CROWN only then. A tree record that has a crown ratio is not changed.

**Subroutine CROWN.** Subroutine CROWN is used for two purposes. When LSTART is true, as it is when CRATET calls it, CROWN dubs the missing crown ratios. A tree record with ICR greater than 0 is skipped. At the end of each projection cycle, subroutine GRADD calls CROWN to change the crown ratios, as described in [Computing crown ratio change and crown width](#sec-computing-crown-ratio-change-and-crown-width).

**Crown ratio models.** The crown ratio of a live tree is dubbed with the crown ratio model of the variant. A dead tree is dubbed with the same model in the variants that have no subroutine DUBSCR for the tree, and with subroutine DUBSCR in the other variants. The models are listed by variant in the next table. In the variants with subroutine DUBSCR other than SN, DUBSCR dubs the live trees that are smaller than a threshold diameter as well, and the model of the variant dubs the larger live trees.

```{r crown-models, echo=FALSE}
crown_models <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Live_Tree_Model, ~DUBSCR_Used_For,
  "AK", "Logistic equation of height, diameter and point density", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "BC", "Percentile regression (V2) or logistic equation of the BEC zone (V3)", "Live trees below 3.0 inches (V2) or 2 cm (V3) and dead trees",
  "BM", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "CA", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "CI", "Weibull, and crown length equations for some species", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "CR", "Crown length equations by species (subroutine GEMCR)", "Not called",
  "CS", "TWIGS", "Not called",
  "EC", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "EM", "Percentile regression, crown length equations, or Weibull, by species", "Live trees below the threshold of the model, and dead trees of the species that use the regression or the Weibull model",
  "HI", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "IE", "Percentile regression, crown length equations, or Weibull, by species", "Live trees below the threshold of the model, and dead trees of the species that use the regression or the Weibull model",
  "KT", "Percentile regression", "Live trees below 3.0 inches and dead trees",
  "LS", "TWIGS", "Not called",
  "NC", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "NE", "TWIGS", "Not called",
  "OC", "Weibull; ORGANON for the trees that are valid for ORGANON", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "ON", "TWIGS", "Not called",
  "OP", "Weibull; ORGANON for the trees that are valid for ORGANON", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "PN", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "SN", "Weibull, with the mean crown ratio from relative stand density index", "Dead trees only",
  "SO", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "TT", "Weibull, and crown length equations for some species", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "UT", "Weibull, and crown length equations for some species", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "WC", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees",
  "WS", "Weibull", "Live trees below 1.0 inch and dead trees"
)

kable(crown_models,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Live Tree Model", "DUBSCR Used For"),
      caption = "Crown ratio models used to dub missing crown ratios",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The CR variant compiles subroutine DUBSCR but does not call it. The dead trees of the CR variant are dubbed with the crown length equations. The BC, EM and IE entries are described under "Variant differences" below.

**TWIGS model (CS, LS, NE and ON).** The crown ratio is predicted from the stand basal area and the tree diameter with equation {3.6.2.5.1}, and the result is rounded to an integer percent.

$$
CRNEW = 10\left[\frac{BCR_1}{1 + BCR_2 \cdot BA} + BCR_3\left(1 - \exp\left(BCR_4 \cdot DBH\right)\right)\right]
\tag{3.6.2.5.1}
$$

Where:

- CRNEW: Crown ratio (percent)
- BCR1, BCR2, BCR3, BCR4: Coefficients by species; BCR4 is negative in LS, NE and ON, and is positive in CS, where the exponent is written as $-BCR_4 \cdot DBH$
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)

**Weibull model.** In the variants that use the Weibull model, the crown ratio is a percentile of a Weibull distribution of the crown ratios of the species, and the percentile is the rank of the tree by diameter. The parameters of the distribution are calculated for each species from the relative stand density index. The steps are as follows.

1. The mean crown ratio of the species, ACR, is calculated with equation {3.6.2.5.2} from RELSDI, where RELSDI is SDIAC divided by SDIDEF (1.0 when SDIDEF is not greater than 0), and is limited to 1.5.
2. The Weibull parameters A, B and C are calculated from ACR with equation {3.6.2.5.3}. B is set to a minimum value that depends on the variant and the species (see the table after the equations), and C is set to 2.0 when it is less than 2.0.
3. The percentile of the tree, X, is the rank of the tree by diameter divided by the number of tree records, multiplied by a density scalar, SCALE. A tree record with a diameter of 0 is given a random rank. The percentile is limited to 0.05 to 0.95.
4. The crown ratio is calculated from the Weibull distribution with equation {3.6.2.5.4}.

$$
ACR = C_0 + C_1 \cdot 100 \cdot RELSDI
\tag{3.6.2.5.2}
$$

Where:

- ACR: Mean crown ratio of the species
- C0, C1: Coefficients by species or species group
- RELSDI: Relative stand density index of the species

$$
A = WEIBA, \qquad B = WEIBB_0 + WEIBB_1 \cdot ACR, \qquad C = WEIBC_0 + WEIBC_1 \cdot ACR
\tag{3.6.2.5.3}
$$

Where:

- A, B, C: Location, scale and shape parameters of the Weibull distribution
- WEIBA, WEIBB0, WEIBB1, WEIBC0, WEIBC1: Coefficients by species or species group
- ACR: Mean crown ratio of the species from equation {3.6.2.5.2}

$$
CR = A + B\left[-\ln\left(1 - X\right)\right]^{1/C}, \qquad X = \frac{ISORT}{ITRN}\cdot SCALE
\tag{3.6.2.5.4}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio in tenths of a percent, which is multiplied by 10 to obtain the percent (in SN the result is already in percent)
- A, B, C: Weibull parameters from equation {3.6.2.5.3}
- ISORT: Rank of the tree record by diameter (1 is the smallest)
- ITRN: Number of tree records
- SCALE: Density scalar, from 0.30 to 1.0

The percentile X of the tree is limited to 0.05 to 0.95.

The mean crown ratio, the scalar, and the minimum of B differ among the variants, as listed in the next table. In SN, RELSDI is ten times SDIAC divided by SDIDEF (6.0 when SDIDEF is not greater than 0), limited to 1.0 to 12.0, ACR is calculated with a function selected by species (for example Hoerl's equation, $ACR = \exp(a + b \ln RELSDI + c \cdot RELSDI)$), and equation {3.6.2.5.4} gives the crown ratio directly in percent. In WS, SCALE is $1.5 - RELSDI$ for the species LP, WB, PM, KP, FP, CP, LM, GP, WE, WJ, UJ and CJ; $1 - 0.00167\,(RELDEN - 100)$ for the species MC; and $1 - 0.00333\,(RELDEN - 50)$ for the other species. In all variants the scalar is limited to 0.30 to 1.0.

```{r crown-weibull-variants, echo=FALSE}
crown_weibull <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~SCALE, ~Minimum_B,
  "BM", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "1.0 for WJ, LM and AS; 3.0 for the other species",
  "CA", "1.5 - RELSDI", "3.0",
  "CI", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "1.0 for WB, PY, AS, WJ, MC, LM, CW and OH; 3.0 for the other species",
  "EC", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "EM", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "1.0",
  "HI", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "IE", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "1.0",
  "NC", "1.5 - RELSDI", "3.0",
  "OC", "1.5 - RELSDI", "3.0",
  "OP", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "PN", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "SN", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "SO", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "TT", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0 for PP; 1.0 for the other species",
  "UT", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "1.0",
  "WC", "1 - 0.00167 (RELDEN - 100)", "3.0",
  "WS", "By species (see the text)", "3.0"
)

kable(crown_weibull,
      col.names = c("Variant", "SCALE", "Minimum B"),
      caption = "Density scalar and minimum of the Weibull parameter B",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Crown length equations.** In the CR variant, and for some species in CI, EM, IE, TT and UT, the crown length of the tree is predicted from the height of the tree and the crown ratio is the crown length divided by the height, as shown in equation {3.6.2.5.5}. The crown length is limited to a minimum of 1.0 foot and a maximum of HF.

$$
CR = \frac{CL}{HF}, \qquad CL = a + b \cdot HF + c \cdot BA
\tag{3.6.2.5.5}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)
- HF: Total tree height at the end of the cycle (feet)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- a, b, c: Coefficients; the two forms used outside CR are $CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552\,HF - 0.01675\,BA$ and $CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703\,HF$

In CR, the equations differ by species, include the diameter and the basal area above the tree, and are in subroutine GEMCR. In the other variants, the species that use a crown length equation, and the equation of each, are listed in the next table.

```{r crown-cl-species, echo=FALSE}
crown_cl_species <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Species, ~Equation,
  "CI", "CW and OH", "CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552 HF - 0.01675 BA",
  "CI", "WJ", "CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703 HF",
  "EM", "GA, CW, BA, PW, NC and OH", "CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552 HF - 0.01675 BA",
  "EM", "RM", "CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703 HF",
  "IE", "CO and OH", "CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552 HF - 0.01675 BA",
  "IE", "PM and RM", "CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703 HF",
  "TT", "NC and OH", "CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552 HF - 0.01675 BA",
  "TT", "PM, UJ and RM", "CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703 HF",
  "UT", "NC, FC and BE", "CL = 5.17281 + 0.32552 HF - 0.01675 BA",
  "UT", "PI, WJ, GO, PM, RM, UJ, GB and OH", "CL = -0.59373 + 0.67703 HF"
)

kable(crown_cl_species,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Species", "Crown Length Equation"),
      caption = "Species that use a crown length equation to dub the crown ratio",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Subroutine DUBSCR.** Subroutine DUBSCR is a species-specific regression that dubs the crown ratio of small live trees and of dead trees. The coefficients, the form of each species, and the standard errors CRSD are in the DUBSCR source file of the variant (the OC variant uses the file of CA, and the OP and PN variants use the file of WC). DUBSCR has two forms, and each returns a crown ratio proportion that is limited to 0.05 to 0.95.

- Crown class form: a crown class code is calculated with a linear function of the height and the stand basal area, as shown in equation {3.6.2.5.6}, and it is converted to a proportion, $CR = ((code - 1) \cdot 10 + 1)/100$. In WC, for example, all species except RW use this form.
- Logistic form: $CR = 1/(1 + \exp(Z + FCR))$, where Z is a linear function of the diameter, the height and the stand basal area. In some variants the function includes more terms (the point crown competition factor, the average height of the largest trees, and the mean annual increment). KT uses $Z = BCR_0 + BCR_1\,DBH + BCR_2\,HT + BCR_3\,BA$. For the species RW in WC, the form is $Z = -1.021064 + 0.309296\ln(12\,HT/DBH) + 0.869720\,PRD - 0.116274\,(DBH/QMDPLT)$ and the standard deviation of FCR is 0.15.

$$
code = BCR_0 + BCR_1 \cdot HT + BCR_2 \cdot BA + FCR
\tag{3.6.2.5.6}
$$

Where:

- code: Crown class code
- BCR0, BCR1, BCR2: Coefficients by species group
- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- FCR: Random error (see below)

The random error, FCR, is drawn from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of CRSD, and is drawn again until its absolute value does not exceed CRSD. In AK, BM, CA, EC, HI, NC, OC, OP, PN, SO, WC and WS the error is always added. In CI, EM, IE, KT, TT, UT and BC (V2) it is added only when DGSD is 1.0 or more. In SN the random error is not implemented. For the species that use the crown class form in CI, TT and UT, and for the species MC in WS, the error is not added to the crown class code.

**Bounds and adjustments.** After a crown ratio has been dubbed for a live tree, the following are applied. The crown ratio of a tree with a broken or dead top (ITRUNC is not zero) is reduced to the crown that remains, as shown in equation {3.6.2.5.7}. A dubbed crown ratio above 95 is set to 95, a value below 10 is set to 10 when CRNMLT is 1.0, and a value below 1 is set to 1. A dead tree that is dubbed is bounded to 10 to 95.

$$
CL = \frac{ICRI}{100}\,HN - HD, \qquad ICRI = \frac{100\,CL}{HN}
\tag{3.6.2.5.7}
$$

Where:

- ICRI: Crown ratio (percent) before and after the adjustment for the broken top
- CL: Crown length that remains (feet)
- HN: Height of the tree without the broken or dead top, NORMHT divided by 100 (feet)
- HD: Length of the broken or dead part, HN minus ITRUNC divided by 100 (feet)

**Keyword CRNMULT.** Keyword CRNMULT multiplies the crown ratios dubbed by CROWN. Field 1 is the date or cycle, field 2 the species, field 3 the multiplier (CRNMLT), field 4 the lower diameter limit (DLOW), field 5 the upper diameter limit (DHI, 99 inches when not given), and field 6 a flag. When DBH is within the limits, the dubbed crown ratio is multiplied by CRNMLT. When field 6 is greater than 0 (ICFLG is 1), the multiplier applies only to the dubbed values and CRNMLT is set to 1.0 after the dubbing.

**Variant differences.** The following variants differ from the description above.

- AK predicts the crown ratio of live trees of 1.0 inch or more with equation {3.6.2.5.8}, without a random error. The dead trees and the live trees below 1.0 inch are dubbed with DUBSCR, which uses the same relationship.
- KT, the species WP, WL, DF, GF, WH, RC, LP, ES, AF, PP, MH, WB, LL and OS of IE, and the species LL of EM use a percentile regression with the habitat type for trees of 3.0 inches or more (equation {3.6.2.5.9}). Trees below 3.0 inches are dubbed with DUBSCR. When DGSD is 1.0 or more, a random error with a standard deviation (CRSD) of 6.35 percent is added at the dubbing in IE and EM.
- IE and EM use the crown length equations for some species (see the table of crown length equations). The remaining species of IE and EM use the Weibull model, with DUBSCR for the trees below 1.0 inch.
- BC uses one of two models that are selected by the BEC zone. The V3 model is used in the zones that contain ICH, IDF, SBS or SBPS, and the V2 model, which is the percentile regression, is used in the other zones. A tree below 3.0 inches (V2) or 2 cm (V3) is dubbed with DUBSCR.
- SN dubs only the dead trees with DUBSCR: $CR = 0.70 - 0.40\,DBH/24$ for DBH of 24 inches or less, and 0.30 for larger trees, bounded to 0.05 to 0.95.
- OC and OP dub the crown ratio of the trees that are valid for ORGANON in subroutine PREPARE, before CROWN is called (see [Dubbing of missing input data and calibration of ORGANON equations](#sec-dubbing-of-missing-input-data-and-calibration-of-organon-equations)). CROWN dubs the other trees with the Weibull model.

$$
X = B_1 + B_2 \ln\left(\frac{12\,HT}{DBH}\right) + B_3\,PRD + B_4\,\frac{DBH}{QMDPLT}, \qquad CR = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(X)}
\tag{3.6.2.5.8}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio (proportion, limited to 0.05 to 0.95)
- B1, B2, B3, B4: Coefficients by species
- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- PRD: Relative density of the inventory point
- QMDPLT: Quadratic mean diameter of the inventory point (inches)

$$
CR = \exp\left(XCRCON + B_7\,DBH + B_8\,DBH^2 + B_9\ln DBH + B_{10}\,HT + B_{11}\,HT^2 + B_{12}\ln HT + B_{13}\,P + B_{14}\ln P\right)
\tag{3.6.2.5.9}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)
- XCRCON: Constant that depends on the species, the habitat type, the stand basal area and the stand crown competition factor
- B7 to B14: Coefficients by species
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- HT: Total tree height (feet)
- P: Percentile of the tree in the basal area distribution, PCT, with a minimum of 0.01

#### Calibrate growth equations

In FVS, trees are considered "large" trees for modeling purposes if they are above some threshold diameter that is both variant- and species-specific; otherwise they are considered "small" trees. The FVS large-tree model is diameter growth driven, and the small-tree model is height growth driven. When periodic increment data are provided with the tree records, FVS calibrates the large-tree diameter growth model and the small-tree height growth model to those data, separately for each species. The calibration is done by subroutine DGDRIV for the large-tree diameter growth model, and by subroutine REGENT for the small-tree height growth model, both called from subroutine CRATET. The calibration logic is introduced in Dixon (2002), sections 6.4 and 7.2. The variables named in this section are defined in the next table.

```{r calib-variables, echo=FALSE}
calib_variables <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variable, ~Definition,
  "DG", "Periodic diameter increment of a tree, inside bark, in inches",
  "DBH0", "Diameter at breast height at the start of the growth measurement period, in inches (WK3)",
  "BARK", "Bark ratio of the tree, the inside bark diameter divided by the outside bark diameter",
  "dds", "Change in squared inside bark diameter over the period",
  "DDS", "Change in squared inside bark diameter predicted by subroutine DGF",
  "YR", "Length of the period on which the increments of the model are based, in years",
  "FINT", "Length of the growth measurement period of the diameter growth data, in years",
  "SCALE", "Conversion of the observed change in squared diameter, measured over FINT years, to the YR-year basis of the model, YR divided by FINT",
  "PROB", "Trees per acre represented by a tree record",
  "r", "Residual of a tree on the logarithmic scale, the observed minus the predicted ln(dds)",
  "FN", "Number of trees in the calibration sample of a species",
  "FNMIN", "Minimum number of trees in the calibration sample, 5 by default",
  "BNY", "Mean of the residuals r of the sample, weighted by PROB",
  "BNX", "Mean of the predicted dds of the sample trees, weighted by PROB",
  "BPOPX", "Mean of the predicted dds of the trees of the species within the diameter range of the sample, weighted by PROB",
  "SLOP", "Slope of the regression of the residual on the predicted dds of the sample trees",
  "SDPRED", "Standard deviation of the predicted dds of the sample trees",
  "DIST", "Distance between the mean predicted dds of the population and of the sample, in units of SDPRED",
  "COR", "Calibration term of the diameter growth model, added to ln(dds)",
  "CORI", "Calibration term before the empirical Bayes weight is applied",
  "WC", "Weight given to the growth sample in the calibration, from 0 to 1",
  "PVAR", "Prior variance of the calibration term (PSIGSQ), set by species in subroutine DGF",
  "SVAR", "Variance of the mean residual of the sample",
  "SIGMAR", "Standard error of the diameter growth model on the logarithmic scale, by species",
  "XNOB", "Number of observations in the data used to fit the model, by species (ATTEN)",
  "HTG", "Periodic height increment of a tree, in feet",
  "EDH", "Height increment predicted by the small-tree height growth model, in feet",
  "NCALHT", "Minimum number of trees in the calibration sample of the small-tree height growth model, 5 by default",
  "HCOR", "Calibration term of the small-tree height growth model, the natural logarithm of the scale factor",
  "RHCON", "User multiplier of the small-tree height growth model, 1.0 unless changed with keyword READCORR",
  "SCALE3", "Conversion of the observed height increment, measured over FINTH years, to the REGYR-year basis of the small-tree model, REGYR divided by FINTH",
  "SFINT", "Years from the start of the projection to the end of the projection cycle",
  "LDGCAL", "Logical variable by species; false when calibration is suppressed with keyword NOCALIB",
  "LHTCAL", "Logical variable by species; false when calibration is suppressed with keyword NOCALIB"
)

kable(calib_variables,
      col.names = c("Variable", "Definition"),
      caption = "Variables used in the calibration of the growth equations",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Diameter growth model.** In most variants, FVS does not predict diameter increment directly. It predicts the change in squared inside bark diameter, dds, from which the diameter increment is derived with equation {3.6.2.6.1} (Dixon 2002, section 7.2.1; Stage 1973; Cole and Stage 1972). The model for ln(dds) is a regression in the site, stand and tree variables of the variant, which subroutine DGF evaluates.

$$
dds = (dib + DG)^2 - dib^2, \qquad DG = \sqrt{dib^2 + dds} - dib
\tag{3.6.2.6.1}
$$

Where:

- dds: Change in squared inside bark diameter over the period (square inches)
- DG: Periodic diameter increment, inside bark (inches)
- dib: Inside bark diameter at the beginning of the period (inches), the bark ratio BARK times DBH

**Calibration sample of the diameter growth model.** A tree record is used in the calibration of a species when it has a diameter increment greater than 0, and when its diameter at the start of the growth period, DBH0, is at least the breakpoint diameter of the species. The records that do not meet the two conditions are not used. When the increment was entered as a second diameter measurement, it is converted to an inside bark increment before the calibration (the increment is multiplied by BARK). The breakpoint diameter is the diameter above which a tree is a large tree, and is listed in the next table. The calibration is done for the species when the sample has FN of FNMIN or more trees, and calibration is not suppressed for the species (LDGCAL is true). By default, FNMIN is 5. Keyword CALBSTAT changes it, with a minimum of 3.

```{r calib-dg-breakpoint, echo=FALSE}
calib_dg_breakpoint <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Species, ~Minimum_DBH,
  "AK", "All", "3.0",
  "BC", "All", "3.0",
  "BM", "All", "3.0",
  "CA", "All", "3.0",
  "CI", "CW and OH", "1.0",
  "CI", "The other species", "3.0",
  "CR", "AF, CB, DF, WF, LP, PP, SW, BS, ES, WS, AS, NC, PW, PB, CI, OS and OH", "1.0",
  "CR", "LM", "2.0",
  "CR", "GF, MH, RC, WL and WB", "3.0",
  "CR", "BC, PI, UJ, GO, AW, EM, BK, SO, AJ, RM, OJ, ER, PM, PD and AZ", "99.0",
  "CS", "All", "5.0",
  "EC", "All", "3.0",
  "EM", "GA, CW, BA, PW, NC and OH", "1.0",
  "EM", "The other species", "3.0",
  "HI", "All", "3.0",
  "IE", "CO and OH", "1.0",
  "IE", "The other species", "3.0",
  "KT", "All", "3.0",
  "LS", "All", "5.0",
  "NC", "All", "3.0",
  "NE", "All", "3.0",
  "OC", "All", "3.0",
  "ON", "All", "3.0",
  "OP", "All", "3.0",
  "PN", "All", "3.0",
  "SN", "All", "3.0",
  "SO", "All", "3.0",
  "TT", "All", "3.0",
  "UT", "NC, FC and BE", "1.0",
  "UT", "WB, LM, DF, WF, BS, AS, LP, ES, AF, PP and OS", "3.0",
  "UT", "PI, WJ, GO, PM, RM, UJ, GB, MC, BI and OH", "99.0",
  "WC", "All", "3.0",
  "WS", "All", "3.0"
)

kable(calib_dg_breakpoint,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Species", "Minimum DBH (inches)"),
      caption = "Minimum diameter of the trees used to calibrate the diameter growth model",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

A minimum diameter of 99.0 inches means that no tree of the species is a large tree in the calibration, and the diameter growth model of the species is not calibrated. The value in CR and UT is set by species in the array BREAK. In OC and OP, the diameter growth of the trees that are valid for ORGANON is calculated by ORGANON, and this section does not describe the calibration of those trees.

**Steps of the diameter growth calibration.**

1. Subroutine DGF is called to predict ln(DDS) for every tree record, with the diameter at the start of the growth period, DBH0.
2. The observed increment is converted to a change in squared inside bark diameter, which is scaled from the FINT-year measurement period to the YR-year basis of the model, and the residual of the tree on the logarithmic scale is calculated with equation {3.6.2.6.2}. A tree with an observed change in squared diameter of 0 is not used.
3. The sums of the sample trees, weighted by PROB, give BNY, BNX, SLOP and SDPRED. BPOPX is the mean predicted DDS of all the trees of the species that are within the diameter range of the sample.
4. The calibration term, CORI, is calculated with equation {3.6.2.6.3}. It is a weighted average of a ratio estimator and a regression estimator.
5. The weight WC is calculated and CORI is multiplied by it, as shown in equation {3.6.2.6.4}.
6. The scale factor is tested, as described below.

$$
r = \ln\left[DG\left(2\,BARK\cdot DBH0 + DG\right) SCALE\right] - \ln\left(DDS\right)
\tag{3.6.2.6.2}
$$

Where:

- r: Residual of the tree on the logarithmic scale
- DG: Observed periodic diameter increment, inside bark (inches)
- BARK: Bark ratio of the tree
- DBH0: Diameter at breast height at the start of the growth measurement period (inches)
- SCALE: YR divided by FINT, which scales the observed change from the measurement period to the YR-year basis of the model
- DDS: Change in squared inside bark diameter predicted by subroutine DGF (square inches)

$$
CORI = \begin{cases}
BNY + (BPOPX - BNX)\,SLOP & DIST \le 1 \\[4pt]
BNY\,\dfrac{DIST}{2} + \left[BNY + (BPOPX - BNX)\,SLOP\right]\left(1 - \dfrac{DIST}{2}\right) & 1 < DIST \le 3 \\[4pt]
BNY & DIST > 3
\end{cases},
\qquad DIST = \frac{|BPOPX - BNX|}{SDPRED}
\tag{3.6.2.6.3}
$$

Where:

- CORI: Calibration term before the weight is applied
- BNY: Weighted mean of the residuals r (the ratio estimator)
- BNX: Weighted mean of the predicted DDS of the sample trees
- BPOPX: Weighted mean of the predicted DDS of the trees of the species within the diameter range of the sample
- SLOP: Slope of the regression of r on the predicted DDS of the sample trees
- SDPRED: Standard deviation of the predicted DDS of the sample trees

The regression estimator is used when the sample is similar to the population of the species in terms of the predicted growth (DIST of 1 or less), and the ratio estimator is used when it is not (DIST above 3).

$$
WC = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-0.5\,TEMP\right)\sqrt{SVAR/PVAR}}, \quad TEMP = \min\left(\frac{CORI^2}{PVAR},\, 72\right), \quad COR = WC \cdot CORI
\tag{3.6.2.6.4}
$$

Where:

- WC: Weight given to the growth sample, from 0 to 1
- CORI: Calibration term from equation {3.6.2.6.3}
- PVAR: Prior variance of the calibration term, set by species in subroutine DGF
- SVAR: Variance of the mean of the residuals r of the sample, which is the sample variance of r divided by FN
- COR: Calibration term of the diameter growth model

The weight is part of an empirical Bayes estimation (Dixon 2002, section 4.3.1.1.3). A weight near 0 means that the model is not adjusted, and a weight near 1 means that the model is adjusted to the sample. The calibration term is added to ln(DDS) in subroutine DGF, so the scale factor of the model is the exponential of COR, as shown in equation {3.6.2.6.5}. The scale factor multiplies the change in squared diameter, and it is in effect a multiplier of the basal area increment.

$$
SF = \exp\left(COR\right), \qquad 0.0821 \le SF \le 12.1825
\tag{3.6.2.6.5}
$$

Where:

- SF: Scale factor of the diameter growth model (reported as "initial scale factors for the DBH increment model")
- COR: Calibration term from equation {3.6.2.6.4}

When SF is outside the range of equation {3.6.2.6.5}, an error message is written to the main output file with the species and the calculated value, SF is set to 1.0 and COR is set to 0.0. This range is $\pm 2.5$ on the logarithmic scale, and a value outside of it is usually the result of a problem with the growth measurements (Dixon 2002, section 7.2). When the sample has fewer than FNMIN trees, when keyword NOCALIB is used, or when the regression of the sample cannot be calculated (the sum of squares of the predicted DDS is negative, in which case a message "POOR SELECTION OF GROWTH SAMPLE TREES DETECTED" is written), the scale factor is 1.0 for the species.

**Variance of the diameter growth model.** The standard error of the model on the logarithmic scale of the species, SIGMA, is also calibrated, as shown in equation {3.6.2.6.6}. The result is used for the random component of the diameter growth described below.

$$
SIGMA = \sqrt{\frac{SSQ + XNOB \cdot SIGMAR^2}{FN + XNOB}}
\tag{3.6.2.6.6}
$$

Where:

- SIGMA: Calibrated standard error of the model on the logarithmic scale
- SSQ: Sum of the squared deviations of the residuals r from their mean
- XNOB: Number of observations in the data used to fit the model of the species
- SIGMAR: Standard error of the model of the species
- FN: Number of trees in the calibration sample

The ratio of the standard deviation of the sample residuals to SIGMAR is reported as the "ratio of standard errors" in the calibration statistics table. A ratio that is consistently above 1.0 indicates that the growth sample varies more than the data used to fit the model (Dixon 2002, section 4.3.1.1.3).

**Small-tree height growth model.** The small-tree model is calibrated with a scale factor that is a ratio of the observed and the predicted height increments. A tree record is used when it has a height increment of at least 0.001 foot, a height at the start of the growth period of at least 0.01 foot, and a diameter below 5.0 inches (3.0 inches in AK). The calibration is done for a species when the sample has NCALHT or more trees (5 by default, changed with keyword CALBSTAT, with a minimum of 3), and LHTCAL is true. The increment predicted for each sample tree is calculated with the small-tree height growth model of the variant, EDH, including the user multiplier RHCON. The scale factor is the ratio of the means of the sample, weighted by PROB, as shown in equation {3.6.2.6.7}, and the calibration term HCOR is its natural logarithm. In subroutine REGENT, the height increment of a small tree is multiplied by RHCON and by the exponential of HCOR. The same range as in equation {3.6.2.6.5} is tested, with the message "SMALL TREE HTG", and the scale factor is set to 1.0 and HCOR to 0.0 when the value is outside the range.

$$
SF_h = \frac{\sum_i PROB_i \cdot HTG_i \cdot SCALE3}{\sum_i PROB_i \cdot EDH_i}, \qquad HCOR = \ln\left(SF_h\right)
\tag{3.6.2.6.7}
$$

Where:

- SF_h: Scale factor of the small-tree height growth model
- PROB: Trees per acre represented by the tree record
- HTG: Observed periodic height increment (feet)
- SCALE3: REGYR divided by FINTH, which scales the observed increment from the measurement period to the REGYR-year basis of the small-tree model
- EDH: Height increment predicted by the small-tree height growth model (feet)
- HCOR: Calibration term of the small-tree height growth model

The height scale factor is a direct multiplier of the predicted height increment. It does not have a weight. The calculation is the same in every variant. In the variants that use more than one small-tree model for different species, the equation for EDH differs by species.

**Attenuation of the scale factors.** The scale factors are attenuated over the projection, because the base model is assumed to be a more stable estimate of long-term growth than the scale factor (Dixon 2002, section 6.4.1). In the first cycle, the attenuation goal, WCI, is set to one half of the initial diameter growth calibration term. At the end of each cycle, the calibration terms for the next cycle are calculated with equation {3.6.2.6.8}. The attenuation applies to the diameter growth calibration term, COR, and to the height growth calibration term, HCOR, of a species when calibration is not suppressed for the species with keyword NOCALIB (LDGCAL is true).

$$
\begin{aligned} WCI &= \frac{COR_0}{2}, \qquad CORMLT = \exp\left(-0.02773\,SFINT\right) \\ COR &= WCI\left(1 + CORMLT\right), \qquad HCOR = WCI + CORMLT\left(HCOR_0 - WCI\right) \end{aligned}
\tag{3.6.2.6.8}
$$

Where:

- COR0: Initial calibration term of the diameter growth model
- HCOR0: Initial calibration term of the small-tree height growth model
- SFINT: Years from the start of the projection to the end of the cycle just projected
- COR, HCOR: Calibration terms used in the next cycle

The factor CORMLT is 0.5 at 25 years, so half of the attenuation takes place in 25 years. The diameter growth term attenuates toward half of its initial value on the logarithmic scale. Because COR is a logarithm, the goal of the scale factor is the square root of its initial value. For an initial scale factor of 2.0 the goal is 1.41, and the values are 1.68, 1.54, 1.48 and 1.45 at 25, 50, 75 and 100 years. The manual (Dixon 2002, section 6.4.1 and figure 6-1) states the goal as one half of the difference between the initial scale factor and one, which is 1.5 in its example of 2.0; the two differ when the factor is not close to 1.0. The height growth term attenuates toward the same goal, WCI, which is one half of the diameter growth term and not one half of its own initial value. When the diameter growth model of a species was not calibrated, COR0 is 0, the goal is 0, and the height growth term attenuates to 0 (a scale factor of 1.0).

**Calibration keywords.** The calibration is controlled with the keywords in the next table. The scale factors are reported in the Calibration Statistics section of the main output file, in the file written with keyword CALBSTAT (records "CAL: LD" for the diameter growth model and "CAL: SH" for the small-tree height growth model), and in the database table FVS_CalibStats.

```{r calib-keywords, echo=FALSE}
calib_keywords <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Keyword, ~Effect,
  "CALBSTAT", "Field 1 is the unit number of the file to which the calibration statistics are written. Field 2 is FNMIN, the minimum number of trees in the diameter growth calibration sample (minimum 3). Field 3 is NCALHT, the minimum number of trees in the height growth calibration sample (minimum 3)",
  "NOCALIB", "Suppresses the calculation of the scale factors for the species or species group in field 1 (all species when blank); LDGCAL and LHTCAL are set to false",
  "READCORD", "Adds the natural logarithm of the value read for each species to the constant of the large-tree diameter growth model, before the calibration (in NE and ON the value multiplies the diameter increment); the values are on the record that follows the keyword",
  "REUSCORD", "Uses the READCORD values of an earlier stand",
  "READCORH", "Adds the natural logarithm of the value read for each species to the constant of the large-tree height growth model, before the calibration",
  "REUSCORH", "Uses the READCORH values of an earlier stand",
  "READCORR", "Sets the multiplier of the small-tree height growth model, RHCON, to the value read for each species (1.0 when not read); for the species of the NI-type model in IE, EM and BC the natural logarithm of the value is added instead"
)

kable(calib_keywords,
      col.names = c("Keyword", "Effect"),
      caption = "Keywords that control the calibration of the growth equations",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Variant differences in the diameter growth calibration.** The calibration of the other variants has the same steps as described above, with the following differences.

- NC, ON and BC calculate the variance SIGMA of equation {3.6.2.6.6} even for a species for which calibration is suppressed with NOCALIB. The other variants use SIGMAR for such a species.
- BC limits the diameter growth calibration term to 1.38629 (a scale factor of 4) in addition to the range of equation {3.6.2.6.5}.
- SO limits TEMP in equation {3.6.2.6.4} to 176 instead of 72, does not test for a negative sum of squares, and for the Warm Springs forest (forest code 10) changes PVAR for some species.
- The prior variance PVAR is set by species in each variant (a data statement in the DGDRIV source file of the variant; 0.0898 or 0.089827273 in most of the variants that have a single value).
- DBSCALIB, which writes the calibration statistics to the database, is not called in ON.
- In OC and OP, the diameter growth of the trees that are valid for ORGANON is not calibrated by DGDRIV; this section does not describe how ORGANON calibrates those trees.

**Randomization.** The random effects of FVS are assigned to the error in the prediction of ln(dds) (Dixon 2002, section 6.4.2; Stage 1973). The error is normally distributed with a mean of 0. Its variance is the variance of the calibrated model, SIGMA, of equation {3.6.2.6.6}, which is a weighted average of the variance of the model and the variance of the growth sample. The error is carried from one cycle to the next with a serial correlation that depends on the cycle length (subroutine AUTCOR). The error is bounded to plus or minus DGSD standard deviations, and DGSD is 2.0 by default (1.7 in CA, CI, EC, HI, PN and WC; 1.5 in BM; 0 in OC and OP), which keyword DGSTDEV changes. When DGSD is less than 1.0, no random variation is added to the diameter growth. The random numbers come from a multiplicative congruential generator (the multiplier is 16807 and the modulus is 2147483647) with one seed, which is reset at the start of each run, and keyword RANNSEED replaces the seed. A normal deviate is made from three uniform numbers. The manual (Dixon 2002, section 6.4.2) describes a Marsaglia-Bray generator with three seeds, which does not match the code.

When the number of tree records is small, the record of each tree is tripled. Each tree record is divided into three records that have the same attributes, with 60, 25 and 15 percent of the trees per acre of the original record, and each of the three records is given a diameter growth that corresponds to one portion of the error distribution, so that the weighted average of the three equals the prediction. Keyword NUMTRIP sets the last projection cycle in which records can be tripled (the default is 2, and 0 in OC and OP), the tripling is done only when the number of tree records is no more than one third of the maximum number of records (MAXTRE), and keyword NOTRIPLE suppresses it. In subroutine DGDRIV, the three growth errors are the constants FU (1.271), FM (-0.14228) and FL (-1.549), multiplied by the standard error SSIGMA and the serial correlation term, and added to the serial correlation of the previous error.

**Multipliers.** The user can also change the model with multipliers. They are of four types (Dixon 2002, section 6.5.2), and each acts at a different point in relation to the calibration.

```{r calib-multipliers, echo=FALSE}
calib_multipliers <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Type, ~Keywords, ~Applied,
  "Computed by the model", "None (the scale factors of this section)", "Calibration; attenuated over the projection",
  "Before calibration", "READCORD, READCORH, READCORR", "Before the calibration; permanent, not attenuated",
  "Regeneration", "HTADJ, STOCKADJ, SPECMULT", "Inside the ESTAB sequence",
  "After calibration", "BAIMULT", "Large-tree diameter growth (DGDRIV, change in squared diameter)",
  "After calibration", "HTGMULT", "Large-tree height growth (HTGF)",
  "After calibration", "REGHMULT", "Small-tree height growth (REGENT)",
  "After calibration", "REGDMULT", "Small-tree diameter growth (REGENT)",
  "After calibration", "MORTMULT", "Mortality",
  "After calibration", "CRNMULT", "Crown ratio change and dubbing (CROWN)",
  "After calibration", "FIXDG, FIXHTG", "Diameter and height growth, at the end of the cycle after the other growth calculations",
  "After calibration", "FIXMORT, FIXCW", "Mortality and crown width"
)

kable(calib_multipliers,
      col.names = c("Type", "Keywords", "Applied To"),
      caption = "Types of multipliers in relation to the calibration",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The multipliers that are applied after the calibration are not attenuated, and their values can be changed from cycle to cycle. Subroutine MULTS returns the species multipliers of a cycle for BAIMULT (DGDRIV), HTGMULT (HTGF), REGHMULT and REGDMULT (REGENT), MORTMULT, and the managed-stand flag. The BAIMULT multiplier enters the prediction of ln(dds) as an additional term, ln(XDMULT). Because of the processing sequence (large-tree diameter growth, large-tree height growth, small-tree height growth, small-tree diameter growth, mortality, crown change), REGHMULT affects the height and the diameter growth of small trees, REGDMULT only the diameter growth of small trees, BAIMULT the diameter and the height growth of large trees, and HTGMULT only the height growth of large trees (Dixon 2002, section 6.5.2.4).

The remaining tasks of the calibration in subroutine CRATET are as follows. If top height, which is the average height of the 40 largest diameter trees, is needed in either of the growth relationships, subroutine CRATET calls subroutine AVHT40 to compute it before DGDRIV; AVHT40 is not called in the IE, CI, CR, EM, KT and BC variants. Subroutine FINDAG estimates total tree age for each tree record. This value is used in estimating height growth in some variants and not needed in others; for those variants that do not use tree age in the small-tree height growth logic, subroutine FINDAG is a "dummy" subroutine that returns control to CRATET without computing tree age. In the IE, CI, CR, EM, TT, UT and BC variants FINDAG is called before DGDRIV, in the other variants it is called after DGDRIV and before REGENT, and AK does not call it.

At this point subroutine CRATET is done with the backdated stand, so it calls subroutines PCTILE, DIST, COMP, and DENSE to compute values related to the initial stand inventory which are needed for output. It then counts and prints the number of tree records with dwarf mistletoe.

Stand Density Index (SDI) is used in many variants for estimating mortality and crown ratio change. For variants using SDI, the last task of subroutine CRATET is to call subroutine SDICHK to see if the SDI of the initial stand inventory is above the maximum SDI specified for the site. If it is, then the maximum SDI is reset and a message is printed to the main output file.

This concludes the model calibration portion of the projection initialization phase but there are still a few more things to do before moving on to the projection cycling phase. Subroutine CRATET returns program control to subroutine FVS for further processing.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is called to see if debug write statements need to be executed in a subroutine.

Subroutine MBACAL is called from subroutines CRATET and DENSE to identify the species representing the most basal area in the stand (i.e. the site species).

Subroutine CCFCAL is called from subroutine DENSE to compute crown competition factor. CCFCAL is also called from other places in FVS for this same purpose and to compute crown width for individual tree records.

Subroutine PCTILE is called from subroutine DENSE to compute tree record percentiles in the basal area distribution.

Subroutine PTBAL is called from subroutine DENSE to compute point basal area in larger trees for each tree record.

Subroutine RDPSRT is called from subroutine CRATET to sort tree records by diameter.

Subroutine SPESRT is called by subroutine CRATET to realign pointers in the species-ordered sort of the tree records.

## Final projection initialization tasks {#sec-final-projection-initialization-tasks}

The remaining projection initialization tasks involve computing stand and tree level variables that have not yet been set, initializing variables used in FVS extensions, and writing initial tree and stand conditions to the various output tables.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine ESFLTR in the regeneration establishment extension to collect inventory information for understory and overstory densities and to flag trees in the inventory as “best trees” for the purposes of regeneration establishment.

The control variable, ICYC, is now set back to a value of 0. It will be used to control the projection cycling phase explained in [Projection Cycling Phase](#sec-projection-cycling-phase).

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine CWIDTH which calls subroutine CWCALC to estimate crown widths for all tree records.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine VOLS to compute volume estimates for the initial inventory. Tree record percentiles in the various volume distributions are then estimated when subroutine FVS calls subroutines PCTILE and DIST for the various volume attributes.

**Volume at the start of the projection (cycle 0).** The logical variable LSTART is set true at the start of the run (`base/fvs.f:90`). Subroutine FVS calls CRATET before it calls VOLS (`fvs.f:197`, `fvs.f:211`), so the initial volumes use the heights and crown ratios that were dubbed in CRATET, and the diameters and heights of the inventory. VOLS adds no diameter increment while LSTART is true: the statement `IF(.NOT.LSTART) D=D+DG(I)/BARK` is skipped (`ie/vols.f:151`, `organon/vols.f:170`, `canada/bc/vols.f:143`, `canada/on/vols.f:132`). The per-tree volumes, biomass and carbon (CFV, BFV, MCFV, SCFV and the biomass and carbon arrays) are multiplied by PROB to give per-acre values for the percentile calculations (PCTILE and DIST), and then divided by PROB again to give per-tree values (`fvs.f:215-310`). Subroutine FVS then calls EXTREE, DISPLY and PRTRLS (argument 1), so the initial stand statistics and the initial tree list contain the volumes of the inventory trees (`fvs.f:321-328`). It calls FVSSTD with argument 1 to store the cycle 0 volumes (`fvs.f:337`), purges the dead trees of the inventory by setting IREC2 to MAXTP1 (`fvs.f:342`), and sets LSTART false (`fvs.f:355`). The per-tree volumes stored by this call are the volumes that the mortality volume in UPDATE and the removed volume in CUTS use in the first projection cycle. The paths of stop and restart that skip this block were not traced.

Subroutine FVS then calls subroutine EXTREE to assign example trees to the arrays which will be used in the Attributes of Selected Sample Trees table in the main output file.

If the cover extension is being used, subroutine FVS makes calls to cover extension subroutines to compute shrub densities, browse statistics, and canopy cover estimates for the initial stand inventory.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine STATS to compute and print stand statistics that describe the distribution of stand attributes among sample plots for the input data. Calculation and printing of this information is controlled by the user with the STATS keyword record. The logical variable LSTATS controls these actions in the code and has a default value of “.FALSE.” and a value of “.TRUE.” if the STATS keyword record is used.

Subroutine FVS next calls subroutine DBSREFERENCE, which writes the inventory reference table (FVS_InvReference: species, maximum SDI, site index, and volume specifications) to the output database when database output is active, and subroutine GHEADS to write the heading for the stand composition table.

Subroutine FVS then needs to write inventory information to various output files. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine DISPLY to write the initial stand statistics to the main output file. Subroutine FVS calls MISPRT to write the dwarf mistletoe infection and mortality information if mistletoe was specified as a damage code in the input data. MISPRT will exist as a subroutine if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the variant or as an entry point in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the variant. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine PRTRLS to write the cycle 0 tree list output if it was called for with the TREELIST keyword record, subroutine FVSSTD to write the cycle 0 information needed by the FVSStand post-processing program if it was called for with the FVSSTAND keyword record, and subroutine NATCRZ to write the cycle 0 information needed by the National Cruise Program if called for with the CRUZFILE keyword record.

Subroutine FVS also calls subroutine DBS_FIAVBC_TRLS to write the FIA-VBC tree list table to the output database when it has been requested, and subroutine SVSTART to create the initial stand visualization.

At this point FVS is done with the dead trees that were present in the initial inventory. Dead trees are not physically purged (i.e. resetting all the storage locations in the tree data arrays that hold dead tree information back to zeroes); they are purged by resetting the variable IREC2, which is a pointer to the location in the tree data arrays where information for dead tree records starts. Dead tree information is stored at the bottom of the tree data arrays. The maximum number of tree records FVS allows is currently set at 3000 (2000 in the ORGANON-FVS variants) and stored in variable MAXTRE in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block. So, storage locations 3000-IREC2 to 3000 (2000-IREC2 to 2000 in the ORGANON-FVS variants) contain dead tree information in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Subroutine FVS resets IREC2 to MAXTP1 (also in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block) which has a value of 3001, or MAXTRE+1, (2001 in ORGANON-FVS variants). In FVS, looping over dead trees goes from IREC2 to MAXTRE, and is preceded by a simple test that if IREC2 is greater than MAXTRE then skip that section of code. So this reassignment of IREC2 effectively frees up those storage locations for later use in storing live tree information.

Subroutine FVS next calls RDMN1 and RDPR to initialize the western root disease model. RDMN1 and RDPR will exist as subroutines if the western root disease extension is part of the FVS executable program, or as entry points in subroutine EXRD if the western root disease extension is not part of the executable program.

Subroutine FVS next calls BRSETP and BRPR to initialize the blister rust model. BRSETP and BRPR will exist as subroutines if the blister rust model is part of the FVS executable program, or as entry points in the EXBR subroutine if the blister rust extension is not part of the executable program.

The final steps in the projection initialization phase are to set the logical flag, LSTART that is carried in the CONTRL labeled COMMON block, to a value of “.FALSE.” indicating the project initialization phase has been completed, and then to call subroutine EVTSTV with an argument of -1 to define the type 1 event monitor variables for the inventory. Some subroutines used in projection initialization (e.g. subroutine DGDRIV) have two similar but distinct sections. One part is used in projection initialization and the other is used in projection cycling. These subroutines check the value of variable LSTART to determine which section should be used.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine COMP is used to calculate the species and tree class percentage composition values for various volume categories.

Subroutine DBCHK is called by various subroutines to see if debug output is to be printed.

Subroutine DIST is used to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points (10, 30, 50, 70, and 90) in the distribution of a stand attribute.

Subroutine ECVOL is used to process volume information for the economics post-processor if an economics analysis is called for.

Subroutine FORTYP is called by subroutine DISPLY to calculate the forest type, size class, and stocking class for printing in the output tables. In the Southern variant (SN), if a user does not specify a maximum stand density index or basal area maximum, then these values are defaulted from the forest type. Consequently, in the SN variant, if forest type changes and user-defined values have not been entered, then the maximum stand density index and basal area maximum are also changed.

Subroutine IAPSRT is called by subroutine ESFLTR to sort trees in the inventory data by plot number.

Subroutine OPFIND is called by subroutine CWIDTH to see if any FIXCW keyword records are scheduled for all cycles.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine CWIDTH to process any FIXCW keyword records scheduled for all cycles, and OPDONE, another entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to list the activity as “DONE”.

Subroutine OPGET2 is called by subroutine ESFLTR to check for a TALLYONE option scheduled within 20 years of the inventory year. Subroutine OPGET2 provides an alternative way to retrieve activities where those scheduled for years beyond the current cycle boundaries can be retrieved.

Subroutine PCTILE is used to calculate percentile points in the distribution of annual total cubic foot accretion.

Subroutine VOLS computes the volumes of the tree records. It first calls subroutine VOLKEY, and then selects the calculation of each tree record by the cubic foot volume method of the species, METHC(i), and the board foot volume method, METHB(i). The default of both is method 6 in every variant (subroutine SITSET changes a method that is still 999 to 6). The methods are used as follows.

1. Methods 6 and 10 (and method 5 in the CS, LS and NE variants) call entry point NATCRS of subroutine FVSVOL, in the file `vvolume/fvsvol.f`. FVSVOL calls subroutine VOLINITNVB of the National Volume Estimator Library (NVEL, the git submodule `volume/NVEL`). For a National Scale Volume and Biomass equation (a name that begins with `NVB`), VOLINITNVB calls subroutine NVBC. For any other equation it calls subroutine VOLINIT, which uses the National Cruise System equations (for example the profile routine PROFILE, and R6VOL for some Region 6 equations). Method 10 is set by the FIAVBC keyword record and selects the National Scale Volume and Biomass equations, which are described in [National Scale Volume and Biomass (NSVB) estimation](#sec-national-scale-volume-and-biomass). Subroutine SITSET chooses the equation of each species and writes a table of the volume equation numbers to the main output file. FVSVOL also calls the variant subroutine FORMCL for the form class.
2. Method 8 calls the variant-specific entry points OCFVOL and OBFVOL of subroutine FVSVOL.
3. The other methods call the variant subroutines CFVOL and BFVOL.

When the board foot method is 5 (CS, LS and NE), 6 or 9 and the cubic foot method is 6 or 10, the board foot volume comes from the same call of NATCRS as the cubic foot volume. Subroutine VOLS calls subroutines CFTOPK and BFTOPK to compute volume lost to broken or dead tops. CFTOPK is not called when an NSVB equation is used or when the FIAVBC keyword record is active; NSVB makes the allowance for the top itself (see the NSVB section). Entry point GETEQN of FVSVOL is used by subroutine NATCRZ to return the volume equation numbers being used when writing an output file for the National Cruise Program post-processor.

Subroutine VOLKEY is called by VOLS to process any keyword records used to change volume standards or volume equations. These keyword records include MCDEFECT, BFDEFECT, VOLUME, and BFVOLUME. After a FIAVBC keyword record has been read, the MCDEFECT and VOLUME records are recognized but have no effect.

# Projection Cycling Phase {#sec-projection-cycling-phase}

The projection cycling phase simulates tree growth, mortality, regeneration establishment, and stand management actions as specified by a user in the keyword record file. This phase is the core of the FVS model. Once this phase is completed FVS will be ready to write the specified output tables.

The projection cycling phase is controlled by the variables ICYC and NCYC. ICYC is the current FVS cycle number and NCYC is the number of FVS cycles in a simulation. The default value of NCYC is 1 but it can be set to a value ranging from 2 to 40 using the NUMCYCLE keyword record. The current maximum, 40, can be changed in the PRGPRM code segment (see [Code Organization and Linking Considerations](#sec-code-organization-and-linking-considerations)).

The FVS control loop and logic can be summed up very simply:

Increment ICYC by 1.

Check the event monitor and simulate harvest, growth, and mortality.

Predict insect and disease effects (if any) and simulate regeneration establishment.

Write end of cycle values to the output files, predict crown ratio change, and update tree records.

Compare ICYC and NCYC; if ICYC is equal to NCYC then the projection cycling phase is completed; if ICYC is less than NCYC then another projection cycle is called for and the process starts over with step 1.

Step 1 happens in subroutine FVS. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine TREGRO which calls subroutine GRINCR to handle step 2 and subroutine GRADD to handle step 3. Both GRINCR and GRADD call several other subroutines, as outlined in the following sections. Subroutine FVS then calls several subroutines to handle step 4, and performs step 5. Steps 2-4 will be explained in detail in the following sections.
