## Event monitor and harvest {#sec-event-monitor-and-harvest}

Checking the event monitor and simulating harvest both occur at the beginning of a projection cycle in FVS. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine TREGRO which calls subroutine GRINCR to control these tasks.

### Subroutines involved and their function

There are some model control tasks that subroutine GRINCR needs to accomplish at the start of each projection cycle. First the cycle length, FINT, is set; next subroutine OPCSET is called to set up the option pointers for the cycle; the logical variable LTRIP is set to control whether record tripling will happen during the cycle; subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND) are called to process any SETSITE keyword records scheduled for the cycle; if a SETSITE keyword record is present, subroutine HABTYP gets called to decode the habitat type, if habitat type is being reset as part of the SETSITE options, and subroutine RCON gets called to recalculate growth equation species-level constants; and various subroutines get called to set up variables needed by FVS extensions (e.g. RDMN2 and RDTRP for root disease, FMSDIT for fire and fuel effects, and others).

Thinning to a relative density target, as done in the SILVAH (Marquis and Ernst 1992) growth model, is a management option in the Northeast (NE) variant. Subroutine GRINCR calls SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, to compute the SILVAH forest type before thinning. For the NE variant, possible values for the SILVAH forest type range from 0 to 5; in all other variants, the SILVAH forest type will be 0.

The event monitor is an integral part of all FVS variants and its’ capabilities are discussed in section 5.5 of the EFVS Guide. A detailed discussion of event monitor structure is presented in [Event monitor logic](#sec-event-monitor-logic) of this document. Subroutine GRINCR next directs the computation of some predefined before-thinning event monitor variables. Subroutine SDICAL is called to compute the before-thinning stand SDI maximum; SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the current stand SDI by two methods (Reineke 1933 and Zeide 1983); and subroutine SSTAGE is called to compute the before-thinning stand structural stage.

Subroutine GRINCR then calls subroutine EVMON to see if any before-thinning actions need to be scheduled. The variable IPH is a local variable in both subroutines GRINCR and EVMON that indicates the event monitor phase number. The value for this variable is passed from subroutine GRINCR to subroutine EVMON through the EVMON argument list. This variable is used in subroutine EVMON to set the event monitor phase number, variable IPHASE that is carried in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block. The phase number is an important variable in controlling event monitor logic. The variable IPH, and consequently variable IPHASE, have a value of 1 if the event monitor is being called before thinning and 2 if the event monitor is being called after thinning. Stop point 1 is processed immediately before this call and stop point 2 immediately after it (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)). Subroutine ECSTATUS is then called with an argument of 0 to evaluate the status of the economics extension before thinning.

#### Checking the event monitor for before-thinning actions {#sec-checking-the-event-monitor-for-before-thinning-actions}

Before-thinning actions include computing predefined and custom output variables based on stand conditions before harvesting occurs, or evaluating expressions that conditionally schedule management activities, such as a thinning, based on before-thinning stand conditions.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVTSTV to load values of predefined event monitor variables in Groups 1, 3, 4, and 5 (see EFVS Table 5-2 for a list of variables in Groups 1, 3, and 4; Group 5 variables are user-defined).

If the cycle number, ICYC, is 2 or greater, subroutine EVAGE is called to age an event that has already occurred and resets it as viable for occurring at some other time.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine ALGEVL to evaluate expressions. Expressions may be used in computing user-defined variables or in keyword record parameter fields using the PARMS format. Subroutine ALGEVL calls subroutine EVLDX to load values of saved variables or results of functions like SPMCDBH into storage registers for further computing.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVPOST to post the year the event occurred. This means changing the second value in the row of the IVENTS(i,j) array (i.e. j = 2, i = the row holding information for this event). This storage location stores the year the activity occurred, if it occurs, or -1 if it does not occur. EVPOST calls subroutine EVALNK to determine if the event is linked to an activity group.

This concludes the event monitor check before thinning and control returns to subroutine GRINCR for further processing.

#### Processing thinning and pruning requests

If the cycle number is greater than or equal to 2, subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine SVOUT to write the beginning-of-cycle output file for the stand visualization post-processor.

Subroutine GRINCR then calls subroutine CUTS to process all pruning and thinning management activities. It is important to note that harvesting occurs at the beginning of a projection cycle. So harvests scheduled at any time during the projection cycle are actually done at the beginning of that projection cycle. If harvesting at a particular year is important to a user, then manipulation of the cycle boundaries using the TIMEINT or CYCLEAT keyword records will be necessary.

Subroutine CUTS is simple in concept, but very complicated in terms of coding; it makes heavy use of logical variables and work arrays. Fortunately, the subroutine is well documented with comment statements. CUTS is responsible for processing minimum harvest constraints (MINHARV keyword record), setting multipliers for use in the harvest priority algorithm (SPECPREF and TCONDMLT keyword records), accounting for portions of a harvest that may be left in the woods (YARDLOSS keyword record), removing portions of a trees’ crown ratio (PRUNE keyword record), and processing all harvest requests scheduled for the cycle (THIN___ and SETPTHIN keyword records).

Subroutine CUTS interfaces with the fire and fuels extension by calling: FMATV to see if the fire extension is active; FMSALV to process harvesting of dead trees with the SALVAGE keyword record; FMSCUT to update the snag list; FMTREM to save removals for processing with the TREEBIO event monitor function; and FMPRUN to update debris pools with pruning slash. FMATV, FMSALV, FMSCUT, FMTREM, and FMPRUN will exist as subroutines if the fire and fuels extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXFIRE if the fire and fuels extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutine CUTS also interfaces with the Economic extension. GetIsPretendActive, an entry point in subroutine ECSTATUS, is called to see if the PRETEND keyword record has been specified. The pretend mode allows users to get an economic analysis of a proposed thinning without actually performing the thinning in FVS. ECHARV is called to accumulate board foot volume removal information. ECHARV will exist as a subroutine if the economics extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXECON if the economics extension is not part of the program executable.

There is an older economics post-processing program called CHEAPOII. Subroutine CUTS calls subroutines ECREMS and ECOUT to produce the necessary information to interface with this program. CHEAPOII has been completely replaced by the ECON extension and is no longer used; code related to the CHEAPOII program should be deleted from the FVS system.

##### How subroutine CUTS works

The harvest concept in subroutine CUTS is to loop over all thinning requests, accumulate the harvest information, and reduce the trees per acre representation for each tree record affected by a thinning. This is done on a “trial basis” first and the accumulated harvest is compared to the minimum harvest constraint. If the minimum harvest constraint is not met, or these thinnings are part of the pretend mode for an economic analysis, then the thinning requests are not finalized. Otherwise, a final pass is made over all tree records and results from the trial thinnings are fully implemented.

Subroutine CUTS calls subroutine OPFIND to see if any thinning requests are scheduled for the current cycle. The trial thinning vector, WK4(i), is loaded with the current trees per acre of tree “i” and is reduced as thinning requests are processed. The removed trees per acre array, WK3(i), is initialized to zero along with other control variables like those used to accumulate removed volumes, and receives the removed trees per acre for tree “i” when the thinning is implemented. The DO 1400 loop processes all thinning requests, one at a time, and accumulates the trial thinning values. For each thinning request scheduled for the current cycle, OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND,  is called to retrieve parameters associated with the thinning request along with the activity number, IACTK, which identifies the type of thinning that is being processed. The IACTK value, or a transformation of it stored in variable ICFLAG, is used within the DO 1400 loop to control the logic needed to process the thinning request.

Within the DO 1400 loop, most thinning requests rank tree records for removal with a priority value stored in WK2(i) in subroutine CUTS. Records are sorted by RDPSRT in descending order of priority and removed from the top of the list until the thinning target is met. The priority of tree record *i* is:

$$P_i = F_d \cdot S_i + SP_s + F_t \cdot IMC_i + F_s \cdot STS_i + F_{pba} \cdot PBA_p + F_{pccf} \cdot PCCF_p + F_{ptpa} \cdot PTPA_p + F_m$$

where:

- $F_d$ is 1 when thinning from above and -1 when thinning from below. In the code the flag is LBELOW, which is reset to false for each thinning request. THINBTA, THINBBA, and thinning below a stocking level in THINAUTO set it true. For THINSDI, THINCC, THINRDEN, THINPT, and THINRDSL, a value of 1 in field 7 sets it true.
- $S_i$ is the size term: DBH, or total height when the height range of the request is narrower than the diameter range. The choice is made by THINBTA and THINATA; THINBBA and THINABA do not set it and use the value left by an earlier request in the same cycle, or DBH if there was none.
- $SP_s$ is the species preference (IORDER) set with the SPECPREF keyword record. It is an integer, defaults to 0, and can apply to one species, a species group, or all species.
- $F_t$, $F_s$, $F_{pba}$, $F_{pccf}$, and $F_{ptpa}$ are the multipliers set in fields 1 to 5 of the TCONDMLT keyword record (TCWT, SPCLWT, PBAWT, PCCFWT, PTPAWT). $IMC_i$ is the tree value class and $STS_i$ the special status code.
- $PBA_p$, $PCCF_p$, and $PTPA_p$ are the per-acre basal area, crown competition factor, and trees per acre estimated for the inventory point *p* where the tree is located (PTBAA, PCCF, PTPA; PTBAA is computed in PTBAL and the others in DENSE).
- $F_m$ is the dwarf mistletoe preference, taken from a table by species and mistletoe rating (PRFMIS, loaded by MISCPF), and added only when the tree has a mistletoe rating greater than zero.

The terms are summed without normalization; the only scaling is the user-supplied preference and multiplier values. A species preference that differs by more than the spread of the size term (DBH or height) between two species determines the order in which those species are removed, regardless of tree size; within a species, the size term still orders the trees. Trees outside the diameter or height limits of the request, and trees of species named in SPLEAVE, are flagged LNOCUT and cannot be selected.

Some requests do not use this equation. THINPRSC takes priority from the prescription codes and THINMIST assigns 1 or 0. THINDBH and THINHT assign 1 to every tree inside the diameter or height limits and 0 to all others, skip the sort, and reduce each tree record inside the limits, in record order, by the cutting efficiency. When a residual trees per acre or basal area target is given, the cutting efficiency is recomputed as the amount to remove divided by the current stocking in the range. THINQFA does not rank trees with this equation. THINSDI, THINCC, THINRDEN, THINPT, and THINRDSL skip the ranking unless field 7 is greater than 0.

The DO 1700 loop implements results from the trial thinnings if minimum harvest constraints are met and the cutting subroutine in not in the pretend mode for an economic analysis.

If the trees per acre representation for a tree record is reduced to zero (i.e. all of the trees represented by that tree record are cut), subroutine CUTS calls subroutine TREDEL to delete those tree records from the tree list. Subroutine SPESRT is then called to realign the species ordered sort for the remaining tree records and subroutine RDPSRT is called to sort the IND(i) array from largest to smallest, in terms of diameter, for residual trees in the stand.

Subroutine CUTS calls several subroutines to produce tree lists for cut tree records and the residual stand. Subroutine PRTRLS produces a cut tree list, requested with the CUTLIST keyword record, and an after treatment live tree list; subroutine FVSSTD is called to write a cut tree list for the FVSStand post-processer, requested with the FVSSTAND keyword record; subroutines DBS_FIAVBC_CUTLST and DBS_FIAVBC_ATRTLS write the corresponding FIA-VBC cut list and after treatment tree list tables to the output database when those tables have been requested; and subroutine SVCUTS is called to write files needed for a stand visualization of the thinning if requested using the SVS keyword record.

**Volume of the removed trees and of the after treatment records.** Subroutine CUTS does not call VOLS. It uses the per-tree volumes that were stored by the last call to VOLS, which is the call of the previous cycle (UPDATE) or, in the first cycle, the initial call of subroutine FVS. CUTS is called near the start of the cycle, before the growth is estimated (`base/grincr.f:292`), so the DBH and HT of the cut records and the volumes of the removed trees are the values of the start of the cycle. For each tree record that is cut, the removed volumes are the products of the trees per acre removed and the stored volumes, as shown in equation {4.1.1.1} (`vbase/cuts.f:1686-1691`). The biomass and carbon of the removed trees follow the same pattern: the non-product values (above-ground and foliage biomass and carbon) are multiplied by PREM, and the product values (merchantable and sawlog biomass and carbon) are multiplied by PREM2 (`cuts.f:1693-1702`). The totals that CUTS accumulates for the trial thinning, CFCUT, CMCUT, SCCUT and BFCUT, use the same stored volumes, with PREM x (1 - PRLOST) for the merchantable, sawlog and board foot volumes, where PRLOST is the proportion lost with the YARDLOSS keyword record (`cuts.f:1394-1397`). The stored volumes are also passed to the economics extension (`cuts.f:1666-1673`) and are used for the distribution of the removed volume (OCVREM and the other removal arrays, `cuts.f:1777-1778`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
WK2 &= PREM \cdot CFV \\
PREM2 &= \max\left(0, \; PREM - DSNG - SSNG\right) \\
WK5 &= PREM2 \cdot MCFV \\
WK7 &= PREM2 \cdot SCFV \\
WK6 &= PREM2 \cdot BFV
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.1.1.1}
$$

Where:

- WK2: Total cubic foot volume removed from the record (cubic feet per acre)
- WK5: Merchantable cubic foot volume removed from the record (cubic feet per acre)
- WK7: Sawlog cubic foot volume removed from the record (cubic feet per acre)
- WK6: Merchantable board foot volume removed from the record (board feet per acre)
- PREM: Trees per acre removed from the record (trees per acre)
- DSNG: Trees per acre of the record left in the stand as down snags by the YARDLOSS keyword record (trees per acre)
- SSNG: Trees per acre of the record left in the stand as standing snags by the YARDLOSS keyword record (trees per acre)
- CFV: Total cubic foot volume of a tree of the record, as stored by the last call to VOLS (cubic feet per tree)
- MCFV: Merchantable cubic foot volume of a tree of the record, as stored by VOLS (cubic feet per tree)
- SCFV: Sawlog cubic foot volume of a tree of the record, as stored by VOLS (cubic feet per tree)
- BFV: Merchantable board foot volume of a tree of the record, as stored by VOLS (board feet per tree)

After the volumes are accumulated, CUTS calls PRTRLS with argument 2 for the cut list and with argument 3 for the after treatment list, and then the corresponding database routines (`cuts.f:1735-1740`). PRTRLS prints the stored CFV, MCFV, SCFV and BFV of each record, and does not calculate volumes (`vbase/prtrls.f:371-425`). The after treatment list holds the residual trees, whose PROB has been reduced by the cut. Their diameters, heights and volumes are the start-of-cycle values as well. All variants, including BC and ON, compile `vbase/cuts.f` (`bin/FVSbc_sourceList.txt:96`, `bin/FVSon_sourceList.txt:107`); BC and ON compile `metric/vbase/prtrls.f` instead of `vbase/prtrls.f` (`bin/FVSbc_sourceList.txt:93`, `bin/FVSon_sourceList.txt:103`), which was not compared. The file `canada/on/cuts.f` is not in the source list of ON.

Processing control returns to subroutine GRINCR to do some post-thinning updating of stand statistics and other control variables. GRINCR calls subroutine DENSE to update stand density statistics if any thinning occurred. GRINCR next computes values of some predefined after-thinning event monitor variables. Subroutine SDICAL is called to compute the after-thinning stand SDI maximum; SDICLS, which is an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the after-thinning stand SDI by two methods (Reineke 1933 and Zeide 1983); SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the after-thinning SILVAH forest type; and subroutine SSTAGE is called to compute the after-thinning stand structural stage. Other code segments are called for extensions that may be part of the model (e.g. CVBROW and CVCNOP for the cover extension). These will be individual subroutines if the extension is part of the model, or entry points in the corresponding “EX__” subroutine if the extension is not part of the model (e.g. subroutine EXCOV for the cover extension). GRINCR is now ready to call the event monitor for processing after-thinning actions.

#### Checking the event monitor for after-thinning actions

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine EVMON, with the event monitor phase number set to 2, to see if any after-thinning actions need to be scheduled. After-thinning actions include computing predefined and custom output variables based on stand conditions after harvesting occurs or evaluating expressions that conditionally schedule management activities based on post-thinning conditions. Stop point 3 is processed immediately before this call and stop point 4 immediately after it. Subroutine ECSTATUS is then called with an argument of 1 to evaluate the status of the economics extension after thinning.

The logic is basically the same as discussed in [Checking the event monitor for before-thinning actions](#sec-checking-the-event-monitor-for-before-thinning-actions). Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVTSTV to load values of predefined event monitor variables in Groups 2 and 5 (see EFVS Table 5-2 for variables in 2; Group 5 variables are user-defined). Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine ALGEVL to evaluate expressions. Subroutine ALGEVL calls subroutine EVLDX to load values of saved variables or results of functions like SPMCDBH into storage registers for further computing. Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVPOST to post the year the event occurred and control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine COMCUP which interfaces with subroutine COMPRS to compress the tree list. This may be necessary when entire tree records are removed as part of the thinning process.

Next, subroutine GRINCR calls various code segments pertaining to insect and disease extensions (e.g. DFTMGO and TMBMAS for the Douglas-fir Tussock Moth extension). These code segments will be individual subroutines if the extension is part of the model, or entry points in the corresponding “EX__” subroutine if the extension is not part of the model (e.g. EXDFTM for the Douglas-fir Tussock Moth extension). These subroutines are used to determine if events like a tussock moth outbreak will occur in this projection cycle.

Subroutine GRINCR is now ready to predict tree growth and mortality for the current projection cycle.

### Auxiliary subroutines

AUTSTK, an entry point in subroutine CUTSTK, is used to compute a value for normal full stocking for the automatic thinning option (THINAUTO keyword record).

CCCLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of canopy cover for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

CLSSTK, an entry point in subroutine CUTSTK, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of trees per acre or basal area for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

Subroutine COMP is used to determine species by tree class composition statistics for removed trees, removed volumes, and residual trees.

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine DIST is used to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points (10, 30, 50, 70, and 90) in the distribution of removed trees and removed volumes.

Subroutine ESTUMP is used to add stumps to the stump list for processing of regeneration sprouting at the end of the projection cycle.

Subroutine ERRGRO is used to post warning and error messages to the FVS output file.

Subroutine LNKCHN is used by subroutine SPESRT to establish the IND2(i) values for residual trees when entire tree records are removed and subsequently deleted by thinning requests.

MISCPF is used to process the mistletoe cutting preference (MISTPREF keyword record) and MISGET is used to retrieve the mistletoe rating for the current tree record. MISCPF and MISGET will exist as subroutines if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the program executable.

OPCHPR, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to change the value of the stored parameter associated with the CUTEFF keyword record.

OPDEL1, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark a thinning request as “DELETED OR CANCELLED” if the thinning request cannot be processed for some reason.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to set the year a thinning option is actually accomplished.

Subroutine PCTILE is used to compute the percentile points in the distribution of removed trees and removed volumes.

RDCLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of relative density (Curtis 1982) for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

RDCLS2, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of relative density (Marquis and Ernst 1992) for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

RDSLTR, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute the relative density (Marquis and Ernst 1992) contribution of a given tree record.

SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of stand density index for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

Subroutine SETUP is called by subroutine SPESRT to establish the IND1(i) and ISCT(i,j) values for residual trees when entire tree records are removed and subsequently deleted by thinning requests.

SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute the forest type according to the SILVAH (Marquis and Ernst 1992) definitions.

Subroutine SVOUT is used to produce a file for post-treatment stand visualization when a salvage removal is called for by the fire and fuels extension and no live trees were removed.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Growth and Mortality {#sec-growth-and-mortality}

Trees are considered “large” trees for FVS modeling purposes when they are larger than some species and variant dependent threshold diameter. These threshold diameters and detailed descriptions of equations used to grow large trees and small trees can be found in the variant overview documents. A general description of the FVS large and small tree models as they are used in model calibration can be found in section 7.2 of the EFVS Guide.

FVS mortality models are of four kinds: 1) the Prognosis-type mortality model; 2) the SDI-based mortality model; 3) individual tree survival models, which are used in the AK variant and in the HI, PN, WC and OP variants; and 4) the ORGANON mortality model. Some variants combine two models by species (EM and TT). A fifth type, the TWIGS based mortality model, has been replaced with the SDI-based mortality model in the Lake States (LS), Central States (CS), and Northeast (NE) variants. A general description of the Prognosis, SDI, and TWIGS mortality models can be found in section 7.3 of the EFVS Guide (Dixon 2002). A description of the ORGANON mortality model can be found in the overview documents for the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants).

### Subroutines involved and their function

The order in which FVS simulates stand-changing events is important. FVS is a forward predicting model. That is to say, it predicts future stand conditions from current stand conditions. Harvesting occurs at the beginning of a growth projection cycle prior to growth prediction. So pruning and harvesting affects growth rates through modified crown ratio and stand density attributes.

Intuitively, if you look at the model flow diagram (figure 2-1), mortality seems to work the other way around; mortality is predicted after growth so it appears that mortality is being predicted at the end of a projection cycle. However, this isn’t really the case. FVS is still in a forward predicting mode and estimating the mortality that will occur during the projection cycle, but taking into consideration competition due to individual tree growth that will occur during the cycle.

The processing sequence through this section of code is to obtain an estimate of:

large tree diameter growth

large tree height growth

small tree height growth

small tree diameter growth

mortality

This is subtly different than the language used in Figure 2-1. Figure 2-1 presents the general processing sequence in conceptual terms; the language here reflects the actual programming sequence. For example, in Figure 2-1 we say “grow large trees (in order: diameter, height)” but here we say “obtain an estimate of: 1) large tree diameter growth, 2) large tree height growth”. Diameter and height growth is estimated for all trees (large and small) using equations in the large-tree portion of FVS; height and diameter growth is estimated for only a portion of the trees using equations in the small-tree portion of FVS; and estimates are combined or discarded as appropriate for the variant and species.

Notice that a trees’ crown ratio change, due to tree growth and changes in stand density, is yet to be predicted. This occurs at the very end of a growth projection cycle and will be discussed in [Updating the tree descriptions](#sec-updating-the-tree-descriptions).

#### Growing the large trees {#sec-growing-the-large-trees}

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine DGDRIV to calculate a large-tree diameter growth estimate for all tree records. DGDRIV is one of those subroutines containing two sections; the top section is used for growth estimation in projection cycling; the bottom section is used for calibration in projection initialization.

Subroutine DGDRIV retrieves any multipliers or management flags scheduled for the current projection cycle with calls to subroutine MULTS.

Large tree diameter growth, expressed as ln(DDS), the natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years, is estimated using a regression equation (or, for some species, another form of equation, as described below) with independent variables being individual tree attributes and current stand conditions. An error term is added to the estimate. Error terms are correlated from cycle-to-cycle so the relative magnitude of an individual trees’ estimate is correlated from one projection cycle to the next. In effect, a tree growing well one cycle is likely to grow well the next cycle, and a tree growing poorly is likely to continue growing poorly, to some extent. The correlation of the errors between cycles is calculated from the autocorrelation function of an autoregressive moving average model, ARMA(1,1), of the annual increments, as described under Serial correlation and random error of the diameter increment. DGDRIV calls subroutine AUTCOR to compute the variance and covariance multipliers for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine DGDRIV calls subroutine DGF to obtain large tree diameter growth estimates for all the tree records. Subroutine DGF contains regression equations for each species. It is structured as nested DO loops with the outside loop controlling species and the inside loop controlling tree records within species. The argument list for subroutine DGF consists of the array of tree diameters to be used. So in the calibration phase of projection initialization subroutine DGF is called with the array of backdated diameters, and in the growth estimation phase of projection cycling it is called with the tree diameters at the beginning of the projection cycle. Subroutine DGF stores estimated diameter growth for each tree record in terms of ln(DDS), the natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter, in work array WK2(i).

**Equation for the large-tree diameter increment.** Subroutine DGF stores in WK2(i) the natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years, ln(DDS), for each tree record i. WK2(i) is not the logarithm of the basal area increment; the two differ by a constant factor, but DGF does not apply the factor. The variables used in this section are defined in the next table.

```{r growth-variables, echo=FALSE}
growth_variables <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variable, ~Definition, ~Units,
  "DBH", "Diameter at breast height outside bark at the start of the cycle (the backdated diameter during calibration)", "inches",
  "DG", "Diameter increment inside bark over YR years", "inches",
  "DDS", "Change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years", "square inches",
  "BARK", "Bark ratio, BRATIO(species, DBH, HT), inside bark diameter divided by outside bark diameter", "ratio",
  "CR", "Crown ratio as a proportion (ICR/100); in the CS and LS variants, as a percent; in the NC species 2, 6 and 9, CRID, the product of the crown ratio and the diameter", "proportion",
  "BA", "Stand basal area", "square feet per acre",
  "BAL", "Basal area in trees larger than the subject tree, (1 - PCT/100) x BA, where PCT is the percentile of the tree in the basal area distribution; in the variants listed in the equation notes, BA is first divided by 100", "square feet per acre",
  "PBAL", "Basal area in larger trees on the point where the tree is located", "square feet per acre",
  "PCCF", "Crown competition factor of the point where the tree is located", "percent",
  "RELDEN", "Stand crown competition factor (CCF)", "percent",
  "RELHT", "Relative height, HT divided by AVH, with a maximum of 1.5 in the variants that use it", "ratio",
  "AVH", "Average height of the 40 largest diameter trees per acre", "feet",
  "SI", "Site index of the species", "feet",
  "ELEV", "Stand elevation (hundreds of feet in most variants)", "feet / 100",
  "SLOPE", "Stand slope as a proportion", "proportion",
  "ASP", "Stand aspect", "radians",
  "COR", "Calibration term of the species, set in subroutine DGDRIV (ln scale; see Calibrate growth equations)", "ln units",
  "COR2", "User-supplied diameter increment multiplier of the species (READCORD), applied as ln(COR2) in DGCON, or as a multiplier of DG in the NE and ON variants", "ratio",
  "DGCON", "Site-specific constant of the ln(DDS) equation, calculated once in the entry point DGCONS", "ln units",
  "YR", "Period length of the growth equations: 10 years, except NC, OC, OP and SN, 5 years", "years",
  "FINT", "Length of the projection cycle", "years"
)

kable(growth_variables,
      col.names = c("Variable", "Definition", "Units"),
      caption = "Variables used in the large-tree diameter increment equations",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "6em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "34em")
```

Most species use the form of equation {4.2.1.1.1}, with coefficients that are arrays subscripted by species. The terms that are included differ by variant and species. The table that follows the equations lists the terms of each variant and species group, and the other forms are given after the table.

$$
\ln(DDS) = CONSPP + DGLD \cdot \ln(DBH) + DGDSQ \cdot DBH^{2} + CR\,(DGCR + DGCRSQ \cdot CR) + DGBAL \cdot BAL + DGDBAL\,\frac{BAL}{\ln(DBH + 1)} + \text{other terms}
\tag{4.2.1.1.1}
$$

Where:

- ln(DDS): Natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years (square inches); the value is bounded below at -9.21
- CONSPP: Constant of the species; it is DGCON + COR, plus a density term in most variants (see the table)
- DGCON: Site-specific constant of the species, calculated once in the entry point DGCONS
- COR: Calibration term of the species; it is zero when no calibration is done
- DGLD, DGDSQ, DGCR, DGCRSQ, DGBAL, DGDBAL: Coefficients of the species (arrays of the same names in subroutine DGF)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)
- BAL: Basal area in larger trees (square feet per acre); the scale of BAL differs by variant and species and is shown in the table
- Other terms: PCCF, RELDEN, RELHT, ln(BA), BA and others, as listed in the table; a term is part of the equation of a species only when the table lists it

In IE, DGCON is given by equation {4.2.1.1.2}. In WC, PN, HI and OP, DGCON = DGFOR + DGEL x ELEV + DGEL2 x ELEV^2 + DGSITE x ln(SI) + (DGSASP x sin(ASP) + DGCASP x cos(ASP) + DGSLOP) x SLOPE + DGSLSQ x SLOPE^2, where the coefficients are those of the species mapped by MAPSPC, ELEV is limited to 30 for the mapped species 14, SI of the mapped species 10 is multiplied by 3.281, and SI of the mapped species 18 (WC) or 19 (PN, HI and OP) is replaced by -37.60812 x ln[1 - (SI / 114.24569)^0.4444]. DGCON of the other variants is calculated in the entry point DGCONS of each file and is not reproduced here.

$$
DGCON = DGHAB + DGFOR + DGEL \cdot ELEV + DGEL2 \cdot ELEV^{2} + \left(DGSASP \cdot \sin ASP + DGCASP \cdot \cos ASP + DGSLOP\right) SLOPE + DGSLSQ \cdot SLOPE^{2}
\tag{4.2.1.1.2}
$$

Where:

- DGCON: Constant of the species in IE; for species LM and PY, 0.001766 x SI is added, and for species AS, MM and PB, 0.00646 x SI is added
- DGHAB: Coefficient for the habitat type of the species
- DGFOR: Coefficient for the national forest or location of the species
- DGEL, DGEL2: Coefficients for elevation and for elevation squared
- ELEV: Elevation (hundreds of feet)
- DGSASP, DGCASP, DGSLOP, DGSLSQ: Coefficients for aspect and slope
- ASP: Aspect (radians); 0.7854 radians is subtracted from the aspect for species LM, PM, RM, PY, AS, MM and PB
- SLOPE: Slope (proportion)

**Equations of the species that grow by a future diameter.** Many species of the IE, EM, CI, BM, SO, TT and UT variants use an equation that predicts the diameter at the end of the period, DF, in place of equation {4.2.1.1.1}. Three forms are used, shown in equations {4.2.1.1.3} to {4.2.1.1.5}. The increment is calculated from the difference of the predicted and current diameters, and is converted to ln(DDS). A fourth form is used for aspen, shown in equation {4.2.1.1.6}. Each row of the next table names the form that each species uses.

$$
\begin{aligned}
DF &= 0.25897 + 1.03129 \cdot DPP - 0.0002025464 \cdot BATEM + 0.00177 \cdot SI, \quad DF \le DPP + 1.0, \quad DF \ge DPP \\
DIAGR &= (DF - DPP) \cdot BARK \\
\ln(DDS) &= \ln\left[DIAGR\,(2 \cdot DPP \cdot BARK + DIAGR)\right] + CONSPP
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.3}
$$

Where:

- ln(DDS): Natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years (square inches), with a minimum of -9.21
- DPP: Diameter at breast height, with a minimum of 1.0 inch (inches)
- BATEM: Stand basal area, with a minimum of 1.0 square foot per acre (square feet per acre)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- BARK: Bark ratio
- CONSPP: Constant of the species, shown in the table

DF is the predicted diameter at the end of the period (inches). If DIAGR is zero or less, ln(DDS) is set to -9.21.

$$
\begin{aligned}
DF &= 0.24506 + 1.01291 \cdot DPP - 0.00084659 \cdot BA + 0.00631 \cdot SI, \quad DF \le 36.0, \quad DF \ge DPP \\
DIAGR &= (DF - DPP) \cdot BARK \\
\ln(DDS) &= \ln\left[DIAGR\,(2 \cdot DPP \cdot BARK + DIAGR)\right] + COR + DGCON
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.4}
$$

Where:

- ln(DDS): Natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years (square inches), with a minimum of -9.21
- DPP: Diameter at breast height, with a minimum of 1.0 inch (inches)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- BARK: Bark ratio
- COR: Calibration term of the species
- DGCON: Constant of the species from equation {4.2.1.1.2}

DF is the predicted diameter at the end of the period (inches). If DIAGR is zero or less, ln(DDS) is set to -9.21.

$$
\begin{aligned}
DF &= 1.05\left[1.55986 + 1.01825 \cdot DPP - 0.29342 \ln(BATEM) + 0.00672 \cdot SI - 0.00073 \cdot \frac{BAU}{BA}\right], \quad DF \ge DPP \\
DIAGR &= (DF - DPP) \cdot BARK \cdot DSTAG \\
\ln(DDS) &= \ln\left[DIAGR\,(2 \cdot DPP \cdot BARK + DIAGR)\right] + COR + DGCON
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.5}
$$

Where:

- ln(DDS): Natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years (square inches), with a minimum of -9.21
- DPP: Diameter at breast height, with a minimum of 1.0 inch (inches)
- BATEM: Stand basal area, with a minimum of 5.0 square feet per acre (square feet per acre)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- BAU: Basal area in the diameter classes that are larger than the class of the tree (square feet per acre); the classes are 1-inch classes numbered INT(DBH + 1), with a maximum of 41, and the basal area of the stand is calculated by subroutine BADIST
- BARK: Bark ratio
- DSTAG: Stagnation multiplier; 1.0 unless the SDIMAX keyword activates the stagnation option (ISTAGF is not 0) for the species, in which case DSTAG = 3.33333 x (1 - RELSDI) when RELSDI is greater than 0.7, where RELSDI is the stand SDI divided by the maximum SDI, with a maximum of 0.85
- COR: Calibration term of the species
- DGCON: Constant of the species from equation {4.2.1.1.2}

DF is the predicted diameter at the end of the period (inches). If DIAGR is zero or less, ln(DDS) is set to -9.21.

Equation {4.2.1.1.3} is the juniper and pinyon form, equation {4.2.1.1.4} is the form of the CR variant for Douglas-fir-type hardwood and other species, and equation {4.2.1.1.5} is the form of the CR variant for spruce and fir. In species GB of the UT variant the DF of equation {4.2.1.1.3} is used with the minimum BATEM of 5.0 and the DSTAG factor of equation {4.2.1.1.5}.

$$
\begin{aligned}
POT &= \left(0.4755 - 3.8336 \times 10^{-6} \, DBH^{4.1488}\right) + 0.04510 \cdot \frac{CR}{10} \cdot DBH^{0.67266}, \quad POT \ge 0.01 \\
FOFR &= 1.07528\left[1 - \exp\left(-1.89022 \cdot \frac{DBH}{RMSQD}\right)\right] \\
GOFAD &= 0.21963 \,(RMSQD + 1.0)^{0.73355} \\
VALMOD &= 1 - \exp\left[-FOFR \cdot GOFAD \sqrt{\frac{310 - BA^{*}}{310}}\right] \\
PREDGR &= POT \cdot VALMOD \cdot (0.48630 + 0.01258 \cdot SI) \\
ASPDG &= \ln\left(2 \cdot DBH \cdot BARK \cdot PREDGR + PREDGR^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.6}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio (percent)
- RMSQD: Quadratic mean diameter of the stand (inches)
- BA*: Stand basal area (square feet per acre), set to 305 when it is 310 or more
- ASPDG: ln(DDS) of the aspen equation (ln square inches); the ln(DDS) of the tree is ASPDG + ln(COR2) + COR
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- BARK: Bark ratio

The next table lists, by variant and species, the equation that DGF uses. CONSPP is the constant of the species. BAL is shown in each row because the scale differs among rows: BAL is (1 - PCT/100) x BA, and in some rows it is divided by 100 as noted. PCCF is the crown competition factor of the point of the tree. The species are listed in the order of the variants.

```{r dgf-forms, echo=FALSE}

  "IE", "WP, WL, DF, GF, WH, RC, LP, ES, AF, PP, MH, WB, LM, LL, PY, OS", "DGCON + COR + 0.01 x DGCCF x RELDEN", "Equation {4.2.1.1.1}: DGLD x ln(DBH) + DGBAL x BAL + CR x (DGCR + DGCRSQ x CR) + DGDSQ x DBH^2 + DGDBAL x BAL / ln(DBH + 1); BAL is (1 - PCT/100) x BA/100", "ie/dgf.f",
```

The BM equation for trees smaller than 10.0 inches, which was fit to 5-year increments, is shown in equation {4.2.1.1.7}. For trees of 3.0 inches and larger, and smaller than 10.0 inches, the large-tree value of the table, DDSL, and the small-tree value, DDSS, are combined with the weight XWT = (10.0 - DBH) / 7.0; XWT is 1.0 for trees smaller than 3.0 inches and 0 for trees of 10.0 inches or larger.

$$
\begin{aligned}
DDSS_{5} &= SMCONS + SMLD \ln(DBH) + SMLBA \ln(BA) + CR\,(SMCR + SMCRSQ \cdot CR) + SMDS \cdot DBH^{2} + SMDBAL \frac{BAL}{\ln(DBH + 1)} + SMPCCF \cdot PCCF \\
TEMDG &= 2\left(\sqrt{DBH^{2} + \exp(DDSS_{5})} - DBH\right), \qquad DDSS = \ln\left[(TEMDG + DBH)^{2} - DBH^{2}\right] \\
\ln(DDS) &= XWT \cdot DDSS + (1 - XWT)\,DDSL
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.7}
$$

Where:

- SMCONS: SMCON + COR; SMCON and the coefficients SMLD, SMLBA, SMCR, SMCRSQ, SMDS, SMDBAL and SMPCCF are arrays of the species group (index SMMAPS) in subroutine DGF
- DDSL: ln(DDS) of the large-tree row of the table
- XWT: Weight of the small-tree value, defined above
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)
- BAL: Basal area in larger trees (square feet per acre), as given in the table
- PCCF: Crown competition factor of the point of the tree (percent)
- ln(DDS): Natural logarithm of the change in squared inside bark diameter over YR years (square inches)

DDSS5 is the ln of the 5-year change in squared diameter of the small-tree equation (ln square inches), and DDSS is that value changed to 10 years; DDSS is 0 when the argument of the logarithm is zero or less.

**Other forms of the equation.** The remaining variants, and some species in the variants above, use other forms. In each form the result is stored in WK2(i) as ln(DDS).

1. **SN.** The equation is ln(DDS) = DGCON + COR + INTERC + LDBH x ln(DBH) + DBH2 x DBH² + LCRWN x ln(ICR) + HREL x RELHT + PLTB x BA + PNTBL x PBAL, plus a forest type term (the coefficient of the forest type group of the stand times a 0 or 1 indicator), and a plantation term (PLANT, with the indicator equal to 1 when the MANAGED keyword is used). RELHT has a maximum of 1.5, and PBAL is replaced by BAL when it is not positive. DGCON contains the site index, slope, slope times cosine and sine of the aspect, and the dummy variables of the ecological unit. ICR is the crown ratio as a percent.
2. **AK.** The annual increment is BASEDG = exp(DGCONB1 + DGDISQ x DBH² + DGLD x ln(DBH) + DGDBAL x PBAL + DGRD x PRD + DGLNCR x ln(CR) + DGEL x ELEV + DGSLOP x SLOPE + DGSASP x SLOPE x cos(ASP) + DGLNSI x ln(SI)), where PRD is the relative density of the point, the Zeide relative density of the point divided by its maximum, and PBAL is the point basal area in larger trees. BASEDG is multiplied by YR and by the permafrost modifier, PFMOD (species TA, WS, LS, BE, OS, PB, AB, BA, AS, CW, WI, SU and OH; PFMOD is 1.0 for the other species), and by 0.45 for species AD, WI and OH, and by 0.65 for species SU. PFMOD is limited to 1.0 or less when permafrost is present and to 1.0 or more when it is absent. The result, DGPRED, is the outside bark increment. It is converted to the inside bark change in squared diameter: ln(DDS) = ln[(DBH + DGPRED)² x BARK² - (DBH x BARK)²] + COR + DGCON.
3. **CS and LS.** The equation is ln(DDS) = DGCON + COR + INTERC + VDBHC / DBH + DBHC x DBH + DBH2C x DBH² + RDBHC x RELDBH + RDBHSQC x RELDBH² + CRWNC x CR + CRSQC x CR² + SBAC x BAGE5 + BALC x BAL + SITEC x SI. RELDBH is DBH divided by the quadratic mean diameter of the trees that are 5.0 inches or larger, BAGE5 is the basal area of the trees that are 5.0 inches or larger, and CR is the crown ratio as a percent. The result is a change in squared diameter outside bark. It is converted to the inside bark scale in the code: DIAGRO = sqrt(DBH² + exp(lnDDS)) - DBH; DIAGRI = DIAGRO x BARK; ln(DDS) = ln[(DBH x BARK + DIAGRI)² - (DBH x BARK)²].
4. **NE.** The potential basal area increment is POTBAG = 0.7 x DGB1 x SI x (1 - exp(-DGB2 x DBH)). The BAL modifier, BAGMOD, is returned by subroutine BALMOD. The squared diameter grows by DELD = POTBAG x BAGMOD (in units of basal area) in each of 10 annual iterations: DBH is replaced by the diameter that has a basal area of 0.0054542 x DBH² + DELD. After the 10 iterations DIAGR = (DBH_end - DBH_start) x BARK, which is multiplied by COR2 when READCORD is used and has a lower bound of 0.0001. Then ln(DDS) = ln[DIAGR x (2 x DBH x BARK + DIAGR)] + COR.
5. **CR.** Subroutine GEMDG selects one equation for each of the 38 species of the variant and for the model type of the stand (IMODTY: 1, southwest mixed conifer; 2, southwest ponderosa pine; 3, Black Hills ponderosa pine; 4, spruce-fir; 5, lodgepole pine). The equations are shown in the table that follows this list. The variables are DPP (diameter, minimum 1.0 inch), BAT (stand basal area), BATEM (BAT with a minimum that depends on the model type: 1.0 for type 1, 21.0 for type 2, 5.0 for types 3 and 4, and 14.0 for type 5), BGTTBA (BAU / BA, the proportion of the stand basal area in diameter classes larger than the class of the tree; it is 0 for model type 1 when BAT is less than 65), SI, CR (proportion), SLOPE, ASP, RELDEN, BAL100 (BAL / 100), PBAL and PCCFI. Equations of the type "DF" predict the future diameter; DF is limited to the maximum diameter of the species, DBHMAX, and to DPP or more, and DIAGR = (DF - DPP) x BARK. Equations of the type "DDS" predict ln(DDS) directly, and DIAGR = sqrt(exp(DDS) + (DPP x BARK)^2) - DPP x BARK. DIAGR is multiplied by DSTAG when ISTAGF of the species is not 0, and by 0.80 for species PP and CI in model type 3. The result is ln(DDS) = ln[DIAGR x (2 x DPP x BARK + DIAGR)], with -9.21 when DIAGR is zero or less, and then WK2(i) = ln(DDS) + COR + DGCON. All 38 species are in a case, so the default case (ln(DDS) = -9.21) is not used.

The constants 60 and 80 in the equations of GF, MH, RC, WL and WB are elevations (in hundreds of feet) fixed in the source; the equations were taken from other variants for a fixed habitat type and elevation, as the source comments state. DGCON for the CR variant is added after GEMDG returns.

6. **ON.** The equation is annual and is in metric units. X1 = -B0 - BBAL x BALM - BHT x HTM - BSI x SIM - BBA x BAM - BDBHQ x QMDM - BAGS x AGS is constant over 10 iterations. In each iteration, ln(DG) = X1 + B1 x ln(DBHM) - B2 x DBHM, which is limited to the range -5 to 5, then exponentiated, limited to the range 0.0001 to B95 (the 95th percentile of the annual growth of the species), and added to DBHM (the diameter in centimeters). The increment in inches, converted to inside bark, is multiplied by COR2 when READCORD is used, and bounded below by 0.0001. Then ln(DDS) = ln[DIAGR x (2 x DBH x BARK + DIAGR)] + COR.
7. **BC.** BC has two equations. When the logical LV2ATV is true, the equation has the form of equation {4.2.1.1.1} with 0.01 x (DGCCF + SEICCF) x RELDEN in the constant. In the other biogeoclimatic zones (ICH, IDF, SBS, SBPS) the annual diameter increment in centimeters is exp(CONSPP + DGLD1 x DBH + DGDSQ1 x DBH² + DGBAL1 x BAL + DGDBAL1 x BAL / DBH + DGDBAL2 x BAL / ln(DBH + 1) + DGCR1 x CR) with a lower bound of exp(-9.21); it is converted to ln(DDS) in square inches.

**Special equations in the variants that use equation {4.2.1.1.1}.** The species in the next list use equations of another form.

- **Red alder.** For species RA in WC, PN, HI, OP, SO and EC, the diameter increment is DG = CONST - 0.166496 x DBH + 0.004618 x DBH² for DBH of 18.0 inches or less, and DG = CONST - (CONST / 10) x (DBH - 18) above 18.0, with CONST = 3.250531 - 0.003029 x BA and a lower bound of 0.1. In WC, PN, HI, OP and SO the bark ratio is evaluated as BRATIO(22, DBH, HT). Then ln(DDS) = ln[DG x (2 x DBH x BARK + DG)] + COR + ln(COR2).
- **Redwood and giant sequoia.** For species RW in WC, PN, HI, OP and NC, RW and GS in CA and OC, and species GS and RW (species 4 and 23) in WS, the outside bark increment is DGLT = exp(CONSPP + 0.185911 x ln(DBH) - 0.000073 x DBH² - 0.001796 x PBAL - 0.42078 x PRD + 0.589318 x ln(100 x CR) - 0.000926 x 100 x SLOPE - 0.002203 x 100 x SLOPE x cos(ASP)). CONSPP does not contain COR for these species. In WC the constant of the species is -3.502444 + 0.415435 x ln(SI), and the coefficient of DBH squared is zero. DGLT is converted to ln(DDS) = ln[((DBH + DGLT) x BARK)² - (DBH x BARK)²] + COR + ln(COR2). PRD is the relative density of the point, the Zeide relative density of the point divided by its maximum. The year basis of DGLT is not stated in the code.
- **Tanoak.** For species TO in CA and OC, DDS is multiplied by 2 (the equation is a 5-year estimate, changed to 10 years, as the source comment states).
- **Oaks in WS.** For species 28 to 40 and 43 of WS, which are 5-year equations, DDS is multiplied by 2.
- **OC and OP.** The equations of the FVS species predict a 10-year increment. After the ln(DDS) is computed, DDS is divided by 2 to give a 5-year estimate.
- **WS, smaller trees.** For trees smaller than 10.0 inches, species JP uses its own equation, and species DF, WF, RF, SF and BD use another. A bound on the maximum ln(DDS), DDSMAX, is coded for some species after WK2(i) is assigned, so it has no effect.

In all variants the lower bound of ln(DDS) is -9.21.

**Where the calibration and user multipliers enter.** COR is included in the equation of the species, as shown above. COR2 is added in DGCON as ln(COR2) when the READCORD or REUSCORD keyword is used. The BAIMULT multiplier, XDMULT, is applied in subroutine DGDRIV, as shown in the steps for the projection cycle, and not in subroutine DGF.

Subroutine DGDRIV has an extra task in the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). That is to direct estimation of large tree diameter and height growth, crown ratio change, and mortality using ORGANON equations for valid ORGANON trees. This step is done by calling the ORGANON subroutine EXECUTE and does not occur in any of the other FVS variants. Processing then continues somewhat as described below, with structural differences as discussed in [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants).

Subroutine DGDRIV then enters its own nested species and trees-within-species DO loops. Before the loops, DGDRIV copies the diameter increment of the previous cycle, DG(i), to work array WK1(i), where the mortality routines use it. In 18 variants (BC, BM, CA, CI, CR, EC, EM, HI, IE, KT, NC, OC, OP, SO, TT, UT, WC and WS) and in PN, which compiles the WC version of DGDRIV, DGDRIV also calls subroutine CLGMULT to load a tree-level growth multiplier from the climate extension into work array WK4(i). For each species, the serial correlation of diameter growth estimates from one cycle to the next is adjusted for the cycle length and diameter growth errors are calculated. The scale factors are attenuated and then the tree loop within species is entered. For each tree record the following steps are made.

1. The diameter inside bark is computed as D = DBH(i) × BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i)). The array DBH(i) is always the diameter outside bark; FVS does not keep an inside bark diameter array.
2. The expected change in squared inside bark diameter is DDS = exp(WK2(i) + ln(XDMULT)). WK2(i) is the ln(DDS) estimate from subroutine DGF, and XDMULT is the species multiplier from the BAIMULT keyword record (1.0 if none). In the variants listed above, DDS is also multiplied by WK4(i).
3. Subroutine DGSCOR returns the error term as a multiplier, FRM. DGSCOR draws an error from a normal distribution about the predicted ln(DDS), combines it with the error of the previous cycle (OLDRN) through the serial correlation, and draws again when the result is more than DGSD standard deviations from zero. The error is zero when DGSD is less than 1.0. It is also set to zero when the predicted ln(DDS) is greater than 5.0, and it is multiplied by (ln(DDS) − 4.0) when the predicted ln(DDS) is between 4.0 and 5.0. FRM is the exponential of the error.
4. The diameter increment is DG(i) = sqrt(D² + DDS × FRM) − D. When record tripling is in effect, the errors of the three records do not come from DGSCOR; see Serial correlation and random error of the diameter increment.
5. In the CI, CR, EM, IE and UT variants, DG(i) is limited so that it does not exceed 1.33 times the expected increment, sqrt(D² + DDS) − D. The limit applies to all species in the CR variant and to selected species in the other four (species 17 and 19 in CI; 11, 13 to 16 and 19 in EM; 19 and 22 in IE; 17 to 19 and 22 in UT).
6. DG(i) is multiplied by the dwarf mistletoe factor, MISDGF(i, species).
7. Subroutine DGBND bounds DG(i). Five versions are compiled. The IE version, which most variants compile, applies only the size limit: when DBH(i) + DG(i) is greater than SIZCAP(species,1) and SIZCAP(species,3) is less than 1.5, DG(i) is set to SIZCAP(species,1) − DBH(i), with a minimum of 0.01. The HI and WC versions (also compiled by OP and PN) first limit DG(i) to 7.92 × exp(−0.03 × DBH(i)), with DBH(i) taken as no more than 150, for all species except species 17, and then apply the size limit. The WS version first limits DG(i) to a species-specific function of DBH(i) (a × DBH^b × exp(c × DBH)) for the species and diameters it lists (DBH of 3.0 or more), and then applies the size limit. The SN version leaves DG(i) unchanged when DBH(i) is at or below the lower species-specific diameter DLODHI(species,1), sets DG(i) to 0.048 when DBH(i) is above the upper diameter DLODHI(species,2), and between the two diameters multiplies DG(i) by 1 + 0.90 x (DBH(i) - DLODHI(species,1)) / (DLODHI(species,1) - DLODHI(species,2)), with a minimum of 0.048, and then applies the size limit. The ON version limits DG(i) to 6.0 × exp(−0.03 × DBH(i)) and has no size limit.

Diameter growth is similarly assigned to tree record triples if record tripling is in effect and control returns to subroutine GRINCR. After subroutine DGDRIV, DG(i) is an inside bark increment on a YR-year basis. YR is 10 years in all variants except NC, OC, OP and SN, where it is 5 years. The source comment in subroutine GRINCR states that DG is returned on the YR basis, and the diameter increment is scaled to the cycle length by subroutine GRADD (see [Diameter increment through the projection cycle](#sec-diameter-increment-through-the-projection-cycle)).

**Serial correlation and random error of the diameter increment.** Subroutine DGDRIV calls subroutine AUTCOR at the start of each cycle (and once at the start of the projection, for the calibration). AUTCOR computes, for the cycle length, the variance multiplier, VMLT, and the covariance multiplier, COVMLT, of the ln(DDS) errors, from the autocorrelation function of an ARMA(1,1) process for the annual increments, as shown in equations {4.2.1.1.8} to {4.2.1.1.10}.

$$
BJRHO_1 = \frac{(1 - \phi\theta)(\phi - \theta)}{1 + \theta(\theta - 2\phi)}, \qquad BJRHO_i = \phi \cdot BJRHO_{i-1}, \quad i = 2, \ldots, 40
\tag{4.2.1.1.8}
$$

Where:

- BJRHO_i: Autocorrelation of the annual errors at a lag of i years (dimensionless)
- φ: Autoregressive parameter, BJPHI; the default is 0.74 in all variants
- θ: Moving average parameter, BJTHET; the default is 0.42 in all variants

$$
VMLT = N + 2 \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} BJRHO_i \,(N - i)
\tag{4.2.1.1.9}
$$

Where:

- VMLT: Variance multiplier of the current cycle (dimensionless)
- N: Length of the current cycle (years); N is INT(YR) at the start of the projection and FINT in the cycles
- BJRHO_i: Autocorrelation of the annual errors at a lag of i years, equation {4.2.1.1.8} (dimensionless)

$$
COVMLT = \sum_{i=1}^{L} BJRHO_i \, T_i
\tag{4.2.1.1.10}
$$

Where:

- COVMLT: Covariance multiplier between the current cycle and the preceding cycle (dimensionless)
- BJRHO_i: Autocorrelation of the annual errors at a lag of i years, equation {4.2.1.1.8} (dimensionless)
- L: Smaller of N plus the length of the preceding cycle, minus 1, and 40
- T_i: Number of pairs of years that are i years apart in the two cycles; T increases by 1 for each lag up to the smaller of the two cycle lengths, stays constant up to the larger of the two cycle lengths, and decreases by 1 for each lag after that

The keyword SERLCORR changes φ and θ. DGDRIV uses VMLT and COVMLT as follows. The correlation of the errors of two successive cycles is CORR = COVMLT / sqrt(VMLT x PVMLT), where PVMLT is VMLT of the preceding cycle. For each species, the standard deviation of the ln(DDS) error is SSIGMA = sqrt(ln[(sqrt(1 + 4 x VARDG x VMLT) + 1) / 2]), and SIG1 is calculated in the same way with PVMLT. The serial correlation of the species is RHO = ln[1 + CORR x sqrt((EVARP1 - 1)(EVARP2 - 1))] / (SIG1 x SSIGMA), where EVARP1 and EVARP2 are the values inside the logarithms of SIG1 and SSIGMA. RHOCP = sqrt(1 - RHO²). VARDG is the variance of the diameter growth error of the species and is calculated from the calibration (SIGMA). Subroutine DGSCOR then computes the error of tree i as FRM = BACHLO(0, SSIGMA) x RHOCP + RHO x OLDRN(i), where BACHLO returns a draw from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of SSIGMA. A new draw is made until |FRM| is no larger than DGSD x SSIGMA. The error is zero when DGSD is less than 1.0. It is also set to zero when the predicted ln(DDS) is greater than 5.0, and it is multiplied by (ln(DDS) - 4.0) when the predicted ln(DDS) is between 4.0 and 5.0. OLDRN(i) is then replaced by FRM, which is stored on the ln scale, and the multiplier of DDS is exp(FRM).

The default value of the keyword DGSTDEV (DGSD) is 2.0 in the AK, BC, CR, CS, EM, IE, KT, LS, NC, NE, ON, SN, SO, TT, UT and WS variants, 1.7 in the CA, CI, EC, HI, PN and WC variants, 1.5 in the BM variant, and 0 in the OC and OP variants. A DGSD of less than 1.0 means that no random error is added. OLDRN is also used in the height growth equation of the CS, LS and NE variants.

When the calibration is done, OLDRN(i) is initialized to the residual of ln(DDS) for the trees in the calibration sample, and, when the calibration conditions are met, to the value of the residual regression at the predicted ln(DDS) of the tree for the other trees. When the calibration is not done, OLDRN(i) is a random draw with a standard deviation of SIGMA, truncated at DGSD x SIGMA. OLDRN is set to zero for new trees from the regeneration establishment model. When record tripling is in effect, the errors of the tripled records do not come from DGSCOR; they are DGDRIV values FRM + CORR x OLDRN(i) for the original record, and FRU + CORR x OLDRN(i) and FRL + CORR x OLDRN(i), with FRU = 1.271 x SSIGMA x RHOCP and FRL = -1.549 x SSIGMA x RHOCP, for the two new records.

Subroutine HTGF has a similar construction as subroutine DGF does. It has nested species and trees-within-species DO loops controlling subroutine execution. Subroutine MULTS is called to retrieve large-tree height growth multipliers. Each trees’ height growth is bounded so current height plus height growth does not exceed a morphological maximum height for the species as entered in the fifth field of the TREESZCP keyword record (999 feet when the field is blank). Height growth estimates are assigned to record triples if record tripling is in effect and control returns to subroutine GRINCR. Height growth estimates at the end of subroutine HTGF are on a cycle-length basis.

For variants using site index curves to estimate height growth, two other subroutines play a major role in large tree height growth estimation. Subroutine HTCALC contains equations for the site index curves being used for each species. Subroutine HTGF calls subroutine FINDAG to estimate a trees’ age based on a trees’ height and species using the equations in subroutine HTCALC. Subroutine HTGF then adds 10 years to this age (5 years in the NC, OC and OP variants) and calls HTCALC to obtain an estimate of tree height at the end of the projection cycle based on tree age and species. Potential height growth is then the difference between the estimated beginning- and end-of cycle heights.

**Large-tree height increment.** Subroutine HTGF estimates the height increment for the cycle for each tree record. The potential height growth, the modifier, and the scaling are described in the following paragraphs for the variants that use the equations; the forms differ by variant, as shown in the table that follows them.

*Potential height growth from the site index curve.* BM, CA, CI (species MC), EC, HI, NC, OC, OP, PN, SO, TT, UT, WC and WS estimate the age of the tree from its height with subroutine FINDAG, and then calculate the height of the tree at the age plus 10 years (plus 5 years in NC, OC and OP) with subroutine HTCALC. FINDAG tries ages from 2 years in steps of 2 years until the site index curve height is within 2.0 feet of the height of the tree, or exceeds it. It returns the age, SITAGE, and the height of the curve at that age, SITHT; SITHT is not the height of the tree. The potential height growth is shown in equation {4.2.1.1.11}.

$$
POTHTG = HTCALC(SITAGE + A) - SITHT
\tag{4.2.1.1.11}
$$

Where:

- POTHTG: Potential height growth over A years (feet)
- HTCALC: Site index curve height of the species at a given age (feet)
- SITAGE: Age of the tree estimated by FINDAG (years)
- A: Age increment, 10 years in BM, CA, CI, EC, HI, PN, SO, TT, UT, WC and WS; 5 years in NC, OC and OP
- SITHT: Height of the site index curve at SITAGE (feet)

If SITAGE exceeds the maximum age of the curve, POTHTG is 0.1 foot. In SN the equation is a closed-form Chapman-Richards curve, H = B1 x SI^B2 x (1 - exp(B3 x AGE))^(B4 x SI^B5), HTCALC inverts it for the age, and the potential growth is the difference between the heights at the age plus 5 years and at the age. When the maximum height, B1 x SI^B2, exceeds the tree height by 1.0 foot or less, the height increment is 0.1 foot. LS, NE and CS use equations of the same kind, with 10 years, and with coefficients of the species taken from the array LTBHEC.

*Modifier of the potential height growth (WC, PN, HI, OP, BM, EC, SO, TT, UT, WS, CI and SN).* For the species that use the site index curve in these variants (the species are listed by case in the file of each variant), the potential height growth is multiplied by a modifier that is a weighted sum of a crown ratio function and a relative height function, as shown in equations {4.2.1.1.12} to {4.2.1.1.14}. The crown ratio function is Hoerl's special function, and the relative height function is a generalized Chapman-Richards function (Donnelly et al. 1992).

$$
HGMDCR = \min\left[1.0,\; CRA \left(\frac{ICR}{100}\right)^{CRB} \exp\left(CRC \cdot \frac{ICR}{100}\right)\right]
\tag{4.2.1.1.12}
$$

Where:

- HGMDCR: Crown ratio contribution (dimensionless), bounded above by 1.0
- ICR: Crown ratio (percent)
- CRA, CRB, CRC: Coefficients of the species; CRA is 100, CRB is 3.0 and CRC is -5.0 in CI

$$
HGMDRH = RHK \left[1 + FCTRKX \cdot \exp\left(FCTRRB \cdot FCTRXB\right)\right]^{FCTRM}
\tag{4.2.1.1.13}
$$

Where:

- HGMDRH: Relative height contribution (dimensionless)
- RHK: Coefficient, 1.0
- FCTRKX: (RHK / RHYXS)^(RHM - 1) - 1, where RHYXS is a coefficient of the species and RHM is a coefficient of the species (1.10 in WC)
- FCTRRB: -RHR / (1 - RHB), where RHR and RHB are coefficients of the species
- FCTRXB: RELHT^(1 - RHB) - RHXS^(1 - RHB), where RHXS is 0
- FCTRM: -1 / (RHM - 1)
- RELHT: HT / AVH, with a maximum of 1.5

$$
HTGMOD = 0.25 \cdot HGMDCR + 0.75 \cdot HGMDRH
\tag{4.2.1.1.14}
$$

Where:

- HTGMOD: Height growth modifier (dimensionless), bounded between 0.1 and 2.0; a value of zero or less is replaced by 0.1
- HGMDCR: Crown ratio contribution from equation {4.2.1.1.12} (dimensionless)
- HGMDRH: Relative height contribution from equation {4.2.1.1.13} (dimensionless)

The height increment for the cycle is HTG = POTHTG x HTGMOD, with a lower bound of 0.1 foot. The coefficients RHR, RHYXS and RHB are arrays of the species in subroutine HTGF (the values of the WC variant are in wc/htgf.f). In SN the lower bound is applied when HTGMOD is 0.1 or less.

*Other forms of the height increment equation.* The forms in the next list are written once. The table that follows lists the variant and species that use each form, with the arrays of coefficients and their lines in the source.

1. **Height from the diameter increment (HDG form).** HTG = exp(CON + HDGCOF x ln(DG)) + BIAS, where CON = HTCON + H2COF x HT^2 + HGLD x ln(DBH) + HGLH x ln(HT). HDGCOF, H2COF and HGLD are arrays of habitat group and species, BIAS is 0.4809 and HGLH is 0.23315 (EM species LL has HGLH written as the term 0.23315 x ln(HT) and a coefficient of -0.1997 on ln(DBH); TT species PP has CON = 2.03035 + 0.7316 - 0.00013358 x HT^2 - 0.5657 x ln(DBH) + 0.23315 x ln(HT) and a coefficient of 0.62144 on ln(DG)). DG is the diameter increment of the cycle from DGDRIV. HTG has a lower bound of 0.1 foot.
2. **Johnson SB form.** The height at the end of the period is predicted from the diameter at the end of the period. The coefficients COF(1) to COF(9) depend on the species group and on the crown ratio group K (K is 1 for crown ratio classes 1 and 2, 2 for classes 3 to 7, and 3 for classes 8 and 9, where the class is INT(ICR/10 + 0.5), with a maximum of 9). The calculation is shown in equation {4.2.1.1.15}.

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1 &= \frac{DBH - 0.1}{COF_1}, \qquad Y_2 = \frac{HT - 4.5}{COF_2}, \qquad F_i = \ln\frac{Y_i}{1 - Y_i} \\
Z &= \frac{COF_4 + COF_6 F_2 - COF_7 \left(COF_3 + COF_5 F_1\right)}{\sqrt{1 - COF_7^{2}}} - ZBIAS + ZADJ + ZACC \\
DIA &= DBH + \frac{DG}{BARK} \\
PSI &= COF_8 \left(\frac{DIA - 0.1}{0.1 + COF_1 - DIA}\right)^{COF_9} \exp\left(\frac{Z \sqrt{1 - COF_7^{2}}}{COF_6}\right) \\
H &= \frac{PSI}{1 + PSI}\, COF_2 + 4.5, \qquad HTG = \max(H, HT) - HT, \quad HTG \ge 0.1
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.1.15}
$$

Where:

- COF(1) to COF(9): Coefficients of the Johnson SB distribution of the species group and crown ratio group (arrays named in the table)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height at the start of the cycle (inches); a minimum of 0.2 inch is used in IE, CI and EM
- HT: Total height at the start of the cycle (feet)
- ZBIAS: Bias correction (BM, SO and TT): AZBIAS + BZBIAS x ELEV, with ELEV - 20 for BM species AS, SO species AS, and TT species AS and MM; ZBIAS is 0 when ELEV is less than 55 or more than 80, and 0 when Z - ZBIAS is 2.0 or more and ZBIAS is negative (the arrays AZBIAS and BZBIAS are zero in BM and SO)
- ZADJ: Adjustment for the bias of the height-diameter model, ZADJ = 0.1 - 0.10273 x Z + 0.00273 x Z^2 with a minimum of 0, added to Z for the species marked in the table
- ZACC: Accelerator for young lodgepole pine, calculated only in the first cycle when the stand age (IAGE) is given: when the age at the start, IXAGE = IAGE + IY(ICYC) - IY(1), is from 11 to 39 years, DBH is less than 9.0 inches, and Z is 2.0 or less, ZACC = 0.3564 x DG x FINT/YR x CLOSUR, with CLOSUR = PCT/100 (1.0 when RELDEN is less than 100), multiplied by 1.1 when the crown ratio class is 8 or 9; Z is then limited to 2.0
- DG: Diameter increment of the cycle from DGDRIV (inches)
- BARK: Bark ratio
- HTG: Height increment (feet); HTG is 0.1 foot when HT is 4.5 feet or less, when DBH is 0.1 + COF(1) or more, when HT is 4.5 + COF(2) or more, or when DIA is 0.1 + COF(1) or more (the distribution is undefined)

3. **Potential height growth of the EM variant (subroutine POTHTG).** For species WB, WL, DF, LP, ES, AF, PP and OS in EM, subroutine POTHTG returns the 10-year potential height growth PHTG. It is then adjusted: PHTG = PHTG x 0.706 x [1 - exp(-10.19 x CR)] x [1 - exp(-0.1 x 18.158 x DG)]^0.944 + 0.0265 x HT, and HTG = PHTG x HTMOD, where HTMOD = min[1.0, exp(2.54119 x ((HT/AVH)^0.250537 - 1))], with a lower bound of 0.1 foot. CR is the crown ratio as a proportion. POTHTG calculates an effective age from the height and site index and returns the difference between the heights at the effective age plus 10 years and at the effective age. Species WB, LP, WL and OS use the curve of Alexander, Tackle and Dahms, with CCF of 125 (A = 9.72443 - 0.00091 x SI100 x CCF - HT, B = -0.23733 + 0.0149 x SI100, C = 0.00160 - 0.00005 x SI100; EFAGE = (-B + sqrt(B^2 - 4AC)) / (2C); PHTG = -2.3733 + 0.00160 x (EFAG10^2 - EFAGE^2) + 0.1490 x SI100 - 0.00005 x SI100 x (EFAG10^2 - EFAGE^2)); species DF uses the height-age curve of Monserud (1985) with SI50; species ES and AF use a curve with asymptote SI100, B = 0.931764, C = 0.01679 and D = 0.302381, H10 = A x (1 - B x exp(-C x EFAG10))^(1/(1 - D)); species PP uses a curve with the constants P1 = 3.635794, P2 = 0.916307, P3 = 6.09478, P4 = 0.96483 and P5 = 0.277025 (see `em/pothtg.f`). EFAG10 is EFAGE + 10.
4. **Height-age curve with the GEMHT model (CR variant).** Subroutine GEMHT computes, for the tree at the start and at the end of the cycle (the age is AP + 10 and the diameter is DBH + DG/BARK), an even-aged height HHE and an uneven-aged height HHU. HHE comes from a site index curve that depends on the model type of the stand (`cr/gemht.f` lines 38 to 199: southwest mixed conifer, southwest ponderosa pine, Black Hills ponderosa pine, spruce-fir and lodgepole pine), multiplied by a ratio with a model-type minimum (0.768, 0.768, 0.793, 0.728, 0.742) of 1 - BAU/BA; the species equations that give HHU are in `cr/gemht.f` lines 200 to 421. The age of the tree, AP, is the age in the tree record, adjusted for the breast-height curves. The TT, UT and WS variants contain an inline version of the same logic for the species listed in the table. HTG = (HHE2 - HHE1) x ADJUST, where ADJUST is the value of the array HTOSI for the model type and the species. If the range of ages in the stand is more than 40 years and BA is 70 or more, trees with PCT of 10 or less get HHU2 - HHU1, and trees with PCT between 10 and 40 get XWT x (HHE2 - HHE1) x ADJUST + (1 - XWT) x (HHU2 - HHU1), with XWT = (PCT - 10) x (10/3) / 100. Species AS and PB are multiplied by 0.6253 + 0.00583 x SI (SI between 30 and 90). A random increment, ZZRAN x 0.1, is added, where ZZRAN is a normal draw truncated at DGSD standard deviations. When the stagnation option is on for the species (ISTAGF not 0), HTG is multiplied by (DSTAG + 1) / 2. HTG has a lower bound of 0.1 foot, and is then multiplied by exp(HTCON) x SCALE x XHMULT. In lodgepole pine (model type 5) trees with a breast-height age of 31 or less are brought to the height H30 = 5.25621 + 0.37515 x SI - 0.00082 x TCCF x SI times the age/31 when this exceeds the growth from the curve, where TCCF is the point CCF (0 when 125 or less).
5. **WS default equation.** HTG = HTCON + HGDG2 x DG + HGRDG2 x sqrt(DG) + HGBA2 x BA + HGBAI2 x [(DBH + DG)^2 - DBH^2] + HGLBA2 x ln(BA) + HGBLT2 x BAL + HGBAD2 x BAL / DBH + HGCR2 x ICR + HGDSQ x DBH^2, where BAL = (1 - PCT/100) x BA with a minimum of 0.001. The result is multiplied by 1.5 for species OS, WF, SF and JP, 1.25 for species DF and BD, 1.2 for species IC and RF, 1.15 for species PP and MP, and 0.75 for species TO, GC, AS, CL, MA and DG.

6. **Redwood and giant sequoia (LTHTG equation).** LTHTG = exp(1.412947 - 0.000204 x DBH^2 + 0.31971 x ln(DBH) + 0.394005 x ln(SI) + 0.399888 x ln(DG10) - 0.451708 x ln(HT)), and HTG = LTHTG x HGBND, where HGBND is 1.0 when HT is less than 217 feet, 1 - (HT - 217) / (380 - 217) with a minimum of 0.1 when HT is from 217 to 380 feet, and 0.1 when HT is 380 feet or more. DG10 is the 10-year outside bark diameter increment calculated in HTGF (0.1 when HT is less than 4.5 feet). In NC, LTHTG is multiplied by 0.5.
7. **CA modifier (CA, OC, and SO species SH and WO).** HTG = POTHTG x XMOD, with POTHTG from equation {4.2.1.1.11} (A is 10 years in CA and SO and 5 years in OC), and XMOD = 1.016605 x [1 - exp(-4.26558 x CR)] x exp[2.54119 x (RELHT^0.250537 - 1)], where CR is the crown ratio as a proportion and RELHT = HT/AVH with a maximum of 1.0 (RELHT is 1.0 when the PCCF of the point is less than 100).
8. **NC modifier.** HTG = POTHTG x XMOD, with POTHTG from equation {4.2.1.1.11} (A is 5 years), and XMOD = -0.02647 + 0.71338 x RELHT^2 + 0.06851 x CR/10 when the PCCF of the point is 50 or more, where CR is the crown ratio as a percent; XMOD is 1.0 otherwise. RELHT = HT/AVH, replaced by (RELHT + 1)/2 when PCCF is less than 100, with a maximum of 1.0.
9. **Chapman-Richards curve with a basal area modifier (LS, NE and CS).** HTCALC inverts the Chapman-Richards curve of the species (the array LTBHEC) for the age, and HTG1 is the difference between the heights at the age plus 10 years and at the age. HTG = HTG1 x (1 + OLDRN) x GMOD, where GMOD = 0.8 x [1 - (1 - GMODB)(1 - RELHTA)], GMODB is the value returned by subroutine BALMOD (the arguments differ among the variants: LS passes BA and RMSQD, CS passes BAL and BA, and NE passes only the species and diameter), RELHTA = min(HT/AVH, 1.0), and OLDRN is the diameter growth error of the tree (see Serial correlation and random error). IVAR is 1 in LS, 2 in CS and 3 in NE.
