In AK the annual increment is BASEHG = exp(B1 + B2 x DBH^2 + B3 x ln(DBH) + B4 x ELEV + B5 x ln(SI) + B6 x ln(DG10)), where the coefficients are the arrays NOPERMH1 to NOPERMH6 (lines 97 to 137 of `ak/htgf.f`), ELEV is in feet, DG10 = DG / BARK (0.1 when HT is less than 4.5 feet), and the permafrost modifier PFHMOD uses the arrays PERMH1 to PERMH6 for species TA, WS, LS, BE, OS, PB, AB, BA, AS, CW, WI, SU and OH (the species in the cases of `ak/htgf.f`). POTHTG = YR x BASEHG x PFHMOD, multiplied by 0.45 for species AD, WI and OH and by 0.65 for species SU, and then by a bound HGBND that is 1.0 below HTLO, 1 - (HT - HTLO) / (HTHI - HTLO) with a minimum of 0.1 between HTLO and HTHI, and 0.1 above HTHI. HTG is 0.1 when DG is 0.04 inch or less. In ON the increment is HTONT(DBH + DG/BARK, QMD10, BA10) - HTONT(DBH, QMD, BA), multiplied by the BAL modifier from BALMOD, with a lower bound of 0.1 foot.

*Scaling and limits.* After the equation of the variant is evaluated, HTG is multiplied by SCALE = FINT / YR, by the user-supplied height growth multiplier XHT (HTGMULT keyword), and by exp(HTCON), where HTCON is the natural logarithm of the READCORH multiplier (zero when no multiplier is given). In ON the READCORH multiplier (XHT2) is used in place of exp(HTCON). HTG is then multiplied by the dwarf mistletoe factor MISHGF, and is limited so that HT plus HTG is no greater than SIZCAP(species, 4), which is the fifth field of the TREESZCP keyword (999 feet when the field is blank). When the limit is applied, the minimum HTG is 0.1 foot. Large-tree height growth is not calibrated automatically; READCORH is the only way to change it (see Calibrate growth equations).

**Maximum height and maximum age in FINDAG.** Subroutine FINDAG returns the age of the tree on the site index curve, SITAGE, the height of the curve at that age, SITHT, the maximum age of the curve, AGMAX, and the maximum heights HTMAX (at the start of the cycle) and HTMAX2 (at the end of the cycle). When the height of the tree is HTMAX or more, SITAGE is AGMAX + (H - HTMAX) / 0.10. The values of HTMAX and AGMAX differ by variant: in WC, PN, HI and OP, AGMAX is 200 years and HTMAX = HDRAT1 x DBH + HDRAT2 (and HTMAX2 uses the diameter at the end of the cycle), where the coefficients are by height-diameter group (MAPHD, `wc/findag.f` lines 43 to 48 and `hi/findag.f` lines 43 to 48); in BM, HTMAX = AHMAX + BHMAX x SI (`bm/findag.f` lines 73 to 95; for species MH the value is multiplied by 3.281); in EC, HTMAX = AHMAX + BHMAX x SI for species WP, WL, DF, SF, RC, GF, LP, ES, AF, PP and WF, HTMAX = AHMAX + BHMAX x SI x 3.281 for species MH and OS, and HTMAX = AHMAX x DBH + BHMAX (and HTMAX2 with the diameter at the end of the cycle) for the species that use the logic of WC (`ec/findag.f` lines 106 to 163); in SO, TT, UT and WS, HTMAX is the array HTMAX of the species (`so/findag.f` line 70, `tt/findag.f` line 84, `ut/findag.f` line 86, `ws/findag.f` line 138); in NC, HTMAX is 300 feet and AGMAX is 200 years (`nc/findag.f` lines 43 and 57); in CA and OC, AGMAX is the array AGEMAX of the species, and 400 years for forests with IFOR of 5 or less (`ca/findag.f` lines 57 and 58).

**Exceptions in the large-tree height increment of BM and EC.** In BM, when the height of the tree is HTMAX or more, HTG = AASM + BASM x RELSI (with a minimum of 0.1 foot) x XHT x SCALE x exp(HTCON), where RELSI = (SI - SLO) / (SHI - SLO), SI is limited to the range SLO to SHI (the range from subroutine SITERANGE) and the arrays AASM and BASM are in `bm/htgf.f` lines 84 to 91. When SITAGE is more than AGMAX, POTHTG is 0.1 foot, and for species PP and OS in BM, POTHTG = -1.31 + 0.05 x SI with a minimum of 0.1 foot; species WJ gets its height growth from REGENT. In EC, for species WH, PY, WB, NF, LL, YC, WJ, BM, VN, RA, PB, GC, DG, AS, CW, WO, PL, WI and OH (the species of the WC case), when HT is more than HTMAX, HTG is 0.5 x DG, with a minimum of 0.1 foot, if HT is also HTMAX2 or more, and is zero otherwise (the code skips the rest of the calculation, although the source comment states that the normal calculation should follow); for the other species, when HT is HTMAX or more, HTG is 0.1 foot. In EC when SITAGE is AGMAX or more, POTHTG is 0.1 foot, and for species PP it is -1.31 + 0.05 x SI with a minimum of 0.1 foot. At the end of the calculation, EC limits HTG so that HT plus HTG is not more than HTMAX2 (the species of the WC case) or HTMAX (the other species), with a minimum of 0.1 foot.

#### Growing the small trees {#sec-growing-the-small-trees}

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine REGENT to estimate height and diameter growth using equations for trees smaller than a threshold diameter. Upon completion of subroutine REGENT, all trees will have an estimate of height and diameter growth. Whether that estimate is the estimate using the large tree equations in subroutines DGF and HTGF or the small tree equations contained in subroutine REGENT, or a weighted average of the two, depends on the attribute being estimated, the diameter of the tree, and one or more threshold diameter.

##### Threshold diameters

Several threshold diameters are used in subroutine REGENT:

For height growth, two threshold diameters are used. These are contained in local arrays subscripted by species, usually called XMIN(i) and XMAX(i). For species i, an estimate of height growth using small tree equations contained in subroutine REGENT is only calculated for trees with diameter (DBH(i)) less than XMAX(i). Height growth estimates from the small-tree model are weighted with the height growth estimates from the large tree model over a range of diameters, XMIN(i) to XMAX(i), in order to smooth the transition between estimates from the two models. In other words, the closer a tree’s DBH(i) value is to the minimum diameter XMIN(i), the more the growth estimate will be weighted towards the small-tree growth model. The closer a tree’s DBH(i) value is to the maximum diameter XMAX(i), the more the growth estimate will be weighted towards the large-tree growth model. If a tree’s DBH(i) value falls outside of the range given by XMIN(i) and XMAX(i), then the model will use only the estimates from the small-tree equations or large-tree equations in the growth estimate. The weight applied to the growth estimate is calculated using equation {4.2.1.2.1}, and applied as shown in equation {4.2.1.2.2}. The range of diameters for each species is shown in the appropriate variant overview document.

$$
XWT =
\begin{cases}
0 & DBH_i < X_{min} \\
\dfrac{DBH_i - X_{min}}{X_{max} - X_{min}} & X_{min} < DBH_i < X_{max} \\
1 & DBH_i > X_{max}
\end{cases}
\tag{4.2.1.2.1}
$$

Where:

- XWT: Weight applied to the growth estimates
- DBH_i: Diameter at breast height of tree i (inches)
- X_max: Maximum DBH, XMAX(i), in the diameter range (inches)
- X_min: Minimum DBH, XMIN(i), in the diameter range (inches)

$$
\text{Estimated growth} = \left[(1 - XWT) \times STGE\right] + \left[XWT \times LTGE\right]
\tag{4.2.1.2.2}
$$

Where:

- Estimated growth: Growth estimate of the tree record: the weighted combination of the small-tree and large-tree estimates
- XWT: Weight applied to the growth estimates, equation {4.2.1.2.1}
- STGE: Growth estimate obtained using the small-tree equations
- LTGE: Growth estimate obtained using the large-tree equations

For diameter growth, the small-tree estimate is considered only for trees with DBH(i) less than a threshold diameter that is specific to the variant and often to the species. The threshold may be contained locally in subroutine REGENT (for example in the arrays XMAX(i), DGMIN(i) or DGMAX(i), or in the variable BKPT), or it may be contained in an array subscripted by species called BREAK(i) in the GGCOM labeled COMMON block and initialized in subroutine BLKDAT. The values are listed in the table in [Diameter increment through the projection cycle](#sec-diameter-increment-through-the-projection-cycle). Trees with DBH(i) greater than or equal to the threshold diameter keep the diameter growth estimate obtained using the large tree equations. For trees below the threshold, the small-tree estimate either replaces the large-tree estimate or is averaged with it, depending on the variant and the species. Averaging is used in the AK, CA, CS, HI, LS, NC, NE, OC, ON, OP, PN, SO, WC and WS variants for the species shown in that table, which also gives the weights. In the other variants, and for the other species of the variants listed, the small-tree estimate replaces the large-tree estimate.

For a few species in some variants, equations contained in subroutine REGENT are used to estimate height and diameter growth for all sized trees. For example, this happens with pinyon pine in the Central Rockies (CR) variant. In these cases, the logic is the same as just discussed with the threshold diameters being set to artificially high values so only estimates using the small tree equations are used.

##### Growth estimation and calibration

Subroutine REGENT is another one of those subroutines containing two sections; the top section is used for growth estimation in projection cycling; the bottom section is used for calibration in projection initialization. The structure of each section is similar, and understanding the top section will lead to understanding the bottom section. First, the overall structure of subroutine REGENT will be described and then this structure will be broken down into more detail.

For most variants, a single pair of nested species and trees-within-species DO loops control subroutine execution. In these variants, height growth is estimated for the period length for which the small tree equations were fit (REGYR: 10 years in the AK, BM, CR, CS, EC, HI, LS, NE, ON, PN, UT and WC variants; 5 years in the CA, NC, OC, OP and SN variants; in SO, 5 years for species SH and WO and 10 years for the others; in WS, 10 years for species GB and MC and 5 years for the others), scaled to the cycle length, and then weighted with height growth estimates previously calculated using the large tree equations. Diameter growth is then estimated for the cycle length and converted to the YR basis used by subroutine DGDRIV. The conversion is made on the DDS scale: DDS = G × (2 × BARK × D + G) × YR/L, then DG(i) = sqrt((D × BARK)² + DDS) − BARK × D, where G is the small-tree increment for the cycle length of L years converted to inside bark, D is DBH(i) and BARK is BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i)). Where the small-tree and large-tree increments are averaged, the small-tree increment is converted before it is averaged with the large-tree increment, which is already on the YR basis. (Species 41 in the WS variant is the exception: its increment is not converted.) Diameter growth is scaled back to the cycle length in subroutine GRADD, not in subroutine UPDATE (see [Diameter increment through the projection cycle](#sec-diameter-increment-through-the-projection-cycle)).

Some variants use a slightly different logic because the small tree height growth equations were fit to 5-year data. To avoid bias associated with projection cycles longer than the period to which the equation was fit, the projection cycle is first divided into periods that are no longer than 5-years in length (the CI, EM, IE, KT, TT and BC variants). The cycle is divided as evenly as possible: the number of periods is the number of whole 5-year periods in the cycle, plus 1 when a remainder exists, the length of each period is the integer quotient of the years that remain and the periods that remain, and the last period receives the remainder (a 10-year cycle has 2 periods of 5 years, a 7-year cycle has periods of 3 and 4 years, and a 13-year cycle has periods of 4, 4 and 5 years). A triple-nested DO loop structure is used to estimate end of cycle tree height for each tree record which gets stored in work array WK3(j), where j is the tree index. The outside loop is over periods, the middle loop is over species, and the inner loop is over tree records within species. Stand density statistics and tree attributes are updated each period. The height estimate for the last period is scaled to the length of the last period. Double nested species and trees-within-species DO loops are then entered. Height growth for the projection cycle is obtained by subtracting the start-of-cycle tree height from the end-of-cycle tree height. This estimate gets weighted with height growth estimates previously calculated using the large tree equations as discussed above. Diameter growth is estimated and then scaled to a 10-year basis for rescaling in subroutine UPDATE.

###### A closer look at the logic

The overall structure will now be broken down into more detail. Small tree height growth is estimated using regression equations with independent variables being individual tree attributes and current stand conditions. Once small tree height growth is obtained, small tree diameter growth is estimated using species-specific height-diameter curves. Default height-diameter curves by species for a variant are detailed in the variant overview document but the default coefficients will have been changed if they were calibrated to the input data as described in [Initialization tasks](#sec-initialization-tasks).

Subroutine REGENT first calls subroutine DBCHK to see if debug output is to be written.

For variants using sub-cycling over periods, the number of periods and length of each period are computed and necessary independent variables containing the beginning-of-cycle values are initialized.

Subroutine REGENT then retrieves any multipliers or management flags scheduled for the current projection cycle with calls to subroutine MULTS.

Mid-cycle measures of stand density are needed by subroutine REGENT in all variants. Trees coming out of the regeneration establishment model (see [Disturbance effects and dynamics](#sec-disturbance-effects-and-dynamics)) use equations in subroutine REGENT to grow trees in height from the time they are age 5 to the end of the projection cycle in which they become established. So estimates of stand density are needed 5 years into a projection cycle. Also, in variants using period sub-cycling, estimates of stand density are needed at the beginning of each period. The methods by which estimates of stand density are computed are completely different depending on whether period sub-cycling is being used.

In the BM, CR, EC, HI, OP, PN, SO, UT, WC and WS variants, when subroutine REGENT is called from the regeneration establishment model, the crown competition factor and the average height of the 40 largest diameter trees are interpolated: each is (5 / FINT) times the value at the end of the projection cycle plus ((FINT - 5) / FINT) times the value at the start of the cycle (after any thinning). In the other calls, and in the other variants, the values at the start of the cycle are used. Remember that values of these variables are needed to estimate growth on trees in the regeneration establishment model which is being called near the end of the projection cycle, after growth has been estimated on all trees previously in the inventory. So values of these variables for the end of the projection cycle, prior to regeneration establishment, can be calculated.

For variants using period sub-cycling, the process is much more complicated since estimates of stand crown competition factor and basal area are needed for the start of each period for normal processing. Note that if the projection cycle is more than 5 years in length, then start of period estimates can be used for calculating the values needed for estimating growth on regeneration establishment trees; if the projection cycle length is less than 5 years in length then all growth on regeneration establishment trees will be estimated in the regeneration establishment subroutines. The contribution of large trees to stand basal area and crown competition factor is computed from 10-year predicted diameter increment. This value is annualized and then multiplied by the period sub-cycle length to determine the contribution of each tree for the sub-cycle. A 1.5% annual rate of mortality is assumed in this calculation (the number of trees is multiplied by 0.985 raised to the number of years). The contribution of small trees is based on growth predictions made for the preceding period sub-cycle. Subroutine CCFCAL is called to estimate the crown competition factor for each tree record in this calculation. If necessary, the height-diameter function used in diameter growth estimation is then adjusted based on stand crown competition factor and average height of the 40 largest diameter trees; this is only needed in some variants using sub-cycling logic.

In variants using period sub-cycling, the triple nested DO loops to estimate tree height at the end of the projection cycle is next. Subroutine CCFCAL is called at several places in the looping structure to estimate the crown competition factor for individual trees for the period sub-cycle.

In all variants, the double nested DO loop structure to estimate diameter and height growth is next. These loops follow the general structure discussed above. Height and diameter growth are then assigned to tripled tree records if record tripling is in effect and program control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine OPFIND to check for any FIXDG or FIXHTG keyword records scheduled for the projection cycle. If any are found, OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to retrieve parameters associated with each of these keyword records. OPDONE, another entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to mark the activities’ disposition.

For a FIXDG activity, a tree record is included when its species matches the species or species group in the record (0 includes all species) and its diameter at the start of the cycle, DBH(i), is at least the lower diameter limit and less than the upper diameter limit. A negative multiplier is set to 0, a negative lower limit is set to 0, and an upper limit that is 0 or less is set to 999. For each included record, DG(i) is multiplied by the multiplier; the tripled records of the tree receive the same multiplier. Because FIXDG is applied after subroutines DGDRIV and REGENT, it multiplies the small-tree increments as well as the large-tree increments, and it multiplies the increment itself (an inside bark increment on the YR basis), not the change in squared diameter. FIXHTG applies a multiplier to HTG(i) with the same species and diameter test; a negative multiplier is set to 0. Unlike FIXDG, the lower and upper diameter limits are not changed when they are negative or zero.

FVS is now done with basic growth estimates. However, growth estimates may be modified later in the projection cycle to account for fertilization or insect and disease effects on growth.

###### Small-tree height equations

**Equations of the small-tree height increment.** The equation of the species and variant is evaluated by subroutine REGENT for trees smaller than XMAX. The following variants use the equations listed. HI, OP, PN and WC use subroutine SMHGDG, which returns the 5-year height and diameter increments from the equation in {4.2.1.2.3} to {4.2.1.2.5}.

$$
DGS = \frac{DMAX}{1 + \exp\left[\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 PTBA + \alpha_2 \ln(PTBA + 2.71) + \alpha_3 PTBAL + \alpha_4 \ln(PTBAL + 2.71) + \alpha_5 BOOST + \alpha_6 CR + \alpha_7 RELHT + \alpha_8 \sqrt{RELHT} + \alpha_9 SI\right]}
\tag{4.2.1.2.3}
$$

Where:

- DGS: Five-year diameter increment (inches)
- DMAX: Coefficient of the species (array in subroutine SMHGDG)
- α0 to α9: Coefficients of the species (the array ALPHA in subroutine SMHGDG)
- PTBA: Basal area of the point where the tree is located (square feet per acre)
- PTBAL: Basal area in larger trees on the point (square feet per acre)
- BOOST: Term of equation {4.2.1.2.4}
- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)
- RELHT: HT / AVHT, with a maximum of 1.5; AVHT is AVH, and for the regular call in the first 5 years AVHT is (5 / FINT) x AVH + ((FINT - 5) / FINT) x ATAVH
- SI: Site index (feet); for species DF in WC, 5.21486 + 0.66486 x SI is used

$$
BOOST =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{1 + \exp(-3.1 + 0.18 \cdot PTBA)} & PTBA < 100 \\
0 & PTBA \ge 100
\end{cases}
\tag{4.2.1.2.4}
$$

Where:

- BOOST: Term of the five-year diameter increment equation {4.2.1.2.3}
- PTBA: Basal area of the point where the tree is located (square feet per acre)

$$
HG5 = \frac{DGS}{BETA}, \qquad DG5 =
\begin{cases}
DGS & HT \ge 4.5 \\
BETA\,(HT + HG5 - 4.5) & HT < 4.5 \text{ and } HT + HG5 \ge 4.5 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{4.2.1.2.5}
$$

Where:

- DG5: Five-year diameter increment (inches)
- DGS: Five-year diameter increment from equation {4.2.1.2.3} (inches)
- BETA: Coefficient of the species (array in subroutine SMHGDG)
- HT: Tree height (feet)

HG5 is the five-year height increment (feet).

In WC, PN and HI the equation is evaluated twice in each cycle to build a 10-year increment, because REGYR is 10 years in those variants; in OP it is evaluated once, with REGYR of 5 years. REGENT then forms HTGR = (HTGR + ZZRAN x 0.1) x XRHGRO x SCALE x CON x WK4(i), where ZZRAN is a normal draw redrawn when it is above 0.5 or below -2.0, XRHGRO is the user-supplied small-tree height growth multiplier (REGHMULT), CON is the calibration multiplier of the species, and WK4(i) is the climate multiplier. HTGR has a lower bound of 0.1 foot.

*Small-tree height increment of the CR variant.* REGYR is 10 years. For species other than AS and PB, the 10-year increment is the product of the potential growth, a density modifier and a vigor modifier, as shown in equations {4.2.1.2.6} to {4.2.1.2.8}.

$$
HTGR = POTHTG \cdot PCTRED \cdot VIGOR \cdot CON, \qquad POTHTG = \frac{SITEAR}{15 - 4 \cdot RELSI} \cdot HTADJ
\tag{4.2.1.2.6}
$$

Where:

- HTGR: Height increment before the weighting with the large-tree estimate (feet)
- PCTRED: Density modifier from equation {4.2.1.2.7}, between 0.01 and 1.0
- VIGOR: Vigor modifier from equation {4.2.1.2.8}; for species BC, PI, UJ, GO, AW, EM, BK, SO, AJ, RM, OJ, ER, PM, PD and AZ, it is replaced by 1 - (1 - VIGOR) / 3
- CON: RHCON x exp(HCOR), the calibrated multiplier of the species
- SITEAR: Site index of the species (feet)
- RELSI: (SI - SITELO) / (SITEHI - SITELO), where SI is bounded by the arrays SITELO and SITEHI of the species
- HTADJ: Adjustment of the species (array in subroutine REGENT; 1.10 for species RC and WL, and 1.00 for the others)

$$
PCTRED = AB_1 + X\left(AB_2 + X\left(AB_3 + X\left(AB_4 + X\left(AB_5 + X \cdot AB_6\right)\right)\right)\right), \qquad X = \min\left[300, \; AVHT \cdot \frac{CCF}{100}\right]
\tag{4.2.1.2.7}
$$

Where:

- PCTRED: Density modifier, between 0.01 and 1.0
- AB_1 to AB_6: 1.11436, -0.011493, 0.43012E-4, -0.72221E-7, 0.5607E-10 and -0.1641E-13
- AVHT: Average height of the 40 largest trees per acre (feet); in the establishment call, interpolated: (5 / FINT) x AVH + ((FINT - 5) / FINT) x ATAVH, and likewise for CCF
- CCF: Stand crown competition factor (percent)

$$
VIGOR = \min\left[1.0, \; 150\, CR^{3} \exp(-6\, CR) + 0.3\right]
\tag{4.2.1.2.8}
$$

Where:

- VIGOR: Vigor modifier
- CR: Crown ratio (proportion)

For species AS and PB, HTGR = [26.9825 x (AGE + 10)^1.1752 - 26.9825 x AGE^1.1752] / (2.54 x 12) x RSIMOD x CON x 0.75, with RSIMOD = 0.5 x (1 + RELSI) and AGE the age of the tree (minimum 5 years). Then HTGR = (HTGR + ZZRAN x 0.2) x XRHGRO x SCALE x WK4(i), where ZZRAN is a normal draw redrawn when it is above 0.5 or below -2.0 (zero when DGSD is below 1.0), and the weighting of the next paragraph is applied. For trees that are not established by the establishment model, SCALE is FNT / REGYR, where FNT is FINT, or FINT - 5 in the establishment call.

*Small-tree height increment of the KT variant.* In the period sub-cycles, the height at the end of the period of a tree of species other than species 11 is H2 = H1 + HTGRL x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO x CON, where HTGRL = RHCONS + BH x H1 + HTHS2 x H1^2 + BBAL x BAL + BBA x ln(BA) + HTPC1 x PCCF1 + (HTCRS + HTCRS2 x CR) x CR, with a lower bound of 0. For species OT (species 11), HTGRL = exp(RHCONS + BH x ln(H1) + BCCF x RDJ + BBALMH x BALMH + HCOR) and H2 = H1 + HTGRL x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO. H1 is the height at the start of the period, KPER is the length of the period, and the coefficients are arrays of the species and habitat group in subroutine REGENT (see `kt/regent.f`).

*Weighting with the large-tree estimate.* The weight, XWT, is shown in equation {4.2.1.2.1}, with XWT = 0 when the call comes from the regeneration establishment model. For species RW in WC, PN and OP, the code averages the small-tree and large-tree estimates when the call is not from the regeneration establishment model, and then applies the weights of equation {4.2.1.2.2} twice.

**Small-tree height growth in the variants with a 5-year sub-cycle.** The CI, EM, IE, KT, TT and BC variants divide the cycle into periods that are no longer than 5 years. The number of periods is the number of whole 5-year periods in the cycle, plus 1 when a remainder exists. The cycle is divided as evenly as possible; the length of each period is the integer quotient of the years that remain and the periods that remain, and the last period receives the remainder. A 7-year cycle has periods of 3 and 4 years, a 10-year cycle has two periods of 5 years, a 12-year cycle has three periods of 4 years, and a 13-year cycle has periods of 4, 4 and 5 years. The height at the end of each period is calculated with the stand density at the beginning of the period. For the trees that are 3.0 inches or larger, the contribution to the basal area and to the crown competition factor at the beginning of the next period is the annualized 10-year increment multiplied by the years of the period, with the number of trees per acre multiplied by 0.985^K, where K is the number of years since the start of the cycle (a mortality rate of 1.5 percent per year).

**Other equations of the small-tree height increment.** The next paragraphs give each form once. In the variants with 5-year sub-cycles (CI, EM, IE, KT, TT and BC), the equations are evaluated for each period of the cycle; the height at the end of the period is H2 and the height at the start is H1.

*SMHTGF of BM, EC and SO.* Subroutine SMHTGF returns the height growth over DTIME years, HHT, as a function of the site index. The Chapman-Richards form is shown in equation {4.2.1.2.9}; the other forms are in the table that follows.

$$
\begin{aligned}
EFFAGE &= 0 \;\; (MODE = 0), \qquad EFFAGE = \frac{\ln\left[\left(1 - \left(\frac{C_1 H}{SI}\right)^{1/C_4}\right) / C_2\right]}{C_3} \;\; (MODE = 1) \\
HHT &= \frac{SI}{C_1}\left[1 - C_2 \exp\left(C_3 \,(EFFAGE + DTIME)\right)\right]^{C_4} - \frac{SI}{C_1}\left[1 - C_2 \exp\left(C_3 \cdot EFFAGE\right)\right]^{C_4}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.2.9}
$$

Where:

- HHT: Height growth over DTIME years (feet)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)
- H: Height of the tree (feet)
- DTIME: Length of the period (years)
- C1 to C4: Constants given in the table
- MODE: Argument of the subroutine, 0 or 1 (EFFAGE is 0 when MODE is 0, and is calculated from H when MODE is 1)

In EC species RC, EFFAGE is 100 when the argument of the logarithm is zero or less.

SO species AF uses equation {4.2.1.2.10}.

$$
DOMHTGR = \frac{5\,(2.2227 + 0.4314 \cdot SI)}{29.0 - 0.05 \cdot SI}, \qquad HHT = DOMHTGR \cdot 1.016605\,\left[1 - \exp(-4.26558\, CR)\right]\exp\left[2.54119\left(RELHT^{0.250537} - 1\right)\right]
\tag{4.2.1.2.10}
$$

Where:

- CR: Crown ratio as a proportion (the percent divided by 100 in SO; the percent divided by 10 in CA and OC, as coded)
- RELHT: HT / AVH
- HHT: Height growth (feet)
- SI: Site index of the species (feet)

*SMHTGF of CA, OC and WS.* The subroutine returns the height growth over 5 years of each species group. FACTOR = SPADJF x (0.80 + 0.004 x (SI - 50)) in CA and OC (SPADJF is an array of the species, `ca/smhtgf.f`), BALT is BAL with a minimum of 5.0, and HTGR has a minimum of 0.1 foot. The equations are listed in the next table.

*Forms of REGENT in the variants with 5-year sub-cycles.* IE, EM, CI and TT assemble the small-tree equations from the variants where the equations of each species originated. The form is selected by species.

1. **NI form (IE species WP, WL, DF, GF, WH, RC, LP, ES, AF, PP, MH, WB, LL and OS; EM species LL).** ln(HTGRL) = CON + BH x ln(H1) + BCCF x RDJ + BBAL x BAL, and H2 = H1 + exp(HTGRL) x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO (x WK4(i) in IE), where KPER is the length of the period, RDJ is the crown competition factor at the start of the period, BH is RHLH, BCCF is RHCCF and BBAL is RHBAL (arrays of the species), and CON is RHCON + HCOR in this form (RHCON x exp(HCOR) in the other forms; `ie/regent.f` lines 410 to 418). The diameter range of the weighting is XMIN to XMAX of the species (`ie/regent.f` lines 170 to 173).
2. **TT form (IE species LM and PY; EM species LM; CI species WB, PY and LM; TT species WB, LM, DF, BS, AS, LP, ES, AF and OS).** BETA1 = exp(B0A + B1A x ln(TPCCF)), BETA2 = exp(B0B + B1B x ln(TPCCF)), HTG1 = BETA1 + BETA2 x CR, STDDEV = HTG1 x (S0 + S1 x CR), and HTGRL = HTG1 + ZRAND x STDDEV, with a lower bound of 0.1 foot, where CR is the crown ratio as a percent, TPCCF is the point CCF for the period (between 25 and 300), and ZRAND is a normal draw between -2.0 and 2.0 that is redrawn when the previous growth was 0.1 foot or less. In IE and CI the constants are B0A = 1.17527, B1A = -0.42124, B0B = -2.56002, B1B = -0.58642, S0 = 1.08720 and S1 = -0.00230; in EM and TT the constants are the arrays B0ACCF, B1ACCF, B0BCCF, B1BCCF, B0ASTD and B1BSTD (subroutine SMHTGF). H2 = H1 + HTGRL x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO x CON (x WK4(i) in IE, CI and TT as coded).
3. **CR and UT form (IE species PM, RM, AS, MM, PB, CO and OH; EM species RM, AS, PB, GA, CW, BA, PW, NC and OH; CI species AS, WJ, MC, CW and OH; TT species PM, UJ, RM, BI, MM, NC, MC and OH).** HTGRL = POTHTG x PCTRED x VIGOR x CON, with PCTRED and VIGOR as in equations {4.2.1.2.7} and {4.2.1.2.8}, and with POTHTG of the species: in IE, POTHTG = (SJ/5) x (1.5 x SJ - H) / (1.5 x SJ) x 0.83 for the species of the CR and UT form (SJ is the site index of the species); in EM, POTHTG = SI / (15 - 4 x RELSI) for species GA, CW, BA, PW, NC and OH, and (SI/10) x (1.5 x SI - H1) / (1.5 x SI) for species RM; in TT, POTHTG = (SJ/5) x (1.5 x SJ - H) / (1.5 x SJ) x 0.83 for the species other than MM. For the aspen species (IE species AS, MM and PB; EM species AS and PB; CI species AS; TT species MM), HTGRL = [26.9825 x (SITAGE + 10)^1.1752 - 26.9825 x SITAGE^1.1752] / (2.54 x 12) x RSIMOD x CON x 0.75, where SITAGE is the age from FINDAG (the age of the tree record, ABIRTH, in the establishment call) in IE, CI and TT, the age of the tree record, ABIRTH, in EM, and RSIMOD = 0.5 x (1 + RELSI). VIGOR is replaced by 1 - (1 - VIGOR) / 3 for species PM and RM in IE, species RM in EM, species WJ in CI, and species PM, UJ and RM in TT. H2 = H1 + HTGRL x SCALE in IE and in CR-type species, with SCALE = NTYR / YR (a 10-year estimate); in EM, H2 = H1 + HTGRL x FINT / 10.
4. **CI form (CI species WP, WL, DF, GF, WH, RC, LP, ES, AF, PP and OS).** HTGRL = SCNST + SHTBA x RELHT x PTBAA + SPBAL x PTBALI + SBAL x TBAL + SHDM1 x RHDM1 + SHDM2 x RHDM2 + SPTBA x PTBAA, and H2 = H1 + HTGRL x SCALE x XRHGRO x CON, where PTBAA is the basal area of the point, PTBALI is the basal area in larger trees on the point, TBAL = (1 - PCT/100) x BA, RELHT is the relative height (maximum 1.5), and SCNST (the array CNST), SHTBA (HTBA), SPBAL (PBAL), SBAL (BAL), SHDM1 (HDM1), SHDM2 (HDM2) and SPTBA (PTBA) are arrays of the species in `ci/regent.f` lines 192 to 259; CON = RHCON x exp(HCOR); XMIN and XMAX are at lines 177 to 182. The potential growth of the CI-origin species of CI that use the CR and UT form is POTHTG = (SJ/5) x (1.5 x SJ - H) / (1.5 x SJ) x 0.83 (`ci/regent.f` line 602).
5. **CI form in TT (TT species PP).** HTGRL = 2.764559 - 0.009643 x BA + 0.025303 x RCR^2, where RCR is the crown ratio class of the tree, ((ICR - 1) / 10) + 1, with a maximum of 9, and H2 = H1 + HTGRL x SCALE x XRHGRO x CON, with SCALE = NTYR / REGYR. In TT the TT form of item 2 uses SCALE = KPER / REGYR, and species AS has HTGRL multiplied by RSIMOD = 0.5 x (1 + RELSI), with RELSI = (SITEAR(AS) - 30) / 70 between 0 and 1.

*Small-tree height increment of the UT variant.* REGYR is 10 years. POTHTG = SJ / 5 for species WB, LM, DF, WF, BS, LP, ES, AF, PP and OS; POTHTG = (SJ/5) x (1.5 x SJ - H) / (1.5 x SJ) x 0.83 for species PI, WJ, GO, PM, RM, UJ, OH, GB, NC, FC, BE, MC and BI; for species AS, HTGR = [26.9825 x (SITAGE + 10)^1.1752 - 26.9825 x SITAGE^1.1752] / (2.54 x 12) x RSIMOD x CON x 0.75. For the other species HTGR = POTHTG x PCTRED x VIGOR x CON, with VIGOR replaced by 1 - (1 - VIGOR) / 3 for species PI, WJ, GO, PM, RM, UJ, GB and OH. PCTRED is calculated as in equation {4.2.1.2.7}. The coefficients AB(1) to AB(6) are 1.11436, -0.011493, 0.43012E-4, -0.72221E-7, 0.5607E-10 and -0.1641E-13 in the CR, UT, BM, EC, SO, TT and WS variants (the DATA statement AB of each `regent.f`); the WC, PN, HI and OP variants have 0.43015E-4 for AB(3).

**Small-tree height increment of CA and OC.** REGYR is 5 years. XMAX is 4.0 inches (10.0 for species GS and RW), XMIN is 2.0 inches, and the diameter threshold of the diameter increment, DGMIN, is 3.0 inches (7.0 for GS and RW). For each tree, CR = ICR/10, BAL = (1 - PCT/100) x BA, and RELHT = HT/AVH with a maximum of 1.05. Subroutine SMHTGF returns HTGRR (see the table above), and HTGR = (HTGRR x CON + ZZRAN x 0.1) x XRHGRO x SCALE, where CON = RHCON x exp(HCOR), ZZRAN is a normal draw redrawn when above 0.5 or below -2.0, and SCALE is FNT/REGYR. The weighting of equation {4.2.1.2.2} is applied once for all species; for species GS and RW, HTGR is first averaged with the large-tree increment, (HTGR + HTG)/2, unless the call is from the regeneration establishment model, and then weighted (`ca/regent.f` and `oc/regent.f`).

**Small-tree height increment of BC.** REGYR is 5 years. XMAX and XMIN are 4.0 and 2.0 inches for all species when LV2ATV is false, and, when LV2ATV is true, XMAX is 10.0 inches (5.0 for species PL) and XMIN is 2.0 inches (1.0 for species PL) (`canada/bc/regent.f` lines 209 to 212). The height at the end of each period is as follows.

- LV2ATV true, species flagged by subroutine SEISTHG (LSPPOK): HTGRL = STHG_CON + B1X + B3X + RAN, where STHG_CON = -0.00101 x ELEV (m), B1X = 0.518176 x ln(H1 in meters), B3X = -0.003254 x RDJ, and RAN is a draw from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.62921; H2 = H1 + exp(max(-40, HTGRL)) x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO x 3.28084.
- LV2ATV true, other species: the NI form (item 1 above), H2 = H1 + exp(max(-40, HTGRL)) x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO.
- LV2ATV false, zone SBS: HTGRL = (STG%CON + STG%HT x H1m) / [1 + STG%EXPMLT x exp(STG%HCCFL x H1m / max(CCFL, 36) + STG%CCFSL x CCFS / max(CCFL, 36))] x 0.0328084 x exp(RHCON), where H1m is H1 in meters; H2 = H1 + HTGRL x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO.
- LV2ATV false, other zones: HTGRL = exp(max(-88, STG%CON + RHCON + STG%LNHT x ln(max(2, H1m)) + STG%HT x max(2, H1m) + STG%BAL x BAL x 0.2295643 x 0.01 + STG%CCF x RDJ)) x 3.28084; H2 = H1 + HTGRL x (KPER / REGYR) x XRHGRO.

The random increment is drawn with ZZRAN between -1.5 and 1.0: HTGR = HTGR1 x exp(ZZRAN x HSIGMA) when LV2ATV is true, and HTGR = max(0, HTGR1 + ZZRAN x STG%SD) otherwise.

**Small-tree height increment of WS.** REGYR is 10 years for species GB and MC and 5 years for the other species. XMAX and XMIN are arrays of the species (`ws/regent.f` lines 166 to 178; XMAX is 3.5 inches for most species, 4.0 or 10.0 for others, and XMIN is 2.0 inches for most species and 1.0 inch for several), and SMTMAP (line 180) assigns the species to the groups of subroutine SMHTGF. CR = ICR/10, BAL = (1 - PCT/100) x BA, and CON = RHCON x exp(HCOR). The species use the following equations.

- Species MC (from the SO variant): VIGOR = min[1.0, 150 x X^3 x exp(-6 X) + 0.3], with X = ICR/100; POTHTG = ((1.47043 + 0.23317 x SI) / (31.56252 - 0.05586 x SI)) x 10; HTGRR = POTHTG x PCTRED x VIGOR, with PCTRED from equation {4.2.1.2.7}.
- Species GB (from the CR variant, through UT): the same VIGOR, replaced by 1 - (1 - VIGOR) / 3, and POTHTG = ((SI / 5) x (1.5 x SI - H) / (1.5 x SI)) x 0.83; HTGRR = POTHTG x PCTRED x VIGOR.
- All other species: HTGRR is returned by subroutine SMHTGF (see the table above).

Then HTGR = HTGRR x CON, and HTGR = (HTGR + ZZRAN x 0.2) x XRHGRO x SCALE x WK4(i) for species GB and (HTGR + ZZRAN x 0.1) x XRHGRO x SCALE for the others, where ZZRAN is a normal draw redrawn when above 0.5 or below -2.0 and SCALE is FNT/REGYR. The weighting of equation {4.2.1.2.2} is applied once; for species GS and RW the small-tree value is first averaged with the large-tree value, (HTGR + HTG)/2, unless the call is from the regeneration establishment model.

**Coefficients of BC.** In the BC variant the coefficients STG%CON, STG%LNHT, STG%HT, STG%CCF, STG%BAL, STG%EXPMLT, STG%HCCFL, STG%CCFSL and STG%SD are copied from the array ST_COEF for the species and the biogeoclimatic zone (`canada/bc/regent.f` lines 2050 to 2100), with STG%CON = ST_COEF%CON + (ST_COEF%SLP + ST_COEF%CASP x cos(ASP) + ST_COEF%SASP x sin(ASP)) x SLOPE; the coefficients LTH of the large-tree equation V3HTG are copied in the same way from the arrays LTSP and LTHG (`canada/bc/htgf.f` lines 1765 to 1790). The large-tree equation V3HTG, in meters, is HTGM = (CN + CNSI + DG1 x DGM + DG2 x DGM^2) x HTM^(DBH1 + DBH2 x D) x exp(HT2 x HTM^2) for species with the new V3 model (BC species PL, SE, EP, AT, AC and OH), and HTGM = (A1 + SI) x HTM^(B1 + B2 x D + B3 x DGM) x exp(C x HTM^2) for the other species, with D in centimeters, HTM the height in meters and DGM the diameter increment in centimeters; V3HTG = HTGM x 3.28084 x MLT, and V3HTG is 0 for species that were not fit.

#### Diameter increment through the projection cycle {#sec-diameter-increment-through-the-projection-cycle}

The diameter increment array DG(i) is an increment of the **inside bark** diameter. The tree diameter array DBH(i) is the diameter **outside bark** at all times. The conversion between them uses the bark ratio function BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i)), which is variant-specific. The table follows DG(i) through one projection cycle in the order the subroutines are called.

```{r dg-sequence, echo=FALSE}
dg_sequence <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Step, ~Subroutine, ~What_Happens_To_DG, ~Basis_Afterward,
  "1", "DGDRIV", "Computed for every tree record, large and small, from the large-tree ln(DDS) estimate, the error term, the dwarf mistletoe factor and the size bound", "Inside bark; YR years",
  "2", "REGENT", "Replaced by, or averaged with, the small-tree estimate for trees below the threshold diameter, depending on the variant and species; trees at or above the threshold keep the DGDRIV value", "Inside bark; YR years",
  "3", "GRINCR (FIXDG)", "Multiplied by the FIXDG multiplier for records in the species and diameter range", "Inside bark; YR years",
  "4", "FFERT", "Recomputed on the DDS scale for the fertilizer response", "Inside bark; YR years",
  "5", "GRADD (MPBCUP, DFBDRV)", "Called before the scaling; the source comment states that DG must be on the YR basis for the mountain pine beetle model (MPBMOD)", "Inside bark; YR years",
  "6", "GRADD (scaling)", "DDS = DG × (2 × BARK × D + DG) × FINT/YR, then DG = sqrt((D × BARK)² + DDS) − BARK × D; done only when FINT is not equal to YR; a DG that is not positive is set to 0", "Inside bark; FINT years",
  "7", "GRADD (MISTOE, TMCOUP and later calls)", "Called after the scaling, so any change is to the cycle-length increment; TMCOUP subtracts DGLOSS from DG", "Inside bark; FINT years",
  "8", "GRADD (stop point 5)", "Not changed; available through the API as the attribute dg", "Inside bark; FINT years",
  "9", "UPDATE (VOLS)", "Not changed; VOLS computes volume at D = DBH + DG/BARK", "Inside bark; FINT years",
  "10", "UPDATE (diameters)", "Not changed; DBH(i) = DBH(i) + DG(i)/BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i)), with HT(i) already updated", "DBH is outside bark",
  "11", "DGDRIV, next cycle", "Copied to WK1(i) as the previous increment, then overwritten", "Inside bark; FINT years"
)

kable(dg_sequence,
      col.names = c("Step", "Subroutine", "What Happens to DG", "Basis Afterward"),
      caption = "The diameter increment DG(i) through one projection cycle",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "3em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "30em")
```

**Large and small trees.** Subroutine DGDRIV computes a large-tree diameter increment for every tree record, including the small ones. Subroutine REGENT is called next and changes DG(i) only for trees below a threshold diameter. For height growth, REGENT blends the small-tree and large-tree estimates between the diameters XMIN and XMAX of each species. Diameter growth is handled differently in each variant. The table lists, for each variant and species group, the threshold diameter, whether the small-tree increment replaces the DGDRIV value or is averaged with it, and how the small-tree increment is obtained. Trees at or above the threshold keep the DGDRIV value in every case. The table lists the variants that have a source list in the repository. A threshold of 99.0 means that the small-tree equations are used at all diameters, and "None" means that the test is not made for the species. The threshold values for the ON variant are as coded in the source.

**How the small-tree increment is obtained.** In every variant except HI, OP, PN and WC (species other than 17) the small-tree diameter increment is derived from the height growth of the same cycle, not from a diameter regression. REGENT does the following for a tree below the threshold.

1. The height increment HTG(i) is computed first, with the small-tree and large-tree height estimates weighted as described under threshold diameters.
2. When HT(i) + HTG(i) is 4.5 feet or less, DG(i) is set to 0 and DBH(i) is raised by a small amount. Otherwise the species height-diameter relation gives the diameter at the height before the increment and at the height after the increment.
3. The difference between the two diameters is multiplied by the small-tree diameter growth multiplier (REGDMULT) and by the bark ratio, which gives an inside bark increment. When either diameter is negative, most variants use 0.2 × HTG(i) × BARK × the multiplier instead.
4. The increment is bounded below (by 0 in some variants and by 0.1 in others) and, in many variants, above by a species maximum. It is then converted to the YR basis as described above, raised if DBH(i) + DG(i) would be less than the species minimum diameter DIAM, and bounded by DGBND.

In the HI, OP, PN and WC variants, the small-tree diameter increment of every species except species 17 comes from subroutine SMHGDG, which returns both the small-tree height and diameter increments. The diameter increment is multiplied by the climate multiplier WK4(i), the bark ratio and the REGDMULT multiplier, bounded, and converted to the YR basis.

The small-tree diameter increment depends on the height increment of the same cycle, whereas the large-tree increment depends on the ln(DDS) regression and the error term. Subroutine DGSCOR is not called in any REGENT subroutine, so the large-tree error term is not applied to the small-tree increment.

YR is the period length of the growth models and is set in subroutine BLKDAT: 10 years in all variants except NC, OC, OP and SN, where it is 5 years. FINT is the cycle length.

#### Mortality {#sec-mortality-models}

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine MORTS once in each projection cycle to estimate mortality, after the diameter and height increments of the cycle have been estimated. Subroutine MORTS and the subroutines it calls store the trees per acre that die in the work array WK2(i) for each tree record i. They do not change the trees per acre of the record, PROB(i). Subroutine UPDATE subtracts WK2(i) from PROB(i) at the end of the cycle. The mortality models are described in Dixon (2002), section 7.3. The variables named in this section are defined in the next table.

```{r mort-variables, echo=FALSE}
mort_variables <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variable, ~Definition,
  "PROB", "Trees per acre represented by a tree record",
  "WK2", "Trees per acre of a tree record that die in the cycle",
  "WKI", "Trees per acre of the current tree record that die in the cycle, stored in WK2",
  "FINT", "Length of the projection cycle, in years",
  "D", "Tree diameter at breast height, in inches",
  "DG", "Diameter increment of the cycle predicted for the tree, outside bark, in inches",
  "G", "Diameter increment of the tree in the units stated in the text, in inches",
  "BARK", "Bark ratio of the tree",
  "BA", "Stand basal area at the start of the cycle, in square feet per acre",
  "BAMAX", "Maximum stand basal area, in square feet per acre",
  "T", "Stand trees per acre at the start of the cycle",
  "DQ10", "Quadratic mean diameter of the stand 10 years hence, in inches",
  "D10", "Quadratic mean diameter of the stand at the end of the cycle, in inches",
  "SDIMAX", "Maximum stand density index of the stand, the basal area weighted mean of the species maxima",
  "PMSDIL", "Lower limit of density related mortality, as a proportion of the maximum SDI, 0.55 by default",
  "PMSDIU", "Upper limit of density related mortality, as a proportion of the maximum SDI, 0.85 by default",
  "RELDBH", "Diameter of the tree divided by the average diameter of the stand",
  "Rb", "Annual stand mortality rate for the approach to the maximum basal area (RZ in the code)",
  "Ra", "Annual mortality rate of an individual tree record (RIP in the code)",
  "RIPP", "Annual mortality rate of an individual tree record after Ra and Rb are combined",
  "RI", "Annual background mortality rate of an individual tree record in the SDI-based model",
  "RN", "Annual density related mortality rate of the stand in the SDI-based model",
  "X", "Mortality multiplier of the tree record, from keyword MORTMULT",
  "MORTEXP", "Trees per acre that ORGANON predicts to die for a tree record"
)

kable(mort_variables,
      col.names = c("Variable", "Definition"),
      caption = "Variables used in the mortality models",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

**Mortality models by variant.** Four kinds of mortality models are in the compiled code: the Prognosis-type model, the SDI-based model, an individual tree survival model that is applied to every tree record (AK, and the HI, PN, WC and OP variants), and the ORGANON model. Some variants combine models by species. The models are listed by variant in the next table. Subroutine MORTS calls a distribution subroutine in the variants that have one, which distributes the number of trees to kill over the tree records. In the other variants, MORTS calculates the trees per acre that die of every tree record directly. Subroutine SEAMRT is compiled in AK but is not called.

```{r mort-models, echo=FALSE}
mort_models <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Model, ~Distribution_Subroutine, ~CLMORTS_Called,
  "AK", "Individual tree survival", "None", "Yes",
  "BC", "Prognosis-type, with a BC-specific individual rate Ra", "None", "Yes",
  "BM", "SDI-based", "BMTMRT", "Yes",
  "CA", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "Yes",
  "CI", "Prognosis-type", "None", "Yes",
  "CR", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "Yes",
  "CS", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "No",
  "EC", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "Yes",
  "EM", "SDI-based for WB, WL, DF, LP, ES, AF, PP and OS; Prognosis-type for the other species", "None", "Yes",
  "HI", "Individual tree survival", "None", "Yes",
  "IE", "Prognosis-type", "None", "Yes",
  "KT", "Prognosis-type", "None", "Yes",
  "LS", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "No",
  "NC", "SDI-based", "NWCMRT", "Yes",
  "NE", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "No",
  "OC", "ORGANON, or SDI-based when ORGANON gives no mortality", "VARMRT", "Yes",
  "ON", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "No",
  "OP", "ORGANON, or individual tree survival when ORGANON gives no mortality", "None", "Yes",
  "PN", "Individual tree survival", "None", "Yes",
  "SN", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "No",
  "SO", "SDI-based", "SCOMRT", "Yes",
  "TT", "SDI-based, and Prognosis-type for PP", "TTMRT", "Yes",
  "UT", "SDI-based", "UTMRT", "Yes",
  "WC", "Individual tree survival", "None", "Yes",
  "WS", "SDI-based", "VARMRT", "Yes"
)

kable(mort_models,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Mortality Model", "Distribution Subroutine", "CLMORTS Called"),
      caption = "Mortality models by variant",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The OC variant uses the VARMRT source file of the CA variant. In the ON variant, VARMRT has a fourth argument and uses metric equations. The variants that call CLMORTS compile the climate version when the climate extension is part of the executable, and an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM otherwise.

**Steps common to the models.** Subroutine MORTS calls subroutine DBCHK to see if debug output is called for. It calls subroutines OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in OPFIND) and OPDONE (another entry point in OPFIND) to process any mortality multipliers scheduled for the projection cycle with keyword MORTMULT. The multipliers are stored by species in XMMULT, with the lower and upper diameter limits XMDIA1 and XMDIA2, and the multiplier of a tree record is X.

Maximum basal area and maximum stand density index are two measures of the maximum capacity of an area to grow trees. Maximum basal area can be entered with keyword BAMAX. Maximum SDI of the species can be entered with keyword SDIMAX, whose fields 5 and 6 also change the limits PMSDIL and PMSDIU. The maximum SDI of the stand, SDIMAX, is the average of the species values weighted by the basal area of the species. When a maximum basal area has not been entered, subroutine MORTS calls subroutine SDICAL, which sets BAMAX to SDIMAX x 0.5454154 x PMSDIU. This step also serves the climate extension.

##### Prognosis-type mortality model

The Prognosis-type model combines two annual mortality rates: a stand rate for the approach to the maximum basal area, Rb, and an individual rate for each tree record, Ra (Dixon 2002, section 7.3.1). The rates, the combination and the trees that die are calculated for every tree record. The model is used in CI, IE and KT, in BC, in EM for the species that are not SDI-based, and for PP in TT.

*The approach to the maximum basal area.* The quadratic mean diameter 10 years hence, DQ10, is calculated from the diameter increment of the cycle. The basal area increment that results does not account for mortality. The basal area is projected forward 10 years assuming that the proportion BA/BAMAX of the predicted basal area increment is lost to mortality, so when the stand basal area is equal to BAMAX all of the predicted increment is absorbed by mortality. The trees per acre that correspond to the projected basal area are converted to an annual rate Rb with equation {4.2.1.4.1}.

$$
\begin{aligned}
DQ10 &= \sqrt{\frac{\sum P\left(D^2 + 2\,D\,G + G^2\right)}{T}}, \quad G = \frac{DG}{BARK}\\
\Delta BA &= 0.005454154\, DQ10^2\, T - BA\\
BA10 &= BA + \frac{BAMAX - BA}{BAMAX}\,\Delta BA\\
TB &= \frac{BA10}{0.005454154\, DQ10^2}\\
TTB &= \min\left(\frac{T - TB}{T},\; 0.9999\right)\\
R_b &= 1 - \left(1 - TTB\right)^{0.1}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.4.1}
$$

Where:

- P: PROB, trees per acre of a tree record
- D: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- DG: Diameter increment of the cycle, outside bark (inches)
- BARK: Bark ratio of the tree
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- BAMAX: Maximum stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- T: Stand trees per acre
- Rb: Annual stand mortality rate for the approach to the maximum basal area

*The individual rate.* The annual mortality rate of each tree record, Ra, is calculated with equation {4.2.1.4.2} from the tree diameter, the diameter increment of the tree, the relative diameter, the stand basal area, a species constant, and a habitat or national forest effect.

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= 2.76253 + 0.222310\sqrt{D} - 0.0460508\sqrt{BA} + 11.2007\,G - \frac{0.554421}{D} + B_5 + 0.246301\,RELDBH + 6.07129\,\frac{G}{D}\\
R_a &= \frac{REIN}{1 + \exp(z)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.4.2}
$$

Where:

- D: Diameter at breast height (inches), with a minimum of 0.5
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- G: Diameter increment multiplied by GMULT, described below (inches per year)
- B5: Species constant PMSC (equal to B0 in TT)
- RELDBH: Diameter of the tree divided by the average diameter of the stand
- REIN: Potential factor, described below
- Ra: Annual mortality rate of the tree record

The logit z of the annual survival rate is limited to -70 to 70 for the species WB, PY, AS, WJ, MC, LM, CW and OH of CI and in BC, and to -88.5 to 88.5 for the other species of CI and for PP in TT (the limits of the other variants are in the source file `morts.f` of the variant).

The increment G is the diameter increment of the previous cycle, WK1, divided by the length of the previous cycle, OLDFNT, and by the bark ratio. In the first cycle, and when the previous increment is 0, and the predicted increment is more than 0.5 inch, G is the predicted increment divided by the bark ratio and 10. The previous increment is not less than 0.05 inch per year for a tree of 1.0 inch or less, and not less than 0.05(5 - D)/4 for a tree between 1.0 and 5.0 inches. The increment is multiplied by GMULT(1) for a tree larger than 5.0 inches and by GMULT(2) for a tree of 5.0 inches or less. GMULT and REIN are calculated once by subroutine MORCON with equation {4.2.1.4.3}.

$$
\begin{aligned}
GMULT_1 &= \frac{0.90}{POTEN_1}, \qquad REIN_1 = \frac{1 - \left(POTEN_1/20 + 1\right)^{-1.605}}{0.06821}\\
GMULT_2 &= \frac{2.50}{POTEN_2}, \qquad REIN_2 = \frac{1 - \left(POTEN_2 + 1\right)^{-1.605}}{0.86610}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.4.3}
$$

Where:

- POTEN1, POTEN2: Value of the potential array POT for the habitat type or plant association of the stand, for trees larger than 5.0 inches and for trees of 5.0 inches or less

POT(k) is 0.25 + 0.05(k - 1), for k from 1 to 54, so POT is 0.25 to 2.90.

The index of POT for each habitat type is the array IPDG (larger trees) or IPDG2 (smaller trees), by habitat type (30 values) and national forest (11 values in CI, IE and KT, 6 in EM, 15 in BC). These arrays are data statements of subroutine MORTS of the variant, and are not listed here. In TT the indexes are single values. The national forest is mapped to one of the IE national forests in CI by the array MAPFOR. The species constants PMSC of the Prognosis-type species are listed in the next table; the other species of the variant have a constant of 0.0.

```{r mort-pmsc, echo=FALSE}

*The combination of the two rates.* The two rates are combined with equation {4.2.1.4.4}, which is the weighted average of Rb and Ra, with the weight BA/BAMAX on Rb (Dixon 2002, section 7.3.1). The combined rate is not less than Ra and is not more than 1.

$$
RIPP = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{BA\cdot R_b + \left(BAMAX - BA\right) R_a}{BAMAX} & BA \le BAMAX\\[8pt]
\dfrac{BA\cdot R_b}{BAMAX} & BA > BAMAX
\end{cases},
\qquad R_a \le RIPP \le 1
\tag{4.2.1.4.4}
$$

Where:

- RIPP: Combined annual mortality rate of the tree record
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- BAMAX: Maximum stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- Rb: Annual stand rate from equation {4.2.1.4.1}
- Ra: Annual rate of the tree record from equation {4.2.1.4.2}

*Trees that die.* The trees per acre that die are calculated with equation {4.2.1.4.5}. In BC, equation {4.2.1.4.2} gives Ra in the V2 zones (the zones that do not contain ICH, IDF, SBS or SBPS); in the other zones Ra comes from a BC-specific model of the diameter, the basal area in larger trees and the stand density.

$$
WKI = P\left[1 - \left(1 - RIPP\right)^{FINT}\right] X\, M
\tag{4.2.1.4.5}
$$

Where:

- WKI: Trees per acre of the tree record that die in the cycle
- P: PROB, trees per acre of the tree record
- RIPP: Combined annual rate from equation {4.2.1.4.4}
- FINT: Length of the cycle (years)
- X: Multiplier from keyword MORTMULT when the diameter is within its limits, otherwise 1.0, multiplied by the factor that protects the best trees of the regeneration establishment model, as described below
- M: Species multiplier of the variant, as listed in the next table

The mortality multiplier of keyword MORTMULT therefore multiplies the whole combined rate in the Prognosis-type model. The establishment model protects the trees that it has marked as best trees for 20 years after the disturbance date: X is multiplied by $1 - XCHECK$, where XCHECK is the number of years to the end of the protection divided by FINT, limited to 0 to 1. The species multiplier M applies a proportion of the rate of the northern Idaho model (the NI rate in the code comments) to the species that are listed in the next table.

      col.names = c("Variant", "Species", "M"),
      caption = "Species multiplier of the Prognosis-type mortality rate",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

KT and TT (species PP) have no species multiplier, and BC does not apply one.

##### SDI-based mortality model

In the SDI-based model, subroutine MORTS first estimates the number of trees that die in the stand from the trajectory of the stand density, and then distributes it to the tree records. Because the quadratic mean diameter at the end of the cycle depends on which trees die, the calculation is repeated until it converges (Dixon 2002, section 7.3.2). Two kinds of mortality are estimated: background mortality, which is not attributable to competition, and density related mortality, which is a function of stand density, tree vigor, social position and shade tolerance.

*Stand trajectory.* The quadratic mean diameter at the end of the cycle, D10, is calculated from the diameter increment of the cycle, $G = (DG/BARK)(FINT/10)$ (FINT/5 in NC). The maximum number of trees per acre for a quadratic mean diameter is the maximum SDI line of equation {4.2.1.4.6}, limited to 35000. The lower and upper limits of density related mortality are the proportions PMSDIL and PMSDIU of the line.

$$
CONST = \frac{SDIMAX}{0.02483133}, \qquad TMD(d) = \min\left(CONST\cdot d^{-1.605},\; 35000\right)
\tag{4.2.1.4.6}
$$

Where:

- SDIMAX: Maximum SDI of the stand
- TMD(d): Maximum trees per acre for a quadratic mean diameter d
- d: Quadratic mean diameter (inches), DIA0 at the start of the cycle and D10 at the end

The trees per acre remaining at the end of the cycle, TN10, are then calculated with the rules of the next table. All trees die when SDIMAX is less than 5. TN10 is not more than T, and is set to 0 when it is less than 0.1.

```{r mort-sdi-zones, echo=FALSE}
mort_sdi_zones <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Condition, ~TN10,
  "T above the upper limit at DIA0, PMSDIU x TMD(DIA0)", "The upper limit at D10, PMSDIU x TMD(D10)",
  "T between the lower and the upper limit at DIA0, and within 5 trees per acre of the upper limit", "The upper limit at D10",
  "T between the lower and the upper limit at DIA0, and more than 5 trees per acre from the upper limit", "exp(CEPMRT + SLPMRT ln D10), not more than the upper limit at D10",
  "T below the lower limit at DIA0 and above the lower limit at D10", "exp(CEPMRT + SLPMRT ln D10), with the line determined by a direct calculation from T",
  "T below the lower limit at DIA0 and at D10", "T (no density related mortality)"
)

kable(mort_sdi_zones,
      col.names = c("Condition", "Trees per Acre Remaining, TN10"),
      caption = "Trees per acre remaining after density related mortality in the SDI-based model",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The line between the lower and the upper limit is a straight line in the logarithms, $\ln TN = CEPMRT + SLPMRT \ln d$. It passes through the point of the stand, $(DIA0, T)$, and is determined iteratively. The point at the lower limit is $d_{55}$, found from $\ln(TEM) = \ln(PMSDIL \cdot CONST) - 1.605\,d_{55}$ where TEM starts at $1.1\,T$ and is changed by half of the difference between T and the trees on the line at DIA0 until the difference is 5 trees per acre or less (or 100 steps). The point at the upper limit is $d_{85} = 1.25\,d_{55}$, limited to 0.125 to 5.0 and increased in steps of 0.1 while the slope is greater than -0.5. CEPMRT and SLPMRT are kept for the following cycles, and are calculated again when T differs by more than 1 tree per acre from the trees per acre stored at the end of the previous cycle, or when the stand has no trees.

The annual density related rate RN follows from the trees that die, as shown in equation {4.2.1.4.7}.

$$
R_N = 1 - \left[1 - \frac{T - TN10}{T}\right]^{1/FINT}
\tag{4.2.1.4.7}
$$

Where:

- RN: Annual density related mortality rate of the stand
- T: Stand trees per acre at the start of the cycle
- TN10: Trees per acre remaining at the end of the cycle
- FINT: Length of the cycle (years)

*Background mortality.* A background rate RI is calculated for each tree record with equation {4.2.1.4.8}, and then multiplied by 0.5 (except in SN). RI is not less than 0.0001 for some species of CA, NC, OC and WS (see the source file of the variant). The coefficients B0 (PMSC) and B1 (PMD) are arrays by species, or by species group in some variants (see the source file `morts.f` of the variant). EM adds the term $B_2 D^2$.

$$
RI = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(B_0 + B_1\,D\right)}
\tag{4.2.1.4.8}
$$

Where:

- RI: Annual background mortality rate of the tree record
- B0, B1: Coefficients by species
- D: Diameter at breast height (inches)

*Mortality rate of the tree record.* The rate applied to each tree record is the background rate RI when density related mortality is not in effect, and the density related rate RN when it is. Density related mortality is in effect for a tree record when T is more than the lower limit at D10, $PMSDIL\cdot TMD(D10)$, and RN is more than 0. The trees that die are $WKI = P\,[1 - (1 - RIP)^{FINT}]\,X$, where RIP is RI or RN. The multiplier X of keyword MORTMULT, within its diameter limits, is applied only when the background rate is used; it is 1.0 when density related mortality is in effect.

*Distribution and iteration.* Subroutine MORTS then calls the distribution subroutine of the variant when the trees to kill, TN10, are 0.1 per acre or more. The distribution subroutine (for example VARMRT) distributes the trees to kill over the tree records. It calculates an efficiency for each tree record, EFFTR, from the percentile of the tree in the basal area distribution, PCT, as shown in equation {4.2.1.4.9}, and scales the mortality so that the total matches. A new quadratic mean diameter is calculated from the result. When it differs from the previous estimate by more than 0.1 inch (0.2 inch in ON), the calculation is repeated with the new value, up to 10 passes. The number of trees to kill is taken from the stand total when the last tree processed has the density related rate, and from the sum of the background mortality otherwise.

$$
PEFF = 0.84525 - 0.01074\,PCT + 0.0000002\,PCT^3, \qquad 0.01 \le PEFF \le 1.0
\tag{4.2.1.4.9}
$$

Where:

- PEFF: Relative efficiency of mortality as a function of the percentile of the tree
- PCT: Percentile of the tree in the basal area distribution of the stand

In the version of VARMRT of CA, EFFTR is PEFF multiplied by an adjustment by species, VARADJ, and by 0.1. The constant, the use of PCT, and the other factors in EFFTR differ among the distribution subroutines; they are in the source file of each subroutine.

##### Individual tree survival models

In the AK variant, an annual survival probability of each tree record is calculated with equation {4.2.1.4.10}, and the trees that die are $WKI = P\,[1 - RIP^{FINT}]\,X$ with RIP limited to 0.99999 (RIP is set to 0 when it is less than 0.001). The diameter is not less than the species value DSURV, to avoid mass mortality of seedlings. When the stand density at the end of the cycle is above SDIMAX x PMSDIU, or the basal area above BAMAX, the mortality of every record is multiplied by the number of the pass, in repeated passes (up to 100), until the density and the basal area are within the limits.

$$
RIP = \frac{\exp(x)}{1 + \exp(x)}, \qquad x = BM_1 + BM_2\,D_t + BM_3\,D_t^2 + BM_4\,PTBAL + BM_5\,\frac{PTBAL}{D_t}
\tag{4.2.1.4.10}
$$

Where:

- RIP: Annual survival probability of the tree record
- BM1 to BM5: Coefficients by species
- Dt: Diameter of the tree, not less than DSURV for the species (inches)
- PTBAL: Basal area in trees larger than the tree, on the inventory point (square feet per acre)

In the HI, PN, WC and OP variants, the annual mortality rate of each tree record is calculated with survival equations that were derived from the ORGANON equations (the WC and PN equations replaced earlier equations that applied mortality too evenly by size). The form of the equation of a species is selected by the array MORTMAP among six forms, as shown in equation {4.2.1.4.11}, with coefficients BM0 to BM5 by species. WC and PN compile the same source file, and OP uses the same forms and coefficients, with a different treatment of DF described below.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Form 1: } p_5 &= \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\left[BM_0 + BM_1\sqrt{D} + BM_3\,CR^{0.25} + BM_4\left(SI_1 + 4.5\right) + BM_5\,BAL\right]\right)}\\
\text{Form 2: } p_5 &= \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\left[BM_0 + BM_1\,D + BM_4\left(SI_1 + 4.5\right) + BM_5\,BAL/D\right]\right)}\\
\text{Form 3: } p_5 &= \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\left[BM_0 + BM_1\,D + BM_2\,D^2 + BM_3\,CR + BM_4\left(SI_2 + 4.5\right) + BM_5\,BAL\right]\right)}\\
\text{Form 4: } p_5 &= \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\left[BM_0 + BM_1\,D + BM_2\,D^2 + BM_3\,CR + BM_4\left(SI_1 + 4.5\right) + BM_5\,BAL\right]\right)}\\
&\qquad\qquad RIP = 1 - \left(1 - p_5\right)^{0.2} CRADJ \quad \text{(forms 1 to 4)}\\
\text{Form 5: } RIP &= 1 - \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-6.6707 + 0.5105\ln\left(5 + BA\right) - 1.3183\,RELHT\right)}\\
\text{Form 6: } RIP &= \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(2.901447 + 0.578694\,D - 0.001793\,PTBAL\right)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2.1.4.11}
$$

Where:

- RIP: Annual mortality rate of the tree record
- D: Diameter at breast height (inches), with a minimum of 0.5
- CR: Crown ratio of the tree, as a proportion
- BAL: Basal area in trees larger than the tree, $(1 - PCT/100)\,BA$ (square feet per acre)
- PTBAL: Basal area in trees larger than the tree, on the inventory point (square feet per acre)
- SI1: Site index of species 16 (DF), SITEAR(16); in WC it is converted from the Curtis to the King site index, $5.21486 + 0.66486\,SITEAR(16)$ (feet)
- SI2: Site index of species 19 (WH), SITEAR(19) (feet)
- CRADJ: Crown ratio adjustment, $1 - \exp\left(-(25\,CR)^2\right)$ when CR is 0.17 or less, otherwise 1.0
- RELHT: Height of the tree divided by the average height of the 40 largest trees, with a maximum of 1.5
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- BM0 to BM5: Coefficients by species, in the next table

For a tree of less than 3.0 inches, except the species RW (species index 17), the small-tree equation of Gould and Harrington replaces the form above, as shown in equation {4.2.1.4.12}.

$$
RIP = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(a_1 + a_2\,\dfrac{PTBAL\cdot A}{\sqrt{DBHA + 1}} + a_3\,RELHT\right)}, \qquad DBHA = D + BETA\cdot HBH
\tag{4.2.1.4.12}
$$

Where:

- RIP: Annual mortality rate of the tree record
- a1, a2, a3: -4.4384, 0.0053 and -0.6001
- PTBAL: Basal area in trees larger than the tree, on the inventory point (square feet per acre)
- A: Value of the array MVALUES (1.0, 1.5, 2.25, 3.375 and 5.062) for the class of the species, from the array MCLASS
- BETA: Coefficient by species (0.216823 for most species)
- HBH: Height of the tree, with a maximum of 4.5 feet
- RELHT: Height of the tree divided by the average height of the 40 largest trees, with a maximum of 1.5
- D: Diameter at breast height (inches)

The rate RIP is not less than 0.001 (and, in WC and PN, not more than 0.999). The trees that die are $WKI = P\,[1 - (1 - RIP)^{FINT}]\,X$. The mortality of every record is then multiplied by the number of the pass, in repeated passes (up to 100), until the SDI is less than SDIMAX and the basal area is less than 550 square feet per acre. The form and the coefficients of each species are listed in the next table. The species of the WC, PN and OP variants differ only in the species of index 6 (blank in WC and SS in PN and OP), 23 and 24 (WA and PB in WC and PN, and MA and TO in OP).
