##### Steps after the mortality of the tree records

*Mature stand boundary (SDI-based variants).* The breakup of an overmature stand can be simulated with the parameters of keyword MORTMSB. When the quadratic mean diameter is above the boundary diameter QMDMSB (999 by default, so the boundary is off), MORTS calculates the additional mortality in trees per acre that is needed, and calls subroutine MSBMRT to distribute it over the tree records within the diameter limits of the keyword.

*Morphological diameter limit.* In all variants, a check is made for additional mortality of the trees that reach the diameter limit entered with keyword TREESZCP. For a tree whose end of cycle diameter, D + G, is at least the limit SIZCAP(1), and for which the flag SIZCAP(3) is not 1, the trees that die are set to the larger of WKI and $P\cdot SIZCAP(2)\cdot FINT/10$ (FINT/5 in NC). This is a user-controlled surrogate for senescence mortality.

*Basal area check (SDI-based variants).* When holding the SDI to a maximum, the basal area can increase. After the mortality above, the basal area at the end of the cycle is calculated. If it is more than 1 square foot per acre above BAMAX, the trees per acre that die are adjusted upward in proportion, for each tree record, to bring the basal area back to BAMAX. The check is not made in the Prognosis-type and individual tree survival variants.

*Climate and user mortality.* In the variants that call it, subroutine MORTS calls CLMORTS, which modifies the mortality to account for a change in climate. It exists as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the executable program and as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM otherwise. Subroutine MORTS then uses OPFIND, OPGET and OPDONE to process the activities scheduled for the cycle with keyword FIXMORT. The keyword replaces the mortality, adds to it, sets a minimum, or multiplies it, depending on the option of the keyword (the values are $WK2 = PROB \cdot m$, $WK2 + \max(0, PROB - WK2)\,m$, $\max(WK2, PROB\cdot m)$ and $\min(PROB, WK2\cdot m)$, where m is field 2), within the diameter limits of the keyword.

FVS is now done simulating mortality not related to insects, disease, or fire; program control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

*ORGANON variants.* In the OC and OP variants, subroutine MORTS adds the ORGANON mortality estimates, MORTEXP, over all tree records. These were calculated by subroutine EXECUTE, called from DGDRIV. When the sum is greater than 0 and ORGANON is on (LORGANON is true), the trees that die are MORTEXP x FINT/5 for all tree records. The multiplier of keyword MORTMULT is not applied to these values. When the sum is 0, which includes the case where no "big 6" species is present and EXECUTE was skipped, OC calculates mortality with the SDI-based model described above (with VARMRT) and OP calculates it with the individual tree survival model described above. In OC, ORGANON mortality skips the distribution subroutine and the basal area check. Structural differences in the two ORGANON-FVS variants are discussed in more detail in [Structural differences in the ORGANON-FVS variants](#sec-structural-differences-in-the-organon-fvs-variants).

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine DGBND is called by subroutine REGENT to check for compliance with any morphological maximum tree diameters.

Subroutine DUBSCR is called by subroutine REGENT in the IE, KT, EM and BC variants. When the diameter of a tree at the end of the cycle is projected to reach 3.0 inches (2 cm in the BC V3 model), DUBSCR assigns a crown ratio to the tree. In IE, EM and BC the crown ratio is assigned only when the tree does not already have one, and EM skips the species that are dubbed with the Weibull model of EM.

Subroutine MULTS is used by:

Subroutine DGDRIV to retrieve a flag entered with the MANAGED keyword record indicating the stand should be considered as a “managed stand” for modeling purposes (this affects diameter growth rates in some variants) and any large-tree diameter growth modifiers entered with the BAIMULT keyword record.

Subroutine HTGF to retrieve any large-tree height growth modifiers entered with the HTGMULT keyword record.

Subroutine REGENT to retrieve any small-tree height growth modifiers entered with the REGHMULT keyword record or any small-tree diameter growth modifiers entered with the REGDMULT keyword record.

Subroutine MORTS to retrieve any mortality multipliers entered with the MORTMULT keyword record.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark the disposition of growth or mortality activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to see if any growth or mortality activities are scheduled during a projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve parameters associated with any growth or mortality activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

CLGMULT is called by DGDRIV to get a diameter growth multiplier due to climate change. CLGMULT will exist as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM, which returns a multiplier of 1.0, if the climate extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Record tripling and final adjustments

Following estimation of tree growth and mortality, there are two more tasks that are part of the projection cycling phase. Tree records must be tripled when the number of records is small, and the effects of fertilizer treatments on tree growth must be simulated.

### Subroutines involved and their function

**When records are tripled.** Subroutine GRINCR sets the logical variable LTRIP at the start of each projection cycle, with the condition in equation {4.3.1.1}. The condition is evaluated again in every cycle.

$$
LTRIP = \left(ICYC \le ICL4\right) \;\text{and}\; \left(ITRN \le \frac{MAXTRE}{3}\right) \;\text{and}\; \left(\text{not } NOTRIP\right)
\tag{4.3.1.1}
$$

Where:

- LTRIP: Logical variable that is true when the records of the cycle are tripled
- ICYC: Projection cycle number
- ICL4: Number of the last cycle in which records can be tripled; the default is 2 in all variants except OC and OP, where it is 0, and keyword NUMTRIP sets it
- ITRN: Number of tree records at the start of the cycle
- MAXTRE: Maximum number of tree records (3000 in the variants whose limits were checked, so the limit on ITRN is 1000)
- NOTRIP: Logical variable that is true after keyword NOTRIPLE, which has no fields, or after keyword COMPRESS

When the root disease model is active in a variant that includes it, subroutine RDTRP replaces the condition of equation {4.3.1.1} with ICYC <= ICL4 and ITRN <= IRRTRE / 3 and not NOTRIP, where IRRTRE is 1500, so that the limit on ITRN is 500 records. LTRIP is saved with the stand for stop and restart, with NOTRIP and ICL4.

The sequence in subroutine GRINCR is: DGDRIV, HTGF and REGENT estimate the growth; the FIXDG and FIXHTG activities are applied; MORTS estimates the mortality; and, when LTRIP is true and ITRN is greater than 0, subroutine TRIPLE triples the records, ITRN is multiplied by 3, subroutine REASS realigns the pointers, and IREC1 is multiplied by 3. Subroutine FFERT is called last. Subroutines GRADD and UPDATE, called later from subroutine TREGRO, work with the tripled list. The tripled records are permanent records of the list; the code has no step that combines them again, except subroutine COMPRS, which merges records when the COMPRESS keyword is used. Subroutine ESTAB does not triple the records that it creates (it calls REGENT with the logical variable LESTB true).

**Growth of the three records.** The records have the same attributes, but not the same growth. The records are, in the order that they are stored, the original record (60 percent of the trees per acre), the second record (25 percent) and the third record (15 percent). The next table lists how each is assigned.

```{r tripling-growth, echo=FALSE}
tripling_growth <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Attribute, ~Original_Record, ~Second_and_Third_Records, ~Where_Assigned,
  "DG(i), diameter increment", "FRM = FM x SSIGMA x RHOCP, error = FRM + CORR x OLDRN(i); DG = sqrt(DSQ + DDS x exp(error)) - D", "FRU = FU x SSIGMA x RHOCP for the second record, and FRL = FL x SSIGMA x RHOCP for the third record, with error = FRU (or FRL) + CORR x OLDRN(i) of the original record; FU = 1.271, FM = -0.14228 and FL = -1.549", "DGDRIV (subroutine DGSCOR is not called); OLDRN is stored for each record",
  "HTG(i), height increment, large trees", "Estimated once", "The same value as the original, limited so that HT plus HTG does not exceed SIZCAP(species,4) for the height of each record", "HTGF",
  "HTG(i), height increment, small trees", "Estimated first", "A new estimate with its own random draw for each record", "REGENT",
  "FIXDG and FIXHTG multipliers", "Applied to DG(i) and HTG(i)", "The same multiplier is applied to the two new records; the diameter limits are tested on DBH(i) of the original record", "GRINCR",
  "WK2(i), mortality, trees per acre", "0.60 of the amount", "0.25 and 0.15 of the amount", "TRIPLE",
  "PROB(i), trees per acre", "0.60 of the value", "0.25 and 0.15 of the value", "TRIPLE"
)

kable(tripling_growth,
      col.names = c("Attribute", "Original record", "Second and third records", "Where assigned"),
      caption = "How the three records of a tripled tree are assigned",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "8em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "14em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "22em")
```

**Subroutine TRIPLE.** For each tree record I, from 1 to ITRN, subroutine TRIPLE stores the second record at ITFN = ITRN + 2I - 1 and the third record at ITFN + 1, as shown in equation {4.3.1.2}. The original record stays at position I. If the original tree list contains 30 tree records, the records of the first tree are 31 and 32, and the records of the 30th tree are 89 and 90. The trees per acre and the mortality are divided as shown in equation {4.3.1.3}; the 25 percent record is the second record, and the 15 percent record is the third record. The trees per acre of each record is therefore a fraction of the original value; it is not computed from the error distribution. The multiplier that inflates PROB for the sample tree display, TRM, is multiplied by 0.6.

$$
ITFN_{2} = ITRN + 2I - 1, \qquad ITFN_{3} = ITRN + 2I
\tag{4.3.1.2}
$$

Where:

- ITFN_2, ITFN_3: Index of the second and third new record of the tree record I
- I: Index of the original tree record
- ITRN: Number of tree records before tripling

$$
PROB(ITFN_{2}) = 0.25\, PROB(I), \qquad PROB(ITFN_{3}) = 0.15\, PROB(I), \qquad PROB(I) \leftarrow 0.60\, PROB(I)
\tag{4.3.1.3}
$$

Where:

- PROB: Trees per acre of the record; WK2, the trees per acre that die in the cycle, is divided in the same way
- I: Index of the original tree record
- ITFN_2, ITFN_3: Index of the second and third new record, equation {4.3.1.2}

The attributes of the original record are copied to the two new records, as shown in the next table. The new records are given the same crown width, volume, defect, damage and identification values as the original record.

```{r tripling-arrays-copied, echo=FALSE}
tripling_copied <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Group, ~Arrays, ~Treatment,
  "Size and condition", "HT, ICR, IMC, ISP, ITRE, ITRUNC, NORMHT, KUTKOD, DEFECT, ISPECL, CULL, DECAYCD, WDLDSTEM, CRWDTH, HT2TD(,1) and HT2TD(,2)", "Copied unchanged",
  "Volumes", "BFV, CFV, MCFV, SCFV, PTOCFV, PMRBFV, PMRCFV, PSCFV, NCFDEF, NBFDEF, PDBH, PHT", "Copied unchanged",
  "Percentiles and work arrays", "OLDPCT, PCT, WK1, WK3", "Copied unchanged",
  "Identification", "IESTAT, ABIRTH, LBIRTH, IDTREE, ZRAND", "Copied unchanged",
  "Biomass", "ABVGRD_BIO, MERCH_BIO, CUBSAW_BIO", "Copied unchanged",
  "Biomass and carbon", "FOLI_BIO, ABVGRD_CARB, MERCH_CARB, CUBSAW_CARB, FOLI_CARB, CARB_FRAC", "Assigned at index ITRN in the source, so the new records are not given these values",
  "Trees per acre and mortality", "PROB, WK2", "Multiplied by 0.25 and 0.15 for the new records, and by 0.60 for the original record",
  "Diameter and height increments", "DBH of the new records, DG, HTG, OLDRN", "Assigned in subroutines DGDRIV, HTGF and REGENT, not in TRIPLE"
)

kable(tripling_copied,
      col.names = c("Group", "Arrays", "Treatment"),
      caption = "Arrays assigned by subroutine TRIPLE",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "8em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "22em")
```

Subroutine TRIPLE calls subroutine SVTRIP once for each original record, before the copy. SVTRIP assigns the stand visualization objects of the tree among the three records: the original record keeps NR x 0.6 rounded objects, the second record receives 0.625 of the others, rounded, and the third record receives the rest; nothing is changed when the tree has one object or fewer.

Various FVS extension specific code segments are called by subroutine TRIPLE to triple parameter values associated with the extension. For each new record they are called with the index of the new record, the index of the original record and the weight, and they are called again for the original record with a weight of 0.6. The calls are ORGTRIP (ORGANON), MISGET and MISPUT (the dwarf mistletoe rating of the tree), and RDTRIP, BRTRIP, BMTRIP and FMTRIP (the root disease, blister rust, beetle and fire models). The routines exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the program executable, and as entry points of the stub subroutines of the extension if it is not (EXMIST for the dwarf mistletoe extension, EXRD for root disease, EXORGANON for ORGANON, EXBRUS for blister rust and EXBM for the beetle model). FMTRIP copies and multiplies the tree-level arrays of the fire model (FMPROB, FMICR, OLDHT, OLDCRL, GROW, OLDCRW and CROWNW) when the fire model is active; the header of the source file says it triples the fire and snag attributes. The next table shows which variants include each extension; the routines BRTRIP and BMTRIP are not in the source list of any variant, so the stubs are used.

```{r tripling-hooks, echo=FALSE}
kable(tripling_hooks,
      col.names = c("Variant", "SVTRIP", "FMTRIP", "MISGET and MISPUT", "RDTRIP and RDTRP", "ORGTRIP", "FFERT"),
      caption = "Subroutines called for record tripling and fertilizer, by variant (Yes: the routine of the extension is in the source list; Stub: the stub is used)",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "4em")
```

**Subroutine REASS.** Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine REASS to realign the FVS internal pointers following tripling. REASS copies IND1 into IND2 in species order and rewrites IND1 so that each group of three entries lists the second record (ITFN = IREC1 + 2I - 1), the original record (I) and the third record (ITFN + 1) of a tree. It then rewrites the species segments, ISCT(species,1) and ISCT(species,2), the first and last positions of the species in IND1, which hold three times the number of records. Finally, it rewrites the array IND in the same way. Subroutine RDPSRT, called later from subroutine GRADD, sorts the records again.

**Fertilizer effects.** Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine FFERT to compute adjustments to diameter and height growth due to effects of applying fertilizer. FFERT is the routine of the variants (the stub in BC and ON, where the FERTILIZ keyword is an error). The FERTILIZ keyword record (activity code 260) has the date or cycle, the nitrogen (pounds per acre), phosphorus and potassium, and a multiplier of the effect, FEFF, with a default of 1.0. Only an application of 200 pounds of nitrogen per acre can be represented: a blank or any other value of nitrogen is set to 200, and the phosphorus and potassium values are ignored. When several FERTILIZ activities are scheduled for the same cycle, FFERT uses the last one and deletes the others (OPDEL1).

The effect starts at the beginning of the cycle in which FFERT finds the activity (IFFDAT = IY(ICYC)), whatever the date entered, and lasts 10 years. The number of years of the effect in the present cycle is shown in equation {4.3.1.4}. The effect continues in the later cycles with the same parameters, until the 10 years have passed. The tripled records are processed like the others.

$$
IFSTRT = IY(ICYC) - IFFDAT, \qquad IFFIN = \min\left(10, \; IFSTRT + IFINT\right), \qquad IFLEN = IFFIN - IFSTRT
\tag{4.3.1.4}
$$

Where:

- IY(ICYC): Year at the start of the cycle
- IFFDAT: Year at the start of the cycle in which the activity was found
- IFINT: Length of the cycle, FINT (years)
- IFLEN: Number of years of the cycle that are affected by the fertilizer (years); FFERT does nothing when IFSTRT is more than 10 or IFLEN is 0 or less

For each tree with a diameter greater than 0, FFERT calculates the ratio of the diameter increment with and without fertilizer, RDDS, as shown in equation {4.3.1.5}, and the new increments, as shown in equations {4.3.1.6} and {4.3.1.7}.

$$
BAL = \left(1 - \frac{PCT}{100}\right) BA, \qquad RDDS = \min\left[2.6, \; \exp\left(0.1108 \ln(DBH) + 0.003004 \,\frac{BAL}{\ln(DBH + 1)}\right)\right]
\tag{4.3.1.5}
$$

Where:

- RDDS: Ratio of the diameter increment with fertilizer to the increment without it, with a maximum of 2.6
- PCT: Percentile of the tree in the basal area distribution (percent)
- BA: Stand basal area (square feet per acre)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)

$$
\begin{aligned}
DIB &= DBH \cdot BARK, \qquad DDS = 2 \cdot DIB \cdot DG + DG^{2} \\
DDSIT &= \frac{DDS}{YR}\left[RDDS \cdot IFLEN \cdot FEFF + \left(IFINT - IFLEN\right)\right] \\
DG &\leftarrow \sqrt{DIB^{2} + DDSIT \cdot \frac{YR}{FINT}} - DIB
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.3.1.6}
$$

Where:

- DG: Diameter increment inside bark on the YR basis (inches)
- DBH: Diameter at breast height (inches)
- BARK: Bark ratio, BRATIO(species, DBH, HT)
- RDDS: Ratio of the diameter increment with fertilizer to the increment without it, equation {4.3.1.5}
- IFLEN: Number of years of the cycle that are affected by the fertilizer, equation {4.3.1.4} (years)
- IFINT: Length of the cycle, FINT (years)
- FEFF: Multiplier of the effect of the FERTILIZ keyword (the fourth parameter of the activity)
- YR: Period length of the growth models (years), set by the variant (CONTRL.F77)
- FINT: Length of the cycle (years)

$$
HTG \leftarrow \frac{HTG}{YR}\left[RHT \cdot IFLEN \cdot FEFF + \left(IFINT - IFLEN\right)\right] \frac{YR}{FINT}, \qquad RHT = 1.1626
\tag{4.3.1.7}
$$

Where:

- HTG: Height increment (feet)
- IFLEN: Number of years of the cycle that are affected by the fertilizer, equation {4.3.1.4} (years)
- IFINT: Length of the cycle, FINT (years)
- FEFF: Multiplier of the effect of the FERTILIZ keyword (the fourth parameter of the activity)
- YR: Period length of the growth models (years), set by the variant (CONTRL.F77)
- FINT: Length of the cycle (years)

The result remains an inside bark increment on the YR basis, which subroutine GRADD scales to the cycle length. The effect of the fertilizer is on the 10 years; the response of a cycle that is shorter than 10 years is the response of IFLEN years, and FFERT prints a warning when IFLEN is not 10 (including a 5-year cycle in which the whole cycle is affected), and calls subroutine RCDSET with the code 1 after each warning. FFERT also prints a warning when the habitat code ICL5 is not 520 or 530, and when the contribution of the species with the sequence numbers 3 and 4 to the stand crown competition factor, (RELDSP(3) + RELDSP(4)) / RELDEN, is less than 0.5; these species are Douglas-fir and grand fir in the variants where those are the species 3 and 4 (the Inland Empire variant is an example), as shown in the next table.

```{r ffert-species, echo=FALSE}
ffert_species <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~Species_3, ~Species_4,
  "AK", "YC", "TA",
  "BM", "DF", "GF",
  "CA", "RC", "WF",
  "CI", "DF", "GF",
  "CR", "DF", "GF",
  "CS", "SP", "VP",
  "EC", "DF", "SF",
  "EM", "DF", "LM",
  "HI", "GF", "AF",
  "IE", "DF", "GF",
  "KT", "DF", "GF",
  "LS", "RN", "RP",
  "NC", "DF", "WF",
  "NE", "WS", "RS",
  "OC", "RC", "GF",
  "OP", "GF", "AF",
  "PN", "GF", "AF",
  "SN", "PI", "PU",
  "SO", "DF", "WF",
  "TT", "DF", "PM",
  "UT", "DF", "WF",
  "WC", "GF", "AF",
  "WS", "WF", "GS"
)

kable(ffert_species,
      col.names = c("Variant", "Species 3", "Species 4"),
      caption = "Species tested by the species composition warning of subroutine FFERT",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "4em")
```

FFERT is called after subroutine MORTS, so fertilizer treatments do not affect tree mortality through increased competition in the cycle of the treatment. In the variants where subroutine MORTS uses DG(i), the increment of the treated cycle does enter the diameters of the later cycles. Moving the call to subroutine FFERT before the call to subroutine MORTS should be considered; it would have to be done before subroutine TRIPLE, which then would have to give the adjusted increments to the new records.

Subroutine GRINCR is now done with its’ tasks; program control is returned to subroutine TREGRO for further processing.

**ORGANON tripling (OC and OP).** ORGANON subroutine GROW has its own record tripling, which is separate from the FVS tripling above. It is controlled by the ORGANON flag INDS(5), where 0 means no tripling and 1 means tripling (`common/ORGANON.F77:134`, `organon/execute2.f:104-106`). The default is 0 ("ORGANON TRIPLING OFF") in `oc/grinit.f:360` and `op/grinit.f:358`, and no other statement in the source files assigns INDS(5), so the tripling of subroutine GROW does not run in OC and OP. The record tripling of FVS is controlled by LTRIP and ICL4 instead (equation {4.3.1.1}); the ORGANON array IORG is copied to the new FVS records by subroutine ORGTRIP (`organon/orgtrip.f`). The ORGANON setting is printed as "TRIPLING: No" or "TRIPLING: Yes" in the ORGANON table of the output (`vorganon/orgtab.f:183-188`).

When the flag is 1, subroutine GROW triples in the diameter growth loop and again in the loop of height growth of the major species groups (the groups up to IB), through subroutines DGTRIP and HGTRIP, and subroutine XTRIP copies the other tree variables (`organon/grow.f:60-153`, `organon/tripleorg.f`). Each loop first chooses a mode M from the number of records, with a limit of 2000 records (`grow.f:75-90`, `grow.f:115-130`). M is 1 (every tree is tripled) when three times the number of records that have trees per acre above 0 fits in 2000, and the total with the records that have no trees fits as well. Otherwise M is 2 (every other tree is tripled) when twice the number fits, and otherwise M is 0 (no tripling). Records with trees per acre of 0 or less are not grown or tripled. In the height loop the count is made for the major groups only, with the records that are not in a major group counted once. After each loop NTREES is set to the new number of records (`grow.f:110`, `grow.f:153`), and the height loop runs over all those records, so a record of a major group that was tripled in the diameter loop is also a candidate in the height loop.

Each tripled record keeps the attributes of the original record, and each of the three records has one third of the trees per acre, of the mortality expansion and of the other expansion arrays (`organon/tripleorg.f:115-135`, `tripleorg.f:309-330`); the split differs from the 60, 25 and 15 percent split of the FVS tripling. The growth is different for the three records, as shown in equations {4.3.1.8} and {4.3.1.9}, where the first record is the original record, the second record is stored at J and the third at J + 1. The residuals L and U are those of the species group, in subroutines DGRES_SWO, DGRES_NWO and DGRES_SMC (`tripleorg.f:178-198`, `200-217`, `219-234`) for diameter growth and HGRES_SWO, HGRES_NWO and HGRES_SMC (`tripleorg.f:345-373`, `375-402`, `404-431`) for height growth. The diameter growth residuals are constants for each species group. The height growth residuals are polynomials of the height growth and exist only for the major groups, five groups in model type 1 and three in model types 2 and 3 (`tripleorg.f:345-431`).

$$
\begin{aligned}
DG_1 &= \max\left[0, \; DG - \left(L + U\right)\sqrt{DG}\right] \\
DG_2 &= DG + U \sqrt{DG} \\
DG_3 &= \max\left[0, \; DG + L \sqrt{DG}\right]
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.3.1.8}
$$

Where:

- DG_1, DG_2, DG_3: Diameter growth of the original record, the second record and the third record (inches)
- DG: Diameter growth of the original record before tripling (inches)
- L: Lower residual of the species group, DGLRES(g) of the subroutine DGRES_SWO, DGRES_NWO or DGRES_SMC
- U: Upper residual of the species group, DGURES(g) of the same subroutine

$$
\begin{aligned}
HG_1 &= \max\left[0, \; HG - \left(U + L\right)\right] \\
HG_2 &= HG + U \\
HG_3 &= \max\left[0, \; HG + L\right] \\
L &= \min\left(0, \; A_0 + A_1 HG + A_2 HG^{2}\right) \\
U &= \max\left(0, \; C_0 + C_1 HG + C_2 HG^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.3.1.9}
$$

Where:

- HG_1, HG_2, HG_3: Height growth of the original record, the second record and the third record (feet)
- HG: Height growth of the original record before tripling (feet)
- A_0, A_1, A_2: Coefficients HGLRES(g, 1), HGLRES(g, 2) and HGLRES(g, 3) of the species group, in the subroutine HGRES_SWO, HGRES_NWO or HGRES_SMC
- C_0, C_1, C_2: Coefficients HGURES(g, 1), HGURES(g, 2) and HGURES(g, 3) of the species group, in the same subroutine

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to see if any fertilizer activities are scheduled during a projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve parameters associated with any fertilizer activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark the disposition of fertilizer activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

Subroutine OPDEL1 is used by subroutine FFERT to delete the fertilizer activities of a cycle other than the last.

Subroutine RCDSET is used by subroutine FFERT to set return codes used by FVS. FFERT calls it with the code 1 after each warning; the projection continues.

Subroutine SVTRIP is used to adjust the stand visualization file for record tripling.

Subroutines ORGTRIP, MISGET, MISPUT, RDTRIP, BRTRIP, BMTRIP and FMTRIP, and the entry point RDTRP, are the extension routines that are called for record tripling.

## Disturbance effects and dynamics {#sec-disturbance-effects-and-dynamics}

Forest disturbance agents can include insects, diseases, and fire. Dynamics associated with each of these disturbance agents and their effects on tree growth and mortality need to be simulated if those disturbance agents are part of the variant. In addition, some disturbances can be simulated using FVS base model keyword records whether the extension associated with the disturbance agent is part of the variant or not. Lastly, using the stop and restart capabilities, and FVS as a shared library that is called from some other program, disturbances can be modeled outside of FVS and the effects applied using the FVS API calls (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)).

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine TREGRO calls subroutine GRADD, which among other tasks, checks to see if any of the insect and disease extensions are active. Calls are made to MPBCUP to see if there is a mountain pine beetle outbreak this projection cycle; DFBWIN and DFBDRV for Douglas-fir beetle; MISTOE for dwarf mistletoe; TMCOUP for Douglas-fir tussock moth; BWECUP for western spruce budworm; FMMAIN and FMKILL for the fire and fuels extension (FMKILL is called a second time after the blister rust and root disease calls); BRTREG for blister rust; and RDTREG for western root disease. These auxiliary routines will exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the program executable, or entry points in the corresponding externals routine (e.g. subroutine EXRD for western root disease) if the extension in not part of the program executable. These extensions may modify or replace growth and mortality estimates computed previously in the projection cycle by the base FVS subroutines.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine HTGSTP to process any HTGSTOP or FIXHTG keyword records. These keyword records can be used to modify or stop estimated height growth and are useful for simulating effects of disturbance agents such as tussock moth or budworm instead of using the extension itself.

### Auxiliary subroutines

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine HTGSTP to mark the disposition of activities associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine OPFIND is called by subroutine HTGSTP to find activities associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine HTGSTP to retrieve parameters associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine OPSTUS is called by subroutine GRADD to check whether conditions under which a fire will be simulated have been set. Fire conditions, such as wind speed, temperature, and fuel moistures, are set using the SIMFIRE keyword record which is specific to the fire and fuels extension. This subroutine checks to see if the activity has been accomplished, deleted, or awaits accomplishment without taking any action to change its status.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Updating the tree descriptions {#sec-updating-the-tree-descriptions}

FVS is now finished with estimation of growth and mortality for the projection cycle. The next tasks are to update the tree descriptions using these estimates, resort the tree records, calculate new stand density statistics, and make any computations needed for the cover extension.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine SVMORT to update the file needed for stand visualization. This update includes the effects of mortality that occurred during the projection cycle. Subroutine SVMORT assumes that all mortality trees are standing snags for purposes of stand visualization. SVMORT calls subroutine SVRMOV to remove tree records associated with mortality (normal, fire-caused, beetle-caused, etc.) from the file needed for stand visualization. Stop point 5 is processed immediately after this call, before the tree records are updated.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine UPDATE to update tree descriptions. Subroutine UPDATE adds the growth increments, deducts mortality, computes new volume statistics, and calculates some summary information. For each tree record j, the following is done in this order:

1. Tree height is increased by the height increment, HT(j) = HT(j) + HTG(j). When the normal height, NORMHT(j), is greater than 0, 100 × HTG(j) is added to it (rounded to an integer).
2. The mortality is capped at the trees per acre of the record, WKI = min(WK2(j), PROB(j)), and trees per acre is reduced, PROB(j) = max(0, PROB(j) − WKI). The mortality volume is WK6(j) = WKI × CFV(j)/FINT, which is added to the array SPCMO by species and tree class.
3. After all records are processed, subroutine VOLS computes tree and stand volumes. When LSTART is false, VOLS uses the end-of-cycle diameter D = DBH(j) + DG(j)/BARK, where BARK = BRATIO(species, DBH(j), HT(j)) and HT(j) is the updated height.
4. At the end of UPDATE, the tree diameter is increased, DBH(j) = DBH(j) + DG(j)/BRATIO(species, DBH(j), HT(j)), using the same expression for the bark ratio. DG(j) is an inside bark increment on the cycle-length basis (scaled by subroutine GRADD before stop point 5), and dividing it by the bark ratio converts it to an outside bark increment. UPDATE does not change DG(j).

Tree diameters are therefore updated at the very end of the subroutine, while other values are updated at the beginning of the subroutine. Subroutine VOLS, which computes tree volumes, adds the diameter growth to the diameter itself in its calculations (step 3), so volumes are computed for the end-of-cycle diameters while DBH(j) still holds the start-of-cycle values.

Subroutine UPDATE updates the array storing mortality-related volume information by tree species and tree value class, SPCMO(sp,vc). It calls subroutine PCTILE to compute percentiles in the distribution of mortality-related volume, and subroutine DIST to compute percentile points in the distribution of mortality-related volume. Subroutine COMP is called to compute percentages of mortality-related volume by species and tree value class.

Subroutine UPDATE calls subroutine VOLS to compute tree and stand volume statistics. It then updates tree diameters and returns control to subroutine GRADD.

Subroutine GRADD needs to recalculate some control and summary variables based on the updated tree records. GRADD calls subroutine RDPSRT to resort the tree records by updated diameter values. It then calls subroutine DENSE to recalculate stand density statistics based on updated trees per acre values.

The next step is dependent on whether the cover extension is part of the variant. Subroutine GRADD calls CVGO to see if the cover extension is active. If it is, then CVBROW is called to compute shrub density and browse statistics. CVGO and CVBROW will exist as subroutines if the cover extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXCOV if the cover extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutine GRADD then updates the array containing actual or approximated tree age, ABIRTH(j) for each tree record j. Stop point 6 is processed next, before regeneration establishment.

FVS is now ready to simulate regeneration establishment.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine ECVOL is used to process volume information for the economics post-processor if an economics analysis is called for.

Subroutine VOLS computes the volumes of the tree records. It first calls subroutine VOLKEY, and then selects the calculation of each tree record by the cubic foot volume method of the species, METHC(i), and the board foot volume method, METHB(i). The default of both is method 6 in every variant (subroutine SITSET changes a method that is still 999 to 6). The methods are used as follows.

1. Methods 6 and 10 (and method 5 in the CS, LS and NE variants) call entry point NATCRS of subroutine FVSVOL, in the file `vvolume/fvsvol.f`. FVSVOL calls subroutine VOLINITNVB of the National Volume Estimator Library (NVEL, the git submodule `volume/NVEL`). For a National Scale Volume and Biomass equation (a name that begins with `NVB`), VOLINITNVB calls subroutine NVBC. For any other equation it calls subroutine VOLINIT, which uses the National Cruise System equations (for example the profile routine PROFILE, and R6VOL for some Region 6 equations). Method 10 is set by the FIAVBC keyword record and selects the National Scale Volume and Biomass equations, which are described in [National Scale Volume and Biomass (NSVB) estimation](#sec-national-scale-volume-and-biomass). Subroutine SITSET chooses the equation of each species and writes a table of the volume equation numbers to the main output file. FVSVOL also calls the variant subroutine FORMCL for the form class.
2. Method 8 calls the variant-specific entry points OCFVOL and OBFVOL of subroutine FVSVOL.
3. The other methods call the variant subroutines CFVOL and BFVOL.

When the board foot method is 5 (CS, LS and NE), 6 or 9 and the cubic foot method is 6 or 10, the board foot volume comes from the same call of NATCRS as the cubic foot volume. Subroutine VOLS calls subroutines CFTOPK and BFTOPK to compute volume lost to broken or dead tops. CFTOPK is not called when an NSVB equation is used or when the FIAVBC keyword record is active; NSVB makes the allowance for the top itself (see the NSVB section). Entry point GETEQN of FVSVOL is used by subroutine NATCRZ to return the volume equation numbers being used when writing an output file for the National Cruise Program post-processor.

Subroutine VOLKEY is called by subroutine VOLS to process any keyword records used to change volume standards or volume equations. These keyword records include MCDEFECT, BFDEFECT, VOLUME, and BFVOLUME. After a FIAVBC keyword record has been read, the MCDEFECT and VOLUME records are recognized but have no effect.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## National Scale Volume and Biomass (NSVB) estimation {#sec-national-scale-volume-and-biomass}


The National Scale Volume and Biomass (NSVB) system estimates tree volume, biomass and carbon with one set of equations for the United States (Westfall and others, 2023). The equations are in the National Volume Estimator Library (NVEL), which FVS includes as the git submodule `volume/NVEL` (FMSC-Measurements/VolumeLibrary). The calculation is in subroutine NVBC of the file `nsvb.f`. NSVB is used in an FVS run only after the **FIAVBC** keyword record has been read. Without it, FVS uses its usual volume methods and does not estimate biomass or carbon.

### The FIAVBC keyword record

When the FIAVBC record is read in subroutine INITRE, the logical variable LFIANVB is set to true. The first FIAVBC record in a run also does the following:

1. The cubic foot volume method of every species, METHC(i), is set to 10.
2. The user's cubic foot defect (CFLA0, CFLA1, CFDEFT) is set to none.
3. The merchantability standards of every species are set to 0: the minimum DBH, top diameter and stump height of the cubic foot product (DBHMIN, TOPD, STMP) and of the sawlog cubic foot product (SCFMIND, SCFTOPD, SCFSTMP).

Every FIAVBC record then does the following:

1. Field 1 selects the merchantability standards. A blank or 0 selects the FIA standards, and the cruise type CFCTYPE is set to `I`. A value of 1 selects the National Forest System (NFS) standards, and CFCTYPE is set to `F`. Any other value is reported as an error and the FIA standards are used.
2. Field 2 has been disabled. A value in it is reported as an error, and the cruise type comes from field 1.
3. Field 3 names the species or species group for the standards in fields 4 to 9. The fields set, in order, the cubic foot minimum DBH, top diameter and stump height, and the sawlog cubic foot minimum DBH, top diameter and stump height. A field left blank keeps its value.

The keyword records that change cubic foot volume or defect are recognized but have no effect after FIAVBC: MCFDLN, MCDEFECT, VOLUME and the cubic foot part of DEFECT. The board foot records BFFDLN and BFDEFECT, and the board foot part of DEFECT, still apply to board foot volume only. The merchantability standards in effect are listed in the FVS_InvReference table.

### Selection of the equation

Subroutine SITSET of each variant calls subroutine NVB_REGION_CHECK and, for each species with METHC(i) equal to 10, subroutine NVBEQDEF. NVB_REGION_CHECK sets the last digit of the ecological division code ECOREG to 0 and checks the result against a list of 19 divisions (130, 210, 220, 230, 240, 250, 260, 310, 330, 340 and the mountain divisions M130, M210, M220, M230, M240, M260, M310, M330 and M340). A code that is not on the list is replaced by `0000` and a warning is written.

NVBEQDEF builds the equation name, VEQNNC(i), as `NVB`, the four character division code and the three digit FIA species code. The letter `P` is added in position 11 for managed plantations of species 111 and 131 when the division is `0000` or `0230`. Sixteen woodland species (FIA codes 62, 63, 65, 66, 69, 106, 133, 134, 143, 321, 322, 475, 803, 810, 814 and 843) are not given an NSVB equation. NVBEQDEF assigns them regional equations by state (for example `R03CHO0065`, `400DVEW133` and `200DVEW475`), and a warning is written when the state code ISTATE is 0.

### Call sequence

Subroutine VOLS calls the entry point NATCRS of subroutine FVSVOL for species with a cubic foot volume method of 6 or 10. FVSVOL calls subroutine VOLINITNVB of NVEL, which calls subroutine NVBC when the equation name begins with `NVB`. FVSVOL passes, among other values, the diameter, total height, merchantability standards, crown ratio, live or dead status, cull percent, decay code, FIA species code and the cruise type. When a live tree has a broken or dead top (top kill), the height of the break is passed as well; it is taken from ITRUNC(i), which holds the truncation height in hundredths of a foot. For the woodland species the region used is set from the state, and the number of stems per tree is passed instead of the form class.

NVEL does not call NVBC for a tree that has a diameter but no height. Its biomass is estimated with the Jenkins equations, which give above ground biomass, foliage and branch components but no volume. The woodland species are handled separately in VOLINITNVB with regional biomass equations.

### Calculation in subroutine NVBC

Subroutine NVBC returns three arrays of 15 elements: the volumes VOL, the dry weights DRYBIO and the green weights GRNBIO. The following steps are made for a tree.

1. The species data (species group, specific gravity of the wood, softwood or hardwood indicator SFTHRD, carbon fraction, and green and dry weight factors) are looked up by species code. The merchantability rules for the region are retrieved with subroutine MRULES. When the total height is missing it is estimated from the heights and diameters at the tops of the products or from the broken height and diameter.
2. When the tree has a broken top, the proportion of the stem that remains (Rrem) is computed from the ratio equation, and the proportion of the branches and foliage that remain (BrchRem) is computed from the crown ratio, or from the average crown ratio of the division when the crown ratio is not given.
3. The total stem wood volume inside bark, the total stem bark volume and the total stem volume outside bark are computed from equations of the form given in the supplementary tables of Westfall and others (2023). The equation of the species (or of its Jenkins species group, or the default of the national table) is selected from the equation name. The equations are functions of diameter at breast height and total height. Five forms are coded, among them a power function of the form a × D^b × H^c. The soundness adjustments are applied: Rrem for broken tops and the cull percent for rot.
4. The volumes of the stump, the sawlog, the topwood and the tip are obtained from a taper ratio equation, R = (1 − (1 − h/H)^a)^b, which gives the proportion of the total stem volume below height h. The diameter at a height is obtained from the same equation. For the FIA cruise type (`I`) the sawlog and topwood volumes are the ratio volumes between the stump, the top of the sawlog product and the top of the topwood product. For the other cruise types the stem is divided into logs, with the trim between logs, and the log volumes are summed and scaled to the merchantable ratio volume. The board foot volumes (Scribner and International 1/4 inch) are computed from the log diameters and lengths. A tree can have at most 20 logs.
5. The dry weights of the stem wood (volume times specific gravity), the stem bark, the branches and the above ground total are computed from the supplementary tables. The component weights are reduced for broken tops and for dead trees. The above ground total from its own equation is kept, and the difference between it and the sum of the components is shared among the wood, bark and branches in proportion to their weights, so that the components add up to the total. The foliage is computed for live trees only.
6. The weights of the stump, sawlog, topwood and tip are the volumes times the adjusted wood and bark densities.
7. Carbon is the above ground biomass times the carbon fraction of the species, rounded to three decimals. For a dead tree with a decay code the carbon fraction of the decay class is used.
8. Green weight is the dry weight times (1 + the moisture content), where the moisture content is computed from the green weight factor of the region and species and the dry weight factor of the tree.
9. Cord volume is the sawlog cubic volume divided by 90 (79 in regions 3, 8 and 9).

A live tree takes the decay code as 0. For a dead tree with no decay code, class 3 is used. The values for the decay classes are in the next table.

```{r nsvb-decay, echo=FALSE}
nsvb_decay <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Decay_Code, ~Bark_Remaining, ~Branches_Remaining, ~Density_Softwood, ~Density_Hardwood, ~Carbon_Softwood, ~Carbon_Hardwood,
  "1", "1.0", "1.0", "0.97", "0.99", "0.501", "0.470",
  "2", "0.8", "0.5", "1.00", "0.80", "0.504", "0.473",
  "3", "0.5", "0.1", "0.92", "0.54", "0.506", "0.481",
  "4", "0.2", "0.0", "0.55", "0.43", "0.520", "0.480",
  "5", "0.0", "0.0", "0.55", "0.43", "0.527", "0.472"
)

kable(nsvb_decay,
      col.names = c("Decay Code", "Bark Remaining", "Branches Remaining",
                    "Density Proportion, Softwood", "Density Proportion, Hardwood",
                    "Carbon Fraction, Softwood", "Carbon Fraction, Hardwood"),
      caption = "Proportions used by NSVB for dead trees",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

The softwood columns are used when the softwood or hardwood indicator SFTHRD of the species is 0. The remaining proportions of bark and branches are the same for both groups. The density proportion is applied to the stem wood, bark and branch weights of a dead tree.

The elements of the DRYBIO and GRNBIO arrays are listed in the next table.

```{r nsvb-elements, echo=FALSE}
nsvb_elements <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Element, ~Contents,
  "1", "Above ground biomass, without foliage",
  "2", "Total stem wood",
  "3", "Total stem bark",
  "4", "Stump wood",
  "5", "Stump bark",
  "6", "Sawtimber (primary product) wood",
  "7", "Sawtimber bark",
  "8", "Topwood (secondary product) wood",
  "9", "Topwood bark",
  "10", "Tip wood",
  "11", "Tip bark",
  "12", "Branches",
  "13", "Foliage",
  "14", "Top and limbs (above ground biomass less the stump and the sawtimber and topwood wood and bark)",
  "15", "Carbon content"
)

kable(nsvb_elements,
      col.names = c("Element", "Contents"),
      caption = "Elements of the DRYBIO and GRNBIO arrays returned by NVBC",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "4em")
```

### Use of the results in FVS

Subroutine VOLS stores the total cubic foot volume of the tree in CFV(i), the merchantable cubic foot volume in MCFV(i), and, with FIAVBC, the sawlog cubic foot volume in SCFV(i). The biomass and carbon of each tree are stored in the arrays of per-tree values in ARRAYS.F77:

1. ABVGRD_BIO(i) is DRYBIO element 1, and ABVGRD_CARB(i) is element 15.
2. FOLI_BIO(i) is element 13, and FOLI_CARB(i) is element 13 times 0.5.
3. MERCH_BIO(i) is the sum of elements 6 and 8 for trees at or above the minimum DBH DBHMIN(i), and CUBSAW_BIO(i) is element 6 for trees at or above the sawlog minimum DBH SCFMIND(i). Both are 0 otherwise.
4. MERCH_CARB(i) and CUBSAW_CARB(i) are MERCH_BIO(i) and CUBSAW_BIO(i) times the carbon fraction CARB_FRAC(i), which is the species carbon fraction, or the fraction of the decay class for a dead tree.
5. For the 16 woodland species, the merchantable and sawlog volumes, biomass and carbon are set to 0.

Subroutine GRADD multiplies these per-tree values by PROB(i) to get per-acre values, computes the percentile points of their distributions (the arrays OAGBIOCUR, OMERBIOCUR, OCSAWBIOCUR, OFOLIBIO and the matching carbon arrays), and divides them by PROB(i) again. Subroutine CUTS computes the same percentile points for the removed trees. The summary table FVS_FIAVBC_Summary is written from these distributions, divided by the stand area and by 2000 (tons per acre), and the FVS_FIAVBC_TreeList, FVS_FIAVBC_CutList and FVS_FIAVBC_ATRTList tables are written from the per-tree arrays (see the Database Input and Output Extension chapter and Appendix C).

When FIAVBC is active, the snag volume subroutine of the fire and fuels extension (FMSVOL) passes the live or dead status to the volume routine: `D` for standing dead trees, and the status of the tree for snags created by CUTS. The sawlog volume field (field 4) of the MINHARV keyword record is accepted in every variant. The decay code (DECAYCD) of the input data is used for dead trees (see the column mapping table of the Database Input and Output Extension chapter).

## Regeneration establishment {#sec-regeneration-establishment}

The regeneration establishment extension is part of all variants. Regeneration is added near the end of the growth projection cycle. Climate may have an influence on regeneration if the climate extension is also part of the variant. The regeneration establishment extension is described in section 5.4 of the EFVS guide and any variant-specific parameter settings are given in the variant overview documents. Also, [Regeneration establishment in FVS variants](#sec-regeneration-establishment-in-fvs-variants) of this document presents a more detailed discussion of the regeneration establishment model structure.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRADD calls CLAUESTB to determine if any regeneration is occurring because of changes in climate. CLAUESTB will exist as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM if the climate extension is not part of the program executable. The climate extension simulates regeneration due to climate change by adding planting activity records (i.e. PLANT keyword records) to the activity list. These planting activities will then get processed when the FVS regeneration establishment model is called at the next step.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine ESNUTR, which is part of the regeneration establishment extension to simulate any regeneration occurring this projection cycle. Regeneration can occur through stump sprouting if a sprouting species was harvested, planting activities scheduled with the PLANT keyword record, or natural regeneration scheduled with the NATURAL keyword record or occurring automatically in some variants.

Regeneration can also be added from an external source using the ADDTREES keyword record. Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESADDT to add trees from an external source.

Parameter settings specified using the SPECMULT, STOCKADJ, and HTADJ keyword records are retrieved and processed with calls to subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND).

#### Stump and root sprouts

Subroutine ESNUTR adds stump sprouts next. This is done in two steps: 1) if necessary, the tree list is compressed so there will be room to add sprouts, and 2) sprouts get added. Sprouting is one form of automatic regeneration that occurs whenever a designated sprouting species is harvested and the user has not turned sprouting off using the NOSPROUT keyword record or the SPROUT keyword record with a multiplier (field 2) of zero.

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESCPRS to direct compression of the tree list. The tree list is compressed only if the sprouts would not fit in the tree list (the maximum number of tree records is parameter MAXTRE in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block). In that case it is compressed to the larger of MAXTRE minus the number of sprout records needed and 40% of MAXTRE. Subroutine ESCPRS calls subroutines: COMPRS to compress the tree list; SPESRT to reset the species-ordered sort; RDPSRT to reset the diameter sort; PCTILE to reset the distribution of trees per acre and trees per acre by species and tree class; FINDAG to estimate any missing tree ages; DIST to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points in the distribution of trees per acre; COMP to compute the percentage of trees per acre by species and tree class; and OPADD to add a compression (i.e. COMPRESS keyword record) to the activity schedule and signal the year that it was done.

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESUCKR to create tree records corresponding to stump and root sprouts from sprouting species harvested at the beginning of a projection cycle. ESUCKR first processes any activities scheduled for the projection cycle using the SPROUT keyword record and stores that information. Next it loops over all tree records for which harvesting occurred and checks to see if the species associated with that tree record is a designated sprouting species for that variant. If it is a sprouting species and sprouting has not been turned off, ESUCKR calls NSPREC, ESASID, and ASSPTN (which are entry points in subroutine ESSPRT) and subroutine ESSPRT to determine the number of sprout records to create for this tree record. The number of sprout records to create will be an integer number. A sub-loop over the number of sprout records to create is then entered to actually create the new sprout records. If subroutine ESUCKR runs out of room to create the necessary sprout records, then another compression of the tree list may become necessary. Subroutine ESUCKR calls SPRTHT, another entry point in subroutine ESSPRT, to determine sprout height which is species and variant dependent. Subroutine ESUCKR calls subroutine CWCALC to calculate crown width and MISPUTZ to initialize the dwarf mistletoe rating for the newly created sprout record to zero. MISPUTZ will exist as a subroutine when the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXMIST when the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the program executable. When all harvested tree records have been processed and sprouting has occurred, then a sprouting regeneration report is written and ESUCKR returns program control back to subroutine ESNUTR.

If sprouting has occurred, subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine SPESRT to reset the species order sort, and subroutine RDPSRT to reset pointers in the diameter sort. The variable IFST is set to 1 to signal FVS to select new sample tree records the next time subroutine DIST gets called. New sample tree records are selected whenever the FVS tree list changes due to regeneration.

#### Regeneration tallies

Next, subroutine ESNUTR checks for regeneration tallies. Regeneration tallies may be scheduled automatically by FVS in variants having the full establishment model, or by using the TALLY, TALLYONE, or TALLYTWO keyword records in any variant. A tally sequence is also initiated when an ESTAB keyword record is specified. A detailed description of tally sequences and which kinds of tree records get passed to the FVS tree list at the two kinds of tallies are discussed in section 5.4 of the EFVS guide.

#### Natural regeneration and planted trees

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESTAB to add regeneration tree records to the FVS tree list in a tally. Compression of the tree list may be necessary to hold the tree records resulting from a regeneration tally. If a tally is scheduled and more than 70% of the tree list is in use (i.e. less than 30% of MAXTRE is available), subroutine ESCPRS is called to compress the tree list to 40% of MAXTRE. The tally activity is actually marked as accomplished through a call to OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, before subroutine ESTAB gets called. This is because ESTAB calls OPFIND and nested calls to OPFIND are not allowed in the FVS code (i.e. subroutine ESTAB is being called for a tally “found” by subroutine ESNUTR).

Subroutine ESTAB establishes tree records associated with PLANT and NATURAL keyword records in all variants, and tree records resulting from natural regeneration in variants with the full establishment model. This subroutine is very complex.

##### Initialization steps

Initialization of variables and replication of the inventory plots occurs first. The regeneration establishment model creates tree records on 1/300th acre plots. Plots are replicated until at least 50 plots are available so within-stand variations in seedling density, species composition, and heights can be achieved.

Site preparation activities scheduled using the MECHPREP or BURNPREP keyword records are then processed. Subroutine ESTAB calls subroutine ESETPR is called to process these keyword record requests; default probabilities are scheduled by subroutine ESPREP. A site preparation type (none, mechanical, or burn) is assigned randomly to each plot.

Activities associated with any PLANT and NATURAL keyword records are each checked. Unless the number of trees being established by one of these requests is greater than 0.001 trees per acre, the request is “DELETED”.

Sums are accumulated for calculation of shade adjustments. Shading affects the trees per acre representation assigned to regeneration tree records.

##### Creating the new tree records

Subroutine ESTAB is now ready to create the new tree records. Triple-nested DO loops are entered with the outside loop being over the number of plots on which regeneration is being simulated; the middle loop over the site preparations (note: the number of plots is replicated for each of the site preparation types); and the inside loop over the number of replications of each plot by site preparation combination.

In variants with the full establishment model, natural regeneration is simulated first within this triple-nested DO loop structure. Natural regeneration is regeneration that comes in automatically following a harvest (called an automatic tally in regeneration establishment jargon) or ingrowth which occurs after the regeneration period has passed. A regeneration period is the number of years during which regeneration becomes established as a result of a disturbance (such as a harvest). Automatic tallies can be turned off using NOAUTALY keyword record; ingrowth can be turned off using the NOINGROW keyword record; both can be turned off using the STOCKADJ keyword record with a probability of stocking set to zero; both, along with stump sprouting, can be turned off using the NOAUTOES keyword record.

To simulate natural regeneration in the full establishment model, first, the probability of stocking is calculated using subroutine ESTOCK. When an actual inventory is used to initiate FVS, the full establishment model adjusts for differences between the actual inventory and the predicted stocking. This feature adjusts the stocking curve (predicted stocking) to coincide with a known reference point (the actual inventory). Next, the probability of advanced, subsequent, and excess species is calculated using subroutines ESPADV, ESPSUB, and ESPXCS, respectively. Third, variables that control creation of the natural regeneration tree records are calculated. This third step is rather involved because of the regeneration establishment rules discussed in section 5.4.1 of the EFVS guide: the number of tree records on a stocked plot is determined using subroutine ESTPP; the number of species on the plot is calculated using subroutine ESNSPE; species which will occupy the plot are designated in array IBEST(i), i = 1 to MAXSP, as a value of 1 if the species is present and 0 if the species will not be present; the first tree of each species is assigned a status of advanced or subsequent using subroutines ESPADV and ESPSUB; heights are then assigned to the tallest trees by species and the advanced or subsequent designation using subroutines ESADVH and ESSUBH, respectively; next, a check is made to make sure there is a non-zero probability of trees which will classified as “excess” trees if a “best” tree of the same species was chosen for the plot. And fourth, the tree records corresponding to natural regeneration are created: tree species and height are assigned to the first tree of each species; and species and heights are assigned to excess trees using subroutine ESXCSH; other variables such as tree age are also assigned.

For all variants, tree records resulting from PLANT or NATURAL keyword records are created next. Tree heights are estimated using subroutine ESSUBH and tree ages are also assigned.

For variants using the full establishment model, the “best” trees get chosen next. Best trees are the two tallest trees regardless of species; the one tallest tree of each additional species represent on the plot; and if four trees have not yet been designated as best trees, then select in order of descending height from any of the remaining trees.

At this point, regeneration tree records in all variants still exist only in the regeneration establishment model extension; they must be “passed” to the FVS tree list. A check is made to make sure there is adequate room in the FVS tree list to handle the incoming tree records from the regeneration establishment model. If the tree list is within 99 records of the maximum number of tree records that can be handled (MAXTRE, or a smaller limit when the root disease extension is active), a call to subroutine ESCPRS compresses the FVS tree list to ½ of that maximum. Tree records are then passed to the FVS tree list with the full complement of variables assigned (species, trees per acre, diameter, height, etc.).

For all variants, subroutine ESGENT is called to grow the regeneration trees from the time they are 5-years old to the end of the projection cycle. Subroutine ESGENT calls subroutine REGENT, which contains the small tree growth equations, to accomplish this task. Subroutine CWCALC is called to calculate the crown width for seedlings and sprouts. The regeneration summary tables are printed.

After the regeneration summary tables are printed, program control returns to subroutine ESNUTR. ESNUTR calls subroutine RDPSRT to reset the FVS diameter sort of the tree list which now includes regeneration tree records. Program control is returned to subroutine GRADD.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine SVESTB to update files used for stand visualization since the FVS tree list now includes tree records created by the regeneration establishment model. It then calls subroutine ECCALC to calculate the costs and revenues for the cycle when the economics extension is active, and subroutine DENSE to calculate the post-establishment stand density statistics. This concludes tasks associated with the regeneration establishment extension. Next will be the calculation of crown ratio change.

### Allocation of regeneration to tree records

This subsection gives the arithmetic that subroutine ESTAB uses to turn the PLANT and NATURAL keyword records and the predicted natural regeneration into tree records. The line numbers are in `estb/estab.f` unless a file is named.

**Plot replication.** The regeneration model processes each inventory plot DUP times, where DUP is the smallest number of copies for which the number of plots times DUP is at least MINREP, or the largest number for which the number of plots times DUP + 1 does not exceed MAXPLT (`estab.f:199-208`). MINREP is 50 by default (`estb/esinit.f:59`), and the MINPLOTS keyword sets it with a minimum of 20 (`estb/esin.f:587-588`). The copies of a plot are split among the site preparations (`estab.f:450-469`), and the records of the following paragraphs are created once for each copy, so the number of records is multiplied by the number of copies.

$$
DUPNPT = NPTIDS \times DUP
\tag{4.7.1.1}
$$

Where:

- DUPNPT: Number of plot copies that are processed
- NPTIDS: Number of inventory plots
- DUP: Number of copies of each inventory plot, as described above

**Planted trees.** The PLANT and NATURAL keyword records have the fields species, trees per acre, percent survival, age, height and shade code (`estb/esin.f:206-243`). A survival percent outside 0.001 to 100 is set to 100 (`esin.f:234`), and a request with trees per acre or survival of 0.001 or less is deleted (`estab.f:415-422`). At most 99 requests are processed in a call; the others are cancelled with a warning (`estab.f:979-984`). For each request and each plot copy, the trees per acre of the record is PTREE, equation {4.7.1.2} (`estab.f:986-1014`). The shade code is 0 (no adjustment), 1 (more trees on plots with more basal area) or 2 (more trees on plots with less basal area).

$$
PTREE = \frac{TPA \cdot S / 100}{DUPNPT} \times f, \qquad
f = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{shade code 0} \\[1ex] \dfrac{NPTIDS \cdot BAA}{SUM1} & \text{shade code 1} \\[1ex] \dfrac{NPTIDS \cdot SUM1 / BAA}{SUM2} & \text{shade code 2} \end{cases}
\tag{4.7.1.2}
$$

Where:

- PTREE: Trees per acre of the record of the request on one plot copy (trees per acre)
- TPA: Trees per acre of the request, field 2 of the keyword record (trees per acre)
- S: Survival of the request, field 3 of the keyword record (percent)
- DUPNPT: Number of plot copies from equation {4.7.1.1}
- NPTIDS: Number of inventory plots
- BAA: Basal area of the plot, BAAA of the plot, limited to 1.0 to 400 (square feet per acre; `estab.f:482-484`)
- SUM1: Sum over the inventory plots of BAAA, each limited to 1.0 or more (square feet per acre; `estab.f:426-438`)
- SUM2: Sum over the inventory plots of SUM1 divided by BAAA, each BAAA limited to 1.0 or more (`estab.f:434-442`)

The height of a planted tree is from ESSUBH, or, when field 5 is 0.1 or more, a lognormal draw around the given height that is kept within 0.5 and 2 times the given height; HTADJ is added, and the height is limited to the species minimum XMIN and maximum HHTMAX (`estab.f:1018-1040`). The age is field 4, set to 2.0 when it is below 0.5 and limited to 10.0 (`estab.f:987-989`). A record that is passed to the tree list is split when it has more than 10 trees per acre, as in equation {4.7.1.7}.

**Natural regeneration.** In the variants with the full establishment model, the probability of stocking of a plot copy is PROB1, equation {4.7.1.3} (`estab.f:575-584`). The number of trees on a stocked plot, ITPP, is from ESTPP and is limited to 1 to MAXTPP of the habitat group (and to MAXING in ingrowth) (`estab.f:675-686`). NEWTPP is the increase in ITPP from the previous tally, with a minimum of 0. The number of species is from ESNSPE, and is limited by MAXSPP of the habitat group and by the number of species with a probability of advanced or subsequent regeneration above 0.0001 (`estab.f:693-737`). The species of the first trees come from the advanced and subsequent probabilities (PADV, PSUB) and the species of the other trees from the excess probabilities (PXCS) (`estab.f:738-926`). When STOADJ is below 0.0001 no natural trees are created (`estab.f:958-963`).

$$
PROB1 = \begin{cases} PNN + 0.0001 & P < PNN \\ P & P \ge PNN \end{cases}, \qquad
P = \min\left[0.9990, \; \max\left(0.0001, \; \frac{STOADJ}{1 + e^{-\left(PN + ESB - ESB1\right)}}\right)\right]
\tag{4.7.1.3}
$$

Where:

- PROB1: Probability of stocking of the plot copy at the end of the cycle
- STOADJ: Stocking adjustment multiplier, which is set to 0.001 when it is below 0.001 (`estab.f:578`); keyword STOCKADJ sets it
- PN: Logit of the probability of stocking at the end of the cycle, from subroutine ESTOCK
- ESB: Logit of the stocking of the inventory, calculated from the regeneration trees per acre of the inventory, and 0 when no correction applies (`estab.f:288`, `estab.f:302-326`)
- ESB1: Logit of the stocking that the model predicts at the time of the inventory, from subroutine ESTOCK (`estab.f:536-537`)
- PNN: Probability of stocking of the plot copy at the previous tally

$$
ESPROB_i = \begin{cases} \max\left(0.0001, \; PROB1 - PNN\right) & i \le ITPP - NEWTPP \\[1ex] \max\left(0.0001, \; PROB1\right) & i > ITPP - NEWTPP \end{cases}
\tag{4.7.1.4}
$$

Where:

- ESPROB_i: Probability of stocking assigned to natural tree i of the plot copy
- PROB1: Probability of stocking from equation {4.7.1.3}
- PNN: Probability of stocking of the plot copy at the previous tally
- ITPP: Number of natural trees on the stocked plot
- NEWTPP: Number of natural trees that are new in this tally

In ingrowth (NTALLY of 99) and when the first tally of a stand follows an inventory more than 20 years after the disturbance (`estab.f:237`), ESPROB_i is PROB1 × NEWTPP / ITPP for every tree, with the same minimum (`estab.f:944-952`).

**Best trees.** When there are 5 or more natural and planted records in the plot copy, the best trees are the two tallest trees, then the tallest tree of each other species, then the tallest remaining trees until there are at least 4; when there are fewer than 5 records all of them are best trees (`estab.f:1078-1143`). The natural records are not eligible when PROB1 is below 0.00011 (`estab.f:1088`).

**Passing the records to the tree list.** The records are passed in three groups (`estab.f:1196-1446`). Every new record has DBH 0.1, a crown ratio of 0 and no growth, and is on the real plot of the copy; the new record count is ITRN + 1, and ESGENT then grows the records to the end of the cycle (`estab.f:1493`).

1. **Natural best trees.** A record is created for a natural best tree when ESPROB is 0.00011 or more. The record is not subject to mortality for 20 years (IESTAT = IDSDAT + 20), and the tree value class IMC is 1.

$$
PROB = \frac{ESPROB \times 300}{DUPNPT}
\tag{4.7.1.5}
$$

Where:

- PROB: Trees per acre of the record, PROB(ITRN) (trees per acre)
- ESPROB: Probability of stocking of the natural best tree from equation {4.7.1.4}
- DUPNPT: Number of plot copies from equation {4.7.1.1}
- 300: Number of 1/300th acre plots in an acre

2. **Natural excess trees.** The trees of a species that are not best trees are accumulated by species. They are passed in INT(EXCESS/5 + 1) records of the species (`estab.f:1280-1359`), each with IMC 2 and the mean height of the excess trees of the species. The total number of excess trees that are passed per plot copy and species is limited to PASMAX, which is 5 by default (`estb/esinit.f:51`) and 15 in ingrowth (`estab.f:249`); field 1 of the PASSALL keyword sets it, with a minimum of 1 (`esin.f:556-557`). When the sum of ESPROB of a species is below 0.00011 it is added to the next species.

$$
\begin{aligned}
n &= \mathrm{INT}\left(\frac{EXCESS}{5} + 1\right) \\
PROB &= \frac{\left(SUMESP / EXCESS\right) \times 300 \times \min\left(EXCESS, PASMAX\right) / n}{DUPNPT}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.7.1.6}
$$

Where:

- n: Number of records of the species on the plot copy
- PROB: Trees per acre of each record (trees per acre)
- EXCESS: Number of excess trees of the species on the plot copy
- SUMESP: Sum of ESPROB of the excess trees of the species
- PASMAX: Maximum number of excess trees passed per plot copy and species, 5 by default and 15 in ingrowth
- DUPNPT: Number of plot copies from equation {4.7.1.1}

3. **PLANT and NATURAL trees.** A request with ESPROB below 0.00011 is added to the next request (`estab.f:1369-1373`). Each remaining request is split into INT(ESPROB/10 + 1) records of equal size, with IMC 1, or 2 when the tree is not a best tree and STOADJ is above 0 (`estab.f:1374-1386`). The total trees per acre of the request over the plot copies is then TPA × S / 100.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \mathrm{INT}\left(\frac{PTREE}{10} + 1\right) \\
PROB &= \frac{PTREE}{m}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.7.1.7}
$$

Where:

- m: Number of records of the request on the plot copy
- PROB: Trees per acre of each record (trees per acre)
- PTREE: Trees per acre of the request on the plot copy from equation {4.7.1.2} (trees per acre)

The next table lists the attributes of the three kinds of record.

```{r regen-record-kinds, echo=FALSE}
regen_record_kinds <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Record_Kind, ~Trees_Per_Acre, ~IMC, ~IESTAT, ~WK4, ~ABIRTH,
  "Natural best tree", "Equation 4.7.1.5", "1", "IDSDAT + 20", "HTIMLT of the tree", "AGADSB of the tree",
  "Natural excess trees", "Equation 4.7.1.6", "2", "0", "STOMLT of the species", "AGEXC of the species",
  "PLANT or NATURAL tree", "Equation 4.7.1.7", "1, or 2 for a non-best tree when STOADJ > 0", "0", "HTIMLT of the request", "AGEPL of the request"
)

kable(regen_record_kinds,
      col.names = c("Record kind", "Trees per acre", "IMC", "IESTAT", "WK4", "ABIRTH"),
      caption = "Attributes of the regeneration tree records (source: estb/estab.f:1196-1446)",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "9em")
```

After all plots are processed, GENTIM is added to ABIRTH of every new record (`estab.f:1496-1505`). When ITRN is within 99 records of the maximum, ESTAB calls ESGENT and ESCPRS, which compress the tree list to half of the maximum (`estab.f:1183-1188`). The limits of the allocation are in the next table.

```{r regen-limits, echo=FALSE}
regen_limits <- tibble::tribble(

  "PLANT and NATURAL requests per call", "99", "estab.f:979-984",
  "Request deleted when trees per acre or survival is", "0.001 or less", "estab.f:417",
  "Minimum ESPROB of a record", "0.0001 (record is created from 0.00011)", "estab.f:951, 1203, 1369",
  "Stocking probability PROB1", "0.0001 to 0.9990, then at least PNN + 0.0001", "estab.f:581-583",
  "Excess trees passed per plot copy and species (PASMAX)", "5 by default, 15 in ingrowth; PASSALL sets it", "estb/esinit.f:51, estab.f:249, estb/esin.f:556",
  "Records per species for excess trees", "INT(EXCESS / 5 + 1)", "estab.f:1289",
  "Records per PLANT or NATURAL request", "INT(PTREE / 10 + 1)", "estab.f:1374",
  "Best trees", "At least 4, when 5 or more records", "estab.f:1078-1143"
)

kable(regen_limits,
      col.names = c("Item", "Value", "Source"),
      caption = "Limits and constants of the regeneration record allocation",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
```
