## Producing final FVS reports


### Subroutines involved and their function

After the last cycle, subroutine FVS processes stop point -1, which signals that stopping can no longer continue for this stand (see [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api)). It then increments ICYC and sets the scalar variable ICL6 to a value of -99 which will be used to signal subroutine DISPLY that the projection is complete. It saves some parameter values that will be needed when writing the final lines of the output tables and calls SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, to compute the stand SDI at the end of the projection. Subroutine FVS then calls subroutine DISPLY to write the final stand and tree statistics to the stand composition, sample tree, and summary statistics tables.

Once the final lines of the output tables have been written, subroutine DISPLY writes an end-of-file marker on the scratch file containing the summary tree information and calls subroutine PRTEXM. An unformatted scratch file containing output table information has been written as the projection was running. Subroutine PRTEXM reads data from the unformatted scratch file that comprises the example tree and stand attribute table and writes the table in line printer format on unit JOSTND which is the main output file.

Subroutine DISPLY then calls ECEND to write the last lines of economic output. ECEND will exist as a subroutine if the variant executable contains the economic extension; it will exist as an entry point in subroutine EXECON if the variant does not contain the economic extension.

The summary output table is written next. Subroutine DISPLY calls subroutine GROHED to produce header information for the table; subroutine LBSPLW to write the stand policy label set if one was entered using the SPLABEL keyword record (see section 6.6 of the EFVS guide for a description of policy labeling); and subroutine SUMOUT to write the summary statistics table contents.

Subroutine SUMOUT also calls subroutine DBSSUMRY, which writes the FVS_Summary table to the output database when it has been requested. Subroutine DISPLY calls subroutine OPLIST to produce the Activity Summary table; OPLIST calls subroutine DBSCMPU, which writes the FVS_Compute table to the output database when it has been requested. When DISPLY is called after the inventory (that is, at the end of each cycle and again at the end of the projection), it calls subroutine DBSSUMRY2, which writes the FVS_Summary2 rows for the cycle, and subroutine DBSCARBBIOSUMRY, which writes the FVS_FIAVBC_Summary rows. DISPLY then returns program control back to subroutine FVS.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine SSTAGE to compute the structural stage classes for the stand at the end of the projection.

Subroutine SVOUT is called by subroutine FVS to print information that will be used in the end-of-projection stand visualization if this was selected by the user.

Code segments that write end-of-projection output for other extensions are called next. These will exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the variant executable or as an entry point in the corresponding externals subroutine if it is not. These code segments are: ESOUT for the regeneration establishment extension; CVOUT for the cover extension; MPBOUT for the mountain pine beetle extension; DFBOUT for the Douglas-fir beetle extension; TMOUT for the tussock moth extension; BWEOUT for the budworm extension; and BRROUT for the blister rust extension. The western root disease model no longer has an end-of-projection call; its output is written through the multiple report file by GENPRT.

Subroutine FVS then calls GENPRT, an entry point in subroutine GENRPT, which reads the reports that were saved in the multiple report scratch file as the projection ran and writes them to the main output file in report number order, so that the reports from each extension appear as complete tables for the entire projection of this stand.

### Auxiliary subroutines

DBSCMPU is called by subroutine OPLIST and is used to populate a database with values of computed variables if a database is being used. DBSCMPU will exist as a subroutine in the database directory if the database extension is part of the program executable; it will exist as an entry point in subroutine EXDBS in the FVS base directory if the database extension is not part of the variant.

DBSSUMRY is called by subroutine SUMOUT and is used to populate the database with summary output information if a database is being used. DBSSUMRY2 (FVS_Summary2) and DBSCARBBIOSUMRY (FVS_FIAVBC_Summary) are called by subroutine DISPLY. DBSSUMRY will exist as a subroutine in the database directory if the database extension is part of the variant executable; it will exist as an entry point in subroutine EXDBS in the FVS base directory if the database extension is not part of the variant.

ECLBL is used to output label information used by the economics extension. ECLBL will exist as a subroutine in the economics extension source directory if this extension is part of the program executable; it will exist as an entry point in subroutine EXECON in the FVS base source directory if the economics extension in not part of the program executable.

Subroutine FORTYP is used to compute the FIA forest type based on stand stocking levels.

Subroutine GRDTIM is used to retrieve the date and time the projection was made for labeling the output tables.

Subroutine OPBISR is used to find activity codes. Activity codes are used to retrieve information for printing the activity summary table.

Subroutine OPCYCL is used set pointers to activities which were accomplished during a projection cycle. These pointers are used in printing the activity summary table.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to set the year any RESETAGE, FVSSTAND, or TREELIST activities are accomplished.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to find any RESETAGE, FVSSTAND, or TREELIST activities scheduled for the projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve any RESETAGE, FVSSTAND, or TREELIST activities scheduled for the projection cycle.

Subroutine OPSORT is used to sort activities by projection cycles for printing in the activity summary table.

Subroutine REVISE is called to retrieve the date of the last git commit at the time of the build, for labeling output tables.

Subroutine SDICAL is called to compute the end-of-cycle SDI maximum.

Various code segments are used to retrieve keyword record names used in an FVS extension for printing in the activity summary table. These include: ESKEY for the regeneration establishment extension; TMKEY for the tussock moth extension; MPKEY for the mountain pine beetle extension; CVKEY for the cover extension; DBSKEY for the database extension; BRKEY for the blister rust extension; MISKEY for the dwarf-mistletoe extension; BWKEY for the budworm extension; DFB key for the Douglas-fir beetle extension; BMKEY for the west-wide beetle model extension; RDKEY for the root disease extension; FMKEY for the fire and fuels effects extension; and ECKEY for the economics extension. These subroutines will exist as subroutines in the extension’s source directory if the extension is part of the program executable; they will exist as entry points in the corresponding externals file in the FVS base source directory if the extension is not part of the program executable (e.g. EXCOV for the cover extension).

## Running more than one stand {#sec-running-more-than-one-stand}

Processing of the stand is now complete, but other stands might need to be run. Subroutine FVS returns to its caller, which calls FVS again; each call begins by setting the logical variables LSTART and LFLAG to “.TRUE.” and the variable ICYC to 0, and calling subroutine INITRE discussed in [Processing keyword record requests](#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests-subroutines-involved-and-their-function). The run terminates if the next keyword record read is a STOP keyword record; if the keyword record is any other FVS keyword record, then processing of the next stand begins.

As discussed in [General Flow Overview](#sec-general-flow-overview), a run consisting of a single stand is called a single stand serial run. A run consisting of multiple stands organized as discussed in the paragraph above is called a multiple stand serial run. A multiple stand serial run may contain as many individual stand projections as you want. Each stand projection might be a projection of a different stand, different projections (i.e. different management alternatives) of the same stand, or a combination of the two. The projection of each stand follows the same logic outlined in [Processing keyword record requests](#sec-processing-keyword-record-requests) through [Running more than one stand](#sec-running-more-than-one-stand).

A parallel model run follows virtually the same flow as its serial counterpart for each stand in the project initialization, projection cycling, and output reporting phases. Details of a parallel model run are covered in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api).

# Option Processing Logic {#sec-option-processing-logic}

This section provides an overview of the option processing logic. To some degree, the topic has been covered in the descriptions of how keyword records are processed, options scheduled, retrieved, and accomplished (or not). Consider two cases that could be called setting an option: (1) setting the stand elevation is something that is done immediately when FVS reads the STDINFO keyword record, where (2) specifying that a thinning should be accomplished 40 years into a simulation is scheduling the option to occur during the simulation. Here we are discussing options that are scheduled to be done sometime during the simulation (see [Scheduling the Option](#sec-scheduling-the-option)).

```{r fvs-seq-options, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  htmltools::tags$div(`data-fvs-seq` = "options")
} else {
  cat("The interactive figure is available in the HTML version of this document.")
}
```

**Figure 6-1. Option (activity) processing: how an activity is posted, found, retrieved, and marked. Select a box to show the steps involved.**

## General logic and table structure

When a keyword record indicates an option that needs to be scheduled, for example THINDBH, the program needs to store the option, the year it is scheduled, and its parameter values. This is done by calling subroutine OPNEW with an activity code corresponding to the option, the year (internally called a date and stored in vector IDATE in the labeled COMMON block OPCOM), and the parameter values associated with the option, which are typically stored in the PARMS vector. The array IACT(i,j) is an important 2 dimensional array in the labeled COMMON block OPCOM that stores this information, or pointers to that information. When the PARMS feature of an activity is used, the parameter values are entered as expressions. When this is the case, the compiled operations code (created by subroutine ALGCMP) associated with the option is stored in the array IEVCOD(k) in the labeled COMMON block OPCOM.

Activities might be specified as part of an IF-THEN-ENDIF keyword record sequence. In that case, the option is not scheduled until the event occurs. The year field (so-called date) is interpreted as a number of years after the event occurs. When the event does occur, the number of years after an event occurs is added to the year the event occurs and that sum becomes the scheduling year.

The labeled COMMON block OPCOM stores all the data associated with these processes. The comment statements in OPCOM further explain these variables and their use.

Naming conventions for subroutines that support the option processing logic are useful to know. Those subroutines named ALG___ are for the expression compiling and evaluation logic ([Event monitor logic](#sec-event-monitor-logic)). One of these, subroutine ALGSLP, computes a linear interpolation and is used in several extensions, including the fire and fuels extension and climate extension. Subroutines named EV___ are directly related to the event monitor; that code supports the IF-THEN-ENDIF constructs in the keyword record file (see [Event monitor logic](#sec-event-monitor-logic)). Those subroutines named OP___ support options and are generally used to schedule and retrieve activities.

Label processing is supported by those subroutines named LB___. If the AGPLABEL and SPLABEL keyword records were ever removed from the FVS system, the label processing subroutines and the data structures they use can be deleted from FVS.

One more detail: a few options have character strings as parameters, not numbers. The ability to schedule a database query is an example; the SQL statement is a string stored in the option processor code that is returned when the query is run. Storing and retrieving a character string is supported by subroutine OPCACT (for storing the activity) and by OPGETC (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND) for retrieving the character string. Storing and retrieving a vector of numbers is accomplished using OPGET (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND) and subroutine OPGET2.

## Understanding option codes and activity numbers

Every option that is scheduled has an associated activity number (or code) that was chosen by the programmer creating the option; every keyword record name has an associated keyword record number that is the index to the location in the array TABLE(i) where the keyword record name is located. There is a relationship between an activity number and a keyword record number. For example, THINABA is the 27th keyword record name in the array TABLE(i) of all base model keyword record names (so the keyword record number is 27), and has an option process activity code of 226. This fact is stored in two arrays in the subroutine OPLIST. The first is a sorted list of activity codes, array ITRSL1(i), and the second is corresponds to the keyword record number (or index) in the array TABLE(i), array ITRSL2(i). Since the activity code, 226, is in the 38th position in the sorted order of activity codes, ITRSL1(38) = 226, and the corresponding ITRSL2(i) = 27.

This translation scheme is used to output the activity schedule and the activity summary tables in the FVS main output file. Note that when an activity is part of an extension, there is an extension coding system that relates the activity code to the keyword record. Take care to insure these two tables stay in sync and “look” good when adding a keyword record. This table would be a mess to interpret if every programmer just modified it and stuck the new codes in without keeping the table nicely formatted.

Subroutines that accomplish activities access them via the activity codes. This is explained in more detail in [Adding new keyword records](#sec-adding-new-keyword-records).

## Adding new keyword records {#sec-adding-new-keyword-records}

The inner workings of the option processing logic are complicated. However, the ability to quickly add new activity keyword records to the system, including the ability to have their parameter values be computed during a simulation (on-the-fly), is supported by this logic.

FVS maintenance often involves adding a new keyword record, or new “activity”. The process to do this can be broken down into seven steps. If the keyword record being added contains a year/cycle field, then all seven steps need to be followed; if the keyword record does not contain a year/cycle field then steps 3 and 5 can be skipped. These seven steps are illustrated with the base model CRNMULT keyword record.

Steps in adding a new keyword record to the FVS code:

### Adding the keyword record name

1. Make sure the TABLE(i) array in the labeled COMMON block KEYCOM is big enough to hold the new keyword record:

    a. Look in subroutine KEYWDS and see if there are any vacant spots at the end of the TABLE(i) array where the new keyword record name can be inserted. If there are vacant spots, then go to step 2. If there aren’t any vacant spots, then go on to 1b.

    b. In the labeled COMMON block KEYCOM, change the date of revision, if appropriate, and expand the dimension of the TABLE(i) array by modifying the variable ISIZE in the PARAMETER statement.

2. Add the new keyword record name to the TABLE(i) array in subroutine KEYWDS:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. If the variable ISIZE in step 1 was not changed, then simply insert the new keyword record name in a vacant spot. If the variable ISIZE in step 1 was changed, then expand the last DATA statement, inserting the new keyword in the next spot, and padding out the TABLE(i) array with blank entries to correspond to the length specified in step 1 (i.e. if the variable ISIZE was incremented by 5, then expand the last data statement by 5 and insert the new keyword record name in the first vacant spot followed by 4 blank spots to accommodate future additional keywords). Note the location (i.e. array index number) where the new keyword record name was inserted since it may be needed later.  For example, the keyword CRNMULT is located in array location 96 (i.e. TABLE (96)).

### Add the activity code (if necessary)

3. Modify the ITRSL1(i) and ITRSL2(i) arrays in subroutine OPLIST.  (do this step ONLY if the new keyword record has a year/cycle field):

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. First choose a new activity code that will be associated with the new keyword record name. If the activity code is going to be added to an existing subroutine (CUTS, for example, which already handles several activities), then the new code should fit in to the set of existing codes being performed by CUTS. Activity codes in array ITRSL1(i) are in ascending order. Look in this array and find an activity code that is not currently being used. Enter this activity number in the proper sequence (ascending order) in the array ITRSL1(i). Make sure you either omit a zero off the end of the array, or expand the array dimension, parameter NTRSLT, as appropriate. Note the position (array location) where this activity code is entered. For example, the CRNMULT keyword was assigned activity number 81 and this activity number was entered in the third location in ITRSL1 (i.e. ITRSL1(3)) (at least it was the third location at the time this document was written; it may be in a different location now if keyword records have been added with activity numbers less than 81).

    c. Modify the ITRSL2(i) array by inserting the index from step 2b (i.e. the index to the location in the TABLE (i) array where the keyword record name is located) into the position in array ITRSL2(i) corresponding to the location where the activity number was entered in array ITRSL1(i) in step 3b. Once again, remember to remove a zero from the end of the ITRSL2(i) array if appropriate. For example, the CRNMULT keyword occupies location 96 in the TABLE(i) array (from step 2b). So the number 96 gets loaded into the ITRSL2(i) array in the location corresponding to the location occupied by the CRNMULT activity number in array ITRSL1(i). In this case, and at the time this was written, this is the third location. So ITRSL1(3) contains the activity number (81) for the CRNMULT keyword and ITRSL2(3) contains the array index (96) which says the CRNMULT keyword record name is in location TABLE(96).

### Adding code to read and process the keyword record

4. Add code to the appropriate subroutine to read and process the keyword record. For a base model keyword this is subroutine INITRE; if the keyword record applies to an extension, then this may be a different subroutine (e.g. ESIN for a regeneration establishment model keyword record). However, the steps are basically the same. Go into subroutine INITRE and:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Modify the computed GO TO statement which is after the 90 CONTINUE statement by inserting an unused statement label into the position corresponding to the location number noted in step 2b. For example, for the CRNMULT keyword, statement label 9800 was entered in position 96 of this GO TO statement.

    c. Go to the appropriate place in INITRE and insert a CONTINUE statement with the statement label from step 4b, followed by the appropriate code to process the new keyword. For example, see the code following the 9800 CONTINUE statement for the code which processes the CRNMULT keyword. Also, note the comment statements immediately preceding the 9800 CONTINUE statement.

    When adding code to read the keyword record to the input subroutine, follow established patterns. Find call sequences utilizing subroutine OPNEW and/or subroutine OPNEWC to store the parameter values, subroutines KEYDMP and ERRGRO to process keyword record errors, subroutine SPDECD to process species codes and species groups, and so forth, and duplicate those patterns.

5. Add code to the subroutine that will process the activity code (do this step ONLY if the new keyword record has a year/cycle field). Go into the subroutine where this activity will be processed:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Add code to the subroutine to process the activity. In some cases, where the subroutine is already checking for activities, this is as simple as adding the activity number from step 3b to the array containing activity codes processed by this subroutine, usually the MYACTS(i) array, and then inserting the code at the appropriate place in the subroutine to implement the activity. In other cases, if the subroutine is not currently processing any activities, it involves defining and dimensioning a MYACTS(i) array and adding calls to the option processing subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND).

    If the activity is being implemented in a base model subroutine, this step may only require that you change one subroutine. However, if the activity is being processed in a variant dependent subroutine, it will require changing every version of the subroutine for all the variants. For example, the activity associated with the CRNMULT keyword record is processed in subroutine CROWN that is a variant dependent routine. So subroutine CROWN for every variant needed to be changed.  The changes involved defining and dimensioning the MYACTS(i) array; loading the CRNMULT activity number (81) into the MYACTS array; inserting calls to the option processing routines to find, retrieve, process the activity, and mark it “DONE”; and inserting other code in the routine to use the parameter values contained on the CRNMULT keyword record.

    When adding code to implement an activity in a subroutine, follow established patterns. Two examples come to mind; subroutines CWIDTH and FFERT both “accomplish” one activity and can be used as templates for coding the important sequences of calling subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND). On the other hand, subroutine CUTS deals with 23 different activities that are organized into 3 groups. If you want to review a more complicated example, see that code.

6. This step may be required; it may not. For some keyword records containing a year/cycle field their implementation is completely handled in step 5; other keyword records containing a year/cycle field get processed as in step 5 and then associated parameter values get passed to other subroutines through argument lists. Keywords not containing a year/cycle field get processed in subroutine INITRE and typically change the value of variables that are contained in COMMON blocks. For those keyword records this step may be required to actually implement the purpose of the keyword record.  Go into the appropriate subroutine, or subroutines:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Insert the code necessary for implementing the keyword record purpose.

### Assign parameter default values and add variables to subroutines GETSTD and PUTSTD

7. This step is needed if new variables were created in association with the keyword record and added to a COMMON block. Be aware of possible impacts on the COMMON statements when deciding how to get keyword parameters from one place to another in the code. Make sure the variable names picked do not currently exist in any COMMON block, or in any subroutine that will implement the keyword record purpose. Go into subroutine GRINIT and:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Make sure the labeled COMMON block containing the new variables is available through an INCLUDE statement.

    c. Initialize the new variables to a default value for use when the keyword record is not present.

    d. Add the new variables to subroutines GETSTD and PUTSTD. This step is needed so the FVS STOP / RESTART feature will work correctly.


# Event monitor logic {#sec-event-monitor-logic}

As described in [Option Processing Logic](#sec-option-processing-logic), activities can be scheduled to occur after an event happens. Events happen when a logical expression that defines the event is determined to be true. For example, an event can be defined as the culmination of mean annual increment, detected by comparing mean annual increment to current annual increment. Another example may be the time during a simulation when the stand density index exceeds a percentage of maximum. This section describes the code that supports event processing.

## General logic and structure

An event is a logical expression that is entered with the IF keyword record. Subroutine EVIF is called to store information about the event. One of the first steps is to read and compile the logical expression by calling subroutine EVCOMP, which in turn calls subroutine ALGCMP. The logic of the expression is stored in memory areas in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block. Some of these memory arrays are described in [Option Processing Logic](#sec-option-processing-logic).

The 2 dimensional array IEVACT(i,j), in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, stores the relationships between activities and events. The idea of an “activity group” is important to this logic. An activity group is the set of activities that are all scheduled when an event occurs. IEVNTS(i,j) is another 2 dimensional array, in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, where each row stores pointers to the operation code associated with the event. That is, when an IF keyword record is read, the logical expression is compiled into operations code (by subroutine ALGCMP) and stored in vector IEVCOD(k). The location of that operation code inside IEVCOD(k) is stored in IEVNTS(i,j).

Operations code is a set of integer values that define a sequence of operations in post-fix notation. Post-fix notation is also called Reverse Polish notation (RPN) and is a mathematical notation in which every operator follows all of its operands, in contrast to Polish notation, which puts the operator in the prefix position. For example, the adding of 3 and 4, in prefix position is: 3+4 and in RPN it is 3 4 +. Expressions entered in prefix notation are converted to postfix by subroutine ALGCMP. Operations codes are used in this logic. For example, consider the expression: BTOPHT GT 80. Table 7-1 shows how this expression would be converted to a sequence of 4 integers stored in IEVCOD(k):

```{r tbl-7-1, echo=FALSE}
df <- data.frame(
  c1 = c(
    "1",
    "2",
    "3",
    "4"
  ),
  c2 = c(
    "109",
    "1001",
    "6",
    "0"
  ),
  c3 = c(
    "load the pre-defined event monitor variable BTOPHT onto a stack (a vector of real numbers)",
    "load constant number 1 which has the value 80, and is stored in the first location of array PARMS(i) (called CONSTS in ALGCMP), onto the stack structure ",
    "GT, compare the two values on the stack, put the result on the logical stack, and pop the numeric stack ",
    "signals that the expression is finished and the result in on the logical stack"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(df,
      col.names = c("Sequence", "Op code", "Description"),
      caption = "Table 7-1: Example showing how the expression BTOPHT GT 80 is converted to a sequence of 4 integers in FVS.",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```


The comments in subroutine ALGKEY provide a comprehensive list of operations codes. That information is repeated in subroutine ALGEVL. Keeping these comments up to date is essential.

Functions, are powerful and are used extensively to compute new variables and in defining events. An example is the MIN function, operations code 109NN, where NN is the actual number of arguments (up to 99), each separated by a comma. For example, consider this expression: MIN (10,BBA,ABA,1), where BBA and ABA are the pre-defined event monitor variables for total stand basal area before-thinning and after-thinning, respectively. Table 7-2 shows how this expression is converted to operations code:

```{r tbl-7-2, echo=FALSE}
df <- data.frame(
  c1 = c(
    "1",
    "2",
    "3",
    "4",
    "5",
    "6"
  ),
  c2 = c(
    "1002",
    "107",
    "205",
    "1001",
    "10904",
    "0"
  ),
  c3 = c(
    "load constant number 2, which has the value 10, and is stored in the second location of array PARMS(i) (called CONSTS in ALGCMP), onto the stack structure",
    "load the pre-defined event monitor variable BBA, before-thinning total stand basal area ",
    "load the pre-defined event monitor variable ABA, after-thinning total stand basal area ",
    "load constant number 1 which happens to have the value 1, and is stored in the first location of array PARMS(i) (called CONSTS in ALGCMP), onto the stack structure",
    "find the min of 4 values (because NN=4), place it at the top of the stack and pop 3 times)",
    "signals that the expression is finished and the answer is on the top of the numeric stack"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(df,
      col.names = c("Sequence", "Op code", "Description"),
      caption = "Table 7-2: Example showing how the expression MIN (10,BBA,ABA,1) is converted to operations code in FVS.",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```


Subroutine EVMON manages the process of evaluating an expression, first by loading the values of variables used in expressions by calling subroutine EVTSTV. The logical expressions that define events are evaluated twice every cycle. The first time happens at the beginning of the cycle just before subroutine CUTS, and is called phase 1. The second call happens after subroutine CUTS, and is called phase 2. A first step in evaluating expressions is to compute user-defined variables so that they can be used in the logical expressions.

Subroutine EVTSTV loads state variables into vectors used for evaluation and deals with user-defined variables (those defined with the COMPUTE - END keyword record sequence). It provides an interface for extensions to set, unset, and interrogate the value of event monitor variables the extension may be responsible for managing (for example, the variable PNV, which is present net value, is managed by the economics extension).

Key rules in the evaluation process include the concept of a variable being defined or not defined. If an expression includes a variable that is not defined, the expression is also not defined. A logical expression that is not defined is not true. In the example, MIN (10,BBA,ABA,1), the variable ABA is not defined during phase 1, so the result is not defined in phase 1. It is tried again in phase 2 where ABA is defined and so the expression is defined.

A frequent programming task is to add new functions to FVS (see [Steps in adding a new event monitor function to FVS](#sec-steps-in-adding-a-new-event-monitor-function-to-fvs)). The name and operations code is added to subroutine ALGKEY (see the comments in that code and follow the establish patterns). They are evaluated in subroutine ALGEVL; read that code to see how the evaluation logic is programmed.

Variables are divided into groups depending on when they are defined. Those defined during phase 1, for example the variable BADBH that is the before thin average diameter at breast height, are in group 1. Those that are always known are also in group 1. They have corresponding operations codes that are in the hundreds. Variables added more recently include BGMD (code 159, the before thin generalized mean diameter, which is the Reineke diameter computed by the Zeide method and held in the variable DR016) and LOCCODE (code 160, the location code, KODFOR) in group 1, and AGMD (code 238, the after thin generalized mean diameter) in group 2. Subroutine DENSE now computes DR016 whether or not the Zeide method is used for SDI, and the labeled COMMON block CONTRL holds its values at the end of the previous cycle (ODR016, set before thinning) and after thinning (ATDR016).

A multiplier or an expression can be coded on the THEN (or ALSOTRY) keyword records to modify the branch weighting factor of the former Parallel Processing Extension when the event occurs. This capability was included to support decision-tree analytics. The Parallel Processing Extension has been removed, so the feature has no effect; however, column 6 of IEVACT still stores the setting (it is set in subroutine EVTACT and tested in subroutine OPSAME), so deleting column 6 would require changing both subroutines.

## Adding new pre-defined variables and functions

FVS maintenance often involves adding a new event monitor variable or function. The steps to do this are shown below.

### Steps in adding a new event monitor variable to FVS

Pre-defined event monitor variables are useful for many purposes. Values for pre-defined variables are stored in 5 single dimension arrays, TSTV1(i), TSTV2(i), TSTV3(i), TSTV4(i), and TSTV5(i), located in the labeled COMMON block OPCOM. Array TSTV1(i) is used for variables that are defined before thinning (aka phase 1) from cycle 1 forward; TSTV2(i) is used for variables that are only defined after thinning (aka phase 2) from cycle 1 forward; TSTV3(i) is used for variables that are defined before thinning from cycle 2 forward; TSTV4(i) is used for variables that are only defined when the corresponding logical flag, LTSTV4(i) (also located in the labeled COMMON block OPCOM)  is “.TRUE.” indicating TSTV4(i) is defined; TSTV5(i) is used for variables that are user defined. The steps necessary to add a new event monitor variable are:

1. Expand the dimension of the array to which the variable will be added. In the labeled COMMON block OPCOM:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Expand the dimension of the appropriate TSTV_(i) array by increasing the corresponding PARAMETER value in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block: MXTST1, MXTST2, MXTST3, MXTST4, or MXTST5 for TSTV1(i), TSTV2(i), TSTV3(i), TSTV4(i), or TSTV5(i), respectively. The arrays LTSTV4(i) and LTSTV5(i) are dimensioned by MXTST4 and MXTST5.

2. In subroutine ALGKEY, add the variable name and option code to the appropriate arrays:

    a. Change the date of revision.

    b. Expand the appropriate array dimension (N1, N2, …,N8) depending on how many letters (up to 8) make up the variable name.

    c. Look in the comments at the top of the routine and pick an appropriate instruction code to go with the new event monitor variable name. Add the instruction code and name to the comments.

    d. Add the instruction code and variable name to the appropriate CTAB_(i) and IOPT_(i) arrays.

3. In subroutine EVTSTV, add the code necessary for calculating a value for the new variable.

    a. Change the date of revision.

    b. Insert the code necessary for calculating a value for the variable.

### Steps in adding a new event monitor function to FVS {#sec-steps-in-adding-a-new-event-monitor-function-to-fvs}

Event monitor functions are useful for many purposes. The steps necessary to add a new event monitor function are:

1. Add the instruction code and function name to subroutine ALGKEY:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Expand the appropriate array dimension (N1, N2, …,N8) depending on how many letters (up to 8) make up the function name.

    c. Look in the comments at the top of the routine and pick an appropriate instruction code to go with the new event monitor function name. Add the instruction code and name to the comments.

    d. Add the instruction code and function name to the appropriate CTAB_(i) and IOPT_(i) arrays.

2. Add code to subroutine ALGEVL to process the new function:

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Expand the GO TO statement just before the 301 CONTINUE statement, by inserting the appropriate CONTINUE statement label which will execute the code necessary to process the new function.

3. Add code to subroutine EVLDX to process the new function

    a. Change the date of revision, if appropriate.

    b. Insert the code necessary for processing the new function.

Follow the established patterns when modifying subroutines ALGEVL and EVLDX.

# Stop/restart and the FVS API {#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api}

A key source of information regarding stop and restart is in the FVS wiki, currently stored at https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/Stop-Restart. It is essential to understand that document prior to reading more here.

The FVS_API is documented at https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/FVS-API

The code also provides the subroutines fvsGetVersion and fvsGetBuildInfo (source file base/version.f90). Each fills a caller-allocated character buffer and returns the number of characters written. fvsGetVersion returns the version tag followed by the organization in parentheses, and fvsGetBuildInfo returns six labeled lines (Version, Org, Remote, Branch, Commit, and Date). Comments in the source say they can be called from R, Python, or any language with a Fortran or C interface. The command line options --version and --build-info print the same text.

### Stop Point 5 and the Diameter Increment {-}

Stop point 5 is called from subroutine GRADD, after subroutine SVMORT and before subroutine UPDATE. When the stop is taken, GRADD returns up the call stack and the tree list holds the following values.

1. `DBH(i)` is the diameter outside bark at the start of the cycle. It has not been updated.
2. `DG(i)` is the diameter increment for the cycle, **inside bark**, on the cycle-length basis. It includes the large-tree and small-tree estimates, the FIXDG and fertilizer adjustments, the scaling from the YR basis to the cycle length done by GRADD (when FINT is not equal to YR), and any change made by the pest, disease and fire routines called before the stop point (see [Diameter increment through the projection cycle](#sec-diameter-increment-through-the-projection-cycle)).
3. `HTG(i)` is the height increment for the cycle, and `HT(i)` has not been updated.
4. `WK2(i)` is the mortality in trees per acre, and `PROB(i)` has not been reduced.

The API attributes `dg`, `htg`, `mort` and `dbh` read and write `DG`, `HTG`, `WK2` and `DBH` directly (subroutine fvsTreeAttr). No bark conversion and no scaling is applied in either direction. A value written to `dg` is therefore taken as an inside bark increment for the cycle length.

When the run is continued with restart code 5, subroutine TREGRO does not call GRINCR and calls GRADD, which branches to the call to UPDATE. The scaling of DG, the pest and fire calls, SVMORT and the stop point itself are not repeated, so the values in the arrays are used as they are. UPDATE then:

1. adds the height increment to the height, `HT(i) = HT(i) + HTG(i)`;
2. reduces `PROB(i)` by `WK2(i)`, with the mortality limited to the trees per acre of the record;
3. calls VOLS, which computes volumes for the end-of-cycle diameter, `DBH(i) + DG(i)/BARK`; and
4. sets `DBH(i) = DBH(i) + DG(i)/BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i))`.

The bark ratio in the last two steps is evaluated with the diameter at the start of the cycle and the updated height. An outside bark increment of Δ inches is therefore obtained by writing `dg = Δ × BRATIO(species, DBH(i), HT(i) + HTG(i))`. UPDATE does not change `DG(i)` and nothing clears it. At the start of the next cycle subroutine DGDRIV copies it to `WK1(i)`, the previous increment used by the mortality routines, and then recomputes `DG(i)`. Values written to `dg` at stop point 5 therefore also become the previous-cycle increment of the next cycle.

## General logic and structure {#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api-general-logic-and-structure}

First, there are two major components to the stop and restart facility. The first component is the logic built into the program that supports the use of return codes for subroutine calls. It is essential that no FORTRAN STOP be executed except in MAIN. This means that if a fatal error state is created, FVS needs to issue an error message, set a non-zero return code, and return back to the calling routine. Changes were made to FVS in ~2011 to insure that this is always the case. Regardless of how deep into the calling sequence the program might be, if a fatal error condition is detected, control must be passed back up the call stack.

Being able to return back up the call stack from anywhere in FVS provides for the ability to return from an arbitrary place in the sequence of calculations. These arbitrary places are called “stop points”. For example, there is a stop point just prior to the first call to the event monitor. If this stop point has been requested, the program will return from that location. When used as a shared library, where the caller is some other program, FVS returns from the stop point and the caller is free to use the FVS_API to interact with FVS (getting, changing, or both, state variables, for example the tree diameters) prior to calling it again to continue the simulation. When FVS is recalled after stopping at a stop point, it “jumps ahead” to where the program previously left off, and continues the projection until the next stop point is reached or to when the simulation is over.

When FVS is used in a shared library, the stop/restart is made possible by the fact that all essential information about the projection is stored in the global (COMMON blocks) memory of the FVS library. Programmers must, therefore, insure that any variables whose values might be needed upon a restart, must be stored in a COMMON block; otherwise their value may be forgotten (or sometimes not forgotten) leading to difficult-to-find runtime errors.

When used as a program (as opposed to being used as a shared library), FVS must store all the data that defines the state of a simulation onto permanent storage (typically, a disk file) prior to stopping. This is done by writing the value of every variable to the file in a way that allows for those data to be recovered when the program is restarted. This file is called a stop point file and it is created if a stop point is defined along with a stop point file name. The program can be restarted using by specifying the name of a previously created stop point file as a restart file (specified using the –restart command line option, see url:https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/FVS-Command-Line for more information) rather than specifying a keyword record file.

There is a wiki page that also covers the stop and restart logic in FVS stored at url:https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/Stop-Restart; it covers this topic in additional detail.

## Subroutines involved and their function {#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api-subroutines-involved-and-their-function}

Most of the code for supporting stop and restart can be found in subroutine CMDLINE, which contains several short subroutines.

The key variables that control the stop and restart functionality are stored in the labeled COMMON block GLBLCNTL that is in a code segment of the same name.

Subroutine fvsRestart (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) is used to restart the program from a previously created stop point file if it is specified on the command line using the –restart= parameter. This subroutine returns the restart code (see subroutine fvsGetRestartCode in subroutine CMDLINE) as well.

Subroutine fvsStopPoint (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) is called from locations within FVS, for example subroutine GRADD, to find out if the subroutine should return or continue processing.  It is called with the location code within program (for example stop point 5 which is after growth and mortality has been computed, but prior to applying them), and the subroutine compares that code with the stop point that is stored and returns with a flag that indicates if stopping at stop point 5 was requested (using the command line or by calling subroutine fvsSetStoppointCodes (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE)). If the stop point is reached, subroutine GRADD returns back up the call stack. The code in subroutine fvsStopPoint is complicated in that if a stop point is reached and a stop point file name is specified, then subroutine PUTSTD is called to write the stand state variables to mass storage. If the stop point file name is not specified, then the program simply returns up the call stack.

A requested stop is either major or minor. A major stop point (command line option --stoppoint=code,year,file) writes the stand state to the stop point file, if one is named, and ends the stand at that point: the next call to FVS starts the next stand, and a stored stand is continued only by restarting with --restart=file. A minor stop point (subroutine fvsSetStoppointCodes, used by rFVS) writes nothing, and FVS continues the stand from memory when it is called again. In either case a year greater than 0 limits the stop to the cycle that contains that year. A major stop point with a year of 0 is disabled, and a minor stop point with a year of 0 or less is not limited by year.

Subroutine fvsGetRestartCode (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) is called at the beginning of a subroutine to retrieve the prior stop point code. For example, it is called at the beginning of subroutine GRINCR so that subroutine GRINCR will jump ahead to where it left off calculations (its last stopping point) as necessary. The same is true for subroutines TREGRO and GRADD.

Entry point getAmStopping (within subroutine CMDLINE) is called to find out if a stop point has been reached in a called subroutine. For example, subroutine TREGRO calls subroutine GRINCR. When subroutine GRINCR returns to subroutine TREGRO, it may be returning because it has reached a stop point. Subroutine TREGRO can find out if that is the situation by calling getAmStopping. Note that similar logic is used to find out if an error has occurred and subroutine TREGRO should return rather than keep going (this is done by calling subroutine fvsGetRtnCode (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE)).

It is critical that variables computed between stop points be saved in COMMON.

It is also critical that all variables in COMMON be stored in the mass storage file when it is used to store and recover information during a simulation.

The writing and subsequent reading of the stand information is done using subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD. There is a set of subroutines that are called by these two basic functions. The origin of these subroutines is the now-retired Parallel Processing Extension (PPE, Crookston and Stage, 1991). A major difference between how PPE accomplished this task and how FVS does it now, is that the PPE used a single direct-access binary file with fixed records sizes. FVS uses two binary data streams, one for reading and another for writing (support for these binary data streams, where arbitrary read positions can be specified, is relatively new in FORTRAN being specified in the 2003 standard). There is no logical record size, the data is simply pushed out to the file system as a data stream and read by retrieving the data in the order it was stored. There is no requirement that both output and input streams be in use at the same time. There is a built-in ability to position the file before the reading starts so that a specific stand can be loaded, skipping others. So far, this capability is only used to “reload” a current stand, which is useful when the results from applying a set of options to a simulation are wanted on a trial bases. This capability was first used by to support some fuel management analyses where the efficiency of the management action depends on a several-year long projection. Those actions that did not meet decision criteria are ignored by restarting the projection at the time of the actions by calling subroutine fvsRestartLastStand (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE), that restarts from where the most recent stand stopped. Note projections can be stopped without calling subroutine PUTSTD. A call to fvsRestartLastStand without a call to PUTSTD would cause FVS to essentially “back up” to the point in the calculations defined in the restart file for the most recent stand.

### Subroutines

See url:https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/FVS-API for information about the API subroutines. Those listed below are called within the FVS program.

Subroutine PUTSTD is used to write all the state variables for a stand to a stream type, binary output file.

Subroutine GETSTD reads the stand from the binary file created by PUTSTD.

Subroutines IFWRIT, LFWRIT, BFWRIT, CHWRIT (code contained in subroutine PUTGETSUBS) write integer, logical, real, and character variables, respectively, and are called by subroutine PUTSTD (except for subroutine CHWRIT which is called by subroutine CHPUT). Their counterparts are subroutines IFREAD, LFREAD, BFREAD, and CHREAD (code contained in subroutine PUTGETSUBS) that are called by subroutine GETSTD (except for subroutine CHREAD which is called by subroutine CHGET). Subroutine putgetsubs.f also calls subroutines STASH and DSTASH (code contained in subroutine STASH), which contain the actual write and read statements. DSTASH contains logic that supports specification of alternative starting positions within the binary file.

Subroutines VARPUT and VARGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store variant-specific data.

CVPUT and CVGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the cover extension. CVPUT and CVGET will exist as subroutines if the cover extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXCOV if the cover extension is not part of the program executable.

MISACT, MSPPPT and MSPPGT are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the dwarf mistletoe extension. MISACT, MSPPPT and MSPPGT will exist as subroutines if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the program executable.

ECNPUT and ECNGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the economics extension. ECNPUT and ECNGET will exist as subroutines if the economics extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXECON if the economics extension is not part of the program executable.

FMPPPUT and FMPPGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the fire and fuels extension. FMPPPUT and FMPPGET will exist as subroutines if the fire and fuels extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXFIRE if the fire and fuels extension is not part of the program executable.

DBSPPPUT and DBSPPGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the database extension. DBSPPPUT and DBSPPGET will exist as subroutines if the database extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXDBS if the database extension is not part of the program executable.

CLPUT and CLGET are called by subroutines PUTSTD and GETSTD, respectively, to store data owned by the climate extension. CLPUT and CLGET will exist as subroutines if the climate extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXCLIM if the climate extension is not part of the program executable.

Other similar routines exist for the root disease, west-wide pine beetle, and budworm extensions.

Subroutine fvsRestart (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) restarts FVS using a restart file (beginning with the first stand stored in the file); it also returns the restart code.

Subroutine fvsGetRestartCode (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) returns the restart code.

Entry point getAmStopping, in subroutine CMDLINE, returns a flag indicating if a stop point was reached or not.

Subroutine fvsGetRtnCode (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) returns the current return code for the model. The return codes are defined in the labeled COMMON block GLBLCNTL, and generally have values of: 0 = all OK, 1 = error, 2 = run has ended.

Subroutine fvsSetRtnCode (code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) is used to set the return code to 0, 1, or 2.

## The rFVS R Package Interface {#sec-the-rfvs-r-package-interface}

The rFVS package provides a comprehensive R interface to the Forest Vegetation Simulator when it is run as a shared library. This section describes the structure, functionality, and use of rFVS for integrating FVS simulations within R-based analytical workflows.

### Overview and Purpose

rFVS is an R package that enables users to programmatically control and interact with FVS from within the R statistical computing environment. The package leverages the FVS shared library (dynamic link library or .dll on Windows; shared object or .so on Linux/Unix systems) and the FVS API to provide seamless integration between FVS forest growth simulations and R's extensive data analysis, visualization, and statistical modeling capabilities.

**Key Benefits:**

- **Programmatic Control**: Run FVS simulations directly from R scripts without requiring external file management
- **Interactive Workflow**: Start, stop, inspect, modify, and resume simulations at designated stop points
- **Data Integration**: Directly access tree-level and stand-level data as R data frames
- **Batch Processing**: Efficiently process multiple stands or scenarios in automated workflows
- **Advanced Analytics**: Combine FVS projections with R's statistical and machine learning tools
- **Reproducible Research**: Document and share complete analytical workflows using R Markdown

**Package Information:**

- **Version**: 2024.07.01
- **Author**: Nicholas L. Crookston (ncrookston.fs@gmail.com)
- **License**: MIT
- **Requirements**: R version 4.0.0 or higher
- **Repository**: https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator-Interface/tree/main/rFVS

### Architecture and Design

rFVS follows a client-server architecture where R acts as the client and the FVS shared library acts as the server. R code calls functions in the rFVS package, which in turn use the `.C()` interface to call C/Fortran routines in the FVS shared library.

**Component Layers:**

1. **R User Interface Layer**: R functions that users call (e.g., `fvsRun()`, `fvsGetTreeAttrs()`)
2. **R Package Layer**: rFVS package functions that prepare data and handle function calls
3. **C Interface Layer**: C wrapper functions that interface between R and Fortran
4. **FVS Shared Library Layer**: The FVS Fortran code compiled as a shared library
5. **FVS Core**: The FVS model engine with all its growth, mortality, and management logic

This architecture allows the FVS model to maintain its state in memory (via COMMON blocks) between function calls, enabling the stop/restart functionality critical to interactive use.

### Core Functions and Workflow

The rFVS package provides 24 exported functions organized into functional categories:

#### Library Loading and Configuration

**`fvsLoad(fvsProgram, bin)`**

Loads the FVS shared library for a specific variant.

- **Parameters:**
  - `fvsProgram`: Character string specifying the FVS variant (e.g., "FVSie" for Inland Empire, "FVSpn" for Pacific Northwest)
  - `bin`: Directory path where the shared library resides (default: "../../trunk/bin")
- **Process:**
  1. Strips file extensions and adds platform-appropriate suffix (.dll or .so)
  2. Unloads any previously loaded library
  3. Validates that the library file exists
  4. Loads the library using `dyn.load()`
  5. Verifies all required API routines are present
  6. Stores the loaded library name in `.FVSLOADEDLIBRARY`
- **Returns**: Full file path of loaded library (invisibly)

**`fvsSetCmdLine(cl)`**

Sets the command line passed to FVS.

- **Parameters:** `cl` is a character string containing the FVS command line, for example `"--keywordfile=base.key"`. If it is missing, the command line arguments passed to R when it was started (including from Rscript) are used.
- Must be called before running the simulation. Returns the FVS return code, or NULL if no command line is specified.

**`fvsMakeKeyFile(keyFileName, runTitle, standIDs, inDataBase, outDataBase, ncycles, moreKeywords)`**

Writes a simple FVS keyword file suitable for use with `fvsLoad()`, `fvsSetCmdLine()`, and `fvsRun()`.

- Creates keywords for each of the stand identifiers supplied, using the input database (default `FVS_Data.db`) and output database (default `FVSOut.db`), and the number of cycles (default 10).
- `moreKeywords` is either a character vector of keyword lines added to each stand, or a data frame whose first column is a keyword and whose other columns are the keyword fields.
- Returns the name of the keyword file (a unique name is created if `keyFileName` is not given).

**`fvsSetupSummary(asum)`**

Prepares the summary table for plotting.

- **Parameters:** `asum` is the table returned by `fvsGetSummary()`.
- Adds a row for the post-thinning condition in cycles with removals, so that variables such as `Tpa` show the removal as a vertical drop, and adds cumulative total-production columns (`TPrdTpa`, `TPrdTCuFt`, `TPrdMCuFt`, `TPrdBdFt`).

#### Simulation Execution

**`fvsRun(stopPointCode, stopPointYear)`**

Executes the FVS simulation up to a designated stop point.

- **Parameters:**
  - `stopPointCode`: Integer controlling where execution halts:
    - `0`: Never stop
    - `-1`: Stop at every stop location
    - `1`: Stop before the first Event Monitor call (before thinning)
    - `2`: Stop after the first Event Monitor call, before thinning
    - `3`: Stop after thinning, before the second Event Monitor call
    - `4`: Stop after the second Event Monitor call, before growth estimation
    - `5`: Stop after growth and mortality are computed, before they are applied
    - `6`: Stop before the regeneration establishment (ESTAB) routines
    - `7`: Stop after input is read, before missing values are imputed and the model is calibrated
  - `stopPointYear`: A year above 0 stops only in the cycle that contains that year. `-1` means no year limit, so FVS stops in every cycle (any value below 0 behaves the same). For code 7 a year above 0 must be in the first cycle.
- **Return Codes:**
  - `-1`: FVS not initialized
  - `0`: Normal operation
  - `1`: Error detected; reset needed
  - `2`: Processing complete
- **Process**: Implements a loop-based execution model, repeatedly calling the FVS engine and checking for stopping conditions
- **End of stand**: Also returns at the end of each stand, with restart code 100 (even with code 0). The next call starts the next stand.
- **Persistence**: A stop request stays in effect until it is changed. `fvsRun()` with no arguments does not clear it; `fvsRun(0, 0)` turns it off.

**`fvsInteractRun(trace, BeforeEM1, AfterEM1, BeforeEM2, AfterEM2, BeforeAdd, BeforeEstab, SimEnd)`**

Runs FVS and R code together.

- Each argument after `trace` is an optional R code block that is run at the corresponding stop point: just before and just after the first Event Monitor call (`BeforeEM1`, `AfterEM1`), just before and just after the second Event Monitor call (`BeforeEM2`, `AfterEM2`), after growth and mortality are computed but before they are applied (`BeforeAdd`), just before the regeneration establishment model (`BeforeEstab`), and at the end of each stand (`SimEnd`).
- After each code block finishes, FVS runs to the next stop point. When `trace` is true, informative messages are written.
- Returns a list of the stands and years simulated.

#### Data Retrieval Functions

**`fvsGetDims()`**

Returns a named numeric vector of the current and maximum dimensions of FVS data storage: `ntrees`, `ncycles`, `nplots`, `maxtrees`, `maxspecies`, `maxplots`, and `maxcycles`.

**`fvsGetTreeAttrs(vars)`**

Retrieves attributes of the tree records.

- **Parameters:** `vars` is a character vector of attribute names.
- **Returns:** a data frame with one row per tree record and one column per requested attribute.
- **Available attributes (lower case, 25 in all):** `id`, `species` (FVS numeric species index), `tpa`, `mort` (trees per acre predicted to die), `dbh`, `dg` (inside bark diameter increment; it is on the cycle-length basis at stop point 5, after GRADD has scaled it), `ht`, `htg`, `crwdth` (crown width), `cratio`, `age`, `plot` (FVS plot index), `tcuft`, `mcuft`, `bdft`, `ptbal` (point basal area in larger trees), `bapctile` (percentile in the basal area distribution), `defect` (coded 11223344), `mgmtcd` (tree value class), `plotsize`, and `crownwt0` to `crownwt5` (weights of foliage and of crown material in the 0 to 0.25, 0.25 to 1, 1 to 3, 3 to 6, and 6 to 12 inch classes).

**`fvsGetSummary()`**

Retrieves the stand-level summary statistics, one row per period.

- **Returns:** a data frame with 20 columns: `Year`, `Age`, `Tpa`, `TCuFt`, `MCuFt`, `BdFt`, `RTpa`, `RTCuFt`, `RMCuFt`, `RBdFt`, `ATBA`, `ATCCF`, `ATTopHt`, `PrdLen`, `Acc`, `Mort`, `SampWt`, `ForTyp`, `SizeCls`, and `StkCls`.
- **Note**: Returns `NULL` until a simulation has been executed.

**`fvsGetStandIDs()`**

Returns a named character vector with the stand identification (`standid`), stand control number (`standcn`), management identification (`mgmtid`), and `caseID` of the current stand. The values are blank until a run is started.

**`fvsGetSpeciesCodes()` and `fvsGetSpeciesAttrs(vars)`**

Retrieve species-level information.

- `fvsGetSpeciesCodes()` returns a data frame with one row for each species, with the internal FVS species index as the row name and the FVS (`fvs`), FIA (`fia`), and PLANTS (`plant`) codes as columns.
- `fvsGetSpeciesAttrs(vars)` takes a character vector of attribute names and returns the species-level values, for example `spsdi` (SDI maximums), `spsiteindx` (site indices), `baimult` (basal area increment multiplier), `htgmult`, `mortmult`, and the volume specification attributes (`bfmind`, `bftopd`, `bfstmp`, `frmcls`, `bfmeth`, `mcmind`, `mctopd`, `mcstmp`, `mcmeth`).

**`fvsGetEventMonitorVariables(vars)`**

Retrieves the values of Event Monitor variables.

- **Parameters:** `vars` is a character vector of variable names (for example `c("year", "atpa", "aba")`).
- Retrieves pre-defined and user-defined Event Monitor variables; a variable that is not defined is returned as NA.

**`fvsGetRestartcode()`**

Obtains the current restart status code.

- Indicates which stop point was reached (1 to 7), or 100 at the end of a stand
- Returns 0 if no stop point is active, and a negative value right after a stand is reloaded from a stop point file

**`fvsGetSVSDims()` and `fvsGetSVSObjectSet()`**

Retrieve Stand Visualization System (SVS) data.

- `fvsGetSVSDims()` returns the maximum dimensions of the SVS data storage.
- `fvsGetSVSObjectSet()` returns a named list of data frames of trees, snags, and coarse woody debris; the data frames are empty until a run is made using SVS.

**`fvsUnitConversion(name)`**

Returns an FVS unit conversion factor by name (for example `"MtoFT"`, `"INtoCM"`, `"ACRtoHA"`, or `"M2pHAtoFT2pACR"`); see the help page for the full list.

#### Data Modification Functions

**`fvsAddTrees(newtrees)`**

Adds new tree records to the simulation.

- **Parameters:** `newtrees` is a data frame with the columns `dbh` (inches), `species` (FVS species index, see `fvsGetSpeciesCodes()`), `ht` (feet), `cratio` (percent), `plot` (plot index), and `tpa` (trees per acre). No missing values are allowed.
- **Use Cases:**
  - Modeling regeneration from external models
  - Adding underplanting prescriptions
- **Stop point**: Call only at stop point 6 or 7. FVS does not check the stop point.
- Returns 0 if the trees were added and 1 if there was an error.

**`fvsCutNow(propcut)`**

Specifies a thinning for the current cycle as the proportion of each tree record's trees per acre to cut. A single value is applied to every tree record; a vector gives one proportion per record.

- Can only be called at stop point 2; R stops with an error otherwise
- The thinning is carried out using the THINPRSC keyword and can be combined with other thinning keywords such as MINHARV and YARDLOSS.

**`fvsSetTreeAttrs(vars)`**

Modifies attributes of the tree records.

- **Parameters:** `vars` is a named list of numeric vectors, where each name is an attribute (see `fvsGetTreeAttrs()`) and each vector holds a value for every tree record, in order. A typical use is to get attributes with `fvsGetTreeAttrs()`, change them, and pass the result back.
- Returns 0 if the attributes were set and 1 if there was an error.
- **Important**: Changes should be compatible with FVS model assumptions

**`fvsSetSpeciesAttrs(vars)`**

Modifies species-level data.

- **Parameters:** `vars` is a named list of numeric vectors, where each name is a species attribute (see `fvsGetSpeciesAttrs()`) and each vector holds a value for every species, in order.
- Examples include basal area increment, height growth, and mortality multipliers, site indices, and SDI maximums.
- **Caution**: Should only be used by those familiar with FVS internals

**`fvsAddActivity(year, activity, parms)`**

Adds an activity to the FVS activity schedule.

- **Parameters:** `year` is the year the activity is scheduled, `activity` is an activity code (a number or a character string such as `"base_thindbh"`), and `parms` is a numeric vector of the activity parameters.
- Called with no arguments, it returns a named vector of the possible activity codes.
- Returns 0 if the activity was added and 1 if there was an error.

**`fvsSetEventMonitorVariables(vars)`**

Sets the values of Event Monitor variables.

- **Parameters:** `vars` is a named numeric vector (for example `c("myaba" = 100, "another" = 40)`).
- Sets user-defined variables, which can then be used in Event Monitor expressions
- Returns a named numeric vector of the variables, with NA for a variable name that does not exist

#### Utility Functions

**`fvsCompositeSum(allsum)`**

Builds a composite summary table from a list of summary tables.

- **Parameters:** `allsum` is a list of tables returned by `fvsGetSummary()`.
- The composite is a weighted average of the values for the years that are common to all of the tables.

### Typical Workflow

The following sketch of an rFVS session uses the function signatures documented above. It has not been run; the file names are placeholders.

```r
# 1. Load the FVS shared library
library(rFVS)
fvsLoad(fvsProgram = "FVSie", bin = "/path/to/fvs/bin")

# 2. Set up the simulation
fvsSetCmdLine("--keywordfile=base.key")

# 3. Run to stop point 2 (just after the first Event Monitor call)
#    in the cycle that contains the year 2025
fvsRun(2, 2025)

# 4. Inspect the stand
fvsGetStandIDs()
fvsGetEventMonitorVariables(c("year", "bba"))
trees <- fvsGetTreeAttrs(c("dbh", "ht", "tpa"))

# 5. Conditionally specify a thinning for this cycle
bba <- fvsGetEventMonitorVariables("bba")
if (!is.na(bba) && bba > 150) fvsCutNow(0.25)

# 6. Turn the stop point off and run to the end of the stand
fvsRun(0, 0)

# 7. Retrieve and prepare the summary
summaryTable <- fvsSetupSummary(fvsGetSummary())
```

### Integration with FVS API and Stop/Restart

The rFVS package directly utilizes the FVS API functionality described in [Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api). Key integration points include:

**Stop Point Mechanism:**

rFVS's `fvsRun()` function uses the same stop point codes as the FVS API. When execution reaches a stop point:

1. The FVS Fortran code calls `fvsStopPoint()` ([Stop/restart and the FVS API](#sec-stop-restart-and-the-fvs-api-subroutines-involved-and-their-function))
2. Control returns up the call stack to the R environment
3. All FVS state variables remain in memory (in COMMON blocks)
4. R code can call API functions to inspect or modify the simulation state
5. Subsequent calls to `fvsRun()` use `fvsGetRestartCode()` to jump back to the stop point and continue

**Memory Management:**

Unlike standalone FVS with restart files, rFVS keeps all state in memory:

- No need for `PUTSTD`/`GETSTD` file I/O when using rFVS
- Faster execution for iterative analyses
- Variables in COMMON blocks persist between R function calls
- Only limitation is available RAM

**API Function Access:**

All FVS API functions documented at https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki/FVS-API are accessible through rFVS via `.C()` and `.Fortran()` calls. The list below shows the compiled routine that each rFVS function calls. A name that begins with `Cfvs` is a C function in `base/apisubsc.c` that is called with `.C()`; it calls a Fortran routine with a C binding (`fvsXC`), which calls the Fortran API subroutine `fvsX`. The routines `fvsSpeciesCodeC` and `fvsStandIDC` do the work themselves. The other names are Fortran API subroutines that are called with `.Fortran()`.

- `fvsLoad()` calls no API routine. It loads the library with `dyn.load()` and uses `is.loaded()` to check that these routines are present: `CfvsEvmonAttr`, `CfvsFFEAttrs`, `CfvsSVSObjData`, `CfvsSetCmdLine`, `CfvsSpeciesAttr`, `CfvsSpeciesCode`, `CfvsStandID`, `CfvsTreeAttr`, `CfvsUnitConversion`, `fvs`, `fvsAddActivity`, `fvsAddTrees`, `fvsDimSizes`, `fvsGetRestartCode`, `fvsSVSDimSizes`, `fvsSetStoppointCodes` and `fvsSummary`
- `fvsSetCmdLine()` calls `CfvsSetCmdLine`
- `fvsMakeKeyFile()` calls no API routine; it writes a keyword file
- `fvsRun()` calls `fvs`, `fvsGetRestartCode` and `fvsSetStoppointCodes`
- `fvsInteractRun()` calls `fvs`, `fvsGetRestartCode` and `fvsSetStoppointCodes`, and the R functions `fvsGetEventMonitorVariables()` and `fvsGetStandIDs()`
- `fvsGetRestartcode()` calls `fvsGetRestartCode`
- `fvsGetDims()` calls `fvsDimSizes`
- `fvsGetTreeAttrs()` calls `CfvsTreeAttr` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsSetTreeAttrs()` calls `CfvsTreeAttr` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsGetSpeciesAttrs()` calls `CfvsSpeciesAttr` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsSetSpeciesAttrs()` calls `CfvsSpeciesAttr` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsGetSpeciesCodes()` calls `CfvsSpeciesCode` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsGetEventMonitorVariables()` calls `CfvsEvmonAttr`
- `fvsSetEventMonitorVariables()` calls `CfvsEvmonAttr`
- `fvsGetStandIDs()` calls `CfvsStandID`
- `fvsGetSummary()` calls `fvsSummary` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsSetupSummary()` calls no API routine; it adds the columns `TPrdTpa`, `TPrdTCuFt`, `TPrdMCuFt` and `TPrdBdFt` to a summary table
- `fvsCompositeSum()` calls no API routine; it combines summary tables
- `fvsUnitConversion()` calls `CfvsUnitConversion`
- `fvsGetSVSDims()` calls `fvsSVSDimSizes`
- `fvsGetSVSObjectSet()` calls `CfvsSVSObjData` and `CfvsFFEAttrs` (and the R functions `fvsGetSVSDims()`, `fvsGetEventMonitorVariables()`, `fvsGetSpeciesCodes()` and `fvsGetTreeAttrs()`)
- `fvsAddTrees()` calls `fvsAddTrees` (and `fvsGetDims()`)
- `fvsAddActivity()` calls `fvsAddActivity`
- `fvsCutNow()` calls no API routine directly. It calls the R functions `fvsGetRestartcode()`, `fvsGetDims()`, `fvsGetEventMonitorVariables()`, `fvsAddActivity()` and `fvsSetTreeAttrs()`

No rFVS function calls these API routines: `fvsGetKeywordFileName`, `fvsGetStoppointCodes`, `fvsRestartLastStand`, `fvsGetRtnCode`, `fvsSetRtnCode`, `fvsGetICCode`, `fvsCutTrees` (it returns an error because it is not yet implemented), `fvsCloseFile`, `fvsGetVersion` and `fvsGetBuildInfo`. They can be called with `.C()` or `.Fortran()` after `fvsLoad()`.

### Advanced Use Cases

**Sensitivity Analysis:**

rFVS enables sensitivity analyses by changing model parameters at a stop point and comparing the summaries. The following sketch, which has not been run, varies the basal area increment multiplier for all species:

```r
results <- list()
for (m in c(0.8, 1.0, 1.2)) {
  fvsSetCmdLine("--keywordfile=base.key")
  fvsRun(7, 0)                       # stop after input is read
  vars <- fvsGetSpeciesAttrs("baimult")
  vars$baimult[] <- m
  fvsSetSpeciesAttrs(vars)
  fvsRun(0, 0)                       # run to the end of the stand
  results[[as.character(m)]] <- fvsGetSummary()
}
```

**Management Schedules:**

Activities can be added from R with `fvsAddActivity()`, so a schedule can be tested, scored, and changed by an R optimization routine. The call below is adapted from the help page for `fvsAddActivity()` and schedules a diameter-limit thinning and a yard loss in 1993; call `fvsAddActivity()` with no arguments to list the possible activity codes.

```r
fvsAddActivity(1993, "base_yardloss", c(0.50, 0.70, 0.50))
fvsAddActivity(1993, "base_thindbh", c(0.00, 12.00, 1.00, 0.00, 0.00))
```

**Coupling with External Models:**

rFVS can be coupled with external ecological or economic models:

- **Climate Models**: Modify species parameters based on climate projections
- **Economic Models**: Evaluate net present value using R financial functions
- **Wildlife Models**: Export stand structure to habitat suitability models
- **Carbon Models**: Track carbon sequestration across scenarios

**Monte Carlo Simulation:**

Uncertainty can be assessed by running many realizations with randomly varied inputs. The following sketch, which has not been run, scales the species site indices:

```r
nSims <- 100
results <- vector("list", nSims)
for (i in 1:nSims) {
  fvsSetCmdLine("--keywordfile=base.key")
  fvsRun(7, 0)                       # stop after input is read
  vars <- fvsGetSpeciesAttrs("spsiteindx")
  vars$spsiteindx <- vars$spsiteindx * rnorm(1, mean = 1, sd = 0.1)
  fvsSetSpeciesAttrs(vars)
  fvsRun(0, 0)
  results[[i]] <- fvsGetSummary()
}
composite <- fvsCompositeSum(results)
```

### Installation and Configuration

**Prerequisites:**

1. **R** (version 4.0.0 or higher)
2. **FVS Compiled as Shared Library**: FVS must be compiled with shared library flags
   - Windows: Produces `.dll` files
   - Linux/Unix: Produces `.so` files
3. **Build Tools** (if compiling from source):
   - C/Fortran compiler (gfortran recommended)
   - make utility

**Installation:**

```r
# Option 1: Install from GitHub (if available as package)
# devtools::install_github("USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator-Interface",
#                          subdir = "rFVS")

# Option 2: Install from local source
# install.packages("/path/to/rFVS", repos = NULL, type = "source")

# Option 3: Load directly during development
# devtools::load_all("/path/to/rFVS")
```

**Building FVS as a Shared Library:**

Detailed instructions are available in the FVS wiki: https://github.com/USDAForestService/ForestVegetationSimulator/wiki

General steps:

1. Obtain FVS source code
2. Modify build scripts to include shared library flags (`-shared` for Linux, `/LD` for Windows)
3. Compile the desired variant
4. Place the resulting `.so` or `.dll` file in a known directory
5. Specify this directory in `fvsLoad()`

**Package Structure:**

```
rFVS/
├── DESCRIPTION          # Package metadata
├── R/                  # R source code (23 function files)
│   ├── fvsLoad.R
│   ├── fvsRun.R
│   ├── fvsGetTreeAttrs.R
│   ├── fvsGetSummary.R
│   └── ...
├── tests/              # Test suite
└── makefile            # Build automation
```

### Comparison with Other FVS Interfaces

**rFVS vs. FVSOnline:**

- **FVSOnline**: Web-based interface using Shiny; good for single-run analyses and learning
- **rFVS**: Programmatic R package; better for batch processing, optimization, and advanced analytics
- Both use the same underlying FVS shared library

**rFVS vs. Command-Line FVS:**

- **Command-Line FVS**: Standalone executable; processes keyword files sequentially
- **rFVS**: Interactive and programmable; can stop, inspect, modify, and resume
- Command-line FVS can create restart files; rFVS keeps state in memory

### Limitations and Considerations

**Performance:**

- Each call between R and FVS has some overhead
- For very simple runs, command-line FVS may be faster
- For batch processing with data manipulation, rFVS is typically faster overall

**Memory:**

- All simulation state is kept in RAM
- Very large multi-stand analyses may exhaust memory
- Consider processing in batches if memory is limited

**Platform Compatibility:**

- Shared library must match platform (Windows .dll vs. Linux .so)
- Cannot mix 32-bit and 64-bit components
- R and FVS must be compiled with compatible compilers

**Error Handling:**

- Errors in FVS may not always propagate cleanly to R
- Check the return code returned by `fvsRun()` after each call (0 is normal, 1 is an error, and 2 means all stands have been processed)

**Documentation:**

- rFVS function documentation via `?functionName` in R
- FVS model documentation remains essential
- Understanding of FVS internals helpful for advanced use

### Future Developments

Ongoing and potential future developments for rFVS include:

- **Enhanced Documentation**: Vignettes and tutorials for common workflows
- **Helper Functions**: Higher-level functions for common tasks (e.g., `fvsOptimizeThinning()`)
- **Tidyverse Integration**: Functions returning tibbles with standardized names
- **Visualization Tools**: Built-in plotting functions for common outputs
- **Error Handling**: Improved R-side error messages and warnings
- **Unit Tests**: Expanded test suite for reliability
- **CRAN Submission**: Making rFVS available via CRAN for easier installation
- **Multi-threading**: Parallel processing of multiple stands using R's parallel package
